What the simulator **cannot** prove is the thing this check is: that a real phone's write path, a real consumer process, a real orchestrator and a real database, wired to each other out of band, produce the same conversation. That is why the plan refuses to make it a test — it needs a real phone, a real orchestrator and a real project.

**What is in the tree, and what is not — read this before the guard, because a guard that lies wastes your afternoon.** The consumer is merged and registered: `internal/cli/mailbox.go`, with `internal/cli/root.go`'s `newMailboxCmd()` beside `newPairCmd()` (the command list at line 232), the surface `--once`, `--interval`, `--json` and `--no-heartbeat` (`newMailboxCmd`), the M12 exit predicate (`mailboxExit`), the one cancel path (`cancelFromMailbox`), and the keychain read at startup (`mailboxKeyring`, `mailboxKeychain = keychain.System`).

Pairing is merged (`internal/cli/pair.go`: `fugaro pair`, `pair ls`, `pair revoke`), so **nothing here claims pairing is missing**. The app's write path and its voice screen are merged (`mobile/src/mailbox/client.js`; `mobile/src/voice/screen.js` and `speaker.js`, wired by `mobile/index.js`).

The orchestrator **package** is partial, and this is the honest reading: `internal/orchestrator/` and `fugaro orchestrator run` (`internal/cli/orchestrator_run.go`) exist — a real launcher (`launch.go`) and a real daemon lease (`lease.go`) — but that daemon **reads no mailbox** (no `mailbox` reference anywhere in `orchestrator_run.go`), so what the resident, deployed orchestrator of `docs/mobile/design/always-on-orchestrator.md` would act on never reaches it. The provisioning half **has** landed: `deploy/terraform/gcp/modules/installation/orchestrator.tf` carries the account (P5.1b) and its Cloud Run service and tick (P5.1c), and the installation root's `var.orchestrator` has a writer — plain `fugaro update`, which composes the whole block from what the installation already holds and, for an installation with no credentials service, no Firebase backend or no pinned image, leaves it off with one printed line naming why.

One thing is therefore genuinely missing today, and the guard's first leg names it:

- **The consumer's hand-off to the orchestrator.** `mailboxHandOff` (`internal/cli/mailbox.go`'s own declaration, and the `handOff` caller) is a no-op stub returning `nil`, and the file's own comment says the channel between the consumer and the orchestrator "does not exist in this tree". A message the consumer reads reaches no orchestrator, so "the orchestrator acts" cannot be observed — and the account, the service, the tick and the writer that are now in the tree are all behind that one link.

The guard's other legs are the preconditions the rest of this check needs, not missing work: the consumer, the pairing command, the app's two halves, and the writer (`ensureOrchestratorBlock`, run by `fugaro update`) that gives the installation its resident orchestrator so that the process this check drives exists at all. Neither the hand-off nor a leg that would stop is a defect of this check; they are why it is written now and run later.

**The wire, both directions, in one paragraph.** A message is one of five kinds the schema and the template spell (`message`, `prompt`, `answer`, `action`, `registration` — `internal/budget/rules/rules.json.tmpl`), it lives under `mailbox/$mb/{inbox/$msg, outbox/$msg(.acked), heartbeat}`, and every message of every kind and the heartbeat carry a **tag** that is exactly one of `mac` (exactly **64 lowercase-hex characters** — `internal/budget/rules/rules.go`'s `MaxMacLength` and the `MACOK` macro) and `sig` (exactly **86 base64url characters**, an Ed25519 signature — `MaxSigLength` and the `SIGOK` macro), never both and never neither (`TAGOK`).

The rules fence the two writers apart: `USER` (`auth.token.mu == auth.uid` **and** a node at `config/admin/devices/$uid` — `rules.go`'s `userClaim` and `rules.PathDevices`, D166) may write one message into its own inbox and the `acked: true` child of an already-existing outbox message and nothing else — **the inbox has no read grant at all** — while `CONSUMER` (`auth.token.mc == $mb`) is the writer of the outbox and the heartbeat. **The templates prove the shape; only a real project proves the answer** — that is check 81's subject and not this one's.

What **this** check proves is the conversation: the phone's write is a **new** inbox message, the consumer verifies the tag and acts **once**, the orchestrator produces an answer, the reply is signed into the outbox, and the phone **speaks** it and then acks.

**No credential is printed, and none is pasted.** The consumer's own reads use the operator's application-default credential (the plan's C0: the inbox has no read grant for any client, so both the inbox read and the ETag read of the heartbeat are out of band). **The mailbox MAC key lives in the OS keychain, is read by item name and never logged** — the item name is the non-secret `mailbox.keychain_item[<device uid>]` your project config names, and the key itself is never printed, never in a `FACT` line and never in a pull request. The phone's own credential is a credential too and is never pasted. **Nothing in this check waits on stdin, and no step asks you a question.**

**Guard block — re-run this before every step.** It stops unless the checkout carries the consumer, the pairing command, the app's two halves and the writer that turns the resident orchestrator on, and **it stops today** on the one link the conversation is missing: the consumer's hand-off to the orchestrator. A consumer that reads a mailbox and hands it to nothing measures nothing.

```bash
# === Check 80: setup + guard. RE-RUN THIS BLOCK BEFORE EVERY STEP. ===
set -u
ROOT=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null) || { echo "Check 80 stopped: not inside a git checkout; the consumer and the app this check drives are built from this repository" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/internal/cli/mailbox.go" ] || { echo "Check 80 stopped: there is no internal/cli/mailbox.go in this checkout, so there is no consumer to read the inbox and answer it (P4.1)" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/internal/cli/pair.go" ] || { echo "Check 80 stopped: there is no internal/cli/pair.go in this checkout, so the phone cannot be paired and this consumer has no key it could verify (P6.6)" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -d "$ROOT/mobile/src/mailbox" ] || { echo "Check 80 stopped: there is no mobile/src/mailbox/ in this checkout, so the phone has no write path into its own inbox (P3.6)" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -d "$ROOT/mobile/src/voice" ] || { echo "Check 80 stopped: there is no mobile/src/voice/ in this checkout, so nothing on the phone speaks the reply (P3.5)" >&2; exit 1; }
grep -q 'var mailboxHandOff = func(context.Context, mailboxOffer) error { return nil }' "$ROOT/internal/cli/mailbox.go" && {
  echo "Check 80 stopped: the consumer's hand-off to the orchestrator is still the no-op seam — internal/cli/mailbox.go's mailboxHandOff returns nil and its own comment says 'the channel between the two is not in this tree'; a message the consumer reads therefore reaches no orchestrator and 'the orchestrator acts' cannot be observed. The hand-off is the orchestrator's own channel (a pipe, a file, a socket — its to choose) and is still to be written" >&2; exit 1; }
grep -rq --include='*.go' --exclude='*_test.go' -- 'ensureOrchestratorBlock' "$ROOT/internal/cli" || {
  echo "Check 80 stopped: no ensureOrchestratorBlock is written anywhere in internal/cli's own sources (tests are not a writer: they name the function this guard looks for), so the installation root's var.orchestrator cannot be turned on and the resident orchestrator docs/mobile/design/always-on-orchestrator.md names cannot exist: deploy/terraform/gcp/modules/installation/orchestrator.tf ships its account (P5.1b) and P5.1c's service and tick, but this checkout is from before the writer that switches them on — 'fugaro update'" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "Check 80 ready: the phone, the consumer and the orchestrator are all on this tree — this check speaks one message and follows it to the spoken reply, and no key, no keychain value and no credential is printed by it"
```

1. **The phone is paired, and the consumer serves it.** *(Guard block, run by you; then the guard block again in the same shell, so `$ROOT` is the checkout the two commands below were built from.)* Pair your phone with this installation — `fugaro pair` writes the device node at `config/admin/devices/$uid` that the rules' `USER` requires and seals the per-pairing key — and record the item name it prints as `mailbox.keychain_item[<uid>]`. Then run the consumer at your terminal: `fugaro mailbox --once` first, and without `--once` once the one pass reads clean.

   **FACT:** the paired device's **uid** as `fugaro pair ls` prints it, the **keychain item name** (the name, never the value), and the one line — or with `--json` the one document — the first pass printed, naming the pairing, the lease, what was read and what was refused (**by code, never by text**). **FACT:** the lease was **taken** — the heartbeat node `mailbox/$uid/heartbeat` now holds `{at, boot, mac}`, which is the consumer's presence as much as its claim — and a **second** consumer started against the same mailbox is refused the lease rather than sharing it (`TestTwoConsumersOneLease`, `TestMailboxASecondConsumerReadsNothing`). The uid and the item name are **not** secrets; the key is.

2. **The phone writes one inbox message.** *(Guard block, run by you, on the phone.)* From the voice screen speak one **non-destructive** command ("what is running", or the app's own wording for it), letting it complete with the radio on. The app's client reads no key of its own: it reads the per-pairing key out of the platform secure store for the duration of the one call and never holds, logs or stores the plaintext (D111).

   **FACT:** the **message id** the app minted, the timestamp, and that it landed at `mailbox/<uid>/inbox/<id>` as a record of `kind: "message"` carrying `{id, sender, text, at, mac}` (or `sig` in place of `mac`) with `sender == <uid>` and a tag that is exactly one of `mac` and `sig`. Read the node back with **your own IAM credentials**, which bypass the rules — the inbox has no read grant for any client:

   ```bash
   AT=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)   # never printed, never pasted
   curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" "https://<db>/mailbox/<uid>/inbox.json"
   ```
   The message text is yours and may be pasted; `$AT`, the `mac` and any key are **never** pasted. **FACT:** the app wrote **only** that one node and, later, the `acked` child — D113's two writes are the whole of this client's reach, and a third write anywhere is a failure of the check, not a detail of it.

3. **The consumer reads, verifies, and commits before it acts.** *(Guard block, run by you; the consumer from step 1.)* The next pass reads the inbox and takes the message in this order: **verify the tag first** (`internal/mailbox/mac.go`'s `VerifyMAC`, over P6.3's canonical bytes with the direction included), then **hand it to the ledger** (`(*mailbox.Ledger).Perform`, which **commits the delivery before the action runs** — the T4 fence `TestRestartDoesNotRePerform` pins), and only then act.

   **FACT:** the pass printed the delivery as **new** — not `duplicate`, not `refused` — and the ledger at `$XDG_STATE_HOME/fugaro/mailbox/<project>/ledger.json` (0o600, written tmp+rename) now holds exactly that `(sender, id)`. **FACT:** the **negative control** you must run in the same step: a message whose `mac` does not verify is refused with the module's own code and is **never acted on** (`TestMailboxTamperedRecordIsRefused`, `TestMailboxUnsignedMessageAndAnswerAreRefused`) — and, because nothing can retire it, it is read and refused again on every pass until an operator removes the node with their own credential. Record that the **consumer**, not the rules, is what refused it: the rules hold no key and admit any well-formed `mac` (check 81's own note).

4. **The orchestrator acts — the step the guard stops on.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* The consumer carries the message out through the `mailboxHandOff` seam (`internal/cli/mailbox.go`'s `handOff`), which is where the orchestrator attaches; **this check cannot run this step until the hand-off exists and an orchestrator is on the other end of it.**

   When it does: **FACT:** what the orchestrator **did** in answer — the run it launched, the report it wrote, or the prompt it asked — and that what it did is attributable to **this** message and no other (the pass records the offer by id, kind and outcome, never by text, which is §4.3's rule and holds for an answer this consumer produced as much as for one it read). **FACT:** the message was acted on **exactly once** across the whole session, including any pass in which the same delivery arrived twice: the ledger's `(sender, id)` is what refuses the second — a re-delivered record is answered `duplicate` and counted in the pass's `duplicates` counter, not acted on again (`TestMailboxDuplicatePassExitsZero`).

5. **The reply reaches the outbox, signed.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* The consumer builds the answer and **signs it or writes nothing** — `internal/mailbox/outbox.go`'s `WriteReply` builds the value, tags it, validates it against the schema and only then writes it; a signer that errors is a per-write refusal, a recorded outcome of a completed pass and exit 0, never a startup exit.

   **FACT:** the outbox node `mailbox/<uid>/outbox/<id>` now holds a record of the message's **kind** (`answer`, `prompt`, or the kind the reply carries), with a `mac` and, where the kind requires them, `reply_to`, `agent` or `options`; and the operator's read of `mailbox/<uid>/outbox.json` shows **one** answer per question and no unsigned value. **FACT:** the create-only rule the template writes (`CONSUMER && newData.exists() && !data.exists()`) is enforced **in code** for this writer, because the operator's own IAM credential bypasses both the claim and the create-only clause (the plan's C0 and M10) — so one-write-per-answer is this file's to keep, and the check records that the second pass wrote no second copy.

6. **The phone speaks the reply, and only then acks.** *(Guard block, run by you, on the phone.)* The phone's client verifies the outbox message's tag **before it speaks a word**, then speaks it, then writes `acked: true` onto that message — never before.

   **FACT:** the reply was **spoken**, in the app's own voice, and what was spoken is the **signed text** and not a local echo: `mobile/src/mailbox/client.js` drops a message whose tag does not verify, never speaks it and never acks it (the tension (b) resolution), and `mobile/src/voice/speaker.js` is where the words leave the mailbox client. **FACT:** `mailbox/<uid>/outbox/<id>/acked` is `true` **after** the speak and not before, and a speak that failed left the message **unacked** so the next pass tries again (the client's own retry rule). **FACT:** a heartbeat that does not verify is read as **offline**, with its advertised agent list ignored — presence is check **84**'s subject, and this step records only that the same verification gated the reply.

   The comparison this whole step is for is the plan's own: **the simulator said the conversation would go this way, and steps 3–6 are that conversation happening for real.**

7. **What the check did not touch.** *(Guard block, run by you; read-only.)* **FACT:** every write in the whole check came from the app's client with its own credential or from the consumer with the operator's, and the rules are what admit each of them — nothing was written by hand except the two negatives of step 3 (and those are recorded as seeded, proving nothing about the path). **FACT:** `belong` was not named, read or written by any step, and the installation this ran on is `fugaro`. **FACT:** **no credential was printed or pasted anywhere** — not the MAC key, not its keychain value, not the phone's credential, not an ID token; the keychain item was read **by name** and never logged, which is M5's rule for everything this command prints. **FACT:** no step waited on stdin, and no step asked you a question.

**Passes when:** step 1's pairing is the one the consumer serves, the lease is taken by one consumer and refused to a second; step 2's inbox message is one MAC-covered record of kind `message` and the only write the app made; step 3 shows the tag verified before the act and the delivery committed to the ledger before it, with a bad-tag message refused and never acted on; step 4 shows the orchestrator acting on that id **once**, attributable to that message; step 5 shows one signed answer in the outbox with no second copy; and step 6 shows the reply spoken **before** the ack, with a failed speak leaving it unacked.

**Fails when:** any step writes a node by hand that the app or the consumer did not write (a seeded record proves nothing about the path); the inbox message is acted on before its `mac` verifies, or a message with a bad tag is acted on at all; the same `(sender, id)` is acted on twice, or a re-delivered record is acted on rather than answered `duplicate`; the reply is written unsigned, or a second copy of one answer is written; the phone speaks before it verifies the tag, or acks before it speaks; the app writes anything beyond its own inbox message and the `acked` child; `belong` is touched at any point; or a key, a credential or an ID token is printed, pasted into a `FACT` line, or pasted into a pull request.

**Paste back:** the pairing's **uid** and the keychain **item name**; each pass's line, or its `--json` document (the pairing, the lease, what was read, what was refused by code); the inbox and outbox **ids** with their kinds and timestamps, and the message and reply **text** if you choose to (it is your own); the ledger's entry for the `(sender, id)` and the pass's `duplicates` counter; what the orchestrator did in answer; and the two negatives of step 3 (the bad tag's refusal code, and that the node stayed until you removed it). **Never paste a MAC, a keychain value, the pairing key, the phone's credential or an ID token.**

**Restore.** The check's own effects are small and its undos are named:

- The **paired device** stays paired only if you want it: `fugaro pair revoke --uid <uid>` deletes the device node (so the next read from that uid is refused) and removes the keychain item, which is what makes every message that phone signs stop verifying; the config entry `mailbox.keychain_item[<uid>]` is the operator's to edit, and a revoked pairing with no key is served by no pass — the consumer reports it and drops the prompts it was holding.
- The **messages** the check left in the mailbox (`inbox/<id>`, the `outbox/<id>` and its `acked`, and the heartbeat) are removed with your own IAM credentials, exactly as they were read: they are this installation's own, and no sweep deletes them — the offline sweeper's remit is P4.1's own state and **nothing in the store**.
- The **consumer's own state** (`$XDG_STATE_HOME/fugaro/mailbox/<project>/ledger.json` and `pending.json`) is safe to leave: it is a keyed memory of deliveries, it names no secret, and its horizon is the plan's window. Delete the directory if you want a clean first run.
- Nothing else changed: no rules deploy, no node written by hand but the two negatives of step 3, no commit, and nothing on `belong` was ever in reach.

## Check 81: the deployed rules' fence — the signed-in user's two writes and its read grant (`fugaro-dev` only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

The emulator (P2.2 and P6.4, build tag `firebase`, `go test -tags firebase ./internal/budget/rules/...`) proves the mailbox rules against a local RTDB emulator. This check is the half no emulator can prove: that **the document actually deployed in `fugaro-dev`** — the one P2.1's template generates, whose generation check 82 reads back — answers the same way to real Firebase ID tokens minted by the project's own signer, over the real Identity Toolkit and the real Realtime Database. Its subject is the plan's row 81: a signed-in **user** may write **only** its own inbox messages and the ack on a message it has spoken (D113's two writes), and may read **nothing** beyond the nodes D112's user-claim read grant sits at — and their parents are not granted either. Its cases are P2.2's `TestMailboxPhoneWritesItsOwnInbox`, `TestMailboxMessageShape`, `TestMailboxHeartbeatDeleteIsDenied` (from the user's side), `TestMailboxPhoneAcksWhatItSpoke`, `TestMailboxClaimMismatchIsAdmittedNowhere` and `TestMailboxReadsAreTheGrantedSet`, P6.4's `TestDeviceNodeGatesEverythingUserReaches` and `TestMailboxMessagesRequireTheTag`, plus — recorded, not failed — `TestMailboxResidualMintedTokenNeedsTheDeviceNode`, whose subject generation 3 changed: a minted token for an account **with** a device node is that account (step 7), and one for an account without is refused everything.

**What the deployed rules are.** The subtree is `mailbox/$mb/{inbox/$msg, outbox/$msg(.acked), heartbeat}` (`internal/budget/rules/rules.json.tmpl`, the `mailbox` node), and every message of every kind and the heartbeat carry a **tag** that is exactly one of `mac` and `sig` — the shape `TAGOK` checks and the value it cannot (`internal/budget/rules`'s `MaxMacLength` and `MaxSigLength`, the `MACOK` and `SIGOK` macros; P6.7 is what verifies the value) — beside the `kind` that says which of the four shapes the message is (`message`, `prompt`, `answer` or `action`, with the fields that kind carries: `agent`, `options` on a prompt, `reply_to` on an answer, the `action` record on an action, whose `verb` may be the typed `launch` with its `mode` beside it instead of a `confirmation`). Four predicates decide everything (`internal/budget/rules/rules.go`): `USER` (`auth != null && auth.token.mu != null && auth.token.mu == auth.uid && root.child('config/admin/devices').child(auth.uid).exists()` — the last conjunct is D166's device node, and it is what makes an account a *device*: an account whose uid has no node there reads and writes **nothing at all**, not even its own mailbox), `MAILBOX` (`USER && $mb == auth.uid`), `CONSUMER` (`auth != null && auth.token.mc != null && auth.token.mc == $mb`) and `PAIRING` (the `pu` claim a pairing session carries on the `p~<random>` uid it created — the only identity a phone has before it is paired, and what admits it to the two pairing nodes). A **user** — the account whose own uid is its `mu` claim **and whose uid has a device node** — may **write** one message into its own `inbox/$msg` (write-once: `MAILBOX && newData.exists() && !data.exists()`; shape `{id, sender, text, at, mac}` with `id == $msg` and `sender == $mb`, `at` a `TIMESTAMP` and the tag exactly one of `mac` and `sig`) and may write `acked: true` once onto a message already in its own `outbox/$msg` (`MAILBOX && newData.exists() && !data.exists()`, with `data.parent().exists()`; the parent must already exist — that write is the **consumer's**, see below). Nothing else in the subtree is a user's: `$other: {".validate": false}` everywhere, the outbox message and the heartbeat are `CONSUMER`'s, the inbox has **no read grant at all**, and the only reads are `outbox` and `heartbeat` under `MAILBOX`. Outside the mailbox, what a `mu` token may read is exactly **the locations D112's grant sits at, plus its own mailbox's two nodes, the coordinator's subtree, the orchestrator's, the run's outcome node (generation 8) and the two launch-envelope leaves (generation 10)**: `config/caps/{global,defaults,repos/$slug}`, `config/kill/{global,repos/$slug}` and `spend/$day/{global,repos/$slug,runs/$slug/$run}` — `rules.json.tmpl` lines 16–18, 40–41, 114 and 143 carry `TOKEN || USER` (their three `repos/$slug` entries `(TOKEN && auth.token.fs == $slug) || USER`), and line 215, the day's per-run node, carries `RUN || USER`: `USER` is in every one of those disjunctions, which is the whole of what a `mu` token is admitted by — plus its own `outbox` and `heartbeat` (lines 354 and 418, under `MAILBOX`) — plus, since generation 8, `outcomes/$day/$slug/$run` (line 282, `USER` alone: the run's own record, which is how the app names a run that is still going — mobile identity-pairing task J1, F30 and D2797) — plus, since generation 4, `coordinator/**` (line 11, `USER` alone: the coordinator's state, coordinator plan P3, D195) and, since O2 of the stateless orchestrator plan, `orchestrator/**` (the template's own last top-level node, `USER` alone with an explicit `.write: false` beside it: the daemon's state, its lease and its audit, `docs/stateless-orchestrator/implementation-plan.md`'s O2, D1220 and D1241), and, since generation 10, the launch envelope: `config/policy/launch/recipe` (line 23, `USER` alone — the installation's named safe recipe, read by every paired device) and `config/policy/launch/devices/$uid` (line 25, `USER && $uid == auth.uid` — the entry of the device the token belongs to and of no other, mobile plan task P5.1g, the owner's answers Q9 and Q11). An RTDB read grant sits at the location it is written on and cascades **down** only, so those nodes and everything under them are readable and **their parents are not**: `config/caps`, `config/caps/repos`, `config/kill`, `config/kill/repos`, `spend`, `spend/$day`, `spend/$day/repos`, `outcomes`, `outcomes/$day` and `mailbox/$mb` itself are each refused — `TestMailboxReadsAreTheGrantedSet` names every one of them in its denied list. The grant is on the **claim, not the day or the repository**: `spend/<another day>/repos/$slug` and `config/caps/repos/$slug` for a slug that does not exist are readable too (the app shows the day it is looking at), and a read of an absent node is a 200 with `null`, not a denial. `config/limits/**`, `config/mode` and `config/policy/**` are `TOKEN` (the run token: a `fp` claim equal to `/fugaro/project` and a live `fx`) — **except the two launch leaves named above**, which no run token reads and a paired device alone does; `config/admin` — and the device allowlist under it, `config/admin/devices/$uid`, which is `false` to read and to write — and `fugaro/**` are `false`, and under `outcomes` no read is granted at the two parents `outcomes` and `outcomes/$day` — the run's own node under them is the one location there a client reads, the `USER` grant named above, with the run's `.write` beside it; `runs/**` and `agents/**` are `RUN` (`rules.json.tmpl` lines 70 and 245) — the run's own token, `TOKEN` **and** `fs`/`fr` naming that `$slug`/`$run`; and `pairing/$uid/{request,delivery}` belongs to `PAIRING` and to nothing else — the request write-once (`key` and `at`), the delivery read-only, which is how a pairing session is handed its answer and why a `mu` token cannot see it. A `mu` token is none of them.

**What this check does not cover.** The **consumer's** own half of the fence — that a token whose `mc` names a mailbox writes that mailbox's outbox message and heartbeat and is admitted nowhere else (P2.2's `TestMailboxConsumerWritesOnlyItsMailbox`) — is **check 80's**, the mailbox end to end, written by P4.2. This check needs an outbox message to ack and a second one with no ack on it, so the three nodes it reads and acks — step 4's outbox message and heartbeat, and step 5's second outbox message — are **seeded with the operator's IAM credentials** — and the two device nodes steps 1 and 5 write are seeded the same way, **five nodes in all** — which bypass the rules entirely: `FACT:` lines record them, and they prove **nothing about the rules** — what step 4 proves is that the *user* may read them and step 5 that the *user* may ack one and be refused a `false` on the other.

**What changes in the project, and its cost.** Two Firebase Auth accounts (`chk81-alice`, the user, and `chk81-bob`, a second user to prove the binding) that **you** add by hand (D114: an account is an installation's own step; no `fugaro mailbox` command exists and `mobile/` is not built yet, so nothing here is automated). Their names are deliberately not `r~<slug>~<run>`, the only shape the sweeper deletes (`internal/budget/sweep.go`, `DefaultUserMaxAge` 48h), so the sweep leaves them and the Restore removes them. Three nodes under Alice's mailbox are seeded with IAM — step 4's outbox message and heartbeat, and step 5's second outbox message, which the value guard needs because a `false` written to an already-acked message would be refused by `!data.exists()` and prove nothing about the boolean — and so are the **two device nodes** generation 3 requires before an account can read anything at all: `config/admin/devices/$ALICE` in step 1 and `config/admin/devices/$BOB` in step 5 (Bob is deliberately left without one through steps 3, 4 and 6, where he is the account that is not a device). Nothing mints a device node yet — `fugaro pair` is plan task P6.6 and is not built — so those two are written by hand over IAM, exactly as the pairing would write them. **Five nodes in all** carry the operator's IAM credentials, and every one of them is removed by the Restore; everything else is reads and writes over REST with minted ID tokens. **No Cloud Run, no VM, no build, nothing billable**: RTDB reads/writes and Identity Toolkit sign-ins are free at this volume.

**No credential is printed, and the only one that reaches a file is a one-hour custom token.** `$KEY` is the project's restricted web API key and every ID token below is a credential: none is printed, pasted into a `FACT` line or pasted into a pull request, and neither is written to a file — the key and the ID tokens live in the shell's variables, and the custom tokens this check mints are written to `$W/jwt-$uid.txt` under `/tmp/chk81` for the length of the run. **That directory is mode 700** (the guard makes it so before anything is minted into it): a custom token is a bearer credential for as long as its `exp` says, and a world-readable `/tmp/chk81` would hand it to any other local user for the length of the run — the same reason docs/gcp-live-checklist.md:1159 writes its credential-bearing file as `(umask 077; terraform state pull > …)`.

**Guard block — re-run this before every step.** It hard-stops unless the installation is the `fugaro` one on GCP project `fugaro-dev` (never `belong`), reads the four backend values out of the project's own config rather than from memory, and refuses to start without any of them. **Paste it into a file and `source` it, not into an interactive zsh**: the block is bash — the construct that makes it so is `${!v}` in the `for v in DB KEY SA FP` loop below, indirect expansion, which zsh spells `${(P)v}`.

```bash
# === Check 81: setup + guard. RE-RUN THIS BLOCK BEFORE EVERY STEP. ===
P=fugaro-dev                    # hard-coded; the guard below refuses anything else
C=$HOME/.config/fugaro/projects/fugaro.yaml
set -u
[ "$P" = fugaro-dev ] || { echo "Check 81 stopped: this check runs on fugaro-dev only (never belong)" >&2; exit 1; }
command -v fugaro >/dev/null || { echo "Check 81 stopped: no fugaro on PATH" >&2; exit 1; }
fugaro doctor --project fugaro --all 2>/dev/null | grep -q '^project: .*(GCP fugaro-dev,' || {
  echo "Check 81 stopped: installation 'fugaro' is not the fugaro-dev installation on this machine" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -r "$C" ] || { echo "Check 81 stopped: no project config at $C (read the project line of 'fugaro doctor --project fugaro')" >&2; exit 1; }
# DB is the host alone, with no scheme (the same strip check 82's guard and
# docs/gcp-setup.md make), so EVERY url below is written "https://$DB/..." --
# a bare "$DB/..." would be plain HTTP on port 80 and could not answer the
# 200/401 this check requires.
DB=$(sed -n 's|^ *rtdb_url: *||p' "$C" | tr -d "\"'" | sed -e 's|^https://||' -e 's|/*$||' | head -1)
KEY=$(sed -n 's|^ *firebase_api_key: *||p' "$C" | tr -d "\"'" | head -1)
SA=$(sed -n 's|^ *token_signer: *||p' "$C" | tr -d "\"'" | head -1)
# FP is the Firebase project id, which is what Identity Toolkit's
# accounts:signInWithCustomToken and the Restore's accounts:batchDelete address,
# and the project
# the token signer below is an account of (docs/m9-budget-and-dashboard/spec.md: token_signer is
# fugaro-token-signer@<fp>.iam.gserviceaccount.com, and internal/localcfg
# requires exactly that shape) — NOT the GCP project id P above (an
# installation's Firebase project is its own, and the two are the same only by
# coincidence).
FP=$(sed -n 's|^ *firebase_project: *||p' "$C" | tr -d "\"'" | head -1)
for v in DB KEY SA FP; do [ -n "${!v}" ] || { echo "Check 81 stopped: $v is not set in $C (its `budget:` section)" >&2; exit 1; }; done
# W holds the minted custom tokens and their payloads ($W/jwt-$uid.txt,
# $W/payload-$uid.json) for the length of the run: a custom token is a bearer
# credential until its exp (mint() below sets now+3600), so the directory is
# made owner-only -- umask 077 for a fresh one, chmod for one a previous run
# left behind at the default umask.
W=/tmp/chk81
(umask 077; mkdir -p "$W") && chmod 700 "$W" || { echo "Check 81 stopped: cannot make $W owner-only (mode 700)" >&2; exit 1; }
# The two uids this check uses, added by hand before step 1 (D114):
#   ALICE  the user        BOB  a second user (the binding's control)
ALICE=chk81-alice; BOB=chk81-bob
AUD=https://identitytoolkit.googleapis.com/google.identity.identitytoolkit.v1.IdentityToolkit
# The epoch day the counters live under: the plain decimal epoch day, budget.DayKey.
DAY=$(python3 -c 'import time; print(int(time.time()//86400))')
# MAC is the tag every message of every kind and the heartbeat must carry since
# generation 3 (D169/D171): the rules check its *shape* -- a string of exactly 64
# lowercase-hex characters, MACOK -- and never its value, which needs the key
# P6.7 holds. Nothing in this check verifies a tag, and any well-formed one is
# accepted, so a fresh one is drawn here rather than written down.
MAC=$(python3 -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_hex(32))')
# NODE is the slug the granted-node reads use: config/caps/repos/$slug and
# spend/$day/repos/$slug are granted to USER for ANY slug, existing or not, so
# no real repository's slug is needed. NONE is a slug that does not exist, which
# is the other half of the same statement: the grant is on the claim, not on the
# repository, so a read of NONE is a 200 with null and not a denial.
NODE=chk81-probe; NONE=chk81-no-such-repo
echo "Check 81 ready: P=$P firebase=$FP day=$DAY node=$NODE — DB (the database host), KEY (the restricted web API key) and SA (the token signer's service account) are read and never printed; P, FP, DAY and NODE are not secrets, and FP is echoed here on purpose"
```

**The two helpers every minting step uses.** `mint <uid> <claims-json>` signs a custom token with the project's own signer through `iam.serviceAccounts.signJwt` — the path `internal/budget/token`'s `Mint` takes (`IAMSigner.SignJWT`, audience `token.Audience`) and the path check 26's step 7 used; `signin <uid> <claims-json>` exchanges it at `accounts:signInWithCustomToken` for an ID token (`internal/budget/token/exchange.go`), which is what `?auth=` takes below. **`sign-jwt` requires your own credentials to hold `fugaroTokenMinter` on the signer** (`iam.serviceAccounts.signJwt` and nothing else, the `fugaroTokenMinter` role on the signer account): a refusal here is a permission finding, not a fault of this check. The `--project` below is **`$FP`, the Firebase project the signer is an account of** (`token_signer` is `fugaro-token-signer@<fp>.iam.gserviceaccount.com`), not the GCP project id `$P` the guard hard-codes: they are the same only on a same-project installation.

```bash
# === Check 81: the helpers (after the guard block). ===
mint() { # mint <uid> <claims-json-object> -> the custom token on stdout
  local uid=$1 claims=$2 now exp
  now=$(date +%s); exp=$(( now + 3600 ))
  printf '{"iss":"%s","sub":"%s","aud":"%s","iat":%s,"exp":%s,"uid":"%s","claims":%s}' \
    "$SA" "$SA" "$AUD" "$now" "$exp" "$uid" "$claims" > "$W/payload-$uid.json"
  gcloud iam service-accounts sign-jwt "$W/payload-$uid.json" "$W/jwt-$uid.txt" \
    --iam-account="$SA" --project="$FP" >/dev/null || return 1
  cat "$W/jwt-$uid.txt"
}
signin() { # signin <uid> <claims-json-object> -> the ID token on stdout
  local uid=$1 claims=$2 jwt
  jwt=$(mint "$uid" "$claims") || return 1
  curl -sS -X POST "https://identitytoolkit.googleapis.com/v1/accounts:signInWithCustomToken?key=$KEY" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d "{\"token\":\"$jwt\",\"returnSecureToken\":true}" |
    python3 -c 'import json,sys
d = json.load(sys.stdin)
if "idToken" not in d:
    sys.exit("sign-in refused: " + json.dumps(d))
print(d["idToken"])'
}
jwtclaim() { # jwtclaim <jwt> -> the payload, decoded and printed (never the signature)
  python3 - "$1" <<'PY'
import base64, json, sys
p = sys.argv[1].split('.')[1]
p += '=' * (-len(p) % 4)
print(json.dumps(json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(p)), indent=2, sort_keys=True))
PY
}
# TOK keeps the body and puts the status on a line of its own. Every call this
# check makes with `?auth=` -- the rules-facing ones -- goes through it,
# because every one of them is read as a status **with** the body it answered
# with: step 2's write (200 and the message it holds), the refusals of steps
# 3, 4, 5 and 7 (`Permission denied`), and step 6's columns (the node's own
# value, or `null` for an absent one). There is one helper, and no form of it
# throws the body away.
TOK() { curl -sS -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' "$@"; }
```

1. **The two accounts exist, and the tokens carry the claims the rules read.** *(Guard block, then the helpers.)* Add `chk81-alice` and `chk81-bob` as Firebase Auth users by hand — Authentication → Users → Add user in the console, or the Admin SDK; **a `uid` you choose**, not an email you sign in as, since the only sign-in path this project permits is a custom token (`fugaro update --firebase-project` refuses any public sign-up path). Then mint and decode each token **before** exchanging anything:

   ```bash
   jwtclaim "$(mint "$ALICE" "{\"mu\":\"$ALICE\"}")"   # the user: mu == uid
   jwtclaim "$(mint "$BOB"   "{\"mu\":\"$BOB\"}")"     # the second user
   ```
   **FACT:** for each, the values of `aud`, `uid`, `mu` and `exp`, and the signer (`iss`) — **the claims only, never the token**. The audience must be `https://identitytoolkit.googleapis.com/google.identity.identitytoolkit.v1.IdentityToolkit` (`token.Audience`), or the exchange in the next line refuses. Then `AL=$(signin "$ALICE" "{\"mu\":\"$ALICE\"}")` and `BO=$(signin "$BOB" "{\"mu\":\"$BOB\"}")`; **FACT:** the exchange returned an `idToken` for each — the sign-in works with **no sign-in provider enabled** (the property check 21's free identity probe records) — and the ID tokens are in the shell only, never in a file that outlives the run.

   **Then write Alice's device node, and leave Bob without one.** Since generation 3 an account is a device only if `config/admin/devices/<its uid>` exists (D166), and **the rules refuse every client both reading and writing that node** — it is IAM's, and `fugaro pair` (plan task P6.6) is not built, so this step writes it by hand. Bob's node is seeded in step 5: steps 3, 4 and 6 use him as the account that is **not** a device, which is the half of D166 this check can prove with the two accounts it already has.

   ```bash
   AT=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)   # never printed, never pasted
   curl -sS -X PUT "https://$DB/config/admin/devices/$ALICE.json?access_token=$AT" \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d 'true'
   curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" "https://$DB/config/admin/devices.json"
   ```
   **FACT:** the write's status and the read-back — the allowlist holds exactly `$ALICE`, and `true` is a placeholder: the rules read the node's **existence** and no field of it, so nothing personal belongs in it. The three states of one account are what P6.4's `TestDeviceNodeGatesEverythingUserReaches` walks (never written, written, deleted), because a revocation that waits for an ID token to expire is not a revocation (G14) — which is why the owner chose a node over a claim. **FACT:** that `config/admin/devices/$ALICE` exists and `config/admin/devices/$BOB` does not.

2. **The fence's positive half — the user's own inbox write, once, in the one shape.** *(Guard block, helpers, tokens from step 1, Alice's device node from step 1.)* The message id is minted fresh because the write is once-only, and the message carries the tag and the kind generation 3 added:

   ```bash
   MSG=$(printf 'chk81-%s' "$(date +%s)")
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/inbox/$MSG.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d "{\"id\":\"$MSG\",\"sender\":\"$ALICE\",\"text\":\"check 81 step 2\",\"at\":$(date +%s000),\"mac\":\"$MAC\",\"kind\":\"message\"}"
   # The same PUT again: the write is once-only (`!data.exists()`) -- 401.
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/inbox/$MSG.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d "{\"id\":\"$MSG\",\"sender\":\"$ALICE\",\"text\":\"check 81 step 2\",\"at\":$(date +%s000),\"mac\":\"$MAC\",\"kind\":\"message\"}"
   # And each wrong shape -- sender not $mb, empty text, id != $msg, at not a
   # number, no mac at all, a mac that is not 64 lowercase hex characters -- on
   # an id of its own: a refused write leaves nothing behind, so the path stays
   # empty for the next line. All six are 401.
   BAD=$(printf 'chk81-bad-%s' "$(date +%s)")
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/inbox/$BAD.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d "{\"id\":\"$BAD\",\"sender\":\"$BOB\",\"text\":\"x\",\"at\":$(date +%s000),\"mac\":\"$MAC\"}"      # sender: newData.val() == $mb
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/inbox/$BAD.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d "{\"id\":\"$BAD\",\"sender\":\"$ALICE\",\"text\":\"\",\"at\":$(date +%s000),\"mac\":\"$MAC\"}"     # text: length > 0
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/inbox/$BAD.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d "{\"id\":\"chk81-other\",\"sender\":\"$ALICE\",\"text\":\"x\",\"at\":$(date +%s000),\"mac\":\"$MAC\"}"   # id: newData.val() == $msg
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/inbox/$BAD.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d "{\"id\":\"$BAD\",\"sender\":\"$ALICE\",\"text\":\"x\",\"at\":\"now\",\"mac\":\"$MAC\"}"            # at: newData.isNumber()
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/inbox/$BAD.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d "{\"id\":\"$BAD\",\"sender\":\"$ALICE\",\"text\":\"x\",\"at\":$(date +%s000)}"                    # mac: hasChildren([... 'mac'])
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/inbox/$BAD.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d "{\"id\":\"$BAD\",\"sender\":\"$ALICE\",\"text\":\"x\",\"at\":$(date +%s000),\"mac\":\"${MAC:0:63}\"}"   # mac: length == 64 && matches(HEX)
   # The operator's own read of the whole inbox (IAM bypasses the rules): it
   # holds exactly the one message, and none of the refused shapes left a node.
   AT=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)   # never printed, never pasted
   curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/inbox.json"
   ```
   **FACT:** the response body (`{"id":...,"sender":...,"text":...,"at":...,"mac":...}`) and the status, 200. A write the rules refuse answers `Permission denied` with 401 (`internal/rtdb`'s `ErrPermission` is the 401 **or** 403 answer). **FACT:** the second PUT's status (401, write-once `!data.exists()`), each of the six wrong shapes' status (401) with the rule each one fails, and the operator's read of `mailbox/$ALICE/inbox.json`, which holds exactly the one message — no refused shape left a node. (The step 4 seeding reuses `$AT`, which is set here.) The last two lines are the tag generation 3 added (D169/D171): the rules can require a **well-formed** tag and nothing more — they hold no key, so a message with a wrong-but-well-formed tag is admitted here and caught only by `fugaro mailbox` (P6.7), which is P6.4's `TestMailboxMessagesRequireTheTag` at the database and the reason this step records the field and not its value.

3. **The fence's negative half — what the user may not write, and what an account with no device node may not do at all.** *(Guard block, helpers, tokens, operator credentials for the read-back.)* Each line must answer a permission denial; a 200 on any of them is a **failure** of this check, not a question. The last three are D166's: Bob's token carries `mu == uid` and **his account has no device node yet** (step 5 seeds it), so `USER` itself fails and even his own mailbox is closed to him — the state every account is in before it is paired:

   ```bash
   ID2=$(printf 'chk81-%s' "$(date +%s)")
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$BOB/inbox/$ID2.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d "{\"id\":\"$ID2\",\"sender\":\"$BOB\",\"text\":\"x\",\"at\":$(date +%s000),\"mac\":\"$MAC\"}"      # another mailbox: MAILBOX fails ($mb != auth.uid)
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/outbox/$ID2.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d "{\"id\":\"$ID2\",\"sender\":\"$ALICE\",\"text\":\"x\",\"at\":$(date +%s000),\"mac\":\"$MAC\"}"    # the outbox message is CONSUMER's (check 80's half)
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/heartbeat.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d "{\"at\":$(date +%s000),\"boot\":\"chk81\",\"mac\":\"$MAC\"}"                                      # the heartbeat is CONSUMER's
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/inbox/$ID2/secret.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '"x"'   # $other: {".validate": false}
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/agents/$NODE/chk81-run.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"repo":"x","requestedBy":"x"}'
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/outcomes/$DAY/$NODE/chk81-run.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"status":"failed","requestedBy":"x"}'
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/runs/$NODE/chk81-run/exp.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '0'
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/config/mode.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '"enforce"'
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/config/limits/maxReserveMicros.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '1'
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/fugaro/mark.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/config/admin/devices/$BOB.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d 'true'   # the allowlist is IAM's: a user may not write it, not even for another account
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$BOB/inbox/$ID2.json?auth=$BO" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d "{\"id\":\"$ID2\",\"sender\":\"$BOB\",\"text\":\"x\",\"at\":$(date +%s000),\"mac\":\"$MAC\"}"      # no device node: USER fails, so his own inbox is closed to him
   TOK "https://$DB/mailbox/$BOB/outbox.json?auth=$BO"   # no device node: nor his own outbox
   TOK "https://$DB/config/caps/global.json?auth=$BO"    # no device node: nor the nodes D112 grants a mu token
   AT=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)   # never printed, never pasted; the read-back below
   curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" "https://$DB/config/mode.json"; echo
   curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" "https://$DB/config/limits/maxReserveMicros.json"; echo
   curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" "https://$DB/fugaro/mark.json"; echo
   curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" "https://$DB/config/admin/devices.json"; echo
   ```
   **FACT:** the fourteen statuses, each with its refused body (`Permission denied`), and — read back with the operator's credentials, since `config/mode` is `TOKEN`-only and a `mu` token cannot even read it — that `config/mode`, `config/limits/maxReserveMicros` and `fugaro/mark` are unchanged: the three bodies above, which hold the values the installation had before these fourteen refusals. **FACT:** the allowlist read-back holds `$ALICE` and **not** `$BOB` — the refusal above left no node behind. The three `$BO` lines are the device conjunct itself (D166): the same token, the same `mu == uid`, refused everything it would otherwise reach — which is exactly what a phone that deploys generation 3 without being paired sees, and what P6.4's `TestDeviceNodeGatesEverythingUserReaches` walks at the database.

4. **The user reads its own outbox and heartbeat — and reads its own inbox no way at all.** *(Guard block, helpers, tokens, `$MSG` from step 2, operator credentials for the seeding.)* The outbox and the heartbeat carry `".read": "MAILBOX"`; the inbox carries **no** read grant, and neither does `mailbox/$mb` itself. **The two nodes are seeded here by IAM**, which bypasses the rules — the consumer's own write of them is check 80's, and this seeding proves nothing about the rules:

   ```bash
   AT=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)   # never printed, never pasted
   OUT=$(printf 'chk81-out-%s' "$(date +%s)")
   curl -sS -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/outbox/$OUT.json?access_token=$AT" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d "{\"id\":\"$OUT\",\"sender\":\"$ALICE\",\"text\":\"seeded by IAM for check 81\",\"at\":$(date +%s000),\"mac\":\"$MAC\",\"kind\":\"message\"}"
   curl -sS -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/heartbeat.json?access_token=$AT" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d "{\"at\":$(date +%s000),\"boot\":\"chk81\",\"mac\":\"$MAC\"}"
   TOK "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/outbox.json?auth=$AL"      # 200: the grant
   TOK "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/heartbeat.json?auth=$AL"   # 200
   TOK "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/inbox.json?auth=$AL"       # 401: the inbox has no client read grant
   TOK "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/inbox/$MSG.json?auth=$AL"  # 401: nor the message the user just wrote
   TOK "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE.json?auth=$AL"             # 401: nor the mailbox's parent
   TOK "https://$DB/mailbox/$BOB/outbox.json?auth=$AL"        # 401: another mailbox's outbox
   ```
   **FACT:** the six statuses, and — for the two 200s — the bodies, which must hold the seeded message and heartbeat and nothing else. **A user that can read the message it wrote is the failure this step exists to catch**: it would mean the deployed document is not this one. (The 200 with an **empty** body is not this: the grant is on the node, and an absent node answers `null` — the seeding here is what makes the two 200s hold content.) The two seeds carry the `mac` and the `kind` a consumer's own write carries since generation 3: IAM bypasses the rules, so this step proves nothing about them, but a seeded node shaped like a message no writer could have written would make the read-back harder to read than it needs to be.

5. **The user's second write — the ack, once, on a message that already exists — and Bob becomes a device.** *(Guard block, helpers, tokens, `$OUT` from step 4, operator credentials for the second seed and for Bob's device node.)* `acked` is `MAILBOX && newData.exists() && !data.exists()` with `data.parent().exists()`:

   ```bash
   AT=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)   # never printed, never pasted; seeds the second message below
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/outbox/$OUT/acked.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d 'true'   # 200: the one ack
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/outbox/$OUT/acked.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d 'true'   # 401: once only (!data.exists())
   OUT2=$(printf 'chk81-out2-%s' "$(date +%s)")
   curl -sS -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/outbox/$OUT2.json?access_token=$AT" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d "{\"id\":\"$OUT2\",\"sender\":\"$ALICE\",\"text\":\"seeded by IAM for check 81 step 5\",\"at\":$(date +%s000),\"mac\":\"$MAC\",\"kind\":\"message\"}"
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/outbox/$OUT2/acked.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d 'false'  # 401: newData.val() == true, on a message with no ack yet
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/outbox/chk81-absent/acked.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d 'true'   # 401: data.parent().exists()
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$BOB/outbox/chk81-absent/acked.json?auth=$AL" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d 'true'     # 401: another mailbox
   # Bob's device node goes in here, and only here: steps 3, 4 and 6 use him as
   # the account that is not a device (step 6's control read of config/caps/global
   # with $BO is the other half of step 3's three $BO refusals, and needs this).
   curl -sS -X PUT "https://$DB/config/admin/devices/$BOB.json?access_token=$AT" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d 'true'
   curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" "https://$DB/config/admin/devices.json"; echo   # $ALICE and $BOB
   curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/outbox/$OUT.json"; echo   # the read-back: acked: true, text unchanged
   ```
   **FACT:** the five `TOK` statuses and the refused bodies — counted by `TOK` line, the way step 4 counts its own six: the block's four `curl` lines are the two IAM writes and the two read-backs, and none is one of them. The third `TOK` line is refused by the **value** guard (`newData.val() == true`) and not by the write-once one: it is a **different** message from the acked one, seeded here through IAM, because a `false` written to the message the first `TOK` line already acked would be refused by `!data.exists()` and would prove nothing about the boolean — the case P2.2's `c2` tries on a fresh message. The fourth `TOK` line is the guard against an ack that would create its own parent: the message must already exist, which is why the seeding in step 4 is on the path. **FACT:** the allowlist read-back, which now holds `$ALICE` and `$BOB` — and the operator's read of the acked message, which carries `acked: true` and its `text` unchanged (an ack that replaced the message would be a different failure).

6. **The granted read nodes, everything the grant does not name, and the parents of the granted nodes.** *(Guard block, helpers, tokens, Bob's device node from step 5.)* This is `TestMailboxReadsAreTheGrantedSet` in the emulator, which is where these path lists come from — the outcome node's own read, and its refusal under the document behind, is `TestEmulatorRunsADeviceReadsOutcomes`, the neighbour J1 added — plus the device allowlist and the pairing nodes of `TestDeviceNodeGatesEverythingUserReaches` and `TestPairingSessionWritesItsRequestOnceAndReadsOnlyItsDelivery`. Two things make the reading non-obvious and both are in the first column's result: **an RTDB read grant sits at the location it is written on and cascades *down* only**, so the granted nodes and everything under them are readable and their **parents are not** — there is no `.read` at `spend/$day`, `outcomes/$day`, `config/caps` or `config/kill`, and a read of one of them is a **401**, not a 200 — the run's outcome node `outcomes/$day/$slug/$run` is this generation's addition to the grant (mobile identity-pairing task J1, F30 and D2797: the run's own record, so the phone can name a run that is still going), and it is granted to the app's user claim alone, with the run's ledger at `runs/$slug/$run` staying the run's; and **the grant is on the claim, not on the day or the slug**, so a day that is not today and a repository slug that does not exist are readable just the same (the app reads the day it is looking at). A read of an absent node is a 200 whose body is `null`, which is a pass, not a denial:

   ```bash
   for p in "config/caps/global" "config/caps/defaults" "config/caps/repos/$NODE" "config/caps/repos/$NONE" \
            "config/kill/global" "config/kill/repos/$NODE" \
            "spend/$DAY/global" "spend/$DAY/global/counted" "spend/$DAY/repos/$NODE" \
            "spend/$DAY/runs/$NODE/chk81-run" "spend/$DAY/runs/$NODE/chk81-run/spent" \
            "outcomes/$DAY/$NODE/chk81-run" \
            "spend/$((DAY-1))/repos/$NODE" "spend/$((DAY+1))/global"; do
     printf '%-52s %s\n' "$p" "$(TOK "https://$DB/$p.json?auth=$AL")"
   done
   for p in "config" "config/caps" "config/caps/repos" "config/kill" "config/kill/repos" \
            "config/limits" "config/limits/policyRules" "config/mode" "config/policy/shared" "config/admin" \
            "config/admin/devices" "config/admin/devices/$ALICE" \
            "spend" "spend/$DAY" "spend/$DAY/repos" \
            "mailbox" "mailbox/$ALICE" "mailbox/$ALICE/inbox" \
            "fugaro" "fugaro/project" "runs/$NODE" "agents/$NODE" "outcomes/$DAY" \
            "pairing" "pairing/$ALICE/request" "pairing/$ALICE/delivery"; do
     printf '%-52s %s\n' "$p" "$(TOK "https://$DB/$p.json?auth=$AL")"
   done
   # The second user closes the binding: the node is granted to any `mu` token
   # whose account is a device (step 5 wrote BOB's node), and ALICE's mailbox
   # nodes are BOB's to read only if `$mb` were BOB.
   printf '%-52s %s\n' "config/caps/global"     "$(TOK "https://$DB/config/caps/global.json?auth=$BO")"        # 200: granted to any paired mu token
   printf '%-52s %s\n' "mailbox/$ALICE/outbox"  "$(TOK "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/outbox.json?auth=$BO")"     # 401: BOB's mu is BOB
   printf '%-52s %s\n' "mailbox/$ALICE/heartbeat" "$(TOK "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/heartbeat.json?auth=$BO")"  # 401
   ```
   **FACT:** the two columns, each row the body it answered with and then the status (`TOK` puts the status on a line of its own, so the column stays readable under the bodies). The first fourteen are **200**, with the body being whatever that node holds in this installation or `null` if it holds nothing (nothing here is seeded: step 4's seeding is the mailbox's outbox and heartbeat, so `spend/$DAY/global`, the three other-day/absent-slug paths, `spend/$DAY/runs/$NODE/chk81-run` and `outcomes/$DAY/$NODE/chk81-run` are `null` unless the installation has real spend under them — **a 200 with `null` is the pass, and it is the whole point of the line: the read was allowed, the node is simply empty**), and the second twenty-six are **401** with `Permission denied`. **`spend/$DAY` is in the denied column and that is the point**: the grant is at `spend/$day/global`, `/repos/$slug` and `/runs/$slug/$run` (and, for the caps and kill nodes, at `config/caps/global`, `config/caps/defaults`, `config/caps/repos/$slug`, `config/kill/global` and `config/kill/repos/$slug` — nothing at `config/caps`, `config/caps/repos`, `config/kill` or `config/kill/repos`), and a 200 on any of those parents would mean the deployed document grants more than D112 says it does. The **second user** closes the binding with three more: `$DB/config/caps/global.json?auth=$BO` is **200** (the node is granted to any `mu` token whose account is a device — step 5 wrote Bob's node, and without it this line is a 401, which is step 3's last `TOK` line — the last of its three `$BO` lines), while `$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/outbox.json?auth=$BO` and `$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/heartbeat.json?auth=$BO` are **401** (BOB's `mu` is BOB). **FACT:** those three. `config/limits/policyRules` is deliberately in the denied column: the runner reads the marker as a `TOKEN`, and a user that could read it would be reading a node D112's grant does not name. `mailbox` and `mailbox/$ALICE` are in it too — the mailbox's own `outbox` and `heartbeat` are granted, the container above them is not, and step 4 has already read them. The five generation-3 additions are the same statement about D166's and D165's nodes: `config/admin` is `false` and the allowlist under it, `config/admin/devices/$ALICE`, is what makes Alice a device — **the user whose own node it is may not read it** (its content is IAM's, and the rules read its existence and no field), and `pairing/$ALICE/{request,delivery}` is `PAIRING`'s alone, so a `mu` token sees neither the request its own phone would write nor the delivery it would read. **FACT:** those five, whose 401s are what says the deployed document carries D166 and D165 rather than the generation-2 document that had neither node.

7. **A token whose `mu` is not its own uid is admitted nowhere — and the residual P2.2 accepted.** *(Guard block, helpers.)* Two tokens, minted and exchanged only here:

   ```bash
   MI=$(signin "$BOB" "{\"mu\":\"$ALICE\"}")   # uid=BOB wearing ALICE's mu
   TOK -X PUT "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/inbox/chk81-mismatch.json?auth=$MI" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d "{\"id\":\"chk81-mismatch\",\"sender\":\"$ALICE\",\"text\":\"x\",\"at\":$(date +%s000),\"mac\":\"$MAC\"}"   # 401: mu != auth.uid
   TOK "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/outbox.json?auth=$MI"        # 401: USER fails, so MAILBOX does too
   TOK "https://$DB/mailbox/$ALICE/heartbeat.json?auth=$MI"     # 401
   TOK "https://$DB/config/caps/global.json?auth=$MI"           # 401: the granted nodes are USER's too
   TOK "https://$DB/mailbox/$BOB/inbox/chk81-mismatch.json?auth=$MI" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d "{\"id\":\"chk81-mismatch\",\"sender\":\"$BOB\",\"text\":\"x\",\"at\":$(date +%s000),\"mac\":\"$MAC\"}"     # 401: BO's own mailbox is not MI's either
   ```
   **FACT:** the five 401s and their bodies: a `mu` that disagrees with the token's own `uid` buys **nothing**, not even the granted read nodes. **Then the residual, recorded and not failed** (P6.4's `TestMailboxResidualMintedTokenNeedsTheDeviceNode`, which is what P2.2's `TestMailboxResidualMintedTokenPassesUntilPhase6` became): whoever can sign a custom token for the project can mint one whose `uid` **is** Alice and whose `mu` **is** Alice, and Firebase cannot tell it from Alice's own device. Mint exactly that — `signin "$ALICE" "{\"mu\":\"$ALICE\"}"` with a signer identity other than the one step 1 used, if you hold a second — and record that a write of step 2's shape **on a fresh id** succeeds (step 2's `$MSG` is taken, and the write is once-only: a repeat of that PUT is refused by `!data.exists()` and would prove nothing about the token). This is the accepted residual the rules' own comments name (`internal/budget/rules/rules.go`, G13) and its boundary is `iam.serviceAccounts.signJwt` over the whole project, which `fugaro doctor`'s `token-signers` check reports. **Generation 3 puts a second key in front of it and does not close it**: the token alone is not Alice — Alice's **device node** is, which is why a minted token for an account that has none is refused everything (step 3's three `$BO` lines are that state exactly, and the emulator case walks it: refused, then the node goes in, then the same token is Alice). The node is not the minter's to *hold* but it is the minter's to *write*: whoever can sign over the project usually holds `roles/firebasedatabase.admin` too, so they can write the node as well as the token — step 1 writes one over IAM by hand, and a minter does the same. **FACT:** which signer minted it and whether the write succeeded. **The per-pairing MAC (D169/D171) is the field that separates a message the phone spoke from one the minter invented, and the rules can require its shape and nothing more**: verifying a tag is P6.7's (`fugaro mailbox`), which is not built, so a minted token can still speak any message it likes. **A write that succeeds here is today's expected result and not a failure of this check.**

8. **The fence is the deployed document's, not one this checkout generates.** *(Guard block, operator credentials.)* Everything above only means something if the document answering it is P2.1's. Read it as the operator (IAM bypasses the rules) and compare it with what this binary would deploy:

   ```bash
   AT=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)   # never printed, never pasted
   curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" "https://$DB/.settings/rules.json" > "$W/deployed.json"
   test -s "$W/deployed.json" || { echo "the read returned nothing: check \$DB and the token, do not read on"; exit 1; }
   wc -c < "$W/deployed.json"                # the deployed document's size
   grep -o '"mailbox"' "$W/deployed.json" | wc -l              # 1: the subtree is deployed
   grep -o 'auth.token.mu != null' "$W/deployed.json" | wc -l  # 17: the USER predicate, on every node that carries it
   grep -o '"\.validate": false' "$W/deployed.json" | wc -l    # 17: $other's guard is deployed
   grep -o 'config/admin/devices' "$W/deployed.json" | wc -l   # 17: D166's device conjunct, inside every expansion of USER
   grep -o '"pairing"' "$W/deployed.json" | wc -l              # 1: D165's subtree
   grep -o '"mac"' "$W/deployed.json" | wc -l                  # 3: the tag, on both message directions and the heartbeat
   # The comparison the CLI itself makes (infra.SameJSON): the same JSON document,
   # formatting ignored. It needs a checkout of this release, for the golden.
   python3 - "$W/deployed.json" internal/budget/rules/testdata/rules.golden.json <<'PY'
   import json, sys
   a, b = json.load(open(sys.argv[1])), json.load(open(sys.argv[2]))
   if a != b:
       sys.exit("the deployed document is not this release's generated one (JSON, formatting ignored)")
   print("the deployed document is the generated one (JSON-equal)")
   PY
   ```
   **FACT:** the read-back's byte count — **whatever the API stored**: no number is required of it, because `internal/infra`'s `DB.Plan` compares the deployed document with the generated one through `SameJSON`, which unmarshals both and re-marshals them, i.e. **the same JSON document, formatting ignored** — so a document the API stored with other whitespace is the same document at another byte count, which is what the JSON comparison above is for. The one number that exists is the generator's own **75318** bytes, the size `internal/budget/rules/testdata/rules.golden.json` carries and check 82's step 3's plan line prints. The six counts: **1, 17, 17, 17, 1 and 3** for this release's document — they are this document's own numbers and not thresholds: a generation-2 document, the older one this check is written to catch, carries the mailbox and so answers **1** for the first pattern, but **0** for each of the last three. **The patterns are the document's own text, and `auth.token.mu != null` is the one to copy carefully**: the rules render the `USER` predicate expanded, so `mu` is never the first word after a quote and `grep -o '"mu != null"'` matches nothing in a correct document — a pattern that cannot match is a FACT line that reads as a failed deploy of a perfect one, which is why the counts are the generator's and `internal/cli`'s test for this check derives them from `internal/budget/rules/testdata/rules.golden.json`. The last three are generation 3's own: `config/admin/devices` is D166's conjunct and appears as many times as `USER` is expanded, `pairing` is D165's subtree (one node, absent from any generation-2 document), and `"mac"` is the tag on the two message directions and the heartbeat — a document without it is generation 2's, and the deploy that put it there is check 82's. A deployed document **without** `mailbox` is the failure this step exists to catch, and it is the one that makes the rest unreadable in the other direction: **step 3's and step 6's refused columns would pass on a document that grants nothing at all**, which is why the two are read together. If it is `mailbox`-less, stop and run **check 82** (the deploy) before reading any other result of this check.

**Passes when:** step 1 writes Alice's device node and leaves Bob without one; step 2's write and step 5's first ack answer 200; every refused line in steps 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 answers 401 `Permission denied` — including step 3's three `$BO` lines, the account whose `mu` is its own uid and which has **no device node**; step 6's first fourteen reads answer 200 (some with an absent node's `null`) and its second twenty-six 401, including a 401 on each parent of a granted node (`spend/$DAY`, `config/caps`, `config/kill`), a 401 on `config/admin/devices/$ALICE` and on both pairing nodes, and a 200 on the same granted nodes under another day and an absent slug; the user cannot read its own inbox or the message it wrote; and step 8's JSON comparison finds the deployed document equal to `rules.Generate()`'s output (formatting ignored — `SameJSON`), carrying `mailbox`, the `USER` predicate with its device conjunct, `pairing`, the `mac` field and `$other`'s guard (its byte count is the API's to choose; only the generated document is 75318 bytes). Step 7's residual succeeding is expected today and does not fail the check.

**Fails when:** any refusal answers 200 — another user's inbox accepted; the outbox message or the heartbeat accepted from a user; a second, `false`, consumer-less or parent-less ack accepted; an account with **no device node** admitted to its own mailbox, its own outbox or the granted read nodes (step 3's three `$BO` lines); the device allowlist readable by the user whose node it is, or a pairing node readable or writable by a `mu` token; a message with no `mac` accepted; any non-granted read answering 200 (especially `config/mode`, `config/limits/policyRules` or `fugaro/**`); a user reading its own inbox; or a `mu` that disagrees with the token's own `uid` admitted anywhere. **What failing looks like:** a deployed document older than generation 3 — generation 2's has `mailbox` but neither `config/admin/devices` nor `pairing`, so every read in step 6 passes and the app is open to any account that can be signed in; a hand-edited document in the Firebase console that a later deploy overwrote; a `$mb` guard written `auth.token.mu == $mb` instead of `USER && $mb == auth.uid`, which is what makes a mismatch token work. **The fix is the deploy, never a hand-edit in the console** — a document edited there is one this release's template does not generate, and check 82's second run would report the difference as a deploy rather than as "already has the rules". Stop and run check 82.

**Paste back:** every `FACT` line above — the decoded claims (never a token), each status with its refused body, the two read columns and the second user's three, the residual's outcome and which signer minted it, the deployed document's size and its six counts. **Never paste a minted token, an ID token, a refresh token, the web API key, or the signer's token**: a `FACT` line names `$KEY`/`$SA` as variables or not at all. Until this check runs, the mailbox fence is **UNVERIFIED** live — the emulator's cases are the only evidence — and the row above stays **NOT RUN**.

**Restore.** Delete what this check wrote and the two accounts it used, with the operator's own credentials — IAM bypasses the rules, so it can remove what the fence itself refused, and the two Auth accounts go through the admin API, which the web API key cannot authenticate — and in this order:

```bash
# === Check 81: Restore (operator credentials; re-run the guard block first). ===
AT=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)
for p in "mailbox/$ALICE" "mailbox/$BOB" "config/admin/devices/$ALICE" "config/admin/devices/$BOB"; do
  curl -sS -X DELETE "https://$DB/$p.json?access_token=$AT" -o /dev/null -w "$p %{http_code}\n"
done
# The two Auth accounts go through the Identity Toolkit ADMIN API, which is
# authenticated: $KEY is the web API key, and it signs the *client* endpoints
# (accounts:signInWithCustomToken, step 1) -- it is not a credential, so
# `?key=$KEY` here answers 401 and leaves both accounts behind. This is the
# call internal/budget's AuthAdmin.DeleteUsers makes: accounts:batchDelete with
# {"localIds":[...],"force":true} and a Bearer credential that holds
# roles/firebaseauth.admin -- which the installation owner's own gcloud
# credential has through the project's basic roles.
curl -sS -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  "https://identitytoolkit.googleapis.com/v1/projects/$FP/accounts:batchDelete" \
  -d "{\"localIds\":[\"$ALICE\",\"$BOB\"],\"force\":true}"
echo
rm -f "$W"/payload-*.json "$W"/jwt-*.txt "$W"/deployed.json
ls "$W"    # empty (or only the guard's own files): no token survives
rmdir "$W" 2>/dev/null || true   # and the 700 directory itself goes
```

**FACT:** the four RTDB deletes' statuses (200 each) and the `accounts:batchDelete` body — empty when both accounts went, or an `errors` array naming a `localId` and its `message`, where `USER_NOT_FOUND` means that account was already gone, which is the outcome this step wants (the call answers 200 either way: `internal/budget`'s `AuthAdmin.DeleteUsers` says "a 200 can carry per-user errors"). The call is `projects/$FP`, the **Firebase** project id the guard reads out of the config, because Identity Toolkit does not address accounts by the GCP project id — and it carries the owner's own access token, because this is the admin API: with the web API key alone it answers 401 and the two accounts stay, outside the sweeper's reach (`internal/budget/sweep.go` deletes only `r~<slug>~<run>` uids, older than `DefaultUserMaxAge` 48h). And that `/tmp/chk81` holds no token afterwards. Both mailboxes go, and both device nodes with them — an allowlist entry for an account that no longer exists is a node nothing will ever clean up, and nothing else in the project references either account. The two names sit outside the sweeper's `r~<slug>~<run>` shape, so nothing removes them for you. **If a step failed, restore anyway** and record which step's leftovers could not be removed.

## Check 82: the rules deploy and the marker — `config/limits/policyRules` reads back this release's `RulesVersion` (`fugaro-dev` only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

The rules are a **generated artifact** of the CLI, not a file anyone edits: `internal/budget/rules`'s `Generate()` renders `rules.json.tmpl` with `rules.go`'s macros, `internal/budget/rules/testdata/rules.golden.json` (75318 bytes) pins the output, and `TestRulesParity`/`TestRulesGolden`/`TestGeneratedRulesParse` keep the three from drifting. The only path that puts that document on a database is **`fugaro update --firebase-project`**, and the deploy is the write **immediately before the generation marker**: the marker is written **after** the rules, never before (`internal/infra`'s `DB.Plan` and `Apply` — `firebasedb.go` appends the rules action and then the marker's own `d.put` call), which is what makes the marker's presence a statement about the document underneath it and this check is held to the code by `internal/cli`'s tests, so a plan that really changed breaks them. This check is that deploy and the generation it records: `internal/projectpolicy`'s `RulesVersion` (**11** on this release — generation 1 is the policy nodes, generation 2 adds the mailbox, generation 3 the message fields, the device allowlist and the pairing nodes, generation 4 the coordinator's read grant, generation 5 the voice policy node (`config/policy/voice/{shared,repos/$slug}`, `TOKEN`-read and never written, mobile plan task P5.3.1), generation 6 the fields a push registration carries on a mailbox message (`token`, `platform` and `prefs` on a message of the `registration` kind, mobile plan task P5.2.2), generation 7 the four leaves a run's stage report writes per model (`spend/$day/repos/$slug/byModel/$model/{notional,rep,tlo,thi}`, spend-accuracy SA5.0), generation 8 the paired device's read of a run's outcome (`outcomes/$day/$slug/$run`, one node granted to the app's user claim and to nothing else, mobile identity-pairing task J1, F30 and D2797), and generation 9 the credential route a run reads at bootstrap (`config/policy/route/$slug`, one node per repository, granted to that repository's own run token and to nothing else `TOKEN && auth.token.fs == $slug`, a read grant and so a bump, workspace-service task WS22, F23, R3 and R4), and generation 10 the phone's launch envelope and its stop request together (mobile plan task P5.1g, the owner's answers Q9, Q10(c) and Q11: `config/policy/launch`, one node under the policy subtree holding the installation's named safe recipe and one entry per paired device — the repository allow-list narrowed from the project's own `allow_repos`, the launch rate and the daily cost ceiling — read by that device alone and written by no client, plus the `stop` kind the app writes into its own inbox to ask a human to stop what they are looking at, which is a request the human acts on at the console or the laptop and is never a phone-writable kill switch; it bumps for generation 4's read-grant reason and generation 6's client-write reason at once), and generation 11 the two shapes a phone of this release writes (a message and the heartbeat carry a tag that is exactly one of `mac` and `sig` — the unpadded base64url Ed25519 signature a device that holds a key signs with — and an inbox action may be the typed `launch`, whose `mode` names the rigor mode to start in and which needs no `confirmation` where every other verb carries one, mobile identity-pairing task J5r, O6 and O10), and T8's build lease family, a deny that opens no family to a client and so moves no generation), recorded at `projectpolicy.PathRulesMarker()` = `config/limits/policyRules`, which is the generation **check 81's denial cases and the emulator cases are written against**. A binary whose `RulesVersion` is not 11 would deploy a different document; the number this check reads back in steps 3 and 5 is that constant's value, `internal/projectpolicy`'s `RulesVersion`, so a release that bumps it rewrites this check with it.

**No agent applies rules.** The database step asks for the project's name typed at a real terminal, and a coding-agent session cannot confirm it whatever flags it passes (`internal/cli`'s `askOrdinary`: an agent session raises `initflow.AgentError` before anything is shown), so this step is yours alone; nothing here is a CI job and no agent's session is one. **The confirmation is the owner's own, at their own real terminal, not an agent's**: `ask` takes it for an ordinary step from what the owner types there, which is why this check says what to do — read the plan and type the name — rather than claiming the CLI refuses it. (On a project the managed marks answer for, **this command's own run still asks it**: `--firebase-project` is one of the flags that shape the installation, so the run is refused the gate before any mark is read (`shapesTheInstallation`) and every confirmation it gives is the one it always gave. The run that reaches this same deploy with nothing typed at the owner's terminal is a plain `fugaro update`, whose rules stage writes the same generation — and there the gate's verdict **is** the confirmation: the document is this binary's own `rules.Generate()` output and the step hands it to the gate as admitted by construction (`managed.ConvergeAdmitted`, whose `Refuse()` is nil for the class this stage judges, with `rulesAdmittedRules` recording what admitted it), so the step prints the gate's own sentence where the typed name would have been and never reaches this confirmation at all. A document the gate did not admit is refused instead of written: the refusal comes back as an error, `rulesStage.gateStep` turns it into an `initflow.GatedError` and the run stops naming the rules that fired, with nothing written and no `initflow.OwnerProceeded` sentence — that sentence is for the steps the gate's rules never judged, not for one the gate judged. The two paths that do reach this step's ordinary confirmation are the owner's own `--ask` and a second mark read that finds the project is not managed any more, and on both the gate has already stopped standing in (`gateStandsIn` is false under `--ask`, and `initGate.underway` is false once the second read revokes), so the owner's arm is not one of them either and this step keeps exactly the confirmation it had before the ruling. The coding agent's refusal is the same in both.)
