**What changes in the project, and its cost.** One `fugaro update --firebase-project` run: **one rules deploy** of about 74 KB and, at most, the marker write after it. The database step lists every write before it makes any, and
- on an installation whose rules already match this binary's document, it plans **no** rules write — but it **still writes the marker** when the node is absent or holds another generation (`DB.Plan`: the marker write is planned whenever `!markerFound || markerGen != projectpolicy.RulesVersion`, because a database whose rules were deployed before this code existed still has to record which generation it runs);
- the rest of the database step (the Fugaro mark, `fugaro/project`, `config/mode`, `config/limits/maxReserveMicros`) is planned only for the fields that are absent or different, so on a settled installation the run is the marker alone under one confirmation; and
- the settled line — `The database already has the rules, mark, project name and mode.` — is printed when **nothing at all is pending**: no act line, Identity Platform already initialized and no Firestore step (`deployDatabase`: `if len(acts) == 0 && !idp.missing && !fs.Pending()`, `internal/cli/init_firebase.go`), and the run then asks for no confirmation. It is the database step's own line for a settled database — not a Terraform root's `No changes`, which is `applyRoot`'s for an empty plan — and it is **not** a statement about the rules alone: an installation whose rules match but whose marker is absent writes the marker and prints that act line instead.

Nothing is billable: the RTDB REST API, the rules deploy and the marker write cost nothing. **No secret is present**: nothing in this check reads, prints or writes one, and the operator's access token stays in a variable.

**Guard block — re-run this before every step.** It hard-stops unless the installation is the `fugaro` one on GCP project `fugaro-dev` (never `belong`) and reads the backend's address out of the project's own config rather than from memory.

```bash
# === Check 82: setup + guard. RE-RUN THIS BLOCK BEFORE EVERY STEP. ===
P=fugaro-dev                    # hard-coded; the guard below refuses anything else
C=$HOME/.config/fugaro/projects/fugaro.yaml
set -u
[ "$P" = fugaro-dev ] || { echo "Check 82 stopped: this check runs on fugaro-dev only (never belong)" >&2; exit 1; }
command -v fugaro >/dev/null || { echo "Check 82 stopped: no fugaro on PATH" >&2; exit 1; }
fugaro doctor --project fugaro --all 2>/dev/null | grep -q '^project: .*(GCP fugaro-dev,' || {
  echo "Check 82 stopped: installation 'fugaro' is not the fugaro-dev installation on this machine" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -r "$C" ] || { echo "Check 82 stopped: no project config at $C (read the project line of 'fugaro doctor --project fugaro')" >&2; exit 1; }
DB=$(sed -n 's|^ *rtdb_url: *||p' "$C" | tr -d "\"'" | sed -e 's|^https://||' -e 's|/*$||' | head -1)
FP=$(sed -n 's|^ *firebase_project: *||p' "$C" | tr -d "\"'" | head -1)
[ -n "$DB" ] || { echo "Check 82 stopped: $C has no budget.rtdb_url" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -n "$FP" ] || { echo "Check 82 stopped: $C has no budget.firebase_project" >&2; exit 1; }
W=/tmp/chk82; mkdir -p "$W"
echo "Check 82 ready: P=$P firebase=$FP — the operator's token is read and never printed"
```

**What this binary deploys, before anything is run.** *(Guard block.)* The version and the generated document's size, both read-only, so step 3's act lines can be checked against a number rather than remembered:

```bash
fugaro version
fugaro update --firebase-project "$FP" --print-vars    # read-only: the variables it resolved, nothing written
wc -c < internal/budget/rules/testdata/rules.golden.json 2>/dev/null || true    # only if you are in a checkout of this release
```

1. **The before-state, read-only.** *(Guard block.)* What the database is now, so the deploy's effect is a difference and not an impression:

   ```bash
   AT=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)   # never printed, never pasted
   echo "marker:  $(curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" "https://$DB/config/limits/policyRules.json")"
   curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" "https://$DB/.settings/rules.json" > "$W/before.json"
   test -s "$W/before.json" || { echo "the read returned nothing: check \$DB and the token, do not read on"; exit 1; }
   echo "bytes:   $(wc -c < "$W/before.json")"
   echo "mailbox: $(grep -o '"mailbox"' "$W/before.json" | wc -l)"
   fugaro doctor --project fugaro | sed -n '/policy-rules-skew/,+3p'
   ```
   **FACT:** the marker's raw body (**`10`**, or `9`, or `8`, or `6`, or `5`, or `4`, or `3`, or `2`, or `1`, or `null` for an absent node), the deployed document's byte count and its `mailbox` count, and **doctor's `policy-rules-skew` line verbatim — or the record that doctor printed no such line at all**. Which line doctor prints is a function of the marker (`internal/cli/doctor.go`'s `doctorRulesSkew`), and for every marker but this release's own there are five states: an **absent or unreadable** marker prints **no line at all** (there is no generation to compare, so there is nothing to warn about — a `null` here is recorded as "no line", never as a sentence); a marker of **0** prints `rulesMarkerPrePolicyText(0)`, the sentence for rules that predate the policy nodes themselves; a marker of **1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 or 10** prints `rulesMarkerOlderText`, the sentence for rules that carry the policy nodes but predate this release's document; a marker **above 11** prints the "a newer Fugaro deployed them" warning; and a hand-edited non-integer prints "the deployed rules cannot be told apart". A marker of **11** is the sixth state, and the only one the marker does not decide: doctor then reads the deployed document and compares it with the one this binary generates (`infra.SameJSON`, formatting ignored) — **no line at all** when the two are the same document, `rulesSkewText` ("the deployed rules are older than the marker ...") when they differ, which is a hand edit of `/.settings/rules.json` in the console and not of the marker, and an **info** note, never a warning, when the document or this binary's own generated rules cannot be read. On an installation on generation 10 — the before-state of this release's deploy — the line is `rulesMarkerOlderText`'s sentence (`internal/cli/project_cmd.go`) for a marker of 10: *"the policy marker config/limits/policyRules records generation 10, below the generation 11 this Fugaro deploys: these rules carry the policy nodes, the mailbox, the device binding, the coordinator's read grant, the voice policy node, the registration kind's fields, the four day-counter leaves a run's stage report writes per model, the paired device's read of a run's outcome, the credential route a run reads, the phone's stop request and the launch envelope, so runs, a published policy, the mobile app and the coordinator are unaffected — what they predate is this release's own document, which adds the two shapes a phone of this release writes (mobile identity-pairing task J5r, O6 and O10): a message and the heartbeat carry `sig` — the base64url Ed25519 signature a device that holds a key signs with — in place of the `mac` tag, exactly one of the two, and an inbox action may be the typed launch, whose `mode` names the rigor mode to start in and which needs no `confirmation` where every other verb carries one; under these rules a device that signs has every message and every heartbeat refused at the database with no error, and a launch is refused at the verb enumeration, so the app can neither speak nor start anything until the deploy; re-run 'fugaro update' in your own terminal from a Fugaro that deploys generation 11 or newer, which writes that document and records its generation in the marker"*. On one on generation 6, two releases back, the line is the same function's sentence for a marker of 6: *"the policy marker config/limits/policyRules records generation 6, below the generation 11 this Fugaro deploys: these rules carry the policy nodes, the mailbox, the device binding, the coordinator's read grant, the voice policy node and the registration kind's fields, so runs, a published policy, the mobile app and the coordinator are unaffected — what they predate is this release's own document, which adds the four leaves a run's stage report writes per model (spend/$day/repos/$slug/byModel/$model/{notional,rep,tlo,thi}: the subscription part of the model's dollars, the cost the provider reported for the calls that carried one, and the table's charge over those same calls at the two ends of the tier that served them, spend-accuracy D2648 and D2650): a run under these rules that writes them is refused the whole stage report, because Realtime Database applies a multi-path update atomically, so it writes the leaves it knows and none of these until the deploy; re-run 'fugaro update' in your own terminal from a Fugaro that deploys generation 11 or newer, which writes that document and records its generation in the marker"*. On one on generation 5, the before-state of the previous release's deploy, the line is the same function's sentence for a marker of 5: *"the policy marker config/limits/policyRules records generation 5, below the generation 11 this Fugaro deploys: these rules carry the policy nodes, the mailbox, the device binding, the coordinator's read grant and the voice policy node, so runs, a published policy, the mobile app and the coordinator are unaffected — what they predate is this release's own document, which adds the fields a push registration carries (the `token`, `platform` and `prefs` fields of a mailbox message of the new `registration` kind, mobile plan task P5.2.2): the app writes one into its own inbox, and until this is deployed the database refuses that message with no error, so the phone is registered with nothing; re-run 'fugaro update' in your own terminal from a Fugaro that deploys generation 11 or newer, which writes that document and records its generation in the marker"*. On one on generation 4, two releases back, the line is the same function's sentence for a marker of 4: *"the policy marker config/limits/policyRules records generation 4, below the generation 11 this Fugaro deploys: these rules carry the policy nodes, the mailbox, the device binding and the coordinator's read grant, so runs, a published policy, the mobile app and the coordinator are unaffected — what they predate is this release's own document, which adds the voice policy node config/policy/voice/{shared,repos/$slug} (mobile plan task P5.3.1): a run token reads its own project's node there, and no client writes either node; re-run 'fugaro update' in your own terminal from a Fugaro that deploys generation 11 or newer, which writes that document and records its generation in the marker"*. On one still on generation 2 it is the same function's longer sentence, printed for a marker of 2: *"the policy marker config/limits/policyRules records generation 2, below the generation 11 this Fugaro deploys: these rules do carry the policy nodes of generation 1, so a published policy is read and enforced and publishing another is not refused — what they predate is this release's own document, which adds the mailbox subtree and the user-claim read grants the mobile app reads (mobile plan P2.1, design m9 §6.4), and binds that user claim to a device node (mobile plan P6.4, D166): a phone account with no config/admin/devices/<uid> node reads and writes nothing at all, so before you deploy, every account that is meant to reach the app needs one — nothing mints a device node yet ('fugaro pair' is plan task P6.6 and is not built), so today that means adding it by hand; re-run 'fugaro update' in your own terminal from a Fugaro that deploys generation 11 or newer, which writes that document and records its generation in the marker"* (the same sentence with `records generation 1` is what a marker of 1 prints). **On a marker of 1 or 2, read the device node in that sentence before you confirm step 3**: the deploy takes the warning away and leaves every unpaired account refused, which is exactly what it says. A `policy-rules-skew` line that is **neither** of the two above and not the "newer Fugaro" warning is one of two states, and step 1's marker tells them apart. With a **hand-edited marker** this Fugaro cannot read as a generation, record it verbatim and **stop**: the deploy would go over rules a newer Fugaro wrote, and `DB.Plan` refuses exactly that (step 7). With a **marker of 11** the line is `rulesSkewText`, and its remedy is this very step: the marker names this generation and the document underneath it is not the one this binary generates (a console hand-edit of `/.settings/rules.json`, which check 81's "What failing looks like" names), so record it verbatim and **confirm step 3**, which is what the sentence tells you to do.

2. **`--print-vars` and nothing else.** *(Guard block.)* The read-only pre-flight of the installation's order: it resolves and prints the variables — including the Firebase project id every write below will be made in — and writes nothing. **FACT:** the resolved Firebase project and the region — the output is one JSON object with two halves, `{"installation": {...}, "firebase": {...}}`, and the two values are at `installation.region` and `firebase.project` (the project id the local config calls `budget.firebase_project`; the key is not `firebase_project` in this document) — that the command exits 0, and that `$DB/config/limits/policyRules` and the deployed document are still what step 1 read (a read-only run changes nothing).

3. **⚠ CONFIRM — the deploy.** *(Guard block.)* **`fugaro update --firebase-project "$FP"`** in your own terminal, and read the plan **before** typing anything. The database step prints, in this order, only what it would write:

   ```
   rules: deploys the security rules (75318 bytes, generated)
   config/limits/policyRules: records the rules generation (config/limits/policyRules = 11)
   config/limits/credsRules: records the credentials rules generation (config/limits/credsRules = 1)
   config/limits/workspaceRules: records the workspace rules generation (config/limits/workspaceRules = 1)
   config/limits/orchestratorRules: records the orchestrator rules generation (config/limits/orchestratorRules = 2)
   ```
   (the act lines are `internal/infra/firebasedb.go`'s, printed in this order: `DB.Plan` appends the rules action (`Path: "rules"`), then plans the policy marker with its `d.put(projectpolicy.PathRulesMarker(), …)` call, then the credentials marker with `d.put(rules.PathCredsRulesMarker(), …)`, then the workspace marker with `d.put(rules.PathWorkspaceRulesMarker(), …)`, then the orchestrator marker with `d.put(rules.PathOrchestratorRulesMarker(), …)`, and `deployDatabase` prints the plan's actions in slice order, so the rules line comes **first**, the marker lines after it, and the **orchestrator** marker line **last**. The rules line appears only when `SameJSON` says the deployed document differs from the generated one; each marker line appears whenever its marker is absent or holds another generation. The workspace and orchestrator lines are the ones this release adds: `config/limits/workspaceRules` (the workspace family's own generation) and `config/limits/orchestratorRules` are absent on a database no `fugaro update` of this release has converged, and a run against one already converged plans no line for either, so record which lines printed rather than expecting all of them; the credentials line (`config/limits/credsRules`, check 92's own marker) prints in exactly those cases too, one line above the orchestrator's. The other lines — `writes the Fugaro mark (fugaro/mark)`, `writes the project's name (fugaro/project = fugaro), which every run token's fp claim must equal`, `seeds the mode: observe`, `seeds the largest lease (max reserve) at $5` — are planned before all of these, for the fields that are absent, so they print above them.) The confirmation sentence names what it does — `writes the database as listed, as you (project owner, editor or budget admin), and then the local config` — and **this check's step is an *ordinary* confirmation** (`askOrdinary`, `internal/cli/init.go`'s `ask`): the owner gives it by typing the name at their own real terminal, which is why the point is that you read the plan first; what no flag can do is confirm it for a **coding agent's session**, where `askOrdinary` raises `initflow.AgentError` before it prints anything. So: type the project's name. **On a project the managed marks answer for, this step still asks it, and the reason is the command:** `--firebase-project` is one of the flags that shape the installation, so this run is refused the gate before any mark is read (`shapesTheInstallation`; `gateRun` returns without a read) and every confirmation it gives is the one it always gave. The run that reaches this same deploy with nothing typed at the owner's terminal is a plain `fugaro update`, whose rules stage writes the same generation under the gate; **this check's own command is not that run**, so the name this step asks for is typed here, after the plan is read. **FACT:** every act line verbatim, in the order printed; the sentence you confirmed; the byte count in the rules line is `rules.Generate()`'s own **75318**, the size `internal/budget/rules/testdata/rules.golden.json` carries; it is **not** the read-back document's size, which the API may store with other formatting — `DB.Plan` compares the two as JSON through `SameJSON`, ignoring formatting, so only the generated bytes have this number; and that the **policy marker line names 11** — which is how this binary states its own `projectpolicy.RulesVersion`, and the value `internal/projectpolicy` exports — and that the **workspace marker line names 1** and the **orchestrator marker line, the last one, names 1**, which is how this binary states its own `rules.WorkspaceRulesVersion` and `rules.OrchestratorRulesVersion` (`internal/budget/rules`). **A rules line whose byte count is not the generated document's is a stop:** it means the plan is not this release's `Generate()` output, and nothing may be confirmed. **The orchestrator marker is the step's last write, and the rules deploy comes before every marker** (`DB.Plan` appends the rules action and then plans the four markers with `d.put(projectpolicy.PathRulesMarker(), …)`, `d.put(rules.PathCredsRulesMarker(), …)`, `d.put(rules.PathWorkspaceRulesMarker(), …)` and `d.put(rules.PathOrchestratorRulesMarker(), …)`, and `Apply` writes them in that order): that is what makes each marker's presence a statement about the document underneath it — and for `config/limits/policyRules`, the generation this check reads, the rules deploy is still the write **immediately before it**. A deploy that fails on the rules leaves the markers as they were — the policy marker **absent** on a first deploy, which is generation 0, the legacy path under which no policy is read and none can be published, or the **old generation** on an upgrade, which is what the document still deployed carries — rather than recording these generations over rules that never landed. Written the other way round, a failed deploy would have left exactly that claim behind: the state doctor reports as `rulesSkewText`, and the state check 81's steps are written to catch. An absent marker is not itself a refusal: what stops a run is a policy node that exists and cannot be read or decoded (`internal/runner/projectpolicy.go`'s `unreadablePolicy`), not a marker that is not there. A run that prints a **marker** line while no rules line appears above it is the other state: the document already matched, only the marker moved.

   ```

   ```

   (`internal/cli/init_firebase.go`). **FACT:** that line verbatim, that **no confirmation was asked** (no `⚠ CONFIRM`, no typed name, exit 0), and — if the line is *not* what appeared — the act lines that did appear instead, which are what a settled installation's second run would have to explain: a `config/limits/policyRules` line here means the marker write did not land in step 3, and the run that would write it is this one. `Identity Platform: already initialized, left as it is` is a normal line of the same step and is not the refusal: the "already has" sentence is printed only when nothing at all is pending, so a run that prints the Identity Platform line instead has a pending write to read.

5. **The marker reads back the generation, and the document is the generated one.** *(Guard block.)* Read both, read-only, with the operator's credentials (IAM bypasses the rules; `config/limits` is `TOKEN`-only read, so a user token could not read this node at all — check 81 step 6 records that denial):

   ```bash
   AT=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)   # never printed, never pasted
   curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" "https://$DB/config/limits/policyRules.json"; echo
   curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" "https://$DB/.settings/rules.json" > "$W/after.json"

   echo "mailbox: $(grep -o '"mailbox"' "$W/after.json" | wc -l)"
   echo "devices: $(grep -o 'config/admin/devices' "$W/after.json" | wc -l)"
   echo "pairing: $(grep -o '"pairing"' "$W/after.json" | wc -l)"
   cmp -s "$W/before.json" "$W/after.json" && echo "the document is unchanged" || echo "the document changed (step 3's deploy)"
   # The comparison DB.Plan itself makes (infra.SameJSON): the same JSON document,
   # formatting ignored — so this, and not the byte count, is what says the
   # deployed document is this release's. A checkout of this release holds the golden.
   python3 - "$W/after.json" internal/budget/rules/testdata/rules.golden.json <<'PY'
   import json, sys
   a, b = json.load(open(sys.argv[1])), json.load(open(sys.argv[2]))
   if a != b:
       sys.exit("the deployed document is not this release's generated one (JSON, formatting ignored)")
   print("the deployed document is the generated one (JSON-equal)")
   PY
   ```
   **FACT:** the marker's raw body — **`11`**, `internal/projectpolicy`'s `RulesVersion` for this release — the read-back document's byte count (**whatever the API stored**: no number is required of it, because `infra.SameJSON` compares the read-back with `rules.Generate()`'s output by unmarshalling and re-marshalling both, i.e. the same JSON document ignoring formatting); **75318 is the generator's own size**, the one `internal/budget/rules/testdata/rules.golden.json` holds, and the JSON comparison above is what ties the two together; its `mailbox` count (**1**: the mailbox subtree generation 2 adds, which check 81 step 8 requires), its `config/admin/devices` count (**17**: D166's device conjunct, expanded into every `USER`, the new `/orchestrator` node included — check 81 steps 3, 4 and 6 are what a missing one looks like live), its `pairing` count (**1**: D165's subtree, which generation 2 had not), whether the JSON comparison says the document is the generated one, and whether the document changed in step 3. The marker and the document have to agree: a marker of 7 over a document without `mailbox`, without the device allowlist or without `pairing` is the state this check exists to catch, and it is a **failure** — the runner would read the marker, believe the mailbox grant exists, and the app's writes would be refused (or, on a marker below this binary's, the app would be met with a document that has no mailbox at all), and the whole of check 81 would be reading a fence the app cannot see.

6. **The transition off the older generation, for the marker step 1 actually found.** *(Guard block.)* What happens here depends on step 1's marker, and the three cases are the three `doctorRulesSkew` can produce for a marker at or below this binary's generation:

   - **`1` or `2`** — a generation below the binary's, at or above the policy nodes: the before-state was `rulesMarkerOlderText`'s sentence (step 1 recorded it verbatim), and after the deploy the same command must say nothing about a skew:

   - **`null` (the marker was absent)** — **there was no line before, and there is none after**: `doctorRulesSkew` returns early with no line at all when the marker is absent (generation 0 is not a state to warn about — there is nothing to compare), so this step **cannot** observe a warning disappearing. Record exactly that: "the marker was absent; doctor printed no `policy-rules-skew` line before the deploy and none after, so the transition was not observed as a warning" — and check step 5's read-back instead, which is what says the deploy recorded the generation.

   ```bash
   fugaro doctor --project fugaro --all | grep -c policy-rules-skew   # 0
   fugaro doctor --strict --project fugaro >/dev/null; echo "doctor --strict exit: $?"
   ```
   **FACT:** the count (`0`) — a `grep -c` of 0 is the pass, and a line here is a deploy that did not land — and `doctor --strict`'s exit code; when it is not 0, the failing check ids, because a `policy-rules-skew` **warning** here is a deploy that did not land and any **other** warning is a separate finding (`token-signers`, a caps gap) that this check records and does not own. If step 1's marker was already **`11`**, this step is **not run**: record "the installation was already on generation 11; the transition was not observed" — an installation that has been on this release's generation since its deploy is the normal case, and pretending to have watched a transition that did not happen is worse than recording that it was not needed.

7. **The marker above this binary's generation is a refusal — read, not provoked.** *(Guard block, read-only.)* `DB.Plan` reads the marker **first** and refuses the whole plan when it is above this binary's `RulesVersion`, before anything is planned: *"the deployed security rules are generation %d (config/limits/policyRules = %d) and this Fugaro's are generation %d: the rules this database runs under came from a newer Fugaro, and 'fugaro update --firebase-project' would deploy this binary's older rules over them and record generation %d in the marker. Upgrade Fugaro first ('brew upgrade dimipaun/tap/fugaro'), then run 'fugaro update --firebase-project' again with the newer binary; 'fugaro doctor' reports this as policy-rules-skew"* (`internal/infra/firebasedb.go`). **This check does not test that live, on purpose**: provoking it means hand-writing a marker above this binary's generation, and while that value stands the runs under it still read and enforce the policy published there — a marker at or above this Fugaro's generation reads as deployed (`internal/projectpolicy`'s `RulesGeneration`) — while `fugaro update --firebase-project` refuses to deploy this binary's document over the newer one and doctor reports the skew; a hand-edited marker the CLI has no reason to write, on the installation that runs the dogfood. The boundary is covered offline, where it can be driven without a window: `internal/infra`'s `TestDBRefusesToDeployOverNewerRules` is the plan test for the refusal (`DB.Plan` returns it before `d.acts` is cleared, so the refused plan writes nothing and the newer installation's rules and marker are left as they are), and `internal/cli`'s `TestDoctorPolicyChecks` covers the reporting — its `policy-rules-skew` cases include the marker above this binary's generation ("rules newer than this Fugaro"). **FACT:** the sentence above, quoted from the source, and the two test names — and record explicitly that **check 82 did not write a marker by hand**. A live proof of the refusal belongs to a scratch project with no runs in it, not to `fugaro-dev`.

**Passes when:** step 3's act lines hold the marker line naming **11** and (when the document differed) the rules line naming the generated document's byte count, and the confirmation was typed; step 4's second run prints `The database already has the rules, mark, project name and mode.` and asks for no confirmation; step 5's read-back marker is `11` and its document is `infra.SameJSON`-equal to `rules.Generate()`'s output (its byte count is the API's to choose) with `mailbox`, the device allowlist and `pairing` present; step 6's doctor prints no `policy-rules-skew` line after the deploy (or the step is recorded as not run because the installation was already on generation 11, or as not observed because the marker was absent); and step 7 records the refusal's sentence and the offline tests without provoking it.

**Fails when:** the marker line does not name 11 (an older CLI deployed an older document — the fix is `brew upgrade dimipaun/tap/fugaro` and this check again, never a hand-edit); the rules line's byte count is not the generated document's; the second run plans a write (the first run's marker write did not land); the read-back marker is not `11`, or is `11` over a document with no `mailbox`, no device allowlist or no `pairing` (the two disagree, and it is the state that makes every one of check 81's refusals meaningless); or `doctor` still reports `policy-rules-skew` as a warning after the deploy. **What failing looks like:** a rules deploy refused for size or syntax (the RTDB rules endpoint has a size limit — the generated document is 75318 bytes and well inside it, and a refusal is worth recording verbatim); a project where Identity Platform is not initialized, which fails the database step **after** the rules and the marker are deployed (`deployDatabase` runs `db.Apply` — the rules' `PutRules`, the marker and the other database writes — and only then `idp.initialize`, `internal/cli/init_firebase.go`; `internal/cli`'s `TestIdentityPlatformInitializedWhenMissing` is the case: the run succeeds with Identity Platform missing and the mark written), so a failure there leaves generation 11 live and the owner looking for a rules problem that is not there — **and, since generation 3, an installation whose accounts have no device node**: the deploy lands, the warning disappears, and every app read is refused until `config/admin/devices/<uid>` exists for each account (`internal/projectpolicy`'s `RulesVersion` comment; check 81 step 1 writes them by hand because `fugaro pair` is P6.6 and is not built); a CLI older than the release whose document is being deployed, which quietly writes the older generation. **The order is the operator's CLI, then this deploy, then the runner images and any repository image**: a runner built from the new CLI asks the backend for leases the old rules refuse, and the gateway reads a refused write with no cap reason as the backend being unavailable, so the run waits and then halts on the grace period.

**Paste back:** the `fugaro version` and `--print-vars` output (the project and region only — no token); the marker's raw body before and after; the deployed document's byte count and `mailbox` count before and after; **every act line of step 3 verbatim and the confirmation sentence**; step 4's "already has" line verbatim; `doctor`'s `policy-rules-skew` line before and after (or the note that the installation was already on generation 11, or that the marker was absent and doctor printed no line either time); step 7's refusal sentence and the note that nothing was hand-written. **Never paste an access token, a refresh token or the web API key.** Until this check runs, the deployed document's generation is **UNVERIFIED** on a live installation and the row above stays **NOT RUN**.

**Restore.** Nothing: this check's whole point is the write it makes, and there is nothing to undo. The rules and the marker it deployed **stay** — that is the state every later check reads. Two cases that are not a rollback:

- **A step failed before the deploy.** The installation is exactly as step 1 found it, because the database step writes nothing until it is confirmed and stops at its first failed write, leaving no marker (`DB.Plan` orders the marker after the deploy; `Apply` stops there). Re-run the check from step 1.
- **The deploy has to be undone.** Rolling back is the same command from a checkout of the older release (rolling back is the same command from a checkout of the older version), run by you, in your terminal, against this installation — and record it as a **generation downgrade**, because the marker goes back with it and the app's mailbox grant goes away. Never `terraform destroy` the Firebase root for it.

## Check 83: one id, delivered twice, is acted on once — a re-read, a restart, the phone's own re-delivery, and a re-send that is a second message (installation `fugaro`, never `belong`, with your own phone and the consumer in your own terminal; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Task **P4.2** of [mobile/implementation-plan.md](mobile/implementation-plan.md) writes this check, and running it is the owner's; its row is the sentence this check measures — *"Replay and duplicate delivery: the same message delivered
twice is acted on once"* — and the row's own reason it is a check and not a test: it needs a **real network that can actually duplicate**. Every piece of the rule is tested already: `shared/mailbox-sim/`'s wire duplicates, reorders, drops and delays
a delivery over the three merged pure modules with no runtime and no clock, and `internal/mailbox`'s `TestLedgerDuplicateIsNotActedOnTwice` and `TestRestartDoesNotRePerform` prove the ledger over fakes. **What no test can supply is a real
duplicate**: a phone that re-delivers what it already sent, a database that hands the same node back twice, and a process killed between two passes. That is this check.

**The guard stops today, and the reason is the phone.** The host half is built — `internal/cli/mailbox.go` is the `fugaro mailbox` command and is registered in `internal/cli/root.go`, and `internal/cli/pair.go` is `fugaro pair` — but the app cannot
speak: `mobile/index.js` builds **no** mailbox client (it hands the voice session a stand-in whose `send`, `poll` and `licenceRefusal` answer `mailbox-not-wired`, and passes the first screen's pairing seam as `pairingScreen: null`), and
`mobile/package.json` names **no Realtime Database SDK**, so nothing the app builds can sign in or write to `mailbox/<uid>/inbox`. `createMailboxClient` is exported from `mobile/src/mailbox/client.js` and called by no shipped file. **No agent runs
any step of it**, and none performs any step below.

**What a duplicate actually is here, and what it is not.** The mailbox subtree the rules generate (`internal/budget/rules/rules.json.tmpl`) is **write-once**: `mailbox/$mb/inbox/$msg` carries `.write` = `MAILBOX && newData.exists() &&
!data.exists()`, so a **second write to the same `$msg`** is refused by the **database** and is not a delivery the consumer ever sees — it is a denied write (check 81's step 2 records exactly that 401). A duplicate is therefore the **same node
delivered or read twice**, and this check records three shapes of it: a **second pass** over an unchanged inbox node (the consumer deletes nothing in the store — M2's rule that the consumer's ack is its outbox reply plus the ledger, not an inbox
write — so the node is still there to be read again); the consumer **restarted**, a new process being a new holder (`newMailboxBootID`'s fresh `boot-<hex>`) with the **same** ledger on disk; and the **phone's own re-delivery** after a reconnect
(`mobile/src/mailbox/client.js` re-delivers an unacked message with the same record, id and `at` included). What a duplicate is **not**: a **re-send with a new id**. The ledger's key is the pair `(sender, id)` (`mailbox.Perform` → `deliver`'s lookup
by `msg.Sender` and `msg.ID`), so a fresh id is a **second message**, accepted and acted on — step 6 records that difference, because "acted once" must not be read as "acted never".

**The fence, and what a crash leaves behind.** `mailbox.Perform` is the whole ordering in one call: the delivery is decided in memory, the record is written, the ledger is **committed** (a temp file in the destination directory, `0o600`, renamed over
the ledger), and **only then** — and only for `OutcomeActed` — is the callback run that performs the action. A process killed **between the commit and the action** therefore leaves `"status":"acted"` on disk and re-performs **nothing** when it comes
back (`TestRestartDoesNotRePerform` pins that exact state); a process killed **before** the commit has performed nothing at all, and the in-memory ledger is rolled back to what is on disk. Nothing is written for a duplicate — a redelivery must not
re-arm a record and must not rewrite the file — which is the second reading this check takes: the ledger bytes are unchanged by a pass that answered `duplicate`.

**The lease, and where a duplicate is refused first.** `mailbox.Take` takes the lease on `mailbox/<uid>/heartbeat` by the **ETag compare-and-swap** of `internal/rtdb` (`GetETag` / `PutIfMatch`, a 412 answering `ErrPrecondition`), and `mailbox.Renew`
renews it under the same swap — on this path the rules bind nothing (the heartbeat's `.write` is only `CONSUMER && newData.exists()`), and the ETag **is** the fence (M1). Past `mailbox.ActionBound` — `ClaimTTL` (ten minutes) less `MaxClockSkew` (five
minutes) — the holder re-reads the lease before it acts and stops acting when the heartbeat no longer names its own fresh claim. A second consumer's take is refused at the **store**, before any delivery reaches the ledger: the first of the three
fences that make acting at most once (the ledger, the lease, then the run's own claim).

**What the pass reports, and one bound on this check.** A `--json` pass prints one document per pairing carrying `pass` (`read`, `delivered`, `duplicates`, `refused`), the `acted` array and the `refused` array: a duplicate is refused with the
module's own code **`duplicate`** (`mailboxCodeDuplicate`) and counted in `pass.duplicates`, and a record the strict reader cannot decode is `unreadable-record` (`mailbox.CodeUnreadableRecord`, the reader's own code — the reader is `mailbox.ReadInbox`'s, and both consumers of one mailbox read through it). The correct exit code for a pass whose only reading was a
duplicate is **0**, not 1: `mailboxExit` answers 1 only when the pass read at least one message, performed nothing, refused **every** message it read, and at least one of those refusals was an **action** refusal; exit 2 is a database that could not
be reached or written. **The bound**: nothing here drives a record to eviction, because `mailbox.Ledger.Ack` — the step that makes a record `acked`, the only status that may be evicted — has **no caller** in `fugaro mailbox` today, and no phone
`acked` is read either, so every re-read here is a `duplicate` and the watermark's `replay` refusal is not reachable from this check.

**Guard block — re-run this before every step.** It stops unless the checkout carries the ledger, the consumer, the pairing command and the phone's client, and — the reason it **stops today** — unless the app can actually speak: it has no database
SDK and its entry builds no mailbox client, so there is no phone to send a message for this check to duplicate. **No credential is read or printed on any path of it**, and nothing in it waits on stdin.

```bash
# === Check 83: setup + guard. RE-RUN THIS BLOCK BEFORE EVERY STEP. ===
set -u
ROOT=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null) || { echo "Check 83 stopped: not inside a git checkout; the ledger this check reads and the consumer it drives are built from this repository" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/internal/mailbox/ledger.go" ] || { echo "Check 83 stopped: there is no internal/mailbox/ledger.go in this checkout, so there is no dedupe ledger for a duplicate to be a duplicate in (T4; ruling M7)" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/internal/cli/mailbox.go" ] || { echo "Check 83 stopped: there is no internal/cli/mailbox.go in this checkout, so the consumer this check drives (the fugaro mailbox command, P4.1) is not built" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/internal/cli/pair.go" ] || { echo "Check 83 stopped: there is no internal/cli/pair.go in this checkout, so a phone cannot be paired and has no key to sign a message with (P6.6)" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/mobile/src/mailbox/client.js" ] || { echo "Check 83 stopped: there is no mobile/src/mailbox/client.js in this checkout, so the phone side that re-delivers an unacked message after a reconnect does not exist (P3.6)" >&2; exit 1; }
grep -q '@react-native-firebase/database' "$ROOT/mobile/package.json" || { echo "Check 83 stopped: mobile/package.json names no Realtime Database SDK, so no build of the app can reach mailbox/<uid>/inbox and there is no delivery for this check to duplicate" >&2; exit 1; }
grep -q 'createMailboxClient' "$ROOT/mobile/index.js" || { echo "Check 83 stopped: the app's entry builds no mailbox client -- mobile/index.js hands the voice session a stand-in whose send, poll and licenceRefusal answer mailbox-not-wired, and passes the first screen's pairing seam as pairingScreen: null, so there is no phone that can speak the message this check duplicates" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "Check 83 ready: one id delivered twice is acted on once — ran by you, never belong; no message text, key or token is pasted"
```

1. **The pairing, and the one message.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* Pair the phone (`fugaro pair`; the session itself is check 100's territory) and, from the phone, send **one** non-destructive message; then run one pass, `fugaro mailbox --once
   --json`. **FACT:** the message's `id`, its `sender` (the phone's Firebase Auth uid) and its `at`, read with your own credentials from `mailbox/<uid>/inbox` — a key and a time, **never the text** — and the pass's `read`, `delivered`, `duplicates`
   (0) and `refused` with its one entry in `acted`. **FACT:** the ledger file `$XDG_STATE_HOME/fugaro/mailbox/<project>/ledger.json` holds exactly one record for the pair, on disk as `"status":"acted"` **before** the offer it produced — the fence
   itself, step 2's precondition.

2. **The re-read: a second pass, no phone, no restart.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* Run `fugaro mailbox --once --json` again, with the phone doing nothing. **FACT:** the second pass reads the **same** node again (the consumer writes no store-side
   ack and deletes nothing), its `pass.duplicates` is **1**, its `refused` array carries the module's own **`duplicate`** code against that id, and its `acted` array is **empty** — no second offer reaches the orchestrator and no second reply is
   signed into `mailbox/<uid>/outbox`. **FACT:** the exit code is **0** (a duplicates-only pass is not M12's exit 1), and the ledger bytes are **unchanged** — a duplicate writes nothing, and its `now` floor is the only thing that moves.

3. **The store's own write-once, which is the other fence.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* Write the same `inbox/<id>` a second time — over IAM, or from the phone — with the record it already holds. **FACT:** the answer is a **denial** (401) over
   `!data.exists()`, not a delivery the consumer decided: the database's write-once rule and the ledger's dedupe are two different fences, recorded together so a denied write is never read as the ledger working (check 81's step 2 is the rules' half).
   **FACT:** the inbox node is unchanged and holds exactly the one record.

4. **The restart: a new holder, the same ledger.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* Stop the consumer and start a **new** `fugaro mailbox --once --json` process — a fresh `boot-<hex>` holder, the lease re-taken under a **new** claim — over the same
   unchanged inbox. **FACT:** the pass still answers `duplicate` for that id and acts on nothing, `TestRestartDoesNotRePerform`'s live counterpart, and the reason the ledger is on disk (tmp+rename, `0o600`) rather than in memory. **FACT:** the ledger
   file's one record for the pair is unchanged by the restarting pass.

5. **The phone's own re-delivery — the duplicate this check exists for.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* With the consumer stopped, speak a message from the phone and let your consumer act on it, but leave it **unacked** — stop the consumer before its
   reply would be spoken, or keep the phone offline so its `poll` never acks — then reconnect so `mobile/src/mailbox/client.js` **flushes the same record** (same `id`, same `at`) the store already holds. **FACT:** the re-delivered record is answered
   **`duplicate`** and acted on **once** — one offer, one reply in the outbox, one `acted` entry, one more count in `pass.duplicates` — and the phone's outbox shows **one** answer, not two: a real network handed the consumer the same node twice.

6. **The re-send with a new id is a second message, not a duplicate.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* From the phone, say the **same words** again — a **fresh id**. **FACT:** the second message is accepted and **acted on** (its own `acted` entry and
   its own reply), and the ledger holds **two** records, one per id: the key is the pair `(sender, id)`, so a new id is not a replay. **FACT:** the ledger's `id-conflict` refusal is the neighbour to record here — the **same** pair with a
   **different** `at` or kind is refused with `id-conflict` (`TestLedgerIDConflictIsRefused`), and neither the conflict nor the new id is a duplicate.

7. **The lease, and a lease taken by a second consumer.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* Start a **second** `fugaro mailbox --once --json` in another terminal while the first's claim is fresh. **FACT:** the second consumer's take is refused at the
   **store** — the ETag compare-and-swap, `internal/rtdb`'s `PutIfMatch` answering 412, `ErrPrecondition` — and it reads no inbox and acts on nothing; a re-read after `mailbox.ActionBound` is what lets the holder stop when the heartbeat no longer
   names its own claim. **FACT:** the ledger holds the same single record for the pair afterwards, so a delivery in another consumer's window is refused **before** the ledger and two consumers cannot each act on it.

8. **The fail-closed half: losing the dedupe memory is not a fresh start.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* With the consumer stopped, make the ledger unreadable — truncate it, or write a value that is not a ledger — and run `fugaro mailbox --once
   --json`. **FACT:** the command **refuses at startup** (exit 1) naming the ledger file and runs no pass: `OpenLedger` refuses a ledger it cannot read rather than starting from an empty one, which is the whole difference between a lost dedupe memory
   and a re-performed action. Restore the ledger before the next step.

**Passes when:** every delivery of **one id** is acted on once — the re-read of step 2, the restart of step 4 and the phone's own re-delivery of step 5 each answer the module's own `duplicate` with **no** second offer, reply or `acted` entry; the
ledger holds exactly one `acted` record for the pair and its bytes are unchanged by a duplicate; the pass that saw only the duplicate exits **0**; the store's write-once rule is recorded beside the ledger's dedupe as the **other** fence; a re-send
with a **new id** is acted on as a second message, so the record shows the difference between "the same message twice" and "two messages"; and an unreadable ledger stops the command rather than acting on a delivery it could not record.

**Fails when:** the same id is acted on **twice** — two offers, two replies, or two `acted` entries across any two passes; a **denied second write** to `inbox/<id>` is read as the ledger working (it is `!data.exists()`, a database refusal, and proves
nothing about the consumer); a restart re-performs an action the record holds as `acted`; the check never reads the ledger file on disk, so an in-memory answer passes for the on-disk rule; a duplicates-only pass is recorded as a failure because its
exit code is not 1; or the **same sentence spoken twice from the phone** is counted as a duplicate (it is two ids, and two messages).

**Paste back:** the message's `id`, its `sender` uid and its `at` (a key and a time, never its text); each pass's `read`/`delivered`/`duplicates`/`refused` counts, its `acted` array and its exit code; the ledger's one `seen` record for the pair
(status, `at`, kind) with its `now` and `evictedThrough`, and the fact that a duplicate left it unchanged; the store's answer to the second write of the same id (the 401 by `!data.exists()`); the second consumer's lease verdict (the 412 refusal) and
the re-read at `mailbox.ActionBound`; the startup refusal for the unreadable ledger; and the phone's outbox message count after step 5. **No credential is printed or pasted** — no pairing MAC key, no keychain item value, no custom token, no ID token
— and the message's **text** never appears, because the ledger records an id and no text (`TestLedgerFileHoldsNoText`).

**Restore.** Nothing to undo in the project that the check could not undo itself: it writes no seeded store node (the message is the phone's own, the reply the consumer's own), mints no token and changes no setting. Delete the consumer's own state —
`$XDG_STATE_HOME/fugaro/mailbox/<project>/`, the ledger and the pending file — so the next check starts from an empty dedupe memory; remove the phone's own inbox and outbox messages you no longer want (they are yours, and no client may delete them
for you); and `fugaro pair revoke --uid <uid>` if you paired a device for this check alone.

## Check 84: presence — the heartbeat's staleness, the offline state, and a clock skew shown as "clock differs" (installation `fugaro`, never `belong`, with your own paired phone, the consumer in your own terminal, and a database you read the heartbeat from yourself; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Task **P4.2** of [mobile/implementation-plan.md](mobile/implementation-plan.md) writes this check, and running it is the owner's. Its row is the sentence it measures — *"Presence: the heartbeat's staleness, the offline state, and a clock skew shown as 'clock differs'"* — and the row's own reason it is a check and not a test: it **needs a real clock and a real database**.

**The rule, and why the pure half is not this check.** The rule is **P1.4**'s (`shared/presence/index.js`), decided by **D117**. It is a **pure function** of three values — a heartbeat, the current time and the interval — so every branch it can take is already tested with an **injected** `now` (`shared/presence/index.test.js`: *"a heartbeat younger than N intervals is live"*, *"a heartbeat exactly at the band is stale, not live: the band is inclusive"*, *"a heartbeat exactly at the offline band is offline"*, *"a heartbeat in the future beyond the bound is clock differs, NOT offline"*, *"a heartbeat in the future within the tolerance bound is live, not clock differs"*, *"a missing heartbeat is offline and never live"*). **What no test supplies is the two things the row names**: a **real clock** that can be wrong, and a **real database** whose server timestamp is the authority.

**Why a real clock, and a real database.** D117's whole point is that *"the server's timestamp is the authority, never the phone's clock"* — a phone whose clock runs ahead computes a **negative age** for a perfectly healthy heartbeat, and both naive readings of that number are wrong (report `live` for a clock that is wrong, or `offline` for an orchestrator that is fine). Only a phone you can nudge against a database you can read proves the reading the app actually shows. The module states its own **honest limit** in the same breath: a skew in the **past** — a phone behind the server — is **not detectable from one heartbeat**, and no function of one heartbeat can tell a dead orchestrator from a slow clock, so the caller must hand it a **server-anchored `now`** (Firebase's `.info/serverTimeOffset`) and the consumer writes `at` from the server (RTDB's `{".sv": "timestamp"}`). **No test can verify that the caller did.**

**The four states, in the rule's own words** (`shared/presence/README.md`'s rule table, the source of every line below):

- **`live`** — the heartbeat is younger than N intervals (N = 3): the orchestrator is writing on schedule.
- **`stale`** — at or past N intervals, short of the offline band: it may be busy or hung, said without calling it dead.
- **`offline`** — at or past the offline band (12 intervals): minutes of silence, not one dropped write.
- **`clock-differs`** — the timestamp is in the future beyond the tolerance (one interval): the phone's clock, not the orchestrator, is what is wrong.
- **Absent (`null`)** — `offline`, because *"we have heard nothing" must not render as "everything is fine"* — and it is **never** `live`.

**The two future-tolerance bounds, and why they must not be confused.** Presence's `DEFAULT_FUTURE_TOLERANCE_MS` is **one interval** and is the bound this check's `clock-differs` is measured against (jitter and network latency are not a clock problem). `shared/mailbox`'s `DEFAULT_FUTURE_TOLERANCE_MS` is **`MAX_CLOCK_SKEW`** — **five minutes**, `shared/lease/index.js`'s constant — and it produces a **`future-timestamp` refusal** on a message, a different reading of a different thing. A check that reported one bound's number for the other would mis-state the state a skewed phone sees.

**The measurement this check is, beside the states.** **U2** of the always-on-orchestrator design is answered here, not there: *"The heartbeat's write volume at the chosen cadence is negligible against RTDB cost — D117 asks for the measurement and it has not been made — Check 84 (presence, the interval and the clock skew)"*, and §4.10 lists *"the heartbeat writes whose volume D117 asks to measure (check 84's interval)"* among the idle costs. Q4 is already answered — the tick is the heartbeat's **only** writer, one write per tick, at **whatever cadence check 84's measurement supports** — so step 6's number is what fixes the interval the module still calls **provisional**.

**The guard stops today, and the reason is the phone, not the rule.** Every module is in the tree: the rule (`shared/presence/index.js`), the consumer (`internal/cli/mailbox.go`, the `fugaro mailbox` command registered in `internal/cli/root.go`), the pairing command (`internal/cli/pair.go`), the app's mailbox client (`mobile/src/mailbox/client.js`, whose `poll` computes presence through `evaluatePresence`) and the row that would show it (`mobile/src/jobs/heartbeat.js`'s `heartbeatRow`). **But no phone can sign in and no screen carries the verdict**: `mobile/index.js` passes the first screen's pairing seam as **`pairingScreen: null`** and hands the voice session a stand-in whose `send`, `poll` and `licenceRefusal` answer **`mailbox-not-wired`**, and `mobile/package.json` names **no Realtime Database SDK** (`@react-native-firebase/app`, `analytics` and `crashlytics` are there and `database` is not), so nothing the app builds can reach `/mailbox/<uid>/heartbeat`. **No agent runs any step of it**, and none performs any step below.

**What this check does not cover.** It is not the feed's liveness (`mobile/src/feed/view.js`'s own `live`/`stale`/`offline` states, which are a document's freshness and a **different** vocabulary — the view floors a negative age at zero and leaves "clock differs" to this check). It is not a message's `future-timestamp` refusal (that is `shared/mailbox`'s five-minute bound, step 6's neighbour and not its subject). It is not check 80's end-to-end mailbox, check 83's duplicate delivery, or check 100's pairing session — it pairs a phone only to have a heartbeat to age, and it writes no message.

**Scale, and what it costs.** One phone, one paired account, one consumer and one measured window: nothing here launches a run, so nothing here is billable beyond the heartbeat writes **U2** measures — which are the whole reason step 6 exists. The installation this check runs against is `fugaro`, and `belong` is named nowhere except to forbid it.

**Guard block — re-run this before every step.** It stops unless the checkout carries the rule, the consumer, the pairing command, the app's mailbox client and the presence row — and — the reason it **stops today** — unless the app is **wired**: it builds no mailbox client and names no database SDK, so there is no phone to sign in and no screen on which "clock differs" could appear. **No credential is read or printed on any path of it**, and nothing in it waits on stdin.

```bash
# === Check 84: setup + guard. RE-RUN THIS BLOCK BEFORE EVERY STEP. ===
set -u
ROOT=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null) || { echo "Check 84 stopped: not inside a git checkout; the presence rule this check exercises and the consumer it drives are built from this repository" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/shared/presence/index.js" ] || { echo "Check 84 stopped: there is no shared/presence/index.js in this checkout, so the rule whose four states this check reads (P1.4, D117) is not on this tree" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/internal/cli/mailbox.go" ] || { echo "Check 84 stopped: there is no internal/cli/mailbox.go in this checkout, so the consumer that writes the heartbeat this check ages (the fugaro mailbox command, P4.1) is not built" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/internal/cli/pair.go" ] || { echo "Check 84 stopped: there is no internal/cli/pair.go in this checkout, so a phone cannot be paired and there is no account whose heartbeat could be read (P6.6)" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/mobile/src/mailbox/client.js" ] || { echo "Check 84 stopped: there is no mobile/src/mailbox/client.js in this checkout, so the phone side that computes presence through evaluatePresence does not exist (P3.6)" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/mobile/src/jobs/heartbeat.js" ] || { echo "Check 84 stopped: there is no mobile/src/jobs/heartbeat.js in this checkout, so the row that would render a presence verdict, clock-differs among them, is not on this tree (P3.3)" >&2; exit 1; }
grep -q '@react-native-firebase/database' "$ROOT/mobile/package.json" || { echo "Check 84 stopped: mobile/package.json names no Realtime Database SDK, so no build of the app can reach /mailbox/<uid>/heartbeat and there is no phone to show a presence state" >&2; exit 1; }
grep -q 'pairingScreen: null' "$ROOT/mobile/index.js" && { echo "Check 84 stopped: mobile/index.js still passes the first screen's pairing seam as pairingScreen: null, so no phone can sign in and no account's heartbeat can be read on the app" >&2; exit 1; }
grep -q 'mailbox-not-wired' "$ROOT/mobile/index.js" && { echo "Check 84 stopped: mobile/index.js hands the voice session a stand-in whose send, poll and licenceRefusal answer mailbox-not-wired, so the app shows no presence verdict and never the offline refusal" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "Check 84 ready: the four states read on a real phone against a real database, beside U2's write-volume measurement — ran by you, never belong; no heartbeat mac, key or token is pasted"
```

**What you need to have, before step 1.** A phone on which the app is installed (check 89's build), paired by `fugaro pair` (the session itself is check 100's territory), a terminal running `fugaro mailbox` beside the orchestrator, and — for the clock steps — the phone's own Settings, where its automatic time can be turned off and its clock moved. Nothing else: this check creates no cloud resource, launches no run and seeds no node.

1. **The live baseline: a heartbeat written and read as `live`.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* Pair the phone, start `fugaro mailbox` (without `--once`) in your terminal so the consumer takes the lease on `mailbox/<uid>/heartbeat` and renews it every pass (`internal/mailbox/lease.go`'s `Take` and `Renew`, called from `internal/cli/mailbox.go`), and read the node with your own credentials. **FACT:** the heartbeat node is `{at, boot, mac, agents?}` (`internal/budget/rules/rules.json.tmpl`, the `heartbeat` child: `hasChildren(['at', 'boot', 'mac'])`, written under `.write` = `CONSUMER && newData.exists()`) — `at` stamped from the server, `boot` the holder (`newMailboxBootID`'s `boot-<hex>`), `mac` **present** and recorded as present, never as bytes. **FACT:** the phone's state is **`live`** — `mobile/src/mailbox/client.js`'s poll computes it through `evaluatePresence({heartbeat: toPresenceHeartbeat(...), now, intervalMs})` and `mobile/src/jobs/heartbeat.js`'s `heartbeatRow` renders it — with the interval the app handed the rule (`heartbeatIntervalMs`) at `DEFAULT_INTERVAL_MS` (60 000) until step 6 moves it.

2. **Staleness: `live` → `stale` → `offline`, at the bands.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* Stop the consumer and read the phone as the heartbeat ages, with `intervalMs = 60_000`. **FACT:** younger than **3** intervals (`DEFAULT_MISSED_INTERVALS`) is **`live`** (`REASON.FRESH`); at **3** intervals it is **`stale`** (`REASON.MISSED_INTERVALS`, the band **inclusive**); at **12** (`DEFAULT_OFFLINE_INTERVALS`) it is **`offline`** (`REASON.LONG_SILENCE`) — the offline band being four times the stale band, so "minutes of silence" is not "one dropped write". **FACT:** the boundary recorded either side of it, one millisecond short of each band still the younger state, which is the pair `shared/presence/index.test.js` pins (*"one millisecond short of the band is still live"*, *"one millisecond short of the offline band is stale, not offline"*).

3. **The offline state, and the missing heartbeat.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* Read the phone for an account that has **never** had a heartbeat written — a fresh pairing, or a heartbeat node you delete over IAM. **FACT:** the state is **`offline`** with `REASON.NO_HEARTBEAT` and `ageMs: null` — `shared/presence/index.js` answers `state: STATE.OFFLINE` for `heartbeat === null`, and it is **never `live`**. **FACT:** the app's own **offline refusal** — the voice screen shows P1.4's `offline` and **refuses to accept a message** while it holds, `SCREEN_CODES.OFFLINE` in `mobile/src/voice/screen.js`, the spec's *"rather than accepting messages into the void"* (§6) — so the record is the app's refusal, not only its label.

4. **The clock skew, shown as "clock differs".** *(Guard block, run by you.)* Leave the consumer running and move the phone's clock **ahead** of the server — first within the tolerance, then beyond it. **FACT:** a skew within the tolerance (**one interval**, `DEFAULT_FUTURE_TOLERANCE_MS`) is still **`live`** — jitter and latency are not a clock problem — and a skew **beyond** it is **`clock-differs`** (`STATE.CLOCK_DIFFERS`, `REASON.FUTURE_SKEW`), the state the future branch returns **first**, so the verdict is **not `offline`** (an age that "makes no sense" is not silence) and **not `live`** (a negative age is not fresh). **FACT:** the phone's **feed** does not double as a clock verdict — `mobile/src/feed/view.js` floors a negative age at zero and its comment names *"check 84 (P4.2) owns 'clock differs'"* — so the two readings are recorded apart.

5. **The server's timestamp is the authority.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* Put the phone's clock **behind** the server and read the state. **FACT:** a heartbeat that merely *looks* old because the phone lags is **not** derivable from one heartbeat — the module's own limit — so the record is whether the app handed the rule a **server-anchored `now`** (`.info/serverTimeOffset`) rather than `Date.now()`, and that the `at` the consumer wrote came from the server (`{".sv": "timestamp"}`) and not the consumer's clock. **FACT:** the reading a lagging phone shows, recorded as the limit rather than asserted as a pass, with the app's divergence from the server named.

6. **The write volume at the cadence — U2's measurement.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* Timed, count the heartbeat writes the consumer makes at the cadence you chose — one write per pass to `/mailbox/<uid>/heartbeat` (`mailbox.Renew`) — and read the RTDB bill they imply. **FACT:** the number of heartbeat writes in the measured window and the cadence it supports, against `DEFAULT_INTERVAL_MS` (60 000 ms) and `MIN_INTERVAL_MS` (30 000, D117's floor). **FACT:** U2's answer for that installation — negligible against RTDB cost or not — recorded as the number that either **confirms** `DEFAULT_INTERVAL_MS` or **moves** it: the module's comment and the plan's **C4** both hold the interval provisional until exactly this measurement is made.

**Passes when:** steps 1–5 read the four states on a **real phone** against a **real database** — `live` at the baseline; `stale` at 3 intervals and `offline` at 12, both **inclusive**, with the one-millisecond-short boundary recorded; `offline`/`no-heartbeat` for a missing node, never `live`, with the app's **offline refusal** beside it; and `clock-differs` — **never `offline`, never `live`** — for a forward skew beyond one interval while a skew within it stays `live`; and step 6 gives **U2** a measured heartbeat write volume at the chosen cadence, so the interval is either confirmed at 60 s or moved.

**Fails when:** a forward skew is shown as `offline` or as `live`, or a missing heartbeat as `live`; a heartbeat exactly at 3 intervals reads as `live` or one exactly at 12 as `stale` (the bands are inclusive); the state is read from the phone's own clock rather than a server-anchored `now`, so a lagging phone reads a healthy orchestrator as dead; the app's offline state is a label with no refusal behind it, so a message is accepted into the void; or step 6 reports no number and the interval is left provisional **without** a measurement — and, above all, the check is never recorded as run while `mobile/index.js` still passes `pairingScreen: null` and hands the session a `mailbox-not-wired` stand-in, which is today's state and the guard's stop.

**Paste back:** the four states with the **age**, the **interval** and the **band** that produced each; the heartbeat node's `at`, its `boot` and the **presence** of `mac` (never its bytes) and whether `agents` is there; the two skew readings — within the tolerance `live`, beyond it `clock-differs` — with what the app showed for each; the offline refusal's code; and **U2**'s write count over the measured window with the cadence it supports. **No credential is printed or pasted** — no pairing MAC key, no keychain item value, no ID token, no custom token — and the heartbeat's `mac` is recorded as **present**, never as its value.

**Restore.** Nothing the check could not undo itself is written: it seeds no node (the heartbeat is the consumer's **own** write), mints no token and changes no setting.

- Stop `fugaro mailbox`, so the heartbeat stops moving and the next check starts from a state you chose.
- Delete the heartbeat node you wrote by hand for step 3, if you wrote one; the consumer's own node is its own write and needs no undo.
- Turn the phone's automatic time back **on** — the OS restores the clock the check moved — and `fugaro pair revoke --uid <uid>` if you paired a device for this check alone.

## Check 85: the on-device STT/TTS bake-off — the same fixed prompts through the local engine and each admitted remote provider, on the oldest device you support (your own phone, at your own terminal; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Task P4.2 writes this check and running it is the owner's; the design is [design/voice-evaluation-switch.md](mobile/design/voice-evaluation-switch.md) §4.7, whose row it amends in place, and its subject is Voice **D44**/**D46** (D46's cell asks for three numbers per candidate: end-of-turn latency, cost per hour of conversation, and error rate on the identifiers this tree uses) and mobile **D123** (D46 inherited: on-device engines only, chosen by a bake-off on the oldest supported device). **No agent performs any step of it**, no step is a CI job, and no step may wait on a prompt.

**The number is one of this work's ten, and a reserved number is never reused.** The owner allocated **80–89** to the mobile work on 2026-10-16, taken as allocated rather than derived from the next free number in the register, and **all ten are owner-run** — no agent performs any step of any of them ([implementation-plan.md](mobile/implementation-plan.md), the "Check numbers this plan takes (80–89)" block). Check 85 is written by **P4.2** and, under the 2026-10-19 amendment, its scope is the same fixed prompts through the local engine and through each admitted remote provider. **Its row and its section are in the register now**, written by P4.2 on 2026-11-17 (checks 81, 82 and 89 were written by Task **P4.2a** on 2026-10-18), and a check is never run before its text is in the register — so the text is here and the running is yours.

**What it gates, and what it does not.** The design says the switch ships **so that** this check can run through both engines (§10), so the check gates **the design's claims**, not its shape: until it runs there is **no number** for either engine — not first partial, not end-of-speech-to-reply, not name error rate, not cost per hour — and §9 says so in its own words ("the number that matters does not exist yet"). What it gates, exactly (§13): every latency and cost sentence in the design; Voice D44's **second** explicit egress decision — **adopting** remote voice, owed and untaken; the **choice among the three admitted providers**, since §7 records every latency number as **UNVERIFIED** and "which one is fast" cannot be answered from a vendor's page; and the hop's **cold-start** question, which §9 prices as a risk a voice interaction cannot afford. What it does **not** gate: the seven P5.3 tasks, which are written against the design and not against a number — the one thing a measurement changes in the build is the `providers` list in the `config/policy/voice` node and the register's rows, an edit to two files.

**This is not Check 102.** Check 102 records **one** engine's wake-word recognition rate; Check 85 records **latency and cost per engine**, through both the local engine and each admitted remote provider.

**Why a live check, when the switch's logic is tested.** `shared/voice-switch`'s suite and its `mutation-proof.sh` prove the **badge's decisions** over the inputs it is handed — the state table, the fail-closed branches, the invariant that `engine` is remote only for a live, admitted, consented route. They cannot produce any of the four numbers, and Global Constraint 10 forbids a CI case that would: **no test may need a live cloud, a real device or a real microphone.** A provider's true latency on the oldest device, what a real recogniser does to a project name, and what a pass costs are facts about a device, a network and an account, and they are exactly what this check is for.

**How it is run, and by whom.** At **your** own terminal, with the app on your own phone, at the switch you set yourself: no command here waits on **stdin**, no step asks a question or needs a confirmation, and **no agent performs any step** — the app is built and installed by **check 89** and the phone is paired by **check 100**, so this check starts where those two end. Every number is one you read off the screen or your own clock and write down; nothing here is a credential.

**The two halves the row names.** The **local** engine and **each admitted remote provider** are the two sides of the comparison, and each is put the **same** fixed list: the local engine is the app's own on-device speech, reached with both switches at **local**; a remote provider is reached by turning the switch for its direction to **remote** with a consent recorded for that name, and the project's `config/policy/voice` node must admit it — a provider the node does not name is not in the bake-off at all, because the node's default is **deny**.

**What "admitted" means, and where the terms live.** A provider is admitted for a direction when the project's `config/policy/voice` node lists it, its `direction` switch for that direction is true, and `force_local` is not set — three fields, and the node carries **no date** (`internal/projectpolicy/voice.go`). The provider's **retention and training terms** and its **price** are not in the node: they live in the register **with the hop** (§4.3), one row per admitted name, and **an entry is a provider name, never a URL** — a URL there would be a policy-carried redirection, and the reader refuses one at decode.

**What the check does not decide, and what it does not touch.** It does **not** take D44's second egress decision; it produces the table that decision is taken against, and neither that decision nor the choice among the three providers is taken by this check. It does **not** reach a provider the project does not admit: the `config/policy/voice` node's default is **deny** (absent, empty, malformed and unreadable all mean local only — `internal/projectpolicy/voice.go`), so an engine you did not write into the node is not measured here.

**The guard stops today, and here is what is genuinely missing — verified against this tree.** The switch is merged: the policy node's reader is `internal/projectpolicy/voice.go` with `PathVoiceShared`/`PathVoiceRepo` in `internal/projectpolicy/paths.go` and the node itself in `internal/budget/rules/rules.json.tmpl` (P5.3.1, P5.3.2), and the app's half is `shared/voice-switch/index.js` (P5.3.4) and `mobile/src/voice-switch/` (P5.3.6). **The two engines are not.** There is **no local engine**: `mobile/src/audio/index.js`'s own header says the tree is interfaces and fakes only ("no capture path, no speech engine and no audio decoder here"), `mobile/src/voice/index.js` says "there is no speech engine and no speech recognition here", and the app ships **voiceless** (the voice-session reconciliation's **F7**, `mobile/README.md`). There is **no remote half**: `internal/voicesvc/` — the hop that holds the provider key, admits a name and forwards to it (P5.3.3, P5.3.5) — is not in the tree, no provider client exists anywhere in it, and `mobile/src/voice-switch/index.js` says the egress path (P5.3.7) "is not in this directory yet". The guard therefore exits at the first of those gaps you meet — today the hop — and this paragraph names both: **neither engine can be put the prompts through.**

**Guard block — re-run this before every step.** It stops unless the checkout carries the ports, the switch, the policy reader and a build to install, and it stops on the two engines themselves: a bake-off with no engine on one side measures one engine and calls it two.

```bash
# === Check 85: setup + guard. RE-RUN THIS BLOCK BEFORE EVERY STEP. ===
set -u
ROOT=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null) || { echo "Check 85 stopped: not inside a git checkout; this check runs a build of the app in this repository" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -d "$ROOT/mobile/src/audio" ] || { echo "Check 85 stopped: there is no mobile/src/audio/ in this checkout, so the ports the bake-off drives are not on this tree (Task P3.4)" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -d "$ROOT/mobile/src/voice-switch" ] || { echo "Check 85 stopped: there is no mobile/src/voice-switch/ in this checkout, so the app has no switch to put a prompt through a second engine with (Task P5.3.6)" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/shared/voice-switch/index.js" ] || { echo "Check 85 stopped: shared/voice-switch/index.js is missing, so the pure switch the badge comes from is not on this tree (Task P5.3.4)" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/internal/projectpolicy/voice.go" ] || { echo "Check 85 stopped: there is no internal/projectpolicy/voice.go, so the admitted-provider list this check reads its remote engines from is not on this tree (Task P5.3.2)" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -d "$ROOT/internal/voicesvc" ] || { echo "Check 85 stopped: there is no internal/voicesvc/ in this checkout, so the REMOTE half has nothing to call — no hop holds a provider key, no provider client exists, and the same prompts cannot go through a remote engine (Tasks P5.3.3 and P5.3.5)" >&2; exit 1; }
if grep -q "no speech engine" "$ROOT/mobile/src/audio/index.js"; then echo "Check 85 stopped: the audio tree is interfaces and fakes only (its own index.js says so) and mobile/src/voice/index.js says there is no speech engine either, so there is no LOCAL engine to measure — the app is voiceless until an engine ships (Task P3.4 ships the ports, not the engine; F7)" >&2; exit 1; fi
[ -f "$ROOT/mobile/eas.json" ] || { echo "Check 85 stopped: there is no mobile/eas.json in this checkout, so the oldest device has no build to install — check 89 is where the app is built and put on the phone, and this check starts where that one ends" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "Check 85 ready: measuring the same fixed prompts through every engine on the oldest device you support — the audio stays on the device except through an engine you switched on, and nothing is pasted but the numbers"
```

1. **The list, and the engines, written down before the first utterance.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* Write the **fixed prompt list** before you start, so the denominators cannot move: the same list for every engine, prepared **off-device** and **never recorded from `belong`** (Global Constraint 11). The engines to measure are the **local** engine and each name the project's `config/policy/voice` node **admits** (read it with your own IAM credentials; `internal/projectpolicy/voice.go` is what the hop reads it with). The design's §7 register names three — **Google Cloud Speech** (both directions), **Deepgram** (STT), **ElevenLabs** (TTS) — and marks every latency number there **UNVERIFIED**. **FACT:**
   - the device and its OS — the **oldest** you support — and the app's build id and version (check 89's);
   - the engines and the node they came from, and that a provider the node does not name was measured **not at all**;
   - **N**, the fixed prompt list itself (the phrases are not secrets), and that it is the same for every engine;
   - the **conditions** — distance, background — held **identical** across engines. A latency is only comparable to itself under one condition, and the condition is recorded.

2. **The pass, engine by engine.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* Run the whole list through **one** engine, then the next, the same way each time. These are D46's "end-of-turn latency" measured two ways, and a number with no engine, no device and no prompt attached is not a measurement. **FACT:**
   - for **each engine**, for **each prompt**: the **first partial** — milliseconds from the start of speech to the first partial transcript (STT);
   - the **end-of-speech-to-reply** — milliseconds from the end of speech to the first spoken reply, which carries the round trip through the model and the TTS;
   - which engine served each prompt, one at a time, with the switch set to it and the other side left off.

3. **The name error rate, against its own denominator.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* **FACT:**
   - for **each engine**, on the prompts that carry them, which of the **identifiers this tree actually uses** — **project, repository and recipe names** — were transcribed wrong, and the count;
   - that the **error rate** is **names wrong over names attempted**, both numbers given, because the set is exactly the identifiers `internal/watch`'s `clean()` sanitises and clips (`maxText = 200` runes, `internal/watch/json.go`'s `JSONRun.Title`) — and a rate stated without its denominator lets a small set read as a perfect engine;
   - that the rate is for the **identifiers only** and not for the prompt text as a whole: the message may be understood while the project name is not, and it is the name the command needs.

4. **Cost per hour, and where the price came from.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* **FACT:**
   - how the number is computed: the provider's **own price for the pass** (its list price from the register's §7 row — TTS per character, STT per minute — or the provider's metered usage figure if it exposes one) applied to what the pass **actually spent** (characters spoken, minutes streamed), **divided by the pass's measured conversation time in hours**;
   - the **price source and the date it was read** — every price in §7 is a page's listing and not a rate, and §7 marks each provider's retention, training and every latency number **UNVERIFIED**, so the price is the provider's word while the measurement is yours;
