Identity comes from sign-in and access comes from the allowlist, and neither is the code's: sign-in is **custom tokens only** — `internal/cli/init_firebase.go`'s `refusePublicSignUp` refuses an Identity Platform configuration with any public sign-in, because *"The web API key is public, so only custom tokens signed by Fugaro's signer may work"* — and the allowlist is the **device node** `config/admin/devices/<uid>`, which `userClaim` requires to exist and whose generated child is `.read: false, .write: false` for every client token. The entry carries an **administered email**, and pairing **refuses an unverified email**, in the shape `internal/cli/init_members.go`'s `userEmail` (called by `authenticatedUser`) already enforces for the CLI: `email_verified` false is refused, and a service account's address is refused with it.

**The reads below use the values check 81's guard block resolves** — `$DB` (the database host, already stripped of its scheme, so every URL here writes `https://` back), `$KEY` and `$FP` — plus `$AT=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)`, your own Google credentials, which bypass the rules and prove nothing about them. Run that guard block first, in this shell: it is the register's resolver for the backend, it prints the project ids it found and never the key, and it is not repeated here. **No step reads a private key, a token or the MAC key out of anywhere; none is printed and none is pasted.**

**Guard block — re-run this before every step.** It stops unless the checkout has the pairing command and the app screen that scans the code, and it stops a development build of its own: a check of the released pairing path is not a check of a `dev` binary.

```bash
# === Check 100: setup + guard. RE-RUN THIS BLOCK BEFORE EVERY STEP. ===
set -u
ROOT=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null) || { echo "Check 100 stopped: not inside a git checkout; the pairing mints its tokens from a release build of the CLI" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/internal/cli/pair.go" ] || { echo "Check 100 stopped: there is no internal/cli/pair.go in this checkout, so 'fugaro pair' is not built, there is no code to scan and no device token to mint (mobile plan Task P6.6 makes it; this check reads it and does not create it)" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -d "$ROOT/mobile/src/pairing" ] || { echo "Check 100 stopped: there is no mobile/src/pairing/ in this checkout, so the app has no screen that scans the code, keeps its key pair on the phone, decrypts the delivery or shows the fingerprint you type (Task P6.8 makes it)" >&2; exit 1; }
FUGARO=$(command -v fugaro) || { echo "Check 100 stopped: no fugaro on PATH; run the release build that carries 'fugaro pair' (0.10.0 or later)" >&2; exit 1; }
VER=$("$FUGARO" version 2>/dev/null || true)
[ -n "$VER" ] || { echo "Check 100 stopped: 'fugaro version' printed nothing, so the release a pairing was made from cannot be recorded" >&2; exit 1; }
case "$VER" in *dev*) echo "Check 100 stopped: fugaro version prints '$VER' — a development build writes no pairing and no device node, so run the release build (0.10.0 or later)" >&2; exit 1;; esac
echo "Check 100 ready: fugaro $VER at $ROOT — the pairing token, the device token and the MAC key are credentials: they are never pasted back and never handed to an agent"
```

1. **The code, and what it carries.** *(Guard block, run by you; then check 81's guard block in the same shell.)* In installation `fugaro`, run `fugaro pair` and record what it shows **before** the phone scans it. **FACT:** the installation and the Firebase project the code names; that its payload is the project's Firebase config plus **one token** and **no key** — no API key of yours, no private key, no MAC key, nothing that is a credential in its own right; the token's subject as a `p~` uid (the one-shot pairing uid whose request node it may write) and its `exp`, which is **at most five minutes** (P6.6's bound). U5 is exactly that number: every run's token lives the full hour (`internal/budget/token`'s `Lifetime`), and the pairing's is deliberately shorter, so the check settles that sign-in honours an `exp` below an hour rather than quietly extending it. Then read the pairing node back with your own credentials, which bypass the rules:

   ```bash
   AT=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)   # never printed, never pasted
   curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" "https://$DB/pairing.json"
   ```
   **FACT:** the session's uid as the read shows it, and that the node exists and is empty until the phone writes (the request node is the phone's, not the CLI's). A client token's read of the same node is a denial (check 81's step 6 covers that fence for `mu` tokens); this read is yours and proves nothing about it.

2. **The phone's key lands once, and only that field.** *(Guard block, run by you, on the phone.)* Scan the code. The phone generates its key pair **on the phone** (the private half never leaves it), shows a code derived from its own key, and writes the public half. **FACT:** the request node `pairing/<the p~ uid>/request` holds `key` (the phone's public key: base64 or base64url text, the `PUBKEY` macro — `internal/budget/rules/rules.go`'s `PUBKEY` case, `"key": { ".validate": "PUBKEY" }` in `rules.json.tmpl`) and `at` (a timestamp) and **nothing else** — every other field is refused (`"$other": {".validate": false}`); the node did not exist before the scan; and a **second** write of it is refused (`newData.exists() && !data.exists()`), so a phone cannot re-register a different key under a session the operator is about to confirm. **FACT:** the private key is on the phone only, and what the phone stored is what P3.1's storage rule permits (the app's own boundary test is the code's half of this sentence).

3. **The code you type, and what the fingerprint is.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* Compare the code the phone shows with the code the CLI shows and **type it** at the CLI. **FACT:** what the phone showed, what the CLI showed, and that they are the same value (**the fingerprint of the phone's key**, so a phone that scanned a code it was shown cannot complete a session whose key it does not hold). Then the deliberate negative, done first if you want it: **type a wrong code** (the code from a second, unattempted session, or a flipped character) and record that **nothing was minted** — no device node, no delivery, the session still pending — that the CLI refused **before any write**, and that a fourth attempt is not locked out of the right code (the refusal is the wrong decision, not the session). **FACT:** after the right code, the delivery node `pairing/<the p~ uid>/delivery` carries the **device token** (`m~<random>`, `mu` = the device's own uid) and the **per-pairing MAC key**, encrypted to the phone's public key, and the phone holds both in secure storage (the settings keep the keychain item's **name**, Voice D42(2), never the key). **FACT:** the session is then spent — P6.6 deletes the `p~` Auth user and the `pairing/<the p~ uid>` node once the delivery has been read, because the deployed rules put no time limit on a `p~` session and nothing else would remove either — and the delivery's contents were never printed in a terminal, a log or a `FACT` line.

4. **The allowlist entry: the device node and the administered email.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* **FACT:** `config/admin/devices/<the device's uid>` exists after pairing — the same node check 81 step 1 writes by hand, now written by `fugaro pair` over IAM, which needs `roles/firebasedatabase.admin` beside the minter role and **refuses, naming the missing one, without it** — and no client token may read it (its generated child is `.read: false, .write: false`, which is why the check reads it with `$AT`). **FACT:** the **administered email** on the entry, and where it came from: the address `pair` took from **your own** credentials — `authenticatedUser` → `userEmail` — so the entry records who the device belongs to as an administered field, not as a second allowlist that a rule reads. **FACT:** an unverified address is refused at pairing, in the shape `userEmail` already enforces; the refusal is **read, not provoked** (no unverified account exists on this installation and one is not made for a check): what is recorded is that line — a false `email_verified` is refused, and a `.gserviceaccount.com` address with it — beside the pairing the check actually completed with your verified one. **FACT:** sign-in stayed custom tokens only: no provider was enabled by the pairing, and the code changed no Identity Platform setting.

5. **What the newly paired phone reaches, and what the code did not give it.** *(Guard block, run by you, on the phone.)* **FACT:** the paired app reads and writes **exactly** check 81's fence — its own `outbox` and `heartbeat`, the one write into its own `inbox`, the `acked: true` on a message it has spoken, and the read grant's nodes — and everything else is refused, the device node it is defined by and both pairing nodes included. **FACT:** with the **pairing token alone** (before the code was typed at the CLI) the phone could read and write nothing else: the `p~` session wrote its own request node once and read its own delivery node, and every project node was denied — **this is what "discovery, not identity" means in the tree**, and it is the negative the check exists for. **FACT:** the timing U5 names: the `exp` step 1 recorded, and that sign-in accepted it (the exchange returned an ID token with an `exp` below an hour), so the app never had to wait for a short-lived token to be extended.

**Passes when:** step 1's code carries the project's config and one short-lived `p~` token and no key; step 2's request node holds the phone's public key and its timestamp and nothing else, written once; step 3's wrong code mints nothing and the right one delivers a device token and a MAC key that reach secure storage and nowhere else; step 4's device node exists, is unreadable to every client token and carries the administered email your own verified credentials supplied; and step 5's fence is check 81's, with the pairing token alone reaching its own two nodes and nothing else.

**Fails when:** the code carries a key of yours, a private key or a MAC key; a `p~` session can read or write a project node beyond its own two; a second request write is admitted, or a wrong typed code still mints a device token or writes a device node; the device node is readable with a client token; an unverified address pairs; the pairing enables a public sign-in provider or the app signs in by anything other than a custom token; or the MAC key or the device token is echoed to a terminal, a log, a settings file or a `FACT` line — a credential that reaches any of those is a finding in itself, and the fix is on the phone or in P6.6, never in this document.

**Paste back:** the release (`fugaro version`), the installation and Firebase project, the phone and its OS; the `p~` token's subject prefix and its `exp` (**the number, never the token**); whether the code carried a key (it must not); the request node's field **names** and that it was written once; whether the wrong code minted nothing; that the delivery reached secure storage and that both the `p~` Auth user and the pairing node were gone afterwards; the administered email's **domain** and that it is your verified one; the device node's existence and that a client read of it is denied; and the pairing token's own reach. **Never paste a pairing token, a device token, a MAC key, a private key or an ID token.**

**Restore.** The pairing is meant to stay — a paired device is the point — so nothing here is undone except what a step deliberately left:

- The session's own artefacts are already gone: P6.6 deletes the `p~` Auth user and the `pairing/<the p~ uid>` node once the delivery is read, and a session you abandoned mid-step is removed by the sweep, not by you.
- The device node `config/admin/devices/<uid>` and the device's Auth user **stay**: they are the paired device. Removing them is **check 101**'s subject (`fugaro pair revoke`), and doing it here would erase the positive result of this check.
- The phone keeps the token and the MAC key in secure storage; removing the app (or its account) removes them. No key was written to a file by this check, so there is nothing to delete on your machine.
- Nothing else changed: this check makes no commit, no rules change and no project setting.

## Check 101: revocation — deleting the device node denies the next read, and the Auth user's timing (installation `fugaro`, `fugaro-dev`, with the phone check 100 paired; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Task P6.11 writes this check and running it is the owner's; its subject is `fugaro pair revoke` (P6.6) and the reconciliation's **U2**: *developer claims from a custom token persist into refreshed ID tokens, and a deleted Auth user's ID token stays valid until its `exp`*. The half of that sentence this tree can decide, it has already decided — **the allowlist is the device node**, and `userClaim` reads it on **every** request — so revocation does not wait for a token to expire; what stays open is the **timing** around it, and that is what the check records. **The guard stops today**: `fugaro pair revoke` is not built.

**Why the node, and why the order matters.** D166 chose a node over a claim because a claim cannot be withdrawn: `internal/budget/rules/rules.go`'s `userClaim` is `auth != null && auth.token.mu != null && auth.token.mu == auth.uid && root.child('config/admin/devices/' + auth.uid).exists()` — so deleting the node revokes at once, and a token minted while the node existed buys nothing once it is gone. P6.6 revokes in the order the fence requires: it deletes the **node first**, then the Auth user, so there is no window in which the account exists and is denied (harmless) in place of one in which the account is gone and the fence has not been asked yet.

**The reads below use check 81's guard values** (`$DB`, `$KEY`, `$FP`) and `$AT` — your own credentials, which bypass the rules. Run check 81's guard block first, in this shell. **The device's uid is `$DEV`, which step 1 sets and steps 2 and 3 read: it is never `$UID`.** Bash defines `UID` as the caller's numeric user id, so a URL written `config/admin/devices/$UID.json` reads the node of user `1000` — which is absent whether or not the device is revoked — and a revocation check whose negatives pass on the wrong node is a false PASS. The same reason check 81 spells its two accounts `$ALICE` and `$BOB` and never `$USER`.

**Guard block — re-run this before every step. It sets nothing the steps read, so re-running it never clears `$DEV`, `$AT` or `$OLD`.**

```bash
# === Check 101: setup + guard. RE-RUN THIS BLOCK BEFORE EVERY STEP. ===
set -u
ROOT=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null) || { echo "Check 101 stopped: not inside a git checkout; the revocation deletes a device node and an Auth user from a release build of the CLI" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/internal/cli/pair.go" ] || { echo "Check 101 stopped: there is no internal/cli/pair.go in this checkout, so 'fugaro pair revoke' and 'fugaro pair ls' are not built and this check has nothing to run (mobile plan Task P6.6 makes it)" >&2; exit 1; }
grep -q 'func revoke' "$ROOT/internal/cli/pair.go" 2>/dev/null || { echo "Check 101 stopped: internal/cli/pair.go carries no revoke path in this checkout, so the delete-the-node-then-the-user order this check records cannot be exercised (Task P6.6's revoke half)" >&2; exit 1; }
FUGARO=$(command -v fugaro) || { echo "Check 101 stopped: no fugaro on PATH; run the release build that carries 'fugaro pair revoke' (0.10.0 or later)" >&2; exit 1; }
VER=$("$FUGARO" version 2>/dev/null || true)
case "$VER" in ""|*dev*) echo "Check 101 stopped: 'fugaro version' printed '$VER' — revocation is a release-path property, so run the release build (0.10.0 or later)" >&2; exit 1;; esac
# The device's uid is $DEV (step 1) and the old ID token is $OLD (step 2). NEITHER
# IS $UID: bash sets UID to your numeric user id, so a URL written "$UID.json"
# would read node 1000 and both of this check's negatives would pass on a node
# that is absent either way.
echo "Check 101 ready: fugaro $VER at $ROOT — the device token you revoke is a credential: it is never pasted back, and neither is any ID token"
```

1. **The paired device, and what revocation will delete.** *(Guard block, run by you; then check 81's guard block in the same shell. This step sets `$DEV`, which steps 2 and 3 read.)* Read the device off `fugaro pair ls` — the uid it prints is `DEV` — and record what the check is about to delete. **FACT:** `fugaro pair ls` lists the devices paired to installation `fugaro` — the device's uid, the administered email on the entry and when it was written — and **reads no key**: the listing is an IAM read of `config/admin/devices`, and nothing in it is a credential.

   ```bash
   fugaro pair ls                                   # prints the uid, the administered email and when it was written
   DEV=<the device uid it printed>                  # e.g. m~<random> — this, not $UID, is the account in question
   AT=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)             # never printed, never pasted
   curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" "https://$DB/config/admin/devices/$DEV.json"     # exists, before anything is revoked
   ```
   **FACT:** with `$AT`, the same two nodes the check is about: `config/admin/devices/$DEV` (exists, and the value is only `true`: the rules read the node's existence and no field of it) and the device's Auth user (present, with its creation time), recorded **before** anything is revoked. The node's body is read with `$AT` because no client token may read it at all; a `200` here is the operator's IAM, not the app's.

2. **The node goes first, and the very next read is denied.** *(Guard block, run by you, on the phone; this step sets `$OLD`, which step 3 reads, and it reads `$DEV` from step 1.)* On the phone, make one read that works (the app's own overview refreshes: it reads the granted nodes, and it succeeds). Put the ID token the phone is holding into `OLD` **before** revoking — from the app's own debug output or its secure storage, in this shell only: it is a bearer credential, and it is never printed and never pasted. Then, at the terminal, run `fugaro pair revoke --uid $DEV` and **immediately**, on the phone, repeat the same read.

   ```bash
   OLD=<the ID token the phone holds, copied in before the revocation>   # $OLD, never printed, never pasted
   fugaro pair revoke --uid "$DEV"   # the device uid step 1 read off 'fugaro pair ls'
   AT=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)
   curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" "https://$DB/config/admin/devices/$DEV.json"   # must be null now
   ```
   **FACT:** the node is **gone** (the same URL that returned a value in step 1 now returns `null`); the phone's next read is **denied** — a permission denial, not a stale empty answer — and it was denied **while the ID token it held had not expired**: record its `exp` and the wall-clock moment of the denial (the app's own screen shows the refusal, and the same ID token read the granted nodes seconds earlier). That timing is the finding: the fence asks the device node on every request, so revocation is immediate and does not wait for a token's hour. **FACT:** a write is denied the same way (the app's next attempt to write its inbox is refused), and the refusal is the rules', not the app's — the phone is not told to hide anything.

3. **The Auth user goes, and what the old token still does (U2).** *(Guard block, run by you; this step reads `$DEV` from step 1 and `$OLD` from step 2.)* P6.6 deletes the Auth user after the node. **FACT:** with your own credentials, the account is gone (`accounts:lookup` returns no user for `$DEV`). Then `$OLD` — the ID token the phone held **before** the revocation, not a fresh one — used as `?auth=`: **FACT:** every project node is denied to it — the node is gone, so `userClaim` is false whatever the token says — and a fresh exchange with the **custom** token (its `exp` may still be in the future) is refused, because the user it names no longer exists; **FACT:** what the old ID token still is, recorded as U2 asks it: a bearer identity that `accounts:lookup` no longer resolves, valid until its own `exp` for anything that trusts an unexpired token without asking the fence — which is why the check records the `exp` rather than assuming it, and why nothing in this project hands a token to a service that does not ask the rules.

   ```bash
   curl -sS -X POST "https://identitytoolkit.googleapis.com/v1/accounts:lookup?key=$KEY" \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "{\"localId\":[\"$DEV\"]}"
   curl -sS -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' "https://$DB/config/caps/global.json?auth=$OLD"
   ```
   **FACT:** the lookup's empty `users` array, and the denied read (the body is the rules' own `Permission denied`, not an empty value). The `?auth=$OLD` is the whole step: without a token the read is denied as unauthenticated and proves nothing about revocation, so the `exp` recorded in step 2 and this answer are read together.

4. **The phone's other half: re-pairing is a new device.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* Pair the same phone again (check 100), and record the two identities side by side. **FACT:** the new session is a **new** `p~` uid and the device gets a **new** uid and a **new** device node, so the token the first pairing delivered is worthless — it still names the old, node-less uid — and the ACM key is a new one (a rotated pairing is a rotated key, D171). **FACT:** `fugaro pair ls` now shows one device (the old one is not on the list), and the old ID token is denied while the new one is admitted: the contrast is the check.

5. **The sweep leaves a paired device alone.** *(Guard block, run by you; read-only.)* The history sweep carries P6.6's `m~` rule: it removes an `m~` Auth user whose device node is **gone**, and it must never remove one whose node exists — an allowlist entry that a sweep deletes on a bad reading is a phone that stops working. **FACT:** the sweep's own output after it runs (the run records `fugaro`'s history step; P6.6's test `internal/budget/sweep_device_test.go` is the code's half): the re-paired device's user is still present, and the revoked one is gone — the check reads that both facts are true **at the same time**, which is the difference between a sweep and a revoke. **FACT:** no key is read by the sweep, and nothing it deletes is on the allowlist it did not first see gone.

**Passes when:** step 1's listing names the device and reads no key; step 2's node deletion is followed immediately by a **denied** read from a phone whose ID token had not expired; step 3's Auth user is gone, its old ID token is denied everywhere and a fresh exchange with the old custom token is refused; step 4's re-pairing produces a new uid, a new node and a new MAC key, with the old token worthless; and step 5's sweep removes the revoked user and leaves the paired one.

**Fails when:** a revoked phone still reads or writes anything after the node is deleted (the fence is not the node, and the allowlist is a claim again); a read succeeds **because** the token had not expired yet, or a denial arrives only after an hour; the device node is deleted **after** the Auth user, leaving a window the check can see; a re-pairing reuses the revoked uid or key; the sweep deletes an `m~` user whose device node exists; or any token is pasted into the report.

**Paste back:** `fugaro pair ls`'s device uid and the **domain** of its administered email; the node's existence before and its absence after; the sequence with two wall-clock times and the ID token's `exp` (**never the token**); the phone's refusals (read and write) and the rules' own `Permission denied`; the `accounts:lookup` answer; the re-pairing's two uids and that the old token is worthless; and the sweep's effect on both users.

**Restore.** Revocation is the point of this check, so what it leaves is exactly what it means to leave:

- The **re-paired** device stays paired (that is check 100's positive result, and P6.6's own door removes it again if you want it gone).
- The revoked uid's Auth user and node are gone and stay gone; a number that has been revoked is not restored, and if you want the device back you pair it again under a new uid rather than re-creating the old one.
- Nothing on your machine changed: no key file, no config edit, no commit. The ID tokens and the custom tokens live in the shell you ran the steps in.

## Check 102: the wake word's recognition rate, on the oldest device you support (your own phone, at your own terminal; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Task P6.11 writes this check and running it is the owner's; its subject is the reconciliation's **U1** — *on-device engines recognise "Fugaro" reliably enough for a wake word*, with no device measured — and the sentence the reconciliation found **false**: the spec's "never misroutes". `docs/voice-module/reconciliation.md` records that finding (*"the reconciliation found that the spec's 'never misroutes' claim is not true, which is why the recognition rate is proposed live Check 102"*), so this check measures two different things and treats them differently: a **missed** wake word is an annoyance, and an utterance with **no** wake word that is routed anyway is the failure. **The guard stops today**: the app has no way to sign in at all (sign-in is custom tokens only and the token is pairing's, P6.6/P6.8 unbuilt), so there is no paired phone to speak to.

**This is not D123's bake-off.** Check 85 is the engine comparison — the same fixed prompts through the local engine and each admitted remote provider, recording first partial, end-of-speech-to-reply, name error rate and cost per hour, per engine. This check records **one** engine's wake-word behaviour on the **oldest device you support**, and it is the number that decides whether the wake word is the app's front door at all.

**Guard block — re-run this before every step.** It stops unless the checkout carries the voice module and the wake word's own screen, and unless the phone is going to be paired to an installation: a wake word that routes speech to nothing measures nothing.

```bash
# === Check 102: setup + guard. RE-RUN THIS BLOCK BEFORE EVERY STEP. ===
set -u
ROOT=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null) || { echo "Check 102 stopped: not inside a git checkout; this check is run against a build of the app in this repository" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -d "$ROOT/mobile/src/voice" ] || { echo "Check 102 stopped: there is no mobile/src/voice/ in this checkout, so the wake word this check measures is not on this tree (P3.5's voice module; P6.12 extends it with the spoken confirmation)" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/internal/cli/pair.go" ] || { echo "Check 102 stopped: there is no internal/cli/pair.go in this checkout, so a phone cannot be paired to the installation this rate is measured against — sign-in is custom tokens only and the token is the pairing's (Task P6.6; the app screen is P6.8)" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/mobile/eas.json" ] || { echo "Check 102 stopped: there is no mobile/eas.json in this checkout, so the device has no build to install — check 89 is where the app is built and put on the phone, and this check starts where that one ends" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "Check 102 ready: measuring the wake word on the oldest device you support, in airplane mode — the audio stays on the device and nothing is pasted"
```

1. **The list, written down before the first utterance.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* Write the list **before** you start, so the denominators cannot move. It has two halves, and they are counted separately: **N utterances in all** (twenty is enough to be worth recording and short enough to finish), of which **W carry the wake word** — each headed by "Fugaro", and that is the half the recognition rate is measured on — and the other **N − W** carry **no** wake word, three of them beginning with a **near miss** ("Furano", "Fugato", "Go …"). **FACT:** the device and its OS, the app's build (check 89's build id and version), the engine the app is configured to use, N, **W**, and the list itself. The phone goes into **airplane mode** for the whole pass: the number this check records is the **on-device engine's**, and a network round trip would hide a local miss behind a remote success.

2. **The pass.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* Speak the list in order, the same way each time (the same distance, the same background — a rate is only comparable to itself under one condition, and the condition is recorded in step 1). After each utterance, record which way it went. **FACT:** for each of the W wake-word utterances: whether the wake word was **recognised**, **missed** (spoken and not picked up), or **misheard** as something else; and for each of the N − W with no wake word, whether it was routed anyway. Then the two numbers, each against **its own** denominator: the **recognition rate** is **recognised over W** — the utterances that carry the wake word, and only those, because the other N − W can never be recognised and counting them in the denominator would record a perfect engine as roughly W/N — and the **false-accept count** is the utterances **out of the N − W with no wake word** that reached an agent.

3. **The near misses, one at a time.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* **FACT:** for each of the three near misses, whether the app treated it as the wake word. This is the finding the check exists for: an utterance that begins with a similar word and is routed **is speech that was not addressed to the app**, and no rate compensates for it — the spec's "never misroutes" sentence was the claim, and this is the measurement that replaces it. **FACT:** what the app did with a misrouted utterance (which agent received it — the active one, D163 — and that nothing else was switched), and whether the misroute was at least **visible** (the app said what it heard, or the feed showed who received it): an invisible misroute is the worst case, because the user reads the reply as an answer to what they actually said.

4. **The same three utterances a second time.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* Repeat the near misses once more, later in the session, after the app has been used. **FACT:** whether the result was the same. A wake word whose error is stable is a property of the engine and can be worked around (a different phrase, a closer microphone); one whose error is **intermittent** is the answer to U1, and the record is the two passes side by side rather than one number.

**Passes when:** step 2's recognition rate is recorded on the oldest device **against W** — the wake-word utterances, not all N — with its N, W, the device, its OS and its build; the false-accept count is recorded against **N − W**, and step 3 shows the three near misses each behaving the same way on the second pass; and no utterance was misrouted invisibly.

**Fails when:** a near miss is **routed to an agent** — that is the finding this check exists to produce, and it is a failure of the wake word, not of the user; a rate is stated without its N, its W, its device or its conditions, or with the no-wake-word utterances in its denominator; the near misses are omitted because the pass "looked fine"; the audio or the transcript of the pass is pasted anywhere (the recording stays on the device); or the check is run in a way that feeds the utterance to a remote engine and calls the result the wake word's rate — with airplane mode on, that cannot happen silently, and a step that needs the network says so.

**Paste back:** the device, its OS, the app's build and version, the engine, N and **W**, the list (the phrases are not secrets); the counts — recognised, missed, misheard (out of W) and routed-without-a-wake-word (out of N − W) — and the two numbers; the near-miss results on both passes and what the app did with each; and whether any misroute was visible. **The recordings themselves are never pasted**, and nothing here is a credential.

**Restore.** Nothing to undo: this check writes no node, mints no token, makes no commit and changes no setting — it speaks at a phone in airplane mode and records what happened. The app's install and the paired device are check 89's and check 100's, and the phone's own recordings are yours to delete from the device.

## Check 103: a spoken cancel and a spoken merge, and the three refusals — on the sandbox repository only (installation `fugaro`, repository `edgeappinc/fugarosandbox`, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Task P6.11 writes this check and running it is the owner's; its subject is the D128 amendment of 2026-10-17 — the owner's ruling, recorded in `docs/mobile/functional-spec-reconciliation.md` §3.1 and as a dated note in `docs/mobile/reconciliation.md`'s D128 row (cancel, approve/merge and confirming an action are allowed on the phone, with a spoken read-back and an explicit "confirm") — P6.2's state machine (`shared/confirm`, merged, with its vectors) and the reconciliation's **U4**: *`gh pr merge` under the operator's login from the consumer process behaves the same as at the terminal*. **This is the one check of the five whose destructive half is aimed at a real repository**, so it names the sandbox — `edgeappinc/fugarosandbox`, the repository every other owner-run check uses — and it names `belong` nowhere except to forbid it. **The guard stops today**: the consumer that re-validates a confirmation is P6.7's (`internal/cli/mailbox.go`, not built) and the voice screen that speaks the read-back is P6.12's.

**Why a live check, when the state machine is tested.** `shared/confirm`'s tests (and P6.7's Go parity test over its vectors) prove the machine's decisions: a misheard confirm does not confirm, a replayed one authorises nothing the second time, a confirm for another target is refused. They cannot prove the two things this check is for: that a real **speech** recogniser produces the utterance the machine expects (and refuses the near misses a person actually says), and that the **consumer's own login** can act (U4's `gh pr merge`, under branch protection, from a process that is not a terminal).

**Guard block — re-run this before every step.** It stops unless the checkout carries the voice module, the pairing command and the consumer, and it refuses a repository other than the sandbox: the merge below is a real merge on a real pull request.

```bash
# === Check 103: setup + guard. RE-RUN THIS BLOCK BEFORE EVERY STEP. ===
set -u
ROOT=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null) || { echo "Check 103 stopped: not inside a git checkout; the consumer this check drives is built from this repository" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -d "$ROOT/mobile/src/voice" ] || { echo "Check 103 stopped: there is no mobile/src/voice/ in this checkout, so nothing speaks the read-back this check confirms (P3.5's voice module; P6.12 adds the confirmation)" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/internal/cli/pair.go" ] || { echo "Check 103 stopped: there is no internal/cli/pair.go in this checkout, so the phone cannot be paired and has no token to send a command with (Task P6.6)" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/internal/cli/mailbox.go" ] || { echo "Check 103 stopped: there is no internal/cli/mailbox.go in this checkout, so the consumer that re-validates a confirmation and runs the cancel or the merge is not built (P4.1 builds the consumer, P6.7 the enforcement) — and a spoken confirm with nothing behind it confirms nothing" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/shared/confirm/vectors.json" ] || { echo "Check 103 stopped: shared/confirm/vectors.json is missing, so the confirm machine and the consumer's parity test have no shared cases on this tree" >&2; exit 1; }
REPO=${REPO:-edgeappinc/fugarosandbox}
case "$REPO" in edgeappinc/fugarosandbox) : ;; *) echo "Check 103 stopped: REPO is '$REPO'; this check merges a pull request and may only ever do it on edgeappinc/fugarosandbox, never on belong and never on a repository you care about" >&2; exit 1;; esac
echo "Check 103 ready: REPO=$REPO — the sandbox repository is the only one this check may merge in, and no GitHub credential is read by it"
```

1. **The two targets, made on purpose.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* On the sandbox checkout: start a run whose id you will cancel (`fugaro run "<a small task>"` on `edgeappinc/fugarosandbox`), and open a pull request whose merge you will speak (a one-line change; base branch as the sandbox uses it). **FACT:** the run id, the PR number, the PR's **head SHA** as the forge shows it, and that both were made by you in the sandbox and nowhere else. Both are the **resolved targets** the read-back is built from: the machine refuses to read back a target it did not resolve, so an ambiguous "cancel that" cannot be confirmed at all.

2. **The spoken cancel, read back, confirmed once.** *(Guard block, run by you, on the phone.)* Speak "cancel that" (or the phrase the app's grammar admits for a cancel) with the run pending and nothing else pending. **FACT:** the read-back **exactly as it was spoken**, naming the **run id** — never the transcript's words, and never a bare "that": the read-back is built from the resolved target; that a **second** "cancel that" while the first is pending is refused or re-resolved rather than silently re-aimed; then speak the confirmation as a **separate** utterance ("confirm"). **FACT:** the cancel went through the CLI's own cancel path (the run's state in the sandbox's view, and `fugaro logs`/the run's record showing the cancellation), exactly **once** — and that the utterance which issued the command could not have confirmed it (speak the whole thing in one breath and record the refusal). **FACT:** a second "confirm" for the same action, spoken afterwards, authorises nothing: the action id is spent, and the run is already cancelled.

3. **The spoken merge, read back, confirmed once — U4's half.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* Speak "merge that" with the pull request on the sandbox as the target. **FACT:** the read-back names the **repository, the PR number and the PR's current head** (D169: a merge record carries the PR's **head SHA** read back at confirmation, and the consumer **refuses the merge if the head has moved** — `docs/mobile/functional-spec-reconciliation.md`'s D169 row, whose §3.5 lists the head SHA among the fields the MAC covers); then "confirm", and the merge runs through the **consumer's own `gh` login** — not yours at a terminal. **FACT:** U4's answer: whether it behaved as the terminal does — the merge commit and who authored it, whether branch protection or a required check refused it, and if it refused, what the refusal said (a consumer that cannot merge under protection is a finding for P6.7, not a fault of this check); and that a **third** thing did not happen: no force, no admin override, no second PR merged. **FACT:** the sandbox's PR is merged (or the refusal is recorded in full), and the read-back the app spoke is the one that is pasted back, not the transcript.

4. **The three refusals.** *(Guard block, run by you.)* With a **fresh** pending target each time (a second run to cancel), do these three in order and record what the app did, not what the machine would have done:

   - **A misheard confirm.** Say "conform", "confirmed it", "yes" — the words a recogniser actually returns for "confirm" — and record that **nothing was cancelled**: the machine refuses anything that is not the fixed phrase, and "yes" is deliberately not an alias of it. **FACT:** the utterance the app heard, the app's own answer, and the run's state afterwards.
   - **A replayed confirm.** Speak the same confirmation twice (and, if the app exposes an id, re-send the same action id). **FACT:** the first authorises, the second authorises **nothing** — one confirmation is one action — and the run is cancelled once, not twice.
   - **A confirm for another target.** With one action pending, change the pending action (speak a second destructive command before confirming, so the target the read-back named is no longer the pending one). **FACT:** the confirmation is refused, and the target named in the read-back is the one that did **not** happen: a confirmation for another target is exactly the case D128's amendment is about.

5. **What the check did not touch.** *(Guard block, run by you; read-only.)* **FACT:** the merge happened in `edgeappinc/fugarosandbox` and nowhere else; `belong` was not named, read or written by this check; no GitHub credential, token or key was read by any step or pasted into the report; and the only destructive effects are the cancelled run and the merged pull request, both of which are the sandbox's own.

**Passes when:** step 2's read-back names the run id and the cancel runs once through the CLI's own path; step 3's read-back names the repository, the PR number and its **current head**, and the merge runs through the consumer's own login (or its refusal is a recorded protection finding); and step 4's three refusals each leave the target untouched, with the replayed confirmation authorising exactly once.

**Fails when:** a read-back is built from the transcript rather than the resolved target; an ambiguous target can be read back and confirmed; a misheard confirm ("conform", "confirmed it", "yes") acts; the same confirmation authorises a second action, or a replayed id is re-accepted after a consumer restart; a confirmation for a changed target acts on the new one; the merge happens anywhere but the sandbox, or a credential is read or pasted; or the app merges with a force or an admin override to get past a protection.

**Paste back:** the sandbox run id and its cancellation's evidence; the PR number, its head SHA before the confirmation and the merge commit after it, or the protection refusal word for word; the read-back as spoken for both commands; what each of the three refusals heard and what it did; and the app's own answers. **Never paste a token, an ID token, a MAC key or a GitHub credential.**

**Restore.** The check's own effects are the two it made on purpose, and both are on the sandbox:

- The **cancelled run** is cancelled; if it left a branch or a worktree in the sandbox checkout, it is the sandbox's to clean, and nothing on `belong` is touched at any point.
- The **merged pull request** stays merged: it is the sandbox's, it was opened for this check, and un-merging it would make the merge the check recorded untrue. If you want the merge undone, that is a new pull request reverting it, which is what the sandbox is for.
- The app's pending actions are gone — a cancelled confirmation and an expired one both drop the action, and nothing is left pending on the phone.
- Nothing in this repository changed: no node written by hand, no rules change, no commit.

## Check 104: offline — no command is sent and none is queued (installation `fugaro`, your own phone, consumer in your own terminal; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Task P6.11 writes this check and running it is the owner's; its subject is the reconciliation's **U3** — *the Expo/React Native Firebase SDK queues RTDB writes while offline by default* — the spec's §6 open question (*"Behaviour with no network or when a project's backend is unreachable"*) and P6.10's gate. **No agent runs any step of it.** **The guard stops today**: the offline gate is P6.10's (it extends `mobile/src/mailbox/`), and a phone cannot be signed in at all before P6.6 and P6.8 are built (sign-in is custom tokens only, and the token is the pairing's).

**What the check is about, and what a unit test cannot see.** P6.10's tests run over a fake connection state: with no connection, or a stale consumer, nothing is written, the user is told, an action record is never queued, and the client never relies on the SDK's own offline queue. Those tests prove the client's **code**; this check proves the client's **behaviour on a phone** with the radio actually off — the case where the SDK, not this code, decides what happens to a write that was issued anyway. The dangerous shape is a command **replayed on reconnect**: the user spoke it once, offline, was told it was not sent, and a queue delivers it later as if it had been said then.

**Guard block — re-run this before every step.** It stops unless the checkout carries the mailbox client the gate extends, the app's voice module, the pairing command and the consumer: this check is a conversation between all four.

```bash
# === Check 104: setup + guard. RE-RUN THIS BLOCK BEFORE EVERY STEP. ===
set -u
ROOT=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null) || { echo "Check 104 stopped: not inside a git checkout; the app, the consumer and the gate all come from this repository" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -d "$ROOT/mobile/src/mailbox" ] || { echo "Check 104 stopped: there is no mobile/src/mailbox/ in this checkout, so the client the offline gate is part of is not on this tree (P3.6 builds it, P6.10 adds the gate)" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/internal/cli/mailbox.go" ] || { echo "Check 104 stopped: there is no internal/cli/mailbox.go in this checkout, so there is no consumer to be running (or stopped) while the phone is offline — P4.1 builds it and P6.7 gives it the enforcement this check's commands go through" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -f "$ROOT/internal/cli/pair.go" ] || { echo "Check 104 stopped: there is no internal/cli/pair.go in this checkout, so the phone cannot be paired and has no token to speak a command with (Task P6.6)" >&2; exit 1; }
[ -d "$ROOT/mobile/src/voice" ] || { echo "Check 104 stopped: there is no mobile/src/voice/ in this checkout, so no command can be spoken at the phone (P3.5; P6.12 adds the spoken confirmation)" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "Check 104 ready: nothing spoken while the phone is disconnected is sent, and nothing is queued — the mailbox is read back with your own credentials at every step"
```

1. **The baseline: the conversation works.** *(Guard block, run by you; then check 81's guard block in the same shell, which resolves `$DB`. This step sets `$MB`, which steps 2-4 read.)* Pair the phone (check 100) and run the consumer in your own terminal. Read the phone's own uid off `fugaro pair ls` — that uid is the mailbox's `$mb`, so it is `MB` — and speak one non-destructive command with everything connected, letting it complete. **FACT:** the run id or the answer it produced, the message id in `mailbox/$MB/inbox/`, and the timestamp — the **control**: without it, a later "nothing was sent" is unreadable. Read the mailbox back with your own credentials:

   ```bash
   MB=<the paired phone's uid, as 'fugaro pair ls' prints it>   # the mailbox's $mb — never $UID, which is your numeric user id
   AT=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)   # never printed, never pasted
   curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $AT" "https://$DB/mailbox/$MB/outbox.json"
   ```

2. **Airplane mode: the phone cannot send, and says so.** *(Guard block, run by you, on the phone; this step reads `$MB` from step 1.)* Put the phone in **airplane mode**, then speak a non-destructive command and a **destructive** one ("cancel that" for the run from step 1). **FACT:** what the app said — that it is offline, in the app's own words, rather than accepting the command and going quiet; **FACT:** the mailbox with your own credentials: **no new inbox message** (the id count is the same as step 1's), no new outbox message, the consumer logged **nothing** — and the run was **not** cancelled: the phone's action record never left it. **FACT:** the app did not fall back to a second path (no direct write to a REST endpoint, no session queued in the phone's storage): record what the app's own state shows about pending work, and that nothing is waiting to be sent.

3. **A stale consumer, with the network back but the phone's own view offline.** *(Guard block, run by you; this step reads `$MB` from step 1.)* Bring the radio back, **stop the consumer**, and speak a command. The phone's own client already knows this state without the network being down: P3.6's presence reads the heartbeat, and the app shows the consumer as stale rather than online (`mobile/src/mailbox`'s own states). **FACT:** the app's own reason (a long silence, an unsigned heartbeat — the states the client's tests walk), that the command was refused at the phone, that the mailbox gained no message, and that the **consumer did not answer it later** when you start it again: a stale consumer is not a queue. **FACT:** what the app said to you, and that it did not pretend to have delivered anything.

4. **Reconnecting must not replay (U3's half).** *(Guard block, run by you; this step reads `$MB` from step 1.)* With the consumer running again and the connection back, look before you speak: **FACT:** the mailbox shows **nothing new** — the commands spoken in steps 2 and 3 were not delivered late, and no action record exists for them (the consumer's ledger has no entry for them, which is the check U3 is about: the SDK's own offline queue is the mechanism that would have delivered one). Then speak the **positive control**: a fresh non-destructive command. **FACT:** it appears once, the consumer acts on it once, and the answer reaches the app — the same command, in the same session, behaving exactly as step 1's did. The double-delivery case itself is **check 83**'s, not this one's.

5. **What the app is allowed to hold offline.** *(Guard block, run by you; read-only.)* **FACT:** what the phone stored while it was offline — the pending prompt queue (P6.5's, which is legitimate: a queued prompt is a question, not a command) and **no** action record, no outbound message, no confirmation — and that the destructive command you spoke offline produced nothing at all, not a queued action waiting for a consent it already had. **FACT:** that the queue's own bound (the pending-prompt cap, D173/P6.5) is what bounds storage offline, and that the phone was told what happened to each thing it could not send. **FACT:** the app never wrote to the database through a path of its own: every write the check sees came from the app's client with its own token, and the rules would have refused anything else (check 81's fence).

**Passes when:** step 1's control reaches the mailbox and is acted on once; step 2's offline commands produce **no** inbox message, no outbox message, no consumer log and no cancellation, with the app saying it is offline; step 3's stale-consumer command is refused at the phone and never delivered when the consumer returns; step 4 shows nothing replayed and the positive control behaving exactly like step 1's; and step 5 finds prompts (if any) but **no** action record, message or confirmation held on the phone.

**Fails when:** an offline command reaches the mailbox at all — sent directly, through a second path, or delivered when the connection returns (that is the SDK's queue doing what U3 suspected, and P6.10's whole subject); a destructive command spoken offline is cancelled, either when spoken or later; the app accepts a command while offline without telling the user it was not sent; the app treats a stale consumer as online; a command delivered late is acted on twice (check 83's case, arriving here); or the app writes anything the rules do not grant it (check 81's fence, failing in the offline path).

**Paste back:** step 1's control (command, message id, timestamp); what the app said offline and its own reason for the stale consumer; the node counts before and after each offline step, and that nothing new appeared; the consumer's log for the offline window; that no action record was held or delivered; the positive control's result; and what the phone held offline (prompt queue counts only). **Never paste a token, an ID token, a MAC key or a message's `mac`.**

**Restore.** Nothing to undo beyond what the check did on purpose:

- The commands spoken offline were never sent, so there is nothing to withdraw — that is the check's result; the run from step 1 and the positive control are the sandbox installation's ordinary work.
- The phone's prompt queue is whatever it was: a prompt with no answer expires at D118's TTL and the consumer hands the orchestrator its non-destructive answer (P6.5/P6.7) — if the check left one waiting, let it expire rather than deleting it by hand, because the expiry path is what the mailbox is built around.
- Nothing in this repository changed: no node was written by hand (check 81's seeding is not needed here), no rules change, no commit.

## Check 111: the billing picker's failure modes — nothing listed, nothing enabled (installation `fugaro`, throwaway projects only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** This check is new (setup-wizard plan Task W0.3 writes it, Task W6.2 runs it), and number **111** is the first free number above every claim the register above records — 110 is claimed by an open pull request, and a claim is settled at its merge. Its subject is the other half of the billing picker: **Check 27 step 3 is the picker's success path against a real account, and this is what it does when it cannot list one.**

**Nothing here is a claim that any of it works: no mode of it has ever been run.** The setup-wizard implementation plan is *"approved to build; implementation in progress"* (`docs/setup-wizard/implementation-plan.md:13`, the owner's approval of 2026-10-20), and the tree now carries the half of it this check reads: `internal/cli/root.go` registers `setup` and `update` (W1.2–W1.3); `internal/billing/` holds the account-list client (W4.1) and the `gcloud billing accounts list` fallback (W4.2), and `internal/cli/billing_prompt.go` holds the picker itself (W4.3) and D3's answer when the API is off — the typed offer on the project being set up, the refusal naming another quota project (W4.4) — whose tests drive it through a stubbed terminal predicate (`stdinIsTerminal`) rather than a pty; `internal/preflight/google.go`'s `Billing()` reads the same answer the same way (W4.4); and `internal/gcpfake/billing.go` fakes the account list (`billingAccounts.list`) as well as a project's billing *link*. **What has never happened is the run**: the picker has not been exercised against a real service, and no mode below has been run at all. W4.4 is written on this tree, so what modes 1 and 2 expect of the picker — mode 1(a)'s offer and its decline, mode 1(b)'s refusal naming the line and who to ask — is written too; W4.5 (the comments the reversal falsifies, and the one test that keeps the half of the old rule that survives) is still open, and what it leaves unwritten is prose and the picker's own bounds, not a behaviour a mode here reads. This section is written because the plan says so (W0.3), and the owner runs it at **W6.2**, against a release that carries the picker.

**What it settles (D3 and D6, plan Tasks W4.1–W4.5).** The picker lists the owner's **open** billing accounts by number, at a real terminal only, and **prefers the Cloud Billing API with `gcloud billing accounts list` as a fallback** — it says which one answered, and it is never allowed to list anything at all when `canType()` is false (a real terminal, not `--json`, not a coding agent's session). Every failure mode below must therefore end in the **same three places**, and each mode asserts all three:

1. the **guided line** — `gcloud billing projects link <project> --billing-account=<billing-account-id>`, the line `internal/cli/init_project.go`'s `guided()` prints today — reaches the owner, together with how to find the account's ID (the console, or `gcloud billing accounts list`). **The hint is why the words "billing accounts" are expected in the output and are not a leak**; what must never appear is a list of *accounts* — a display name of yours, or an id;
2. **no API's state changed**: none was turned **on** in any project — the only way this check may ever enable one is mode 1(a)'s typed offer, which is **declined** here — and none was turned **off** either, since mode 2 runs against an API that must stay enabled (`S`);
3. **no account list appears in any output** — not on stdout, not on stderr, not in `--json`'s document: no display name, no numbered list, no `billingAccounts/<id>`.

**A mode here is a failure mode only when *neither* source can answer.** The picker prefers the Cloud Billing API and falls back to `gcloud billing accounts list`; if the fallback can answer, it lists the accounts, which is the **designed** behaviour and Check 27 step 3's success path — not this check. So modes 1(a), 1(b) and 2(b) run with the fallback **maimed by hand** (a `gcloud` wrapper that fails only at `billing accounts`, below: the wizard's own `gcloud` calls must keep working, so removing `gcloud` from `PATH` is *not* the way), and mode 2(a) is the one run here where a list **is** expected — through the fallback, and it is recorded rather than failed.

**Rules.** Use the installation **named `fugaro`** (`N`) on your **throwaway** project (`P` — one that **`fugaro setup` created**, so it carries the label `fugaro_created=true` (a project made any other way is refused: `fugaro setup` adopts only one that holds nothing of Fugaro's, and a project with an installation in it does not), and that **exists**, has Firebase and has **no billing account linked to it**: Check 27's own project has one, from its step 3, so unlink it first (`gcloud billing projects unlink "${P:?}"`) or use another project). Two more throwaway projects of yours are needed, and **you prepare them before mode 1** — no step of this check creates a project, enables or disables an API, links an account or writes a config. Every mode runs with `--create-project`, because `P` has a local config (its installation has converged), and a run with a project config registers the project stage only when that flag says so: without it no mode would reach the project stage at all. With it, the stage reads `P`, which `fugaro setup` created, and resumes it rather than refusing it. The flag puts the project stage in the run, and `--gcp-project "${P:?}"` keeps the run on `P` rather than on the id `setup` offers (`fugaro-fugaro`), which would be a different project.

Because `--create-project` on a project `fugaro setup` created that is already there resumes it and creates nothing, the guided line assertion 1 reads is the **project stage**'s — and the stage prints it as its **left-for-you** line only when `P` **exists**, is **`ACTIVE`**, **has Firebase** and has **no billing link**. In modes 3, 4 and 5 that is the only place it can come from, since their picker never runs; in modes 1 and 2 it is the only place too, since there neither source answers (mode 2(a) alone lists, through the fallback, and the owner answers its prompt `none` — see mode 2(a)). So run every mode on a `P` that is there, is `ACTIVE`, has Firebase and is not linked to an account — an installation that has converged, with nothing linked — or assertion 1 reads something else: a project **without Firebase** is a *todo* whose left-for-you is the add-Firebase typed confirmation (the guided line is then in the plan view's detail alone), a project **linked to an enabled account** is reported **done** and prints the line nowhere, and a project that is **not there yet** is a creation run that stops at the project stage's typed confirmation. **A fresh project is not the easy one**: it has no installation, so modes 3, 4 and 5 stop at that typed confirmation, and the guided line they exist to read is not the stage's own.

- **`Q`**, whose Cloud Billing API is **off**: the ADC quota project of mode 1(b), where the API being disabled on the quota project is the whole premise.
- **`S`**, whose Cloud Billing API is **on**: the ADC quota project of mode 2, where the API must be reachable for the caller's missing permission to be what refuses (403), rather than the disabled-API path mode 1 already covers.

Never `belong` (the installation on `edge-devel-dimi`), `fugaro-dev` or `edge-devel-dimi` itself. Run every command in your own terminal, in `bash`, with a **release build** of `fugaro` that carries the picker — **0.10.0 or later** — and record `fugaro version`, the date and the OS first. **No agent runs any step of this check** — and one of its five modes *is* an agent session, so mode 5 must be run by you, in a session you deliberately mark, never by handing the step to an agent. **What this check does reach outside your own shell is your ADC (application-default credentials)** — modes 1(a), 1(b) and 2 repoint its **quota project** (`P`, `Q`, `S`), and mode 2 also changes which **account** it is logged in as; the Restore's first lines put both back, and they are not optional. Every step is otherwise a refusal, so the check itself costs nothing beyond the projects you made.

**Run it:** `bash scripts/live-checks/check111.sh --project <P> --account-names <file> [--account-ids <file>] [--api-off-project <Q>] [--api-on-project <S>] [--second-account <email> [--second-adc <file>] | --role-removed] [--region <region>] [--modes 1a,1b,2a,2b,3,4,5] [--dry-run]` — **you** run it, at your own terminal, and **no agent runs it**: an agent's session is one of the modes it observes, so the script refuses to start in one. It is the whole block below — the guard block, the seven runs, the assertion block and the Restore — as one command that does its own setup. **Mode 2 is the one run whose caller is not you**, and `--second-adc` is how one command gets both callers: it names the second account's own Application Default Credentials saved to a file before the run (the manual line below carries the three commands that make it), and the script copies that file over gcloud's ADC file for mode 2's two runs alone, putting **yours** back, byte for byte, as soon as each of them is done — so a `--modes` list that names 2(a) without 2(b) still leaves the modes after it running as you — and again from its exit trap whatever ends the run, which also removes the copy you passed whenever the run put your own file back — so make it a throwaway (the manual line has you create it with `mktemp`, mode 0600, at a name nobody could prepare in advance) and no copy of a login outlives a run that used one. That per-run swap is what keeps modes 1(a), 1(b), 3, 4 and 5 under the login each of them is written for. `--second-account` **without** `--second-adc` declares that account the caller of the **whole** run, which only a run of modes 2(a) and 2(b) alone may be (`--modes 2a,2b`); any wider combination is refused before anything is called, because mode 1(a)'s project stage reads its own project through those credentials and a caller that lacks `billing.accounts.list` is exactly what mode 2 exists to see. Its scratch directory holds the maimed `gcloud` wrapper, this check's own config root and each mode's capture; it refuses to start when `P`, `Q` or `S` names `belong`, `fugaro-dev` or `edge-devel-dimi`, when `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` was pointed somewhere before it, when your ADC carries no quota project it could put back, or under a trace (a trace of these runs carries the accounts mode 2(a) lists); it takes the IDE extension's `CLAUDE_CODE_SSE_PORT` out of modes 3 and 4's own children alone, because with no terminal that marker is a coding agent's session and those two runs are a person's shell whose input is not a terminal — the marker itself is recorded and not refused, since the IDE extension sets it in a person's own terminal too; it prints a PASS or FAIL per criterion with the exact text it read; and it ends with `CHECK 111 RESULT: PASS|FAIL` and the `FACT` block to paste into the register. The Restore above is its exit trap, so the APIs it disabled are enabled again, your ADC's own quota project is put back, and your own ADC file — not the second account's — is what a run that used `--second-adc` leaves behind, when an assertion fails or you press Ctrl-C as much as on the way out; a swap it could not undo says so in its restore row and names the by-hand login — and a mode that was not run is a `FAIL`, never a pass. **`--dry-run` prints every command a real run would run and every command its Restore would undo, and runs none of them: it calls nothing at all** — use it first, because the real run disables an API in two throwaway projects and repoints your ADC. **One step no script may run for you:** mode 2's premise is a caller without `billing.accounts.list`, which takes a browser (the second account's login) or your own IAM (the billing role removed from your account), so the script prints it as its single manual line — the three commands that log the second account in, save its credentials file aside and log you back in, what to pass to `--second-adc`, and what to paste back. **The status stays `NOT RUN`:** its own test, `scripts/live-checks/check111_test.sh`, drives it against fakes on `PATH` with no network and no cloud project, which is a test of the script and not a run of this check — no agent runs any step of the check itself, and W6.2 is where you run it.

⚠ **Set these, and pass the hard stops, by running ONE block — and re-run that whole block at the start of every mode.** The project ids and the installation's name are **hard-coded in the block, never read from `gcloud`**, and every `gcloud` command below that names a project carries `--project="${VAR:?}"` (or `${VAR:?}` as its argument). **Starting over:** `rm -rf /tmp/chk111`, then run the block again.

```bash
# === Check 111: guard. RE-RUN THIS WHOLE BLOCK at the start of every mode
# (1a, 1b, 2a, 2b, 3, 4, 5). It reads its own state back out of vars.env, so a
# mode typed in a NEW SHELL keeps the same config root. ===
CHK111=/tmp/chk111; mkdir -p "$CHK111"; chmod 700 "$CHK111"
P=fugaro-live-20261020   # YOUR throwaway project, which EXISTS, has Firebase and has NO billing link: HARD-CODED
N=fugaro                 # the installation's NAME: hard-coded, and asserted below
Q=                       # a SECOND throwaway project of yours, Cloud Billing API OFF: mode 1(b) only, checked by need_q below
S=                       # a THIRD throwaway project of yours, Cloud Billing API ON: mode 2 only, checked by need_s below

# This check's own config root. It is written down ONCE, in the check's own
# directory, and read back from there: a later shell has no C of its own, and
# ${C:-…} would only have reused it inside one shell.
# NOTHING of yours is installed here — this check creates no installation at all
# — the root exists so that the machine's own installations are never read or
# written by any mode below.
[ -f "$CHK111/vars.env" ] || printf 'C=%s\n' "$CHK111/config" > "$CHK111/vars.env"
. "$CHK111/vars.env"
# This stop runs BEFORE the export below, and that is the point: it refuses a
# shell that is ALREADY pointed somewhere else (your real ~/.config, or another
# check's root), which is what a half-pasted or skipped block leaves behind.
# After the export it could never fail.
[ -z "${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-}" ] || [ "$XDG_CONFIG_HOME" = "${C:?}" ] \
  || { echo "Check 111 stopped: this shell's XDG_CONFIG_HOME ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME) is not this check's root ($C). Unset it, or start the mode in a fresh shell: the machine's own installations must never be read." >&2; exit 1; }
export XDG_CONFIG_HOME="${C:?}"
mkdir -p "$XDG_CONFIG_HOME"

case "$P" in
  ""|belong|fugaro-dev|edge-devel-dimi|fugaro-belong)
    echo "Check 111 stopped: P=$P is empty or names a project this check never touches (belong on edge-devel-dimi, fugaro-dev). Set P to your own throwaway project." >&2; exit 1;;
esac
case "${C:?}" in
  "$CHK111"/*) ;;
  *) echo "Check 111 stopped: vars.env's C=$C is not under $CHK111 — this check never points XDG_CONFIG_HOME at anything but its own directory" >&2; exit 1;;
esac
[ "$N" = fugaro ] || { echo "Check 111 stopped: this check runs on the installation named fugaro (N=$N)" >&2; exit 1; }
[ "$XDG_CONFIG_HOME" = "$CHK111/config" ] || { echo "Check 111 stopped: the block did not leave XDG_CONFIG_HOME at this check's root (it is $XDG_CONFIG_HOME)" >&2; exit 1; }

# The display names of YOUR billing accounts, one per line, written ONCE before
# mode 1. They are what a leak would print, and no check can know them.
[ -s "$CHK111/account-names.txt" ] || { echo "Check 111 stopped: write your billing accounts' display names to $CHK111/account-names.txt first, one per line — they are the strings a leak would print" >&2; exit 1; }

need_q() {   # mode 1(b): an unset Q must stop the mode, never no-op it
  [ -n "${Q:-}" ] || { echo "Check 111 stopped: mode $1 needs Q — a second throwaway project of yours whose Cloud Billing API is off. Set it at the top of this block." >&2; return 1; }
  [ "$Q" != "$P" ] || { echo "Check 111 stopped: Q must not be P — mode 1(b) is about the quota project being ANOTHER project" >&2; return 1; }
  case "$Q" in belong|fugaro-dev|edge-devel-dimi|fugaro-belong)
    echo "Check 111 stopped: Q=$Q names a project this check never touches" >&2; return 1;; esac
}
need_s() {   # mode 2: same stops for S, and S must be neither of the other two
  [ -n "${S:-}" ] || { echo "Check 111 stopped: mode $1 needs S — a third throwaway project of yours whose Cloud Billing API is ON. Set it at the top of this block." >&2; return 1; }
  [ "$S" != "$P" ] && [ "$S" != "${Q:-}" ] || { echo "Check 111 stopped: S must be its own project — mode 2 is about an API that IS enabled, which P and Q are not" >&2; return 1; }
  case "$S" in belong|fugaro-dev|edge-devel-dimi|fugaro-belong)
    echo "Check 111 stopped: S=$S names a project this check never touches" >&2; return 1;; esac
}
need_s_enabled() {   # the state mode 2's premise requires, asserted BEFORE the run:
  local got           # with the API off on S the mode would take the disabled-API
                      # path mode 1 already covers, and would prove nothing
  got=$(gcloud services list --enabled --project="${S:?}" --filter='config.name:cloudbilling.googleapis.com' --format='value(config.name)' | wc -l)
  # -ge, not =: this check is written for macOS too, where wc pads its count
  # ("       1"), and a string test would stop mode 2 on the very state it
  # requires. ${got:-0} keeps an empty read from being a syntax error.
  [ "${got:-0}" -ge 1 ] || { echo "Check 111 stopped: mode $1 needs cloudbilling.googleapis.com ENABLED on S=$S (it reads $got) — enable it and re-run this block" >&2; return 1; }
}

# The fallback, maimed BY HAND where a mode needs neither source to answer: a
# gcloud that fails only at `billing accounts` and passes everything else to the
# real one, so the wizard's own gcloud calls keep working (removing gcloud from
# PATH would break the wizard long before the billing stage).
PATH=${PATH//"$CHK111/bin:"/}; export PATH   # un-maimed by default, at every mode
REAL_GCLOUD=$(command -v gcloud) || true
[ -n "$REAL_GCLOUD" ] || { echo "Check 111 stopped: no gcloud on PATH — this check needs one" >&2; exit 1; }
export REAL_GCLOUD
mkdir -p "$CHK111/bin"
cat > "$CHK111/bin/gcloud" <<'WRAP'
#!/bin/sh
case "$*" in
  *"billing accounts"*) echo "gcloud: billing accounts list is unavailable in this run" >&2; exit 1;;
esac
exec "$REAL_GCLOUD" "$@"
WRAP
chmod +x "$CHK111/bin/gcloud"
maim_fallback() { PATH="$CHK111/bin:$PATH"; export PATH; echo "the gcloud fallback is maimed: $CHK111/bin/gcloud is first on PATH"; }

# capture <mode> <command…> — a TYPED run, through a pty (script(1)), so the
# prompts, the picker and your answers all land in that mode's own transcript and
# the run still sees a real terminal (canType()). Both streams interleave there.
# (On macOS, script is BSD's: `script -q "$CHK111/mode-$m.log" <command…>`, and
# the exit code is the transcript's last line.)
capture() {
  local m=${1:?}; shift
  local f="$CHK111/mode-$m.log"
  script -q -e -c "$(printf '%q ' "$@")" "$f"
  echo "mode $m exit: $? — transcript in $f"
  # script's own two lines, not the run's: dropped so the capture is what the run
  # printed. Its line endings are the pty's; the greps in assert_mode are not
  # affected by them.
  grep -v -e '^Script started on ' -e '^Script done on ' "$f" > "$f.clean" && mv "$f.clean" "$f"
}
# plain <mode> <command…> — an UNTYPED run (no TTY, the agent marker): both
# streams into one file and NO pty, which is the point of modes 3 and 5.
plain() {
  local m=${1:?}; shift
  "$@" > "$CHK111/mode-$m.log" 2>&1
  echo "mode $m exit: $? — output in $CHK111/mode-$m.log"
}
```

**The stops are the ones a skipped or half-pasted block fails.** An empty or forbidden `P`; an `N` that is not `fugaro`; a shell whose `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` was already pointed elsewhere; a `vars.env` whose `C` is not under `$CHK111`; a block that did not leave `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` at this check's own root; and a missing `account-names.txt`. `Q` stops its own mode through `need_q` and through `${Q:?}` on the one `gcloud` line that names it, and `S` through `need_s` and `need_s_enabled` — **both ship empty on purpose**: an unset `Q` or `S` must stop its mode, not silently point your ADC at nothing (or run mode 2 with the API off on `S`, where it would take mode 1's disabled-API path and prove nothing) while you believe the mode ran.

**Three modes reach outside your shell; the rest are refusals and nothing more.** Modes **1(a)**, **1(b)** and **2** each repoint **your own ADC quota project** — at `P`, `Q` and `S` respectively — which is why the Restore's first line is not optional; mode 2 also has you log ADC in as a second account (below), which the Restore's second line undoes. Run them in the order below or in any other — there is no step here that must come last. Modes 3, 4 and 5 change nothing outside your shell at all: their picker never runs, so the quota project does not decide them, but **put your own back before you leave them behind** rather than ending the day with your machine pointed at a throwaway.

**The five modes** — seven runs, because modes 1 and 2 each split in two. Every run keeps its **own** capture under `$CHK111`, and the assertion block below refuses to read a mode whose capture is missing: a mode that was never run is never read as a pass.

1. **The Cloud Billing API is disabled on the quota project** — and **D3 splits this in two**, which is why it is two sub-modes rather than one. Both disable the API on the project concerned first (`gcloud services disable cloudbilling.googleapis.com --project=<project> --force` — a *throwaway* project only, never one you need), both maim the fallback first (`maim_fallback`: neither source may answer here), and both then run the wizard at a real terminal. What separates them is **which project your ADC quota project is**, and that is the whole of D3:
   **(a) The quota project IS the project being set up.** `gcloud auth application-default set-quota-project "${P:?}"`, then:

    ```bash
    maim_fallback
    capture 1a fugaro setup --create-project --gcp-project "${P:?}" --name "$N" --region us-east5 --budget-mode observe
    assert_mode 1a
    ```

   `--create-project` is what makes this the creation path, and the mode needs it: `P` already has a local config, so without the flag the run registers no project stage, and the guided line this mode asserts would never print. The flag puts the stage in the run, and `--gcp-project "${P:?}"` keeps the run on `P`: `setup` offers the id `fugaro-<name>`, i.e. `fugaro-fugaro`, and accepting that default would create a different project, so the mode would test neither D3(a) nor `P`. This also needs `P` to be in the state the Rules state — it **exists**, is `ACTIVE`, has Firebase and has **no billing link**: the project stage reads it, sees it is there and creates nothing — and a project a run created could not be its own quota project — so no run here creates anything. The wizard **may offer to enable** `cloudbilling.googleapis.com`, naming the project and the API, behind a **typed** confirmation that no flag covers (D3, D12 — and note this is the one place in the whole wizard where enabling an API is offered at all). **Decline it**, and record: the offer's exact text; that no flag took it (it takes your typed answer, and the picker never runs under a flag); and then the assertions — the guided line, `gcloud services list --enabled --project="${P:?}" --filter='config.name:cloudbilling.googleapis.com'` printing **nothing**, and no account list anywhere. **FACT:** the offer, the decline, and that the API is still disabled after it.
   **(b) The quota project is ANOTHER project.** `need_q 1b && maim_fallback`, then:

    ```bash
    gcloud auth application-default set-quota-project "${Q:?}"
    capture 1b fugaro setup --create-project --gcp-project "${P:?}" --name "$N" --region us-east5 --budget-mode observe
    assert_mode 1b
    ```

   Expect a **refusal** — not an offer — that names the exact `gcloud services enable cloudbilling.googleapis.com --project "${Q:?}"` line **and who to ask**, and that enables nothing anywhere. **FACT:** the exact line, the project it names, whether it names a person or a role to ask, that `Q`'s API is still disabled, that `P`'s API is still disabled, and that no account list appeared.
2. **A user without `billing.accounts.list`.** The API is **enabled** here (on `S`, this mode's quota project) and the caller nevertheless lacks the permission, so the API answers **403** — the refusal mode 1's disabled API does not produce. The permission lives on the billing accounts, not on a project: **a second Google account with no billing role is the reliable way** (`gcloud auth application-default login` choosing that account; grant it `roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageConsumer` on `S` so the call is allowed to be made at all, and nothing more), and **removing the role from your own account by hand is the other** — but only for 2(b), because 2(a) needs the *other* source to be able to answer. **Record which route you took.** This mode is two runs, because the two sources must be tried **separately** — with both able to answer, the fallback's answer hides the API's refusal.

   `need_s 2a` and `need_s_enabled 2a` first: an `S` whose API is off would take mode 1's path and prove nothing.
   **(a) The fallback answers — the one run in this check where a list is expected.** ADC is logged in as the second account (no permission) and `gcloud`'s own login is your usual one (which has it), and **no `maim_fallback` here**:

    ```bash
    gcloud auth application-default set-quota-project "${S:?}"
    capture 2a fugaro setup --create-project --gcp-project "${P:?}" --name "$N" --region us-east5 --budget-mode observe
    assert_mode 2a may-list
    ```

   **At the picker's prompt, answer `none` — not a number.** This is the one run where the list itself is what the mode is about, and `none` is the picker's own way out of it: it prints the guided line (`billing_prompt.go`'s `billingLeft`), records no account, and leaves `--link-billing` empty. A number would set it, and the project stage would then take its **link** branch — its plan detail reads `link billing account <ID> (its own typed confirmation; may incur charges)` and its left-for-you is that typed confirmation, so the words `gcloud billing projects link` would appear **nowhere** in the capture and assertion 1 would fail — and typing the confirmation would link that account to `P`, which this section's Rules forbid and which nothing else here undoes. **Record that you answered `none`.**
