## Check 148: the read consumer's stop, rotation and ownership transfer (a sandbox installation with the read mint deployed, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **T0.2** of the Bitbucket-credentials plan
([bitbucket-credentials/implementation-plan.md](bitbucket-credentials/implementation-plan.md), its
"Checks this plan takes (Checks 145–154)" and its task **T3.8**; D367, and **D1961**). The plan's
verdict for T3.8 is **superseded in part, kept in part**: the run-mint half goes with S3, and the
**read half** — the read consumer's own stop, rotation and ownership transfer, with **U13** — is
kept, because the read consumer is merged and shipped and nothing else exercises its rotation. What
this row and section register is that half, which the folder's own reconciliation already carries as
live (**148** "in S2 with only its read half live",
[bitbucket-credentials/reconciliation-secrets-brokering.md](bitbucket-credentials/reconciliation-secrets-brokering.md),
its "Numbers this work holds"; D1961's own cell reads **2026-11-10: recommended**, and the plan's
checks table carries the verdict in place). The script that runs it is this task's —
`scripts/live-checks/check148.sh`, with its own test `check148_test.sh` — and the owner runs it
beside **T2.6**, whose runbook section (**§12**, "The Bitbucket read consumer: creating it, and
stopping, rotating and transferring it") it executes step by step.

**What the check measures.** Three changes to the bundle entry `bitbucket-read-consumer`
(`key`, `secret`, `workspace`), each confirmed against the read mint at
`POST <service>/v1/bitbucket/read-token` with a body of `{"repository":"<owner/name>"}`, and each
read through the credential-carrying checks the drill makes:

- **the stop** — the entry is taken out of the bundle and a read mint is then **refused**, and the
  refusal is the service's own: **503** with `error: state_unavailable` **carrying
  `ErrReadNoConsumer`'s own sentence** — `internal/credsvc`'s `ErrReadNoConsumer` through
  `refuseRead` and `internal/credsvc/wire.go`'s statuses. All three readings are needed, because the
  status and the type are not the missing consumer's alone: `internal/credsvc/bitbucket.go` answers
  the operator's stop switches it cannot read, the kill switch, a bundle that fails to load, a
  failed Bitbucket exchange, a token whose scopes this route will not hand on
  (`ErrReadUnexpectedScopes`) and a failed audit with the same `503 state_unavailable` — an example
  rather than the whole of the list, since an answer it could not build is another — so only the
  message tells them apart. That is the only answer the row counts as a stop: a curl timeout, a
  Cloud Run 429 or 5xx, a `503 state_unavailable` whose message is another state's, or an answer
  that is not a document is the run **not knowing**, so the script keeps waiting and then fails the
  row with the answer it got, rather than reporting a stop that may never have happened. No Fugaro command
  removes a bundle entry (`fugaro creds set` is the bundle's only writer and only ever adds or
  replaces), so the drill makes this version **by hand** — `gcloud secrets versions add`, with the
  version it replaced **disabled** — and that is what the row says it does;
- **the rotation** — the consumer's secret regenerated at Bitbucket **at the step that asks for it**,
  the bundle written again with `fugaro creds set`, and the mint **served** from the new one while the
  **old** secret's own `client_credentials` grant at the OAuth endpoint is **refused**: a rotation
  that leaves the old secret alive is a **FAIL**. The ask is the order the drill turns on: Bitbucket's
  regeneration is what kills the secret the bundle holds, so a run that started with the rotated
  document already written would be minting a dead secret from its baseline row — the drill asks, waits
  for the answer, holds what was written to the consumer file's own key and workspace, and only then
  writes it;
- **the ownership transfer** — a successor consumer created under a **second** sandbox account,
  written into the bundle, and a read mint confirmed against it. What the transfer leaves behind is
  the bundle holding the **successor**, which is what the transfer is, and **one** consumer to delete
  at Bitbucket: the one the drill replaced — the consumer whose secret the rotation regenerated,
  which is also the consumer the transfer replaced, since the rotation and the transfer are about the
  same one — while the successor is the bundle's entry now and stays;
- **U13**, the open question this check exists for: whether a token minted **before** the rotation
  still reads. The drill replays the pre-rotation token against the API root after the rotation and
  records the answer either way — it is an **INFO** line, not a pass or a fail, because the
  reconciliation carries U13 as **UNVERIFIED** and this check is what settles it. If it shows the
  token still reads, the runbook's rotation clause and `SECURITY.md`'s custody paragraph
  (**T2.11**) are corrected in the same sweep, not worked around.

The service serves the **parsed** bundle for 30 seconds (`credsvc.BundleCacheTTL`), so every write
is followed by a bounded wait before the mint is read: a mint read too soon after a write is the old
document's answer, and a check that took it as the new one's would report a stop that had not
happened. The wait cuts both ways, and the served direction is the one a bound alone cannot settle:
the document a write **replaced** answers a 200 too, so a reading taken while that document is still
cacheable cannot tell the write being served from the write not having landed.
`CHECK148_MINT_WAIT` is that bound in seconds (default 90, 0 meaning one attempt), and
`CHECK148_CACHE_WAIT` is the lifetime a reading has to be taken after before it is read as the
write's own document (default 40; the row says the wait it took).

**What you type** (task T3.8's read half, beside T2.6):

```bash
scripts/live-checks/check148.sh \
  --installation <sandbox> --repo <owner/name> \
  --consumer-file <path> --rotated-consumer-file <path> --successor-consumer-file <path>
```

Two of the three files exist before the run: the consumer document the bundle holds today, and the
successor created under the second sandbox account. The third — the same consumer with the secret
Bitbucket regenerates — is **written by you during the run**, at the rotation step that asks for it,
and naming its path here is saying where you will write it. Each is the mapping the entry holds —
`key`, `secret`, `workspace`, one per line — and the script **never
prints, echoes or passes one on a command line**: they reach `fugaro creds set` on stdin and the
shell never holds a value. Its own test (`bash scripts/live-checks/check148_test.sh`, run against
fake tools on PATH and a fake Bitbucket Cloud on a loopback port, with no network and no cloud
project) fails if a secret or a minted token is ever written to the output or left in the scratch
directory, and its fake Bitbucket answers a mint only for a consumer its OAuth state **would
exchange**, not for one the bundle merely holds — which is what makes a drill that wrote the rotated
document before asking for the regeneration fail rather than pass.

The script asks for **two** things, and the second cannot be answered by a flag. One line is the
confirmation: it says what it will write and asks you to type the **project ID**, unless you passed
`--yes`. The other is at the rotation, where it tells you to regenerate the consumer's secret at
Bitbucket **now**, write that document to `--rotated-consumer-file` and type `ROTATED`, and it waits
for you. `--yes` stands for the confirmation alone. Anything else at either prompt stops without
writing.

**What it depends on.** The deployed read mint — **T2.4** (the service's Terraform) and **T2.5**
(the read path) — and **T2.6**'s runbook section, which this check executes; the row and the section
are **T0.2**'s. It is a **sandbox** check: `belong` is refused before any write **by every name it
arrives under** — the one you typed as `--installation`, and the name **and** the project ID the
config in force answers with, which is what catches it, since the owner's installation is named
`belong` in the project `fugaro-belong` and a guard reading only the project ID would pass. Nothing
runs in CI, and **no agent runs any step of it**.

**Restore.** The script cleans up after itself, including on a Ctrl-C: the scratch directory — which
holds the whole bundle document while the stop is being made, and every token the drill mints — is
removed, and its `restore` row says whether it really went. **The bundle is not put back the way it
was**: it ends holding the successor consumer, which is the transfer, and the `restore` row names
**one** consumer to delete at Bitbucket once you have pasted the block back — the consumer the drill
replaced, which is the rotation's and the transfer's same one — while the successor is the bundle's
entry now and stays. A run that stopped before the transfer confirms nothing about the bundle's
entry, and the row says so and sends you to `fugaro creds ls` instead of naming a consumer. **Never
run any step against `belong`**, and **no agent runs any step of it**.

## Check 149: the console shows the stored view on the owner's own machine (your own machine, read-only; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **T0.2** of the Bitbucket-credentials plan
([bitbucket-credentials/implementation-plan.md](bitbucket-credentials/implementation-plan.md), its
"Checks this plan takes (Checks 145–154)" and its task **T1.3**). The script that runs its CLI half
is `scripts/live-checks/check149.sh`, with its own test `check149_test.sh`, and it is the one check
of the block that runs on **your own machine**: it names a sandbox installation and its project,
makes the console's own read of that project's database as you, and writes nothing — no project
state, no run, no credential and no host.

**What the check confirms.** **U9** end to end: whether a console child can make the D364 read — the
coordinator's stored view (`coordinator/repos/<slug>/`), read as the signed-in person through
`roles/firebasedatabase.viewer`, with **no App key and no Bitbucket credential**. U9 is largely
settled by the code already: the console spawns reads that depend on ADC (`budget.show`, through
`console/src/main/spawn.ts`) and `CHILD_ENV_KEYS` carries `HOME`. So what this check confirms is the
**new view**, not the mechanism — the console's project view could not be built while it had to run
`coordinator status` itself, and this is the reading that says the replacement works on a real
machine.

**Run it** (task T1.3, which depends on **T1.2** — the console view — and on **T0.2**):
`bash scripts/live-checks/check149.sh --project <name> [--console-ok]`.

The script is the CLI half as ONE command. It settles `<name>` against this machine's own configs
(`fugaro config list --json`, a local read: it opens no bucket and needs no project selected),
refuses `belong` **whether you typed it or the config answers it**, and requires the installation to
be the one the register's own Preconditions name — `FUGARO_LIVE_GCP_PROJECT` has to be exported and
the config's `gcp_project` has to be it, so a project the register does not name as a sandbox stops
the run rather than reading a project that is not one of its own. It then makes the check's **one**
read — `fugaro coordinator status --from-store --all --json --project <name>`, the register's row
word for word — and turns the answer into facts: that it is the **stored** view for **every**
repository the config lists, which is the command's own report of where its view came from
(`stored: true` on each repository, because "no project record changed" is not something a script
can see from outside — a `stored: false`, the runs-alone fallback, is a **stop**: a coordinator that
has never stored a view is not a run of this check); that the document carries the keys and the
types the console reads (`console/docs/json-contract.md`, its §6.13);
and that nothing the read printed — its document or the command's own message — is
credential-shaped, where the block names the **kinds** it found and never the text. The block never
carries a document: the answer is parsed by one reader that prints counts, yes/no and key paths, so
no pull request title, branch, URL or stale reason reaches what you paste back — and `bash -x` is
refused for the same reason.

**The console window stays yours**, because no script can see it: the run prints one step naming
exactly what to look for — the source line `fugaro coordinator status --from-store --all --json`,
the sentence *the stored view carries no time, so this console claims no age for it*, and the
repository labelled **the last stored view**, with the label that means the console did **not** read
the stored view named beside it (*no stored view: the runs alone*) — and asks you for `y` or `n`.
That one answer is the fact `console-renders-stored-view`. `--console-ok` stands for the answer when
nobody is at the prompt, and its row then says that **nothing was looked at**: the flag is your
word, not a reading. `--dry-run` prints the guards and the plan and runs no fugaro command at all
(not even the local listing). A credential-shaped string in the read's output is a **stop**, not a
FAIL: read the command's own output yourself before pasting the block back, and treat a secret
reaching a CLI's output as the finding. Its own test
(`bash scripts/live-checks/check149_test.sh`) drives the script against a fake `fugaro` alone — no
network, no cloud project, no credential and no console window — and fails if a document's own text
or a sentinel secret ever reaches the block.

**Restore.** Nothing is created, so there is nothing to undo: one local listing of this machine's
configs, one read of the sandbox project's database as you, and one window. No project is written,
no run is launched, no credential is minted, and the check holds no secret to paste back. The script
makes its own scratch directory (0700, outside every git work tree, removed at the end) and its
`restore` row says whether it really went. **Never run any step against `belong`**, and **no agent
runs any step of it.**

## Check 160: the campaign pages' three key events fire in GA4 DebugView after both consents, and none before (the four deployed campaign pages, read-only, on the site's own Firebase project — never an installation's and never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** The go-to-market plan ([go-to-market/implementation-plan.md](go-to-market/implementation-plan.md))
writes it under task **G2.5**, its owner-run half, and the events and the gate it reads are task
**G2.4**'s, in `website/public/scripts/site.js`. **You** run it, as G2.5. There is no script: the check
is one browser session on the four deployed campaign pages with GA4's DebugView open, and **no agent
runs any step of it**.

**What it settles, and what it gates.** Spec §6's "Done when", the sentence at the end of the
landing pages section (*"all key events fire in GA4 DebugView"*), and **F17**: that the funnel's
three events — `install_click`, `whatsapp_click` and
`demo_booked` — reach GA4, one each, and that none of them reaches it before the visitor has
answered. The gate is the site's **analytics** consent, a separate question from the campaign's
**marketing** one (**D401**, `website/src/lib/consent-key.mjs`): `keyEvent()` in
`website/public/scripts/site.js` sends nothing while `measuring` is false — the state a visitor who
has not answered is in, and the state a withdrawal puts them back in — and GA4's own script is not
fetched before that answer either. The second half of the check is the other question's reading:
Calendly's embed is drawn only behind the marketing grant (**D401**), and what a visitor who
declined keeps is the plain link underneath.

**What you do.** The four paths are the `path` entries of `website/data/landing.yaml`: `/save`,
`/control`, `/scale` and `/crew`. The check reads them on a **preview channel**, so that what is
read is not the live site. Each of steps 3 to 5 needs a browser that holds no decision yet, so start
each one in a fresh profile. And **open the two text actions in a new tab** — ⌘-click, Ctrl-click or
a middle press — because `Install free` and `Chat with the founder` are plain same-tab links to the
repository and to WhatsApp (`CampaignCalls.astro` sets no `target`, and the click handler `site.js`
binds sends its event without holding the press back), so a plain press takes the campaign page away
from under the reading, and the events are read off the campaign page's own session:

1. Deploy a preview channel and keep the URL it prints:

   ```sh
   scripts/deploy-website.sh --channel <name> --dry-run
   scripts/deploy-website.sh --channel <name>
   ```

2. Open one of the four pages on it with **GA4's DebugView** in front of you (Admin → DebugView for
   the property the site's measurement id names). The page sets no debug flag of its own, so the
   browser needs GA's debug signal: turn the debug extension on before the page is opened.
3. **Before answering anything**: press `Install free`, press `Chat with the founder` — each in the
   new tab just described, so the campaign page stays open in front of DebugView — and leave the
   banner standing. DebugView shows nothing at all.
4. Press **Accept All Cookies** — on a campaign page a press answers the campaign's question, and the
   site's too when the visitor has not answered it yet, which a fresh profile has not — then press
   `Install free` (`install_click`), press
   `Chat with the founder` (`whatsapp_click`), again each in its new tab, and book through the embed
   the grant has now drawn into `#calendly-embed` (`demo_booked`). Each fires **once**.
5. Then read the analytics-only case, in another **fresh browser profile** — a question this browser
   has answered is not asked again, so a step done in a used profile reads the previous step, not
   this one. Open **Cookie Settings**, and note that the panel is drawn with **nothing ticked**, as
   a browser holding no decision has both questions open: turn **Analytics** **on**, leave
   **Marketing** **off** and press **Save my choices**, which writes exactly those two answers.
   Then press `Install free` and `Chat with the founder` again, each in its new tab, and read the
   closing band. The band carries `website/src/components/CampaignCalls.astro`'s plain `Book a demo`
   link with no frame under it — Calendly's script is fetched after the marketing grant and never
   before — so the third event has no booking to come from.

**What a pass looks like.** Step 3's DebugView shows no event at all, GA4's script not being fetched
before the analytics grant. Step 4's shows `install_click`, `whatsapp_click` and `demo_booked`, one
of each. Step 5's shows `install_click` and `whatsapp_click` for its two presses — analytics alone
measures them — and **no** `demo_booked`, the band holding the link and no `iframe`; the `page_view`
that same grant sends for the page itself is not one of the three. The reading is the one the save
wrote: a save that left **Analytics** off answers both questions **no**, and while its DebugView is
just as empty as step 3's, it is not this reading and does not stand for it. `demo_booked` is read
off a real booking, which is Check 161's test booking when the page was arrived at with a campaign
source on its URL. A press that fires no event after its grant, an event before any grant, a second
event for one press, or a frame in step 5 is the failure.

**Restore.** Delete the preview channel (`firebase hosting:channel:delete <name> --project
fugaro-prod`), cancel the test booking in your own Calendly account, and clear the consent decisions
from the browser profile you used if you want the questions asked again. Nothing in the repository, in
an installation, in the runs bucket or in the site's built artifact is written. **No agent runs any
step of it**, and **never `belong`**.

## Check 161: a test booking carries its UTM source into Calendly (a deployed campaign page, read-only, on the site's own Firebase project — never an installation's and never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** The go-to-market plan's task **G2.5** carries it (its "Checks 160–161"), on the
pass-through task **G2.4** wrote in `website/public/scripts/site.js`, and **you** run it in the same
browser session as Check 160. There is no script, and **no agent runs any step of it**.

**What it settles, and what it gates.** Spec §6's "Done when", its landing pages sentence —
*"a test booking carries its UTM source"* — and **F22**: that the campaign's attribution travels on
the booking's own address and
nowhere else. `bookingURL()` in `website/public/scripts/site.js` copies the campaign parameters the
visitor arrived through onto the address it writes into the embed: the five allow-listed `utm_*` keys,
each value decoded and encoded again, with a key outside the five, an empty value and one over 100
characters dropped. They go there **only** — not into the chat message, not to GA4, and not onto the
plain link a visitor who declined the marketing consent gets, which is the second reading this check
can take. What Calendly does with the address it is handed is Calendly's, so the check reads its
record of the booking and not a field name this repository would be pinning for it.

**What you do.**

1. On the deployed campaign page (Check 160's preview channel, or the live site once it is promoted),
   arrive **with a campaign source on the URL** — for example
   `/save?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=email`. `utm_source` is the one this check reads; the five
   names are the ones `bookingURL()` lists.
2. Grant the marketing consent, so the widget is embedded, and book a test slot through it.
3. Read that booking in your own Calendly account: its record carries the source the visitor arrived
   through.

**What a pass looks like.** The booked event's own record names `newsletter` — the value the URL
carried, and no other. A booking whose source is empty, or names a value the URL did not carry, is the
failure. The second reading is the refusing case: a booking made from the plain `Book a demo` link on
a page where the marketing consent was declined, whose address is the one `website/data/landing.yaml`
writes with nothing appended.

**Restore.** Cancel the test booking in your own Calendly account; that is the whole of it. The page
load, the consent decision and the booking are the only things the check made. **No agent runs any
step of it**, and **never `belong`**.

## Check 162: `fugaro estimate`'s figure against the one the run itself recorded (a sandbox installation and one finished run of a sandbox repository, read-only; never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Registered by task **G6.1** of the go-to-market plan
([go-to-market/implementation-plan.md](go-to-market/implementation-plan.md), its "Check 162") and
**run by you** once tasks **G1.2** and **G1.3** are released — G1.2 is what puts the per-model token
counts on the run record (**F8**) and G1.3 is the command — and **no agent runs any step of it**: the
reading is a comparison you judge.

**What it settles, and what it gates.** Spec §10's demo feature on a real run: that `fugaro estimate`
reprices what a finished run recorded and lands near what that run cost. **F8** is why the run has to
be a recent one (the record's `cost.model_tokens` is what G1.2 added, and there is no backfill), and
**F9** is what the figure means: the command labels it an estimate, assumes the run's own cache ratio,
and cannot reproduce four things about the recorded figure. Check 162 is named in **D404**'s
launch-ready list, and it is the last reading of it.

**What you do.**

1. Pick **one finished sandbox run**: one that a released build carrying G1.2 finalized, so its record
   carries `cost.model_tokens`, and one whose calls all stayed under their model's long-context
   threshold. The run's `model call` lines, from `fugaro logs <run>`, carry the input counts that say
   so; a small task is the easy one to read.
2. Read the catalog the figure will be priced from. `fugaro budget prices` prints the same
   `checked_at` and stale flag the estimate prints beside its figure, and the window is the row's: 30
   days for a provider catalog row (`catalog.StaleAfter`), 90 for the embedded Claude price table
   (`priceStaleAfter`). **A stale catalog is not this check's reading** — a stale provider row is
   priced at the dearest end of its tier until it is regenerated, so the figure would be wrong on
   purpose; regenerate it first (`scripts/gen-price-catalog.sh`, which the release checklist runs).
   "A fresh catalog" in the plan means a date inside that window.
3. Reprice the run at the model it ran on:

   ```sh
   fugaro estimate --run <ID> --model <model>
   ```

   `--run` takes the run's ID, its `slug/id`, or an ending of one, and `--model` is the model that run
   itself ran on, spelled the way the price table spells it: an ID `fugaro budget prices` lists, or
   that row's route ID. The command writes nothing and runs nothing — it reprices the stored counts.
4. Read the two figures it prints: the estimate on the first line, and `the run recorded <figure>
   (<basis>)` under it — the basis is `api-list` (a bill) or `subscription` (a plan's figure). The
   `prices:` line under the model table carries the catalog's source and date, and a stale catalog is
   warned about on stderr.

**What a pass looks like.** The two figures agree within a few percent, from a catalog inside its own
window. They are not the same number and are not expected to be: **F9** names the four things this
command cannot reproduce — a long-context tier, which applies per call and is dropped rather than
charged on the run's summed input; web searches, priced apart from the tokens; the `unattributed`
residual `model_usd` carries; and the calls settled from a reservation (`Unreconciled`,
`UsageUnparsed`). The difference is yours to judge with that list in front of you; the run that is the
clean reading is the one none of the four applies to, and a gap wider than a few percent there is the
finding, and it belongs in this row's result rather than being explained away.

Two refusals are not failures of the check and are not readings either: a run the command refuses **by
name** for carrying no per-model tokens — one that never finalized, or one finalized before this
binary recorded them — is F8's "no backfill", and a `--model` the price table has no row for is
answered with the IDs it has. Both name what to do next.

**What waits on it.** **D404**'s launch-ready list names Check 162, and it is the last reading of it: a
figure that lands wide of the record on a clean run is the finding that list waits on, not a detail to
explain away. The demo line **F7** corrects (`fugaro estimate --pr N --repo owner/name --model
claude-opus-5-5`) is this same command aimed at a pull request's run instead of a named one.

**Restore.** Nothing was created, so there is nothing to undo: one bucket read, one price-table lookup
and the catalog's date. No job, no container, no build, no object and no credential. **No agent runs
any step of it**, and **never `belong`**.

## Check 170: a key verifies offline in the CLI, the console and the app (your own machine and a sandbox installation, read-only, with the network off; run by you; NOT RUN)

**Checks 170–179 are the subscriptions work's, and all ten are written below** — the key service's
own six, the lapse state's two, the coordinator's sweep job, and the merchant's test mode. All ten
are **OWNER-RUN**: **no agent runs any step of any of them**, and no agent mints, holds or reaches a
signing key (R5 as amended by D440).

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **S3.6** of the subscriptions plan
([subscriptions/implementation-plan.md](subscriptions/implementation-plan.md), its "Checks this plan
takes (170–179)"), and run by the owner in task **S3.7** once S3.8's key ring exists and S2.9's
production public half is published — in `ee/licence/keys/production.pub`, the CLI's ring built
from it, and the app's ring; the ring the console verifies with is filled by the CLI release that
takes the key back out of its own environment. Until the service is deployed, a key the
owner mints by hand with S2.10's tool is the same format, and this check measures the same thing
with it.

**What the check confirms.** **R2**'s "no hosted dependency at runtime", measured: a key the service
issued — or the owner minted by hand — licenses an installation with no route to the service at all
([key-signing-service/spec.md](key-signing-service/spec.md) §1 and §2). It is the reading no
hermetic test can produce: each verifier's own tests hold a signature vector, and this holds a key
the owner's own key ring signed.

**What you do:**

1. Install the one key where each product keeps it
   ([licensing/licence-key.md](licensing/licence-key.md), "Storage and hand-off"): the CLI's
   `licence.key` file in its own config directory at mode 0600, the console's key screen, and the
   app's settings screen. The console hands it to the CLI it
   spawns in `FUGARO_LICENCE_KEY` and never in argv.
2. Turn the network off on the machine and on the phone — the interface down, not a browser
   setting — and start each product: the CLI (a build carrying the `ee` tag), the console and the
   app.
3. Record the three readings: the key's state in each product, the same tier, seats and expiry in
   all three, and that none of them reached the network to answer.

**Restore.** The three installs are the owner's own licence and may stay; a hand-minted key is
removed by deleting the CLI's file and clearing the console's and the app's key screens. Nothing is
minted, nothing is deployed, and no credential is pasted back. **No agent runs any step of it.**

## Check 171: the free seat queues a free-mail domain and a second key for one organisation, and refuses a domain with a paid subscription (the key service's intake, staging keys only; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **S3.6** of the subscriptions plan
([subscriptions/implementation-plan.md](subscriptions/implementation-plan.md), its "Checks this plan
takes (170–179)"), and run by the owner in task **S3.7**.

**What the check confirms.** §4.1–§4.3 of the design
([key-signing-service/spec.md](key-signing-service/spec.md)), which is UNVERIFIED **U11**: whether
an email domain, a free-mail list and the code host's API are *enough* to enforce "one per
organisation". The three outcomes are the design's three — **queue** for a free-mail domain,
**queue** for a second application for a domain that already holds a free key, and **refuse** for a
domain the service's event store knows holds a paid subscription — and the first two are the queue
rather than a refusal because **T15** makes an individual an organisation of one, which is exactly
who holds a free-mail address.

**What you do** (against the intake that mints with the **staging** key id — D459 is where that
intake lives — so that nothing this check produces can license a customer):

1. Apply for the free seat with an address at a free email provider. Read the answer: it is the
   **uniform** one (§7.1), and the request is in the queue rather than minted.
2. Apply again for a domain that already holds a free key. The answer reads the same as step 1's,
   the request is queued, and nothing says a key exists for the domain.
3. Buy a Team subscription in the merchant's **test mode** (Check 179), so the event store knows the
   domain, then apply for the free seat with an address on that domain. This one is **refused**:
   §10.2(a) gives a Customer on a Paid Plan no free seat.
4. Record each outcome, the page's own words, and the two requests in the queue — the third never
   reaches it, because §4.3 refuses it at submission.

**Restore.** The two queued applications are the owner's own test data: decline each in the admin
page (Check 173), so no key is minted for either, and leave the store's record of the refusal to
D457's retention.
**No agent runs any step of it.**

([key-signing-service/spec.md](key-signing-service/spec.md)) and the other half of **U11**: that
visibility and licence are read per repository from the code host's API, that **D452**'s proof of
control is required, and that a private repository beside the ones named cannot be seen — the
check's own stated limit, with the Terms as the enforcement.

**What you do** (against the intake that mints with the **staging** key id, and with repositories
the owner controls — never a third party's):

2. Apply with the **all-public** repository under an OSI licence and **without** D452's proof of

   against the staging key id. The applicant's email verifies first, exactly as §4.1's does.
4. Record the four refusals' words and the minted key's claims.

## Check 175: installed keys keep working with the service stopped, and the next key issued 30 days before expiry overlaps the current one (a sandbox installation and the key service; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **S3.6** of the subscriptions plan
([subscriptions/implementation-plan.md](subscriptions/implementation-plan.md), its "Checks this plan
takes (170–179)"), and run by the owner in task **S3.7**.

**What the check confirms.** §8 of the design
([key-signing-service/spec.md](key-signing-service/spec.md)) and **T26**: that validation is
offline, so a stopped service cannot stop an installation's work, and that the 30-day overlap is
what makes an issuing outage bite only past 60 days.

   minter gone, or simply the network off. Launch a run: it works, because nothing in the product

   overlaps the installed key's, or from the service's own renewal path — and read its `expires`:
   it is the end of the term the predecessor covered, not `issued` plus the bare term.
3. Install both keys (the store holds at most two) and read which one applies: the one with the
   later `expires`, with the earlier key still verifying.
4. Restart the service and record that the outage cost nothing but **new** keys.

**Restore.** The sandbox's own key stays; the second key is the store's second entry and may stay
too. **No agent runs any step of it.**

step of it.**

**NOT RUN.** And it is **deferred until enforcement (2026-10-29, D524)**. The check measured the

key-gated job. A key check and its refusal come only with enforcement, and **no key is mounted
today**, so there is no refusal to measure: the two halves written below are what can be read, and
they are run by the owner in task **S1.10** when the enforcement release lands. Registered here by
task **S3.6** of the subscriptions plan
([subscriptions/implementation-plan.md](subscriptions/implementation-plan.md), its "Checks this plan
takes (170–179)").

**What the check confirms.** That the sweep job runs the **tagged** build — the one image the
one-binary release produces (S1.9, E1.4) — so the paid coordinator is what runs where no person
types anything, and that the console's project view still reads the stored view without a key
(D364, Check 149's reading).

**What you do:**

1. On the sandbox installation, run `fugaro update` and read the coordinator's job definition: its
   image is the one built with the `ee` tag, and **no key secret is mounted** (D524).
2. Run one sweep and read its log: `fugaro coordinator` runs the paid build rather than the core
   stub — an untagged build's `fugaro coordinator` is the stub and says why (E1.1, D522).
3. Type `fugaro coordinator status --from-store --all --json --project <name>` and open the
   console's project view: both read the same stored view, and the console's view needs no key.

**Restore.** One `fugaro update` and one sweep on the sandbox installation; no project is written
and no credential is minted. **No agent runs any step of it.**

## Check 179: a purchase in the merchant's test mode mints a staging key production refuses, a renewal reissues it, and a cancellation stops the reissue (the key service and the merchant's test mode, staging keys only; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **S3.6** of the subscriptions plan
([subscriptions/implementation-plan.md](subscriptions/implementation-plan.md), its "Checks this plan
takes (170–179)"), and run by the owner in task **S3.7**, which is also where the merchant's webhook
is configured.

**What the check confirms.** §5 of the design
([key-signing-service/spec.md](key-signing-service/spec.md)) — the paid path end to end: the
signature, the idempotency, the renewal window, the seat change and the cancellation — and the
staging pair, which is the whole of §2's second rule: a test-mode key cannot license a customer
because a production verifier holds production ids only.

**What you do** (in the merchant's **test mode**, so every key this check mints is a staging key):

1. Buy a Team subscription. The service mints a key against the **staging** key id, stating the
   seats the purchase carries.
2. Install it in a **production** verifier — the CLI, the console, the app: each **refuses** it.
   Install it in the sandbox installation, whose verifier holds the staging id: it reads there.
3. Deliver the same event twice: one key, not two. Deliver a replayed or out-of-order event: the
   subscription's state does not move backwards and no key is resurrected.
4. Renew: the next key issues **30 days before** the current one's `expires`, with the seats the
   subscription now states. Change the seats: it reissues.
5. Cancel: the reissue **stops**, and the key the customer holds keeps working until it expires —
   T25's accepted leakage.
6. Record the event ids, the mints and the service's own record of them.

**Restore.** Cancel the test-mode subscription in the merchant's dashboard; the staging keys are the
sandbox's and may stay. **No agent runs any step of it.**

## Check 180: one Bitbucket project or workspace access token serving many repositories (installation `<sandbox>` only, sandbox workspace only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **T1.3** of the Bitbucket workspace-token plan
([bitbucket-workspace-token/implementation-plan.md](bitbucket-workspace-token/implementation-plan.md), its
"Checks this plan takes (Checks 180–189)"), and **run by the owner** in task **T1.4**. It is the only
check of that block written: **182–189 stay unwritten** until a work claims them (181 is Check 181
below). Nothing here has been run, and the workspace U6 left unknown **is known now**: the Premium
sandbox workspace is the owner's own **`dimi_bmb`**, whose plan admits project and workspace access
tokens, and it is the `--workspace` the check defaults to — every repository you name has to be in
it, and you override the flag only if the sandbox workspace moves. That is why D468 = no put the
whole path in 0.13.0 with no claim that it works: the workspace was the missing half, not the code.
The owner types one command, and every argument in it is required:

```bash
scripts/live-checks/check180.sh --installation <sandbox> --token-file <the token file> --repo <owner/name>=<checkout path> --repo <owner/name>=<checkout path> --probe-repo <owner/name>
```

`--token-file` is the file holding the project access token and nothing else, at mode 0600 — the one
place the value lives. Each `--repo owner/name=<checkout path>` is one of the two allow-listed
repositories and the checkout the check runs `fugaro update --repo` in, one pair each.
`--probe-repo` is the sandbox repository added to the same Bitbucket project afterwards (step 7),
which must **not** be in `project_secrets` and **must already exist** when you run the command: the
check reads it with the token as one of the repositories that token has to reach, so a probe
repository created after the command has started reads as a 404 and fails U3 on a run that has
already launched billed runs and opened pull requests. `--workspace` names the sandbox workspace all
three repositories have to be in and defaults to `dimi_bmb`; `--new-token-file`, `--source`,
`--gcloud-config` and `--merge` are optional. The script plans first (`--dry-run` prints the plan and touches nothing) and
refuses `belong` by name at every step — as `--installation`, as `--workspace`, as either
repository's workspace, as the probe repository and as the installation `fugaro doctor --project`
selects. That and one stop
are the whole of its installation guard: it reads the installation you name with `fugaro doctor
--project` and **stops** if the installation the doctor reports is not the name you typed, so a typo
measures nothing — but it accepts **any** installation the doctor agrees with, and only `belong` is
refused outright. **Point it at your sandbox installation and no other**: it stores a project-wide
secret, launches billed runs, pushes, approves, merges and rotates the token, and nothing in the
script proves the installation you named is the sandbox one beyond what the two guards above say. Its
driver is
`scripts/live-checks/check180_test.sh`, which runs offline — fake `fugaro`, `gcloud`, `go` and `git`
on `PATH` and a fake Bitbucket Cloud on a loopback port — inside `go test ./scripts`. **No agent runs
any step of this check**, only that test; and no step types, prints or pastes a token or a key value:
the token is read from the file the owner names and handed to the CLI on stdin.

**What the check settles** (the reconciliation's **U1**–**U5** and **U7**, and **F3**): the reading the
whole Bitbucket workspace-token path rests on and that no offline test can produce — what a **project
access token** with `repository:write` and `pullrequest:write` actually authenticates against
Bitbucket Cloud, which is exactly what D468 = no leaves open. It is also where D490's sentence is
seen: the token reaches the job itself, and a proxy that keeps it out of the job is designed in
[secrets-brokering](secrets-brokering/README.md) and not built. The run's agent and every
launcher of an allow-listed repository hold the token's value (F7), which is why this check runs on a
**Premium** sandbox workspace and nowhere else.

**What you do** (task T1.4; every step on the sandbox installation and a sandbox workspace, never
`belong`):

1. **Create the token** (U7). In the sandbox workspace create a **project access token** with
   `repository:write` and `pullrequest:write` — the minimum a run needs, no admin, webhook, pipeline
   or project-admin scope — and give it a name you want on every pull request, since the name cannot
   be edited later. Record the exact scope names Bitbucket's own page shows (U7), and have the two
   sandbox repositories of one Bitbucket project ready.
2. **Allow-list and store the token.** Write the `project_secrets.bitbucket-token.allow_data_to`
   entry naming the two repositories, run `fugaro update` so the project container exists, and store
   it project-wide with
   `fugaro secrets set bitbucket-token --project-wide < <token-file>`, which reads the value from
   stdin. The store's acceptance is the reading: the entry has to name the repositories the token is
   meant for, or the store refuses.
3. **`fugaro update --repo <path>` on each repository, and record that it asks nothing.** The name is
   covered by the allow-list, so the prompt does not appear. This is the reading the second half of
   D462 turns on: one token for many repositories, with no per-repository copy typed anywhere.
4. **One run per repository.** Launch a run on each and record three things from it: the clone and the
   push, which authenticate as `x-token-auth` with the token's value (U1); the pull request it opens,
   and the author's **name**, which is the token's (U2, D472 — every enrolled repository's pull
   requests carry that one author); and the run's own `fugaro runs ls --repo <owner/name> --json` row,
   where `pushed`, `branch` and `pr` say the push and the pull request happened. `fugaro run` returns
   as soon as the run is **launched**, so the script does not read that row at launch: it polls the
   listing until the row for the run it just launched — picked out by the run's own id, since the
   listing is newest-first and holds other runs — is in a **final status**, up to the cap the plan
   prints. Waiting for each run is the long part of this check; a run still in flight at the cap is
   recorded as a FAIL with the status it had, not as a push that did not happen.
5. **`TestLiveBitbucket` with the token**, and **`GET /2.0/user`** (U2, U7). The live test
   (`internal/gitprov/bitbucket/live_test.go`, build tag `live`) is the harness for the API itself:
   `FUGARO_LIVE_REPO` and `FUGARO_BITBUCKET_TOKEN` set, then
   `go test -tags live -run 'TestLive' ./internal/gitprov/bitbucket/`. Its answer, and what
   `GET /2.0/user` answers about the token's own identity — whether the token even has a user — are
   the two readings U2 is open on.
6. **Approve and merge** (U4). Peer review is out of reach for the token's own account, so this is
   the reading that says whether **approve and merge** are admitted with `repository:write` and
   `pullrequest:write` alone: on the sandbox repository approve the run's pull request and merge it,
   and record what each call answered. A merge cannot be undone; on a sandbox repository that is the
   point, and no step of this check touches `belong`.
7. **A repository added to the Bitbucket project afterwards** (U3, D464). Create one more sandbox
   repository in the same Bitbucket project — **before** the one command above runs, since the check
   reads it with the token during that run — and check that the allow-listed token reaches it
   with no new local-config entry. U3 is the reading D464's wildcard rests on: **added to the
   Bitbucket project afterwards** is what a project-scoped token does rather than what a list of
   names does.
8. **Rotate the token** (F3). Store the new token as a new version of the same secret
   (`fugaro secrets set bitbucket-token --project-wide < <new-token-file>`), wait for the running
   executions to end, then revoke the old token in the Bitbucket UI, and record that **the next run
   uses the new version**: a run launched after the rotation clones, pushes and opens its pull request
   as before, **while the revoked value is refused**. That second half is what makes the first one a
   reading — with the old value still accepted, a job still mounting it (or a pinned version) pushes
   exactly the same way — so the script does not launch that run until it has seen the refusal: after
   storing the new version it **re-reads the first repository** with the old value every 15 seconds,
   tells you to revoke it, and goes on the moment Bitbucket refuses that read with 401 or 403 (up to
   600 seconds, `CHECK180_ROTATION_SECONDS`). That request is the repository read, not
   `GET /2.0/user` — the endpoint step 5 records as open (U7): a token with `repository:write` and
   `pullrequest:write` alone can be refused there from the start, and such a standing 403 would read
   as a revocation that never happened, launching the post-rotation run while the old value is still
   live and reading the row as PASS. The repository read carries no such doubt: it is the request the
   same run already required to answer 200 with that same value, so a refusal of it is a change the
   check watched happen. If the old value is still accepted when the wait runs out, the run
   is **not** launched and the rotation's row reads **UNVERIFIED** with the store's own result
   (`x` versions before, `y` after) — revoke the old token and run the check again with the same
   arguments. The secret's version list is what the script reads back here: it finds the container by
   the labels the store writes on it (`fugaro_secret=bitbucket-token`, `fugaro_project=<name>`, the
   same way the CLI finds it) rather than by its name, which carries a hash suffix, and reads the
   versions with `gcloud secrets versions list`.
9. **A second operator's machine** (U5, D467). On a machine seeded from the shared config with
   `fugaro update --gcp-project <id> --region <region> --name <name> --config-only`, run
   `fugaro update --repo <path> --plan-only` **without** copying the `project_secrets` entry, and
   record what it plans: a per-repository token, because the entry is operator-local by design and
   the shared config never carries it. The script's own second machine is a scratch `HOME` with its
   own `XDG` and git config, so the one thing it has to borrow is the owner's Application Default
   Credentials: `--gcloud-config <dir>` names the directory to read them from, and without the flag
   the script falls back to `$GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`, then `$CLOUDSDK_CONFIG`, then
   `~/.config/gcloud`. The flag is the one that wins: the CLI reads
   `$GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` before the gcloud config directory (`internal/cli/adcpath.go`),
   so the script clears that variable for the two commands the flag is about — an inherited file
   would otherwise be read instead, and the flag would decide nothing. The path is passed through
   and **no credential is copied** into the scratch home. That seed is a write as well as a
   read — it writes the scratch home's local config — and the CLI confirms that write at a real
   terminal. The script's scratch home has no terminal, so a seed that refuses leaves the
   second-machine row UNVERIFIED on every run; run it by hand and your own terminal confirms it (the
   config it writes is the scratch home's, never yours). If the seeded command fails for any other
   reason, the row reads UNVERIFIED and names what it needs, rather than reading as a pass.

**How to read the block.** The script prints one block whose last line is the verdict, and the
verdict is the exit status: `CHECK 180 RESULT: PASS (exit 0)` every criterion was measured and
passed; `FAIL (exit 1)` a criterion was measured and failed; `INCOMPLETE (exit 2)` the run stopped
before it could measure everything — a guard stopped it, a tool is missing, a command was refused,
an error ended it — and the keys it never reached read `FAIL — not reached`, with `aborted` naming
what stopped it; `INCOMPLETE (exit 3)` it ran to the end and at least one criterion was **not
settled**: a row reading `UNVERIFIED`, a step that could not verify its criterion (the rotation
without `--new-token-file` or with the old token still accepted when the wait for its revocation ran
out, the merge without `--merge`, the second machine without credentials it can read the installation
with). A criterion that was not measured is not a pass: **only an all-PASS
block is a PASS**, and a step that could not verify its criterion says so in its own row instead of
leaving the reader to take the block for an answer it never got.

**What the check does not settle.** D474's API-root lock shipped in 0.14.0 (policy version 4,
`bitbucket_api_roots`) and this check does not read it; a workspace access token reaches the whole
workspace rather than one project (the pair is one credential with two reaches, and this check runs
the project token because it is the narrower one); and no part of the path is kept out of the job —
see D490 above.

**Restore.** The script removes its own scratch directory and every file a credential was written
into, and the block's `restore` row says whether they really went — a FAILed row there names what to
remove by hand. It writes nothing to a base branch: the branches it pushes and the pull requests it
opens are the runs' own, and they are left for a person to look at. What a person has to undo by hand
is what the check exists to make: the one extra sandbox repository created in step 7, the merged pull request of
step 6 (which cannot be unmerged), the rotated and revoked token pair of step 8 (the new version is
the live one from then on), and the project-wide secret, which
`fugaro secrets rm bitbucket-token` removes — the container with every version in it and the
`project_secrets` entry that made it reachable, in the same run — once no repository needs it.
**Never run any step against `belong`**, and **no agent runs any step of it**.

## Check 181: a Bitbucket shared project job end to end, and the allow-list refusal at publish, at deploy and at the proxy (installation `<sandbox>` only, the sandbox workspace `dimi_bmb` only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **T2.6** of the Bitbucket workspace-token plan
([bitbucket-workspace-token/implementation-plan.md](bitbucket-workspace-token/implementation-plan.md), its
"Checks this plan takes (Checks 180–189)"), and **run by you** in task **T2.7**. Check 180 beside it
ships as a script, and so does this one: the steps below are what
`scripts/live-checks/check181.sh` runs — `fugaro project policy publish`, `fugaro update` and
`fugaro run --repo <owner/name>`, one command instead of three you type — its own dry driver is
`scripts/live-checks/check181_test.sh`, which runs it against fakes and touches no cloud, and
**no agent runs any step of it**.

The owner types one command, and every argument but `--workspace` and `--profile` is required:

```bash
scripts/live-checks/check181.sh --installation <sandbox> --token-file <the token file> --repo <owner/name> --repo <owner/name> --third-repo <owner/name>
```

`--token-file` is the file holding the project access token of step 1 and nothing else, at mode
0600 — the one place the value lives. The script never holds it in a variable, never puts it on a
command line and never prints it: the only command that ever sees it is `fugaro secrets set
bitbucket-token --project-wide`, which reads it from the file on stdin. The two `--repo` pairs are
the two allow-listed sandbox repositories, one run each, and `--third-repo` is the sandbox
repository the token's block does **not** name — the one steps 3 and 6 are about. `--workspace` is
the **Premium** sandbox Bitbucket workspace all three live in, and it defaults to the owner's own
**`dimi_bmb`**, the value U6 left unknown until 2026-11-23: every repository named has to be in it,
and you override the flag only if the sandbox workspace moves. `--profile` names the Bitbucket
profile a shared job is deployed for, and defaults to `bitbucket-shared`. `--dry-run` prints the
plan and calls nothing at all — no `fugaro`, no `gcloud`, no `git`. The script refuses `belong` as
the installation, as the workspace and as any of the three repositories, refuses to run inside a
coding agent's session (`CLAUDECODE` and the like), and stops on a repository outside
`--workspace`, all of it before the first command. Its block is one `CHECK 181 RESULT` with a
PASS/FAIL row per criterion, and only an all-PASS block is a PASS: a criterion it could not measure
reads UNVERIFIED and the last line says `INCOMPLETE (exit 3)` rather than `PASS`.

Nothing here has been run, and **it cannot run yet**: the four sides of a shared Bitbucket job are
built on this tree — S1's deployer refuses a profile that mounts a Bitbucket credential and admits one
that does not; S2's pairing serves the shared class at the credentials service's Bitbucket proxy;
S3's runner reaches git only through it (`internal/runner`'s `TestSharedBitbucketJobHoldsNoToken` and
`TestSharedBitbucketJobHaltsWhenTheProxyRefusesARepository`); S4's launcher resolves the profile —
and **the two that put such a job in the deployer's hands have landed since this was written**:
docs/shared-jobs-default's **I1** (`internal/infra`'s `sharedJobProviders` admits `bitbucket` beside
`github`) and its **S5** (**`fugaro update` writes the default profile a shared Bitbucket job is
deployed from**). What is still owed is **the service's own admission of the class** — the
`FUGARO_SHARED_JOB_ACCOUNTS` table below, rendered by no module — and not the front door: **B5.2 has
shipped**, and the shared job account's `roles/run.invoker` on the credentials service is written by
`deploy/terraform/gcp/modules/project/sa.tf`.

The first is the one to know before step 5: the service's shared class is its table of
`FUGARO_SHARED_JOB_ACCOUNTS` rows, nothing under `deploy/terraform/` renders that name
(`internal/infra/tf`'s `CredentialsServiceEnvAwaitingTheModule` records it as the name the module does
not carry yet), and an installation whose entry is absent starts with the empty set and **refuses the
whole class** — the caller falls through to the per-repository table and is refused there
(`internal/cli`'s `credentialsServiceSharedJobAccounts` and `internal/credsvc`'s authenticator) — so
the runs of step 5 would be refused by the service before they cloned anything, on a job that holds no
credential to fall back on.

**The second was the front door, and it has shipped.** The shared job's service account holds
**`roles/run.invoker` on the credentials service**: `deploy/terraform/gcp/modules/project/sa.tf`
writes exactly that one member — the job's own account, on that one service, for a profile the
service serves — where the per-repository path's grant is
`deploy/terraform/gcp/modules/workflow/sa.tf`'s (D135), and task **B5.2** is the change that landed
it. The service is IAM-only (its front end states `invoker_iam_disabled = false` and no `allUsers`
member is written anywhere), so the grant is what lets a request into the container at all; a caller
that arrives without a row in the class's table is then refused by **the service's own
authenticator**, and not by Cloud Run's front end. The bare **403** this paragraph used to say you
meet first is therefore no longer the refusal to expect here: what stops the runs of steps 5 and 6 is
the empty class table above, and that is **not** this section's refusal and not a pass of step 6
either.

So what a shared Bitbucket job lacks today is not the provider list, the profile it is deployed from
or the grant that lets its account into the service — all three landed — but the class's own table,
and its consequence is that the runs of steps 5 and 6 are refused by the service before they clone
anything: neither step can read the refusal this check is for until that table is rendered. Run this
section once it has, and read the documents that say so as of 2026-11-16 — [git-providers.md](git-providers.md) and [project-layer.md](project-layer.md).

**What the check settles** (**D460**–**D462**, **D466**, **D2302**; and F11 and F12 of the
[reconciliation](bitbucket-workspace-token/reconciliation-secrets-brokering.md)): the shape a shared
Bitbucket job is meant to have, end to end and at the allow-list — **one** Cloud Run job and **one**
job service account serve every repository of one profile, the job holds **no Bitbucket token at
all**, and its git traffic reaches Bitbucket only through the credentials service's Bitbucket proxy,
which pairs the verified run identity to the repositories the job's own profile admits. Three
readings make it: the token's block is the credential's reach — refused where the list is published
for a profile that mounts it, and held to where a run is served for a job that does not; the job's own
description is a job with the credentials service's address on it and no `bitbucket-token` anywhere
in it; and a repository the allow-list does not name gets no git operation at all, on a job that
could otherwise serve it. No offline test produces any of them — the runner's tests use a fake proxy
and a fake deployment, and the deployer's refusal is a plan, not a project.

**What you do** (task T2.7; every step on the sandbox installation and a sandbox workspace, never
`belong`):

1. **The token and its allow-list** (D461). In the sandbox workspace create a **project access
   token** with `repository:write` and `pullrequest:write` — the narrower of the pair D461 allows,
   no admin, webhook, pipeline or project-admin scope — and treat the two sandbox repositories of
   one Bitbucket project as the repositories it is for. Write the
   `project_secrets.bitbucket-token.allow_data_to` block naming those two, run `fugaro update` so
   the project container exists, and store the token project-wide with
   `fugaro secrets set bitbucket-token --project-wide < <token-file>`. Check 180's steps 1 and 2 are
   the same two, and settle the token itself; this check reads the block as the allow-list the
   publish and the pairing both answer with.
2. **The profile a shared job is deployed for, which mounts no Bitbucket credential (D2302).** In
   the installation's local config write a Bitbucket profile whose `allow_repos` names **the same two
   repositories** the block names and whose `secrets` carry **nothing of Bitbucket's**: the
   project-wide token is step 1's, and the job — shared by every repository the profile admits —
   holds no credential of its own, so `bitbucket-token` is not on this profile at all. The rule that
   says so is `internal/projectpolicy`'s `CheckSharedJobProfile`, and both doors ask it: the publish
   and, one step later, the deployer (step 3 reads the refusal it makes). `fugaro project policy show`
   is how you read back what the publish writes. The profile is the boundary a shared job is built
   from — one service account serves every repository it admits, while the bucket condition on that
   account is the same whole-prefix one every project job account carries, whatever its profile,
   because a profile separates secrets and not bucket objects (SECURITY.md, "The Bitbucket git
   proxy", and its "Known limits").
3. **The lists, and the third repository's three readings** (D2302, and F11 of the
   [reconciliation](bitbucket-workspace-token/reconciliation-secrets-brokering.md)). All three use
   the same third sandbox repository — one the token's block does **not** name.
   - **At the publish, through the subset rule.** Add it to the `allow_repos` of a profile that
     **mounts** `bitbucket-token` — the per-repository shape, and the shape a Bitbucket profile had
     before D2302; the shared profile of step 2 mounts nothing. `fugaro project policy publish`
     **refuses** it through `internal/projectpolicy`'s `CheckBitbucketProfileRepos`, the rule that a
     profile's list may only narrow the block's, naming the repository it is not allowed to admit
     (the same rule is asked at `fugaro project profile` when a profile is edited), and `fugaro
     update` refuses the same node before it plans anything. Record both refusals in their own words,
     then take the credential off that profile and the third repository out of its list.
   - **At the deploy, through the mount rule.** Put `bitbucket-token` on the profile of step 2 and
     read what refuses it: `fugaro project policy publish` refuses the mount through `CheckSharedJobProfile`,
     the same function the deployer asks — which is why a shared job is refused rather than deployed
     with the mount dropped — and once `sharedJobProviders` admits `bitbucket` (I1) `fugaro update`
     refuses the **job** one step later, at the deployer and not at the policy stage, which writes the
     node the config states (the HARD RULE: an update converges). Take the entry off again.
   - **On the profile a shared job is deployed for, through nothing at all.** With the credential off
     that profile, as step 2 leaves it, the third repository added to its `allow_repos` is refused at
     **no** door here: the block is not the profile's to mount, and the token's reach is the service's
     to hold a call to. Record that too — it is the difference between the rule before D2302 and the
     rule now, and the refusal you are looking for is step 6's.
4. **The deploy.** `fugaro update` on the sandbox installation. The reading is the deployment it
   leaves: **one** new Cloud Run job named `fugaro-p-…` for the profile — one job and one job
   service account, named from a profile rather than from a repository
   (`internal/backend/gcp`'s `ProjectJobName`) — with `FUGARO_CREDENTIALS_SERVICE_URL` in its
   environment, written by the deployer because a job that holds no git credential cannot clone
   without it (D2302; git-providers.md's amendment of 2026-11-16), and with **no** secret reference
   to `bitbucket-token` in the job's spec. `gcloud run jobs describe` reads both, and a job that
   carries that mount fails this step: S1's deployer refuses the profile that would produce it, so a
   job holding one was built by something other than this path.
5. **A run of each allow-listed repository.** `fugaro run --repo <owner/name>` for each of the two
   sandbox repositories, one at a time or both at once — sharing the job is the point of the
   profile. Each run has to execute **on that one job**: one `fugaro-p-…` execution, the same
   service account, and no second job's name anywhere in the run's own record. Each has to get as
   far as cloning, committing, pushing and opening its pull request, and that the push lands on a
   job with no `bitbucket-token` in it is the reading: the credential on the wire is the service's,
   paired to the repository the run's own profile admits. A run that never reached its clone has
   skipped the reading rather than passed it, and the case to tell apart at once is a run halted
   **without the allow-list having been asked at all** — with the class's table empty (above) the
   service refuses every shared run of its own accord, and a bare Cloud Run **403** would be the
   grant rather than the table: neither says anything about this profile.
6. **The third repository, refused at the proxy.** Now launch a run of the repository that is not in
   the allow-list, by hand and against the same shared job — `fugaro run --repo <owner/name>`, with
   that repository already on the published node, which is what makes the run resolve the shared job
   instead of one of its own. The credentials service's Bitbucket proxy **refuses** the run, because
   the pairing resolves its identity against the published node and the repositories that profile is
   bound to, and the runner holds no Bitbucket credential of its own to fall back on; the run halts
   on that refusal instead of finding a way around it (S3's
   `TestSharedBitbucketJobHaltsWhenTheProxyRefusesARepository` is that behaviour, offline). **Read
   the refusal before you record it, because two different refusals end a run here and only one of
   them is this step's.** The one this step is about is the **service's own**, after the pairing:
   its words name the repository and the identity it resolved, it is answered by the proxy's code
   with the audit line a refusal is recorded as, and it is the allow-list doing its job. The other is
   the run stopped **before the allow-list is reached at all** — the class's empty table refusing it
   at the service's own authenticator (the paragraph above), or, on an installation whose job carries
   no grant, a bare Cloud Run **403** with no repository in it. Neither is a reading: **record it as
   this step not having run**, not as the refusal, because a check recorded on it would claim the
   allow-list held when nothing of the allow-list was ever asked. Record the refusal's own words
   and the run's final row. **This is the step to be sure of**: if that run clones, the allow-list
   is not the boundary the design says it is, and that is a finding no other check of the block
   would show.
7. **What is left behind.** The two pull requests of step 5 are the runs' own; they are the one
   thing to look at afterwards, and nothing here approves or merges anything.

**Restore.** No command of this check undoes itself: the sandbox repositories and scratch homes you
made are yours to delete, the two pull requests are left open for a person to look at, the profile
and its `fugaro-p-…` job stay on the sandbox installation until you remove them, and the
project-wide secret goes with `fugaro secrets rm bitbucket-token` once no repository needs it — the
container with every version in it and the `project_secrets` entry that made it reachable, in the
same run. The token itself is revoked in the sandbox workspace, where you created it. **Never run
any step against `belong`**, and **no agent runs any step of it**.

(`scripts/live-checks/check190/main.go`).

**The run's facts, as the owner reported them** (the owner's own summary rather than the script's


**What the result settles, and what it leaves open.** The gate's answer is the **FAIL**: a pack above
**32 MiB** does **not** pass Cloud Run on **HTTP/1.1** — the Google Frontend answers **413 Request
Entity Too Large**, and the proxy behind it receives **4 bytes** — so S1 is not built on HTTP/1.1:
B1.5 and the service serve **h2c end to end** (B1.0). That is U2's first two halves measured, and its
third — whether h2c end to end lifts the limit — stays **UNVERIFIED**: B1.0's listener and B1.5's route
are on `main`, but no live step has read a push over h2c, because no run reaches them yet (B1.7, the
runner's own half, is unwritten) and no deployment carrying the chain has been measured. The rest of the check answered as designed: a full clone is **10 s** (3 requests,
1080 B in / 23008 out), a blobless clone **3 s** (5 requests), the first git request after **2100 s**
idle is **1 s** on a **new** instance (D501's scale-to-zero holds), and the unauthenticated
`GET /chk190/health` answered **403**, so no project-level `allUsers` or `allAuthenticatedUsers`
invoker is behind the service.

**Neither of the run's other two rows is a defect of this tree.** Both are rows of the check at the
head the owner read (`a13c125b7`), and `f46ccf0a` (#1409, merged that same day) fixed them: the
throwaway proxy now keeps the separator after its slow route prefix, so the slow path reaches its
upstream instead of answering `502` after **0 s** (and a slow row answered before any hold reads
*not measured*), and the Restore's branch delete now runs **from the clone**, where `git push` can
run, rather than from the scratch directory, which is not a repository — that is why it left
**`chk190/sJRgQCI8`** behind while the block read as cleaned up. So what the run leaves open is a
**re-run of the 3600 s row** against the fixed check (B0.5's own step), and the branch is that run's
leftover for the owner to delete by hand rather than something today's script does.

**What the check settles.** Five things the Bitbucket proxy is designed against and that cannot be
answered offline (reconciliation.md, F13, F14, U2, U7, U8): whether a pack above **32 MiB** can be
pushed through Cloud Run on **HTTP/1.1** (chunked) at all, and what the front end answers when it
cannot; what a **full clone** and a **blobless clone** cost in requests, bytes and time; how large the
**cold start** of the first git request after idle is (D501: the service keeps scaling to zero); and
what happens to a request held open past the service's **3600 s** timeout. It is the gate the run's
result feeds: a large push that passes on HTTP/1.1 is what S1 is built on, and one that does not is
what makes B1.5 serve h2c end to end.

**Prerequisites.** Installation `fugaro` only: the project (`fugaro-dev`) and the region (`us-east5`)
are hard-coded and `fugaro doctor` must answer that this is the `fugaro-dev` installation, so the
check cannot be pointed at another one and refuses to run if it is. Never `belong`. A **sandbox**
repository you may push a throwaway branch to, and its access token in a file at mode `0600`
(`CHECK190_TOKEN_FILE`; any other mode, and an empty file, are refused). `bash`, `mktemp`, `gcloud`,
`git`, `curl`, `awk` and `fugaro` on PATH, `gcloud` authenticated as you, as an account that can
**create a bucket and a registry and set IAM on both** (a project Owner can): the check makes its own
staging bucket `gs://fugaro-dev-chk190-staging` and registry `fugaro-chk190`, and grants the
installation's build account `roles/storage.objectViewer` and `roles/artifactregistry.writer` on
those two only. The installation's own `gs://fugaro-dev_cloudbuild` is not touched, and reading Cloud
Logging is not needed: the build runs with `CLOUD_LOGGING_ONLY` and the check reads its status.
About **two hours** at the terminal: the cold-start wait is 35 minutes and the slow
push is held open for an hour.

**What you type** (the full text, and what to do when a stop ends the run early, are in
[secrets-brokering/check190-steps.md](secrets-brokering/check190-steps.md)):

1. `umask 077 && pbpaste > ~/check190.token`
2. `CHECK190_REPO=<workspace>/<sandbox repository> CHECK190_TOKEN_FILE=~/check190.token bash scripts/live-checks/check190.sh --dry-run`
3. the same without `--dry-run`; paste the `CHECK 190 RESULT` block back
4. `rm ~/check190.token`

**What the check holds before it sends a request.** The deploy line carries
`--no-allow-unauthenticated`, and the check reads the argv a real run would pass rather than trusting
the flag to be there; `gcloud run services get-iam-policy` is read back, and the run stops before any
request if the policy names `allUsers` or `allAuthenticatedUsers`. A service, repository, secret or
bucket of the check's own names that was **already there** is a hard stop too: it never adopts,
writes into or deletes what it did not create. The token reaches the service as a **file** out of its own Secret Manager container, never as an environment variable — `gcloud run
services describe` prints an environment variable back — and the block carries counts, sizes and
times, never the token, a header or a body.

**The one thing only a request sees.** A project-level `allUsers`/`allAuthenticatedUsers` binding
with `roles/run.invoker` does **not** appear in the service's own `get-iam-policy`; an unauthenticated
`GET /chk190/health` is what finds it. A **401/403** is the pass. Any other answer is a **stop**, not
a failed row: the proxy and the sandbox repository's token would be behind a public URL, and the run
ends there rather than spending the next two hours behind it.

**Restore.** A build still running is cancelled, then the service, the image, the Artifact Registry
repository, the Secret Manager container, the staging bucket with the build's source in it (the two
grants go with the registry and the bucket) and the throwaway branches are deleted, from the exit trap
too, so a Ctrl-C in the middle still leaves nothing running; four counts are asserted `0` before the
scratch directory goes, and the directory is **kept** with a message saying where it is when one is not. The branches
are listed with a **freshly minted** identity token, because the one the slow push used has expired
by then, and a listing that fails is reported as a failure rather than read as "the branch is gone" —
a branch holding a 33 MiB blob left behind is the one outcome that would cost the installation. The
bucket is **read back**: `bucket-deleted` says it is gone, and a bucket that cannot be read is a
failure, not a pass. **No agent runs any step of it.**

([secrets-brokering/implementation-plan.md](secrets-brokering/implementation-plan.md), its "B1.11: Checks
191 and 192 written"; the reconciliation's **D493**, and the plan's **G2**, **G4**, **G6** and **G7**),
and **run by the owner** in task **B1.12**, whose steps are
[secrets-brokering/check191-steps.md](secrets-brokering/check191-steps.md) — this section carries no steps
of its own. The script is `scripts/live-checks/check191.sh`, with the test that drives it against fake
tools (`scripts/live-checks/check191_test.sh`). It runs on the **released** build whose **runner**
carries the proxy — **0.22.0**: the plan's Levels table gives the proxy chain 0.15.0, which has no
proxy to measure, and 0.21.0 is the first tag that holds the service's half
(`internal/credsvc/bitbucketproxy.go` landed 2026-11-07) but was cut **without** the runner's, which
landed in the release after it (`internal/cli/recipes_skew.go`'s `proxySince` is the gate `fugaro run`
refuses an older job image with; a CLI that predates it carries no gate and launches a proxied
repository whose runner pushes straight to Bitbucket with the token the job still mounts). And not on
a development build: a build from a checkout resolves no released
credentials-service image to deploy
(`internal/cli/init_credentials.go`, `resolveCredentialsImage`), so `fugaro version` must not print
`dev`. **No agent runs any step of it**, and none
has: every row it reads is a live installation's, a real run's and the credentials service's own answer.

**Why the attempts come from inside a run.** Every row this check exists for is a **refusal**, and a run's
identity is sealed to its own execution: its calls carry a launch token and the job identity, bound to its
run id and its repository. A call made from your machine — with your own credentials, or with the
service's — is answered about **that** identity, not about a run's, so it says nothing about whether a run
in another repository, a push to `main`, a tag, a delete, a write to another pull request of the run's
own repository, a merge or `/workspaces` is refused. Two of the seven attempts are only reachable from
the right target: `other_pull_request` is what a pull-request write earns when the pull request is not
the run's, and the rules refuse a call that names another **repository** for the repository *before*
they look at the pull request — so that attempt has to be a write to a pull request of the run's own
repository that is not the run's own. `call_not_allowed` is the classification's own refusal: merge and
`/workspaces` are not paths this proxy names at all, so they earn it wherever they point. The attempts
are therefore made by a throwaway run's **own check command** and by nobody else — **no
model is in the loop at all**: the sandbox repository's `commands.test` is Check 191's probe, and a check
step is the gate of the recipe's first model call (`internal/runner`'s `agentLoop` runs it as shell in the
run's container, at the run's own identity, before the agent is called), while the run's own git
environment sends every Bitbucket URL to its loopback forwarder (`internal/runner`'s `credentialVars`),
so the credentials service answers every one of the seven. The check reads that run's own line for each
attempt, the answer it got and the service's **audit line** for it — three halves of one reading, and a
refusal the service did not audit is not a pass.

**A probe is a real run.** The working run, and both of Check 192's runs, commit one line, push their
branch and open their pull request. What the working run's agent is asked for is the one line any task
asks for, and Check 191's probe is the run's own check command, which **exits 1 on purpose**: a run whose
check steps all pass ends with **no pull request at all** (`internal/runner`'s `endWithoutPR`, "every check
passed: nothing to fix"), and this run's pushed branch and pull request are half of what the check
measures. A run whose agent commits nothing is **failed** by the runner ("the agent made no commits",
`internal/runner/runner.go` and `shadow.go`, which record an empty commit and push it as a draft anyway),
and the branch and pull request are also the **positive** half of the reading, that the service SERVES the
clone, the push and the pull request the same identity later has refused — a working run whose push or
pull request never happened is a FAIL of `run-outcome`, whatever the agent did or did not commit. Those
branches and pull requests
**stay** on the sandbox repositories: this check holds no Bitbucket credential of its own and neither
deletes nor closes them, and the block names each one.

**Prerequisites.** Installation `fugaro` only: the project (`fugaro-dev`) and the region (`us-east5`) are
hard-coded and `fugaro doctor --project fugaro --all` must answer that this is the `fugaro-dev`
installation (that line is part of doctor's `--all` tail), so
