the check cannot be pointed at another one. Never `belong`, and a repository of that workspace is refused
by name. The installation's **credentials service must be on**, the sandbox repository must be **on the
credentials-service switch** — `agent.auth: cascade` for it, with a model credential in the service's
bundle and its root re-applied — and the sandbox repository must be **published with `proxy: true`** (the
plan's B1.7/B1.8). The check reads both halves: `fugaro project policy show --project fugaro --json` for
the published policy, and the switch from the credentials service's **own IAM policy** (`gcloud run
services get-iam-policy fugaro-credentials --project fugaro-dev --region us-east5 --format=json`) crossed
with the repository's **real jobs** (the jobs whose own `FUGARO_REMOTE` names it, from the job list the
check already reads): it is ON when every one of those jobs runs as an account that policy grants
`roles/run.invoker` to and at least one job exists, OFF when an existing job's account is not granted, and
UNREAD — a row the check could not measure — otherwise. `fugaro doctor`'s `credentials-service-deployed`
sentence is **not** the decision: the released doctor lists job accounts of workflow variants the
repository does not deploy, so that row is read only for the states where the service cannot serve a run
at all — the installation has no credentials service, or it has one that admits every job account and
holds nothing to serve a model credential out of — and its text is carried in the row for context. Those
states are the ones doctor's own row can be trusted for; where the row is about the invoker grant, doctor
answered it before it ever read the bundle, so the check reads the bundle itself (`gcloud secrets
versions list`, of the container `gcloud secrets list` names as the service's own) and stops unmeasured
when it holds no version Secret Manager will serve. It
fails the `proxied` row *before it launches anything* when the repository is not admitted, is admitted
without the proxy, or is off the switch: the published half alone is **inert**, since a repository off the
switch holds its own Bitbucket token and is served by nothing, so the check stops rather than launch three
runs at a path the proxy is not on; its remedy is to set `agent.auth: cascade` for that repository (with
a model credential in the service's bundle), run `fugaro update --repo` for it and run the check again.
The same published node must also **admit the repository to a Claude account** — an `accounts` entry
whose own `allow_repos` names it, since the service offers a run only a credential of an account that
admits its repository. That admission (`internal/credsvc`'s `admittedAccounts`) is the intersection of
**three** published facts: the node's own top-level `allow_repos` (the project's allow-list, the leg
`fugaro project repos rm` takes away), the account's own list, and the repository child node's
`credentials.accounts`. This preflight reads the account's list alone — the other two live in other
objects, and a repository the project's allow-list has stopped admitting is caught at the run-launch
row below rather than here — and a node whose block names none fails `account-admitted` *before it
launches anything*, since no shared Claude credential can ever serve a run of it. The block is keyed by
account-axis value rather than by Claude account: the publisher keys the project's own paid key into it
as `anthropic-api-key--project` and `provider-key--project` (`internal/config`'s `AxisNonAccountValue`
names the two), so an entry naming one of those admits a run to that tier-B credential and settles
nothing here; the gate reads an entry, and the row says what such an entry does and does not settle.
What the working run and the review-only run then meet turns on the node's own `credentials.fallback`:
where it does not spend, the working run's first model call is refused (the `state_unavailable` halt of
0.23.1, or the fallback-forbidden refusal when the service's bundle holds the paid key and the policy
will not spend it), and where it spends (`auto`) that run is served by the project's paid key instead —
a tier-B credential, which needs no admission — as far as the service's bundle holds that key, which is
not a read this check makes. The review-only run is refused in either arm: a review caller's identity is
paired against this same admission, which the fallback never enters (`internal/credsvc`'s `pairReview`).
The ended-identity probe is not part of this reading at all: its first call is the bootstrap git
traffic, refused as an identity before any route — and so before this admission — is reached. The
row's remedy is to add the repository to the account's own list in the
local config (`claude_accounts.<name>.allow_data_to`, or `project_secrets.claude-oauth-token.allow_data_to`
for the default account), name that account in the profile the repository's workflow uses
(`profiles.<profile>.claude_accounts` — `fugaro accounts add <name> --repos owner/name` writes both),
and have the owner run `fugaro project policy publish`. A switch the reading cannot settle — and a
service doctor reports as not there or as having nothing to serve a run's model credential out of,
where every model call of a run is refused — is recorded as **unmeasured** (exit `2`, nothing
launched) rather than as a pass. Three **sandbox** Bitbucket repositories — the proxied one the runs work
in, a second one for the other-repository refusal, and (with `--after-flip`) one the policy does not proxy
— plus the number of an **open** pull request **in the proxied repository itself** (`CHECK191_OTHER_PR`):
the run's own repository, and a pull request that is not the run's own. It has to be that repository's,
because a call naming another repository is refused for the repository before the pull-request rules are
reached, so a pull request of the second repository would earn `other_repository` and never
`other_pull_request`. The proxied repository must also **carry Check 191's probe** —
`scripts/live-checks/check191-probe.sh` copied into it and named in its own `commands.test`, which is what
makes the seven attempts with no model in the loop (the exact diff, the `fugaro.yaml` line and the two
values it is given are in [secrets-brokering/check191-steps.md](secrets-brokering/check191-steps.md)); a
repository that does not carry it is **refused**, exit `2`, with your step printed, rather than read as a
finding about the proxy. `bash`,
`mktemp`, `python3`, `curl`, `gcloud` and `fugaro` on PATH, `gcloud` authenticated as an account that may
read Cloud Logging for the installation, read the job list, **read the credentials service's own IAM
policy** (`gcloud run services get-iam-policy`, the switch's own half), **list the installation's secrets
and read the versions of the credentials service's bundle container** (the check reads them itself where
doctor's row is about the invoker grant), **read the IAM policy of the one labelled
`fugaro_secret=bitbucket-token`** (Check 192's accessor row: the
project-wide container, and a repository that stored the token itself has its own), and
**write and delete one node** in the installation's Realtime Database (the register's Check 95 step 3 is
the same write): the ended-run row is set up by hand, as you, with `gcloud auth print-access-token` and
`curl`, because no call of a run's own can put its identity in that state. The database's URL is read out
of the installation's own `~/.config/fugaro/projects/fugaro.yaml` (`budget.rtdb_url`). About **40 minutes
per run** at the terminal (`CHECK191_WAIT_SECONDS`, 2400 by default): three runs here and two in Check
192, each billed to the installation as any run is. The seven attempts themselves cost **no model call at
all** — the repository's own check command makes them, before the run's first model call — but each run is
still a run: it bootstraps, clones, and its agent commits the one line, pushes it and opens the pull
request the positive half is read from.

**What you type** (the full text, and what to do when a stop ends the run early, are in
[secrets-brokering/check191-steps.md](secrets-brokering/check191-steps.md)):

1. `CHECK191_REPO=<workspace>/<proxied sandbox repo> CHECK191_OTHER_REPO=<workspace>/<another sandbox repo> CHECK191_OTHER_PR=<n> bash scripts/live-checks/check191.sh --dry-run`
2. the same without `--dry-run`; paste the `CHECK 191 RESULT` block back

**The run ids.** Every run this check launches is named from `CHECK191_RUN_ID`, which must be today's
UTC date and a time (`YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS`; the default is now), and each run's id adds four hex characters
of its own. That is the one shape `fugaro run` admits (`internal/task`, `ValidRunID`'s
`^[0-9]{8}-[0-9]{6}-[0-9a-f]{4}$`, which `Spec.Validate` refuses anything else against), and the base's
day is also the day the service looks a run's outcome up under — an id of another day would put the
ended-run probe where the service never reads. A base outside that shape is refused **before anything is
launched**.

**What the block reads.** `proxied` (the published `bitbucket_token` block admits the repository with
`proxy: true`, and the service's own IAM policy puts it on the credentials-service switch);
`account-admitted` (the same node's `accounts` block admits it too — the account leg of the admission
above, so a node whose block names none can never have a shared credential offered to a run there, and
the check stops before any run is launched, naming the fallback in force and, under it, whether the
working run would be refused or served by the project's paid key, and the review-only run's pairing
refusal in either arm, plus the account's `allow_data_to`, the profile that must name it and the
owner-run `fugaro project policy publish` that carries it to the node); `run-launch` and `run-outcome`
(the working run reached a final
status, pushed its branch and opened its pull request); the seven refusal rows
(`refusal-other-repository`, `refusal-other-ref`, `refusal-tag-ref`, `refusal-ref-delete`,
`refusal-other-pull-request`, `refusal-merge`, `refusal-workspaces`), each failing on the run's own line,
on `refused=yes` and on the service's audit line for that call's class (`other_repository`, `other_ref`,
`tag_ref`, `ref_delete`, `other_pull_request`, `call_not_allowed` — a merge and `/workspaces` are the two
`call_not_allowed` attempts); `review-run` (a **review-only** run launched with `--pr`, the working run's
own pull request — a review-mode recipe reviews a pull request and needs exactly one, and such a run has
no branch of its own: the row passes when the service's own lines carry one of the two classes a
review identity's push can earn — `read_only`, or `no_run_branch` for an identity that carries no `fb`
and is not read-only — and fails on any other class the service wrote, `not_admitted` included: that is
the published block's rule about the **repository**, decided before any rule about what an identity may
write, so it is not a reading of a push. The run's own agent is asked to make the attempt, and its
sentence is read against the service's own lines and never taken on its word: a push it reports as
**served** is a FAIL only where that run's lines carry the served call behind it (one line with the one
status that is not a refusal, `StatusOK`). Where the service's lines carry neither a class nor a served
call at all the row is
recorded as one the check could **not measure** (exit `2`), with one line of reason: a review-mode run
has no route to the credentials service (`internal/runner`'s `refreshGitAuth` gives its agent no
forwarder rewrite and no git credential, and a `mode: review` recipe admits exactly one review step and
no repository command), and the owner decided to leave it that way, so no push of it reaches the service
to be refused or served);
`ended-identity` (the
probe's record, the service's own lines and what it wrote, read together: **nothing written, no line for
the probe in the service's own log, and the record's own sentence naming this execution's forwarder
(`/v1/bitbucket/proxy/`) and the `403` an identity refusal is answered with** is the pass — the probe's
first call is the bootstrap git traffic through its own loopback forwarder, not a model call, and git
prints the URL and the status it was answered and never the body, so no wire type and none of the
service's sentence is in the record; a line for the probe is the service having **served** a call of an
ended run, the finding this row exists for, and any other status on that first call — `503` is
`state_unavailable` — is a call the ended-run refusal never reached); and the
`restore` and `scratch-removed` rows. **Exit 0** is every
criterion that was measured holding, **1** is a measured criterion that did not hold or a guard that
stopped the check, and **2** is the check not being able to measure — a missing tool, the
credentials-service switch the `proxied` row could not be read from, the `review-run` row the service's
own lines could not settle (no class and no served call for the review run's identity, which is the
state a review-mode run's push is in, since such a run has no route to the service), or the ended-run
probe that could
not be set up (the node could not be written or did not read back, its record names no forwarder of this
execution, or its first call was never handed to the service). A key the run never reached reads `FAIL —
not reached`; a
key that could not be measured reads `FAIL` with the reason in its own detail, and nothing was launched.
The keys a mode never records are the exception, and read `N/A — not part of this mode (<mode>)` instead:
Check 191 reads the working run's rows and never Check 192's five (`jobs`, `mount`, `accessor`, `doctor`,
`run-still-works`), nor `dry-run` (only a `--dry-run` plan writes that marker), while Check
192 reads those five and none of Check 191's (`proxied`, `account-admitted`, `run-launch`, `run-outcome`,
the seven refusals, `review-run`, `ended-identity` do not exist in that mode). `N/A` is neither a pass nor
a failure — the exit code counts a `FAIL` alone — so a run whose measured rows all held ends `0` however
many `N/A` rows its block carries: six in a Check 191 run, fourteen in a Check 192 one.

**Restore.** The scratch directory, and the one Realtime Database node the check wrote by hand — deleted
and **read back** (the `restore` row is that reading, and a `restore: FAIL` names the node's URL so you can
delete it with `curl -X DELETE` and your own access token), from the exit trap too, so a Ctrl-C in the
middle still deletes it. The runs' records and the branches and pull requests they opened are left; the
block names each one. **No agent runs any step of it.**

## Check 192: the flip — the mount and the accessor gone, and a run that still works (installation `fugaro` only, sandbox repository only, never `belong`; run by you; RUN 2026-11-22: PASSED for its five rows)

**RUN 2026-11-22: PASSED for the five rows it measures.** The owner ran
`bash scripts/live-checks/check191.sh --after-flip` on 2026-11-22 on installation `fugaro` — project
`fugaro-dev`, region `us-east5` — on the released CLI **0.27.0**, against `edgeappinc/fugarosandbox`.
The block's measured rows:

```
fugaro:        0.27.0
project:       fugaro-dev / us-east5
jobs:          PASS — 1 job
mount:         PASS — none (no job mounts the Bitbucket token)
accessor:      PASS — none of the three labelled containers
doctor:        PASS — ok=true
run-still-works: PASS — run 20261122-181135-0004, PR #81 on edgeappinc/fugarosandbox after the flip
               (status=halted, pushed=yes)
```

The sixth row the run measured, `plain-repo`, **FAILED** (no job of `dimi_bmb/billmybanktests`) and was
**removed** the same day by the owner's ruling: it tested a per-repository job, which shared jobs retire
(D2312, D2302: an onboarded repository gets no job of its own, and shared jobs mount no Bitbucket token),
so the row could never pass. A Check 192 block now has five measured rows and no `plain-repo` key. PR #81
and its branch stay on the sandbox repository and are the owner's to delete.

Written by task **B1.11** of the secrets-brokering plan (its `--after-flip` mode:
`bash scripts/live-checks/check191.sh --after-flip`) and run by the owner **after the flip** (the plan's
B1.13 part two; **D500**, **O7**, and the plan's **G1** and **G9**). It is gated on the flip having
happened: without it the mount is still on the job and the row that reads the flip is the one that fails.
Its steps are [secrets-brokering/check191-steps.md](secrets-brokering/check191-steps.md). **No agent runs
any step of it.**

**What it settles.** After the flip a proxied repository's jobs give up their token. Five rows: the
repository's job still carries `FUGARO_REMOTE` and **none mounts the token** — read as the env var
`FUGARO_BITBUCKET_TOKEN` and the **DERIVED Secret Manager ID** its `secretKeyRef` points at
(`deploy/terraform/gcp/modules/workflow/job.tf` mounts `var.secrets[env.value]`; the logical name
`bitbucket-token` is never what a job mounts); no job account of that repository holds a role on the
secret — the IAM policy is read from every secret the installation **labels**
`fugaro_secret=bitbucket-token` (the project-wide container, and a repository that stored the token
itself has one of its own), and a run that finds no such label ends `2` rather than reading a policy it
did not find (`gcloud secrets list` is what carries the label); a run of it still clones, pushes and
opens its pull request, so the credential the job no longer holds is served by the service; the run's
own report names `bitbucket-direct` clean for it (`fugaro doctor --project fugaro --json`, the read the
plan's B1.9 built). It reads no repository that is not proxied: shared jobs mount no Bitbucket token
and a repository has no job of its own.

**Run it from the proxied repository's own checkout** — the directory `fugaro update --repo` was run in,
whose `fugaro.yaml` must select a shared profile with `workflows.<name>.job_profile` — or name that directory with `CHECK191_CHECKOUT`. The `doctor` row is one of the five, and doctor has
no `--repo`: it resolves the repository it answers about from the **working directory**, and prints no
`bitbucket-direct` line at all anywhere else, which would read as a finding about the flip when it is a
finding about where you were standing. The check therefore requires `git` on PATH, resolves the
checkout's own origin remote and **stops before it launches anything** when that is not this
repository's — a second's mistake rather than a run's.

**Prerequisites.** The same as Check 191 — installation `fugaro` only, never `belong`, sandbox
repositories only, `gcloud` authenticated as you — plus `git` (the checkout's origin remote, the
pre-launch guard above). A leftover `CHECK191_PLAIN_REPO` from the retired half is ignored. The jobs are read with `gcloud run jobs list`, matched by the job's own
`FUGARO_REMOTE`.

**What you type** (the full text is in
[secrets-brokering/check191-steps.md](secrets-brokering/check191-steps.md)):

1. `CHECK191_REPO=<workspace>/<the proxied sandbox repo> bash scripts/live-checks/check191.sh --after-flip --dry-run`
2. the same without `--dry-run`; paste the `CHECK 192 RESULT` block back

Its run is named from the same `CHECK191_RUN_ID` base as Check 191's (`YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS`, today by
default, plus four hex characters), for the same reason: that is the only shape `fugaro run`
admits, and the base's day is the day a run's outcome is looked up under.

**What the block reads.** The same fixed key list Check 191 prints, headed `CHECK 192 RESULT`, with this
mode's own five rows measured — `jobs`, `mount`, `accessor`, `doctor`, `run-still-works` — and
the other fourteen (`proxied`, `account-admitted`, `run-launch`, `run-outcome`, the seven refusals,
`review-run`, `ended-identity` and the `dry-run` marker) reading `N/A — not part of this mode (flip)`: this
mode never records them, and `N/A` is neither a pass nor a failure — the exit code counts a `FAIL` alone —
so they do not read as a check that stopped. A key this mode records, which the run stopped before
reaching, still reads `FAIL — not reached`.

**Restore.** The scratch directory and nothing else: this mode writes no Realtime Database node and
deletes nothing. The run it launches opens a branch and a pull request, and the block names them
— they stay on the sandbox repository, and they are the owner's to settle. **No agent runs any step of
it.**

## Check 193: an `api-key` and an `oauth` repository through the credentials service, and the flip (installation `fugaro` only, sandbox repositories only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **B2.5** of the secrets-brokering plan
([secrets-brokering/implementation-plan.md](secrets-brokering/implementation-plan.md), its "B2.5: Check
193 written"; the reconciliation's **D2070 (a)**, **D2071**, **F29** and **U9**), and **run by the owner**
twice: the switch mode in task **B2.6**, and `bash scripts/live-checks/check193.sh --after-flip` in task
**B2.8**, after the flip (B2.7, **D2072**/**G17**). Its steps are
[secrets-brokering/check193-steps.md](secrets-brokering/check193-steps.md) — this section carries no
steps of its own. The script is `scripts/live-checks/check193.sh`, with the test that drives it against
fake tools (`scripts/live-checks/check193_test.sh`). **No agent runs any step of it**, and none has: what
it measures is a live installation, real runs, and the credentials service's own answers about them.

**What it settles.** S2 puts an `api-key` repository and an `oauth` one on the credentials-service
switch: their runs' model calls are served by the service out of the installation's own bundle instead
of by a credential the job holds. Nothing offline settles whether that happens — the service's own audit
lines are the only record of what answered a call — so the check launches one throwaway run in each of
the two repositories and reads the lines back. Four things are measured, and three of them have a second
half that only the flip can show:

- **The switch is really on**, for both repositories: `gcloud run jobs list` holds a job of each (matched
  by the job's own `FUGARO_REMOTE`) and that job's container carries
  `FUGARO_CREDENTIALS_SERVICE_URL`. And the published budget mode is not `off`: the mode is what
  `fugaro update` reads, and a repository whose root was applied while the mode was live and whose mode
  is then `off` is one whose jobs hold no mount — the flip, B2.7 — and whose runs have nothing to be
  served from, because the address follows the same answer (**D2071**, and the state `fugaro project
  policy publish` refuses to create). A repository off the switch **stops the run
  before anything is launched** — a FAIL that costs no run is worth more than one that costs two.
- **The record each run is served against**: the check **reads** `creds/repoauth/<slug>` for each
  repository out of the installation's own Realtime Database (the node `fugaro update --repo` writes,
  **D2070 (a)**) and requires the pair to be one `api-key` and one `oauth`. The `<slug>` is the
  repository's own task slug (`task.Slug`: the readable path, a `-` and 16 hex — never the path spelled
  out of the repository's name), and the check reads it off the `fugaro_repo` label of that repository's
  jobs, which is the key `fugaro update --repo` writes the record under; a repository whose jobs carry
  none leaves the record unread (verdict `2`). It never writes one: the record is the installation's,
  and a check that wrote it would be measuring itself.
- **The credential a run is served, and its tier.** The run's own model calls are answered by the
  service, so the service's own `credsvc: audit` lines, read out of Cloud Logging filtered by
  `jsonPayload.run`, are the answer: the `api-key` repository's run must have a line naming
  `anthropic-api-key` at **tier B** (the paid key), and the `oauth` repository's run a line naming a
  Claude account's token at **tier A** — and a tier-A line names the **account** itself, `default` for
  the unsuffixed `claude-oauth-token` and the bare account name for a named one, never the
  `claude-oauth-token[-<account>]` Secret Manager container the token is stored in — "a run served
  anything else is the boundary not holding".
- **The account the `oauth` run declared** (**D2070 (a)**, `narrowToRepoAuth`). The account comes from
  the **launch** — the check runs `fugaro run` with no `--token`, and a launch that names no account
  declares the repository's default account, `default` — and never from the run's own row: that row's
  `oauth_account` is the credential the service's answers carried, the account the run used **last**
  (`internal/runner`'s `recordCredential`), so a row that read the declaration there would compare the
  answers with themselves and pass a service that served one account the run never declared. Every
  tier-A line of that run must then name `default` and **no other account the repository's own record
  names** — the refusal the check exists for. The row is read off the oauth run's **own lines**, so
  two states leave it **unmeasured** and the verdict `2`: a record naming only one account, with
  nothing this run could have been served besides the account it declared, and an oauth run that
  **never launched** (its own launch row carries the reason), which left the row no lines to read at
  all — a row read off a file nobody wrote would report the boundary as broken on the strength of
  nothing.
- **The proxy, for the one of the two the published policy admits with `proxy: true`** (**F29**, the
  plan's G7). A proxied Bitbucket repository's own git traffic goes **through** the service, which writes
  a line of that run's own under the purpose `git` (a fetch, the receive-pack advertisement, or a push)
  or `bitbucket-api` (the repository's own REST calls) — the check matches those two purposes and never
  the word `bitbucket`, because a **person's** read mint carries a repository and no run at all and would
  answer the row from outside it. Neither repository admitted with `proxy: true` leaves the row
  unmeasured (verdict `2`) rather than reading a direct push as the proxy.
- **`--after-flip` is the second half**, and it is the reading the flip is gated on: **no job of either
  repository mounts a model credential** — read as the env vars `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and
  `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` and as any `secretKeyRef` onto the `anthropic-api-key` or
  `claude-oauth-token*` Secret Manager IDs, because the DERIVED id is what a job mounts; a **provider
  key** left on a job is counted and is **not** a finding (**R6** — the flip takes the model credentials
  and keeps every provider route); a run of each repository **still succeeds**; and a run **started
  before the re-apply** — named by you in `CHECK193_INFLIGHT`, and compared with the repository's jobs'
  own `updateTime` — **kept its own mount and still finished** (**U9**): an execution created before the
  re-apply keeps the container spec it was created with, and the check reads **that spec** — the
  execution's own containers still carry the model credential while the job template the re-apply wrote
  carries none. The service's own lines for that run are not this reading: the flip keeps
  `FUGARO_CREDENTIALS_SERVICE_URL` on the repository (**D2072**), so a switched run reaches the service
  before and after it. A run named there that started **after** the re-apply is refused, not read: it
  was launched by the template the re-apply wrote, and its mount says nothing about U9.

**A run is the only thing that can show this.** The service binds a credential to the run that asked for
it — a run's identity is its own execution's — so a call made from your machine, with your own
credentials, is answered about **your** identity and can say nothing about what a run in a sandbox
repository is served. That is why the check launches throwaway runs: one in each repository in the
switch mode, and one more each with `--after-flip`. Each writes a single line to `CHK193.md`, commits it
on its own branch and opens a pull request, which is also the positive half of the reading — a run that
could not finish would be a run whose model calls nobody answered.

**Prerequisites.** Installation `fugaro` only: the project (`fugaro-dev`) and the region (`us-east5`)
are hard-coded in the script and never read from `gcloud config`, and `fugaro doctor --project fugaro
--all` must print its `project: … (GCP fugaro-dev,` line (the check reads the **line** and not doctor's
status, because doctor exits `1` whenever any check of its own failed), with `fugaro version` not a
development build: a checkout build resolves no released credentials-service image to deploy. Never
`belong`. `bash`, `mktemp`, `python3`, `gcloud`, `curl` and `fugaro` on PATH, with `gcloud` authenticated
as you — the record is read with `gcloud auth print-access-token` and a GET, and nothing else is asked of
your account. **Two sandbox repositories of that installation**, one whose own `fugaro.yaml` records
`agent.auth: api-key` and one whose records `oauth`, both already switched (the check refuses a pair that
is not one of each, and refuses a repository whose job carries no
`FUGARO_CREDENTIALS_SERVICE_URL`), and **a run of one of them already going** for `--after-flip`. If the
Bitbucket one of the two is published with `proxy: true`, the proxy row is measured; name it with
`CHECK193_PROXY_REPO` if the policy admits a repository that is not one of the two.

**What you type** (the full text is in
[secrets-brokering/check193-steps.md](secrets-brokering/check193-steps.md)):

1. `CHECK193_REPOS=<api-key repo>,<oauth repo> bash scripts/live-checks/check193.sh --dry-run`
2. the same without `--dry-run`; paste the `CHECK 193 RESULT` block back
3. after the flip, with a run of one of the two still going:
   `CHECK193_REPOS=<api-key repo>,<oauth repo> CHECK193_INFLIGHT=<that run id> bash scripts/live-checks/check193.sh --after-flip --dry-run`
4. the same without `--dry-run`; paste that block back too, as Check 193 has two runs (B2.6 and B2.8)

Its runs are named from today's date plus four hex characters each (`-0193`, `-0194`, and `-0195`/`-0196`
with `--after-flip`), which is the only shape `fugaro run` admits; set `CHECK193_RUN_ID` to reuse a base.

**Restore.** The scratch directory, and nothing else: this check creates no cloud resource, writes no
record and deletes nothing. The two (or four) runs it launches open a branch and a pull request each,
and the block names them — they stay on the sandbox repositories, and they are the owner's to settle.
**No agent runs any step of it.**

## Check 194: a repository's workflow secrets through the credentials service, and the flip (installation `fugaro` only, sandbox repositories only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **B3.6** of the secrets-brokering plan
([secrets-brokering/implementation-plan.md](secrets-brokering/implementation-plan.md), its "B3.6: Check
194 written"; the reconciliation's **D2073**, **D2074**, **D1262**, **D1264**, **D1267**, **D2313**,
**G18**, **G19**, **F33**, **F4** and **R6**, and **U9** in the flip's half), and **run by the owner**
twice: the switch mode in task **B3.7**, and `bash scripts/live-checks/check194.sh --after-flip` in task
**B3.9**, after the flip (B3.8, **G17**). Its steps are
[secrets-brokering/check194-steps.md](secrets-brokering/check194-steps.md) — this section carries no
steps of its own. The script is `scripts/live-checks/check194.sh`, with the test that drives it against
fake tools (`scripts/live-checks/check194_test.sh`). **No agent runs any step of it**, and none has: what
it measures is a live installation, real runs, and the credentials service's own answers about them.

**What it settles.** S3 stops a repository's job holding its workflow secrets: `fugaro update --repo`
writes a record of the containers a run may fetch from, the service serves a fetch out of them at the
run's bootstrap, and the flip takes the mounts away. Nothing offline settles whether the record names the
containers the job really mounted, whether a run in a second repository is refused the first one's
secret, or whether a value still reaches a run once its job holds none — so the check reads the record,
the jobs and the run's own outcome, and it launches one throwaway run to do it. Five things are measured,
and three of them have a half that only the flip can show:

- **The record**, read out of the installation's own Realtime Database at `creds/workflowsecrets/<slug>`
  — the node `fugaro update --repo` writes (**D2073 (a)**) — where the `<slug>` is the repository's own
  task slug (the readable path, a `-` and 16 hex), read off the **`fugaro_repo` label of its jobs** and
  never spelled out of the repository's name; a repository whose jobs carry no such label leaves the row
  unmeasured (verdict `2`). Four things are one fact: the node is there; its shape is **closed**
  (`version` and `workflows`, `env` and `id` per entry — every member of it is a NAME, and a member this
  release does not model is a FAIL rather than a shrug, because a member nobody reads is one that could
  hold a value, **G18**); it names a container for **each** of the two variables the sandbox workflow
  declares; and each of those is the installation's **project-wide** container
  (`fugaro-project-<installation>-…`, `gcp.ProjectSecretID`) and **never** the repository's own
  (`fugaro-<readable slug>-…`, `gcp.SecretID`). That last reading is **D2313** read off the wire — the
  decision of 2026-11-13, after this check was planned: a repository-level secret is accepted and
  ignored, so a workflow secret's value comes from the project's copy whatever the allow-list entry
  says. The plan's "one per-repository and one project workflow secret" is therefore read as the
  operator-local allow-list read the two ways it can be written: one `workflow_secrets` entry listing the
  repository under test alone, and one admitting the workspace. The check **reads** the record and never
  writes one: the record is what the service serves a run from, and a check that rewrote one and failed
  to put it back would point every fetch of that repository at another container.
- **The mounts** (**F33**, **D1267**): the fetch reads the container the mount reads, so a variable of
  interest a job of the repository carries must be fed from the container the record names for it, no
  job may carry one as a **plain value** (a value written into the job is one a fetch could never be
  seen to replace), and the **execution the run itself ran on** must read both from those containers —
  that last part is what makes the run's own verify a reading about these containers rather than about a
  job spec somebody edited since. A record that could not be settled stops the check **before any run is
  launched** — a FAIL that costs no run is worth more than one that costs two.
- **A run's verify** — the plan's "a run's verify sees both". The sandbox repository's own verify
  command fails on an empty variable (the owner's step: [the steps file](secrets-brokering/check194-steps.md)),
  so a run whose row reads `succeeded` with a pull request reached its verify stage with both values, out
  of the containers the row above reads off the execution it ran on. Which container each value came from
  is the row above and is not guessed from the run's outcome.
- **Another repository's job is refused them** — read where it can be, in the **second** repository's own
  record and its own jobs. The service decides every call from the record of the repository the
  **verified** job account belongs to and is handed nothing else — the call names one environment
  variable and no repository (**G19**, `internal/runner/workflowsecrets.go`) — so the boundary is
  exactly "what is in the caller's own record", and the check reads those same two names against a second
  repository: the entry that lists **one** repository must be refused to the other (no row of its record,
  no mount on its jobs, no variable in their environment), while the entry that admits the workspace is
  served to it too. A second repository that knows the per-repository name at all is the row this check
  exists to catch.
- **`--after-flip` is the second half**, and it is the reading the flip is gated on: **no job of the
  repository hands a run either variable in any form** — not "fed from another container" but not there
  at all — and a run launched after the flip **finishes all the same**, on an execution that carries
  neither variable, with the service's own `credsvc: audit` lines for it naming **both** of the
  record's containers under the purpose `workflow-secret` (a line of another purpose is never read: a
  switched run's git and model calls are served too, and a row that counted them would call the record's
  containers served when they were not). The address the run reaches the service at is **not** a
  reading of the jobs, and the row does not take one there: the flip keeps
  `FUGARO_CREDENTIALS_SERVICE_URL` (B3.8), but it is a **launch-time** entry — `fugaro run` hands it to
  the backend and the backend writes it into the **execution's** container overrides
  (`internal/cli`'s `credentialsServiceLaunchEnv`, `internal/backend/gcp`'s `Launch`) — so no job
  template of a repository carries it, and the repository's own check job could not
  (`internal/infra`'s `platformEnv` is its whole environment but for the check's own spec). What the
  address is for is what the `served` row reads: a run whose job held neither variable and which still
  finished with both values is a fetch that could only have been made with it; the account the run's
  job runs as holds **no `secretAccessor`**
  on either container's own IAM policy (**D2074** — the grants are the service's, one per container the
  job mounts, B3.3 — so after the flip the value reaches the run through the service and the job reads
  nothing itself); and a run **started before the re-apply** — named by you in `CHECK194_INFLIGHT`, and
  compared with the repository's jobs' own `updateTime` — **kept the container spec it was created with
  and still finished** (**U9**): the check reads the execution's **own** spec off
  `gcloud run jobs executions describe`, and it must still read both variables out of the record's
  containers while the job template the re-apply wrote hands a run neither. A run named there that
  started **after** the re-apply is refused, not read: it was launched by the template the re-apply
  wrote, and its spec says nothing about U9. The service's own lines for that run are deliberately not
  this row's reading — the flip keeps the URL, so a run in flight across the re-apply is served before
  and after it.

**Prerequisites.** Installation `fugaro` only: the project (`fugaro-dev`) and the region (`us-east5`) are
hard-coded in the script and never read from `gcloud config`, and `fugaro doctor --project fugaro --all`
must print its `project: … (GCP fugaro-dev,` line (the check reads the **line**, not doctor's status,
because doctor exits `1` whenever any check of its own failed), with `fugaro version` not a development
build — a checkout build resolves no released credentials-service image to deploy, and a development
build is recorded as a FAILed `fugaro-version` row rather than a stop, so read that row before spending
forty minutes on a run. Never `belong`. `bash`, `mktemp`, `python3`, `gcloud`, `curl` and `fugaro` on
PATH, with `gcloud` authenticated as you — the DB read is a `gcloud auth print-access-token` and a GET,
and the rest are read-only reads of `run jobs`, one execution, a secret's IAM policy and Cloud Logging.
**Two sandbox repositories of that installation**: the one under test declares the two workflow secrets
in its own `fugaro.yaml`, with the verify command failing on an empty variable, and the local config's
`workflow_secrets` block holds an entry listing that repository alone and an entry admitting the
workspace (both stored project-wide, both of which the record then names as the installation's project
containers). The **second** repository must not be listed by the per-repository entry — that is what
makes the boundary readable — and both must have been through `fugaro update --repo` since the release
that carries B3.1, because the record is keyed by the slug their jobs carry. For `--after-flip`: a run of
the repository under test that is still going when you re-apply.

**A run is the only thing that can show this.** The service binds what it serves to the run that asked
for it — a run's identity is its own execution's — so a call made from your machine, with your own
credentials, is answered about **your** identity and can say nothing about what a run in a sandbox
repository is served. That is why the check launches throwaway runs: one in the switch mode, one more
with `--after-flip`. Each writes a single line to `CHK194.md`, commits it on its own branch and opens a
pull request, which is also the positive half of the reading — a run that could not finish would be a
run whose job held no value and whose fetch nobody answered.

**What you type** (the full text is in
[secrets-brokering/check194-steps.md](secrets-brokering/check194-steps.md)):

1. `CHECK194_REPO=<the repository under test> CHECK194_OTHER_REPO=<the second repository> bash scripts/live-checks/check194.sh --dry-run`
2. the same without `--dry-run`; paste the `CHECK 194 RESULT` block back
3. after the flip, with a run of the repository under test still going:
   `CHECK194_REPO=<the repository under test> CHECK194_OTHER_REPO=<the second repository> CHECK194_INFLIGHT=<that run id> bash scripts/live-checks/check194.sh --after-flip --dry-run`
4. the same without `--dry-run`; paste that block back too, as Check 194 has two runs (B3.7 and B3.9)

Its runs are named from today's UTC date and time plus four hex characters each (`-0197` in the switch
mode, `-0198` with `--after-flip`); set `CHECK194_RUN_ID` to reuse a base.

**Restore.** The scratch directory, and nothing else: this check creates no cloud resource, writes no
record and deletes nothing. The one run of the switch mode and the one more of `--after-flip` open a
branch and a pull request each, and the block names them — they stay on the sandbox repository, and they
are the owner's to settle. **No agent runs any step of it.**

## Check 195: a Cloud Build step calls an IAM-only Cloud Run service (installation `fugaro` only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **B4.1** of the secrets-brokering plan
([secrets-brokering/implementation-plan.md](secrets-brokering/implementation-plan.md), its "B4.1: Check
195 written"; the reconciliation's **U4** and **U10**), and **run by the owner** in task **B4.2**, whose
steps are [secrets-brokering/check195-steps.md](secrets-brokering/check195-steps.md) — this section
carries no steps of its own. The script is `scripts/live-checks/check195.sh`, with the test that drives
it against fake tools (`scripts/live-checks/check195_test.sh`). **No agent runs any step of it**, and
none has: the ID token this check reads is minted by a real build's metadata server, inside that build,
and only Cloud Run can say whether the grant admits the call.

**What it settles.** S4 gives a repository's build account access to the credentials service, and
nothing offline settles whether that works: the token comes out of the metadata server of a build that
is really running, and whether the service admits it is Cloud Run's answer. So the check makes the
whole path by hand with throwaways — a Cloud Run service deployed with IAM required, a build account
granted `roles/run.invoker` **on that service alone**, and a Cloud Build whose step runs as that
account, mints an ID token for the service's URL and calls it — and reads the answer out of the
build's own line. **PASS on a 200**, with the token's `email` claim printed and never the token. B4.3's
`VerifyBuild` and B4.4's Terraform grant (`google_cloud_run_v2_service_iam_member` for the build
account, as invoker on the service) are both built on this reading. A **FAIL stops S4** and comes back
to the owner as a decision: an account whose own token is refused is a design answer, not a bug to work
around. The owner's gate is task **B4.2**: the dry run, then the run, then the block pasted back.

**Prerequisites.** Installation `fugaro` only: the project (`fugaro-dev`) and the region (`us-east5`)
are hard-coded in the script and never read from `gcloud config`, and `fugaro doctor --project fugaro`
must answer that this is the `fugaro-dev` installation, so the check cannot be pointed at another one.
Never `belong`. `bash`, `mktemp`, `gcloud`, `curl` and `fugaro` on PATH, `gcloud` authenticated as an
account that can create a Cloud Run service, create a service account, set IAM on the service, add one
project-level binding, submit a build and read the build's own lines out of Cloud Logging — a project
Owner can. **Nothing else is needed and nothing is prepared**: no token, no secret, no repository, no
file. The check mints no credential of its own and asks the owner for none, which is the point of it —
the only credential in the path is the ID token the build's own step mints for itself and uses where it
mints it.

**What it creates, and what it costs.** One throwaway Cloud Run service (`fugaro-chk195`), deployed
from Google's own public Cloud Run sample container, so the check builds and pushes no image of its
own; one throwaway service account (`fugaro-chk195-caller`); the `roles/run.invoker` binding on that
service; and one project-level `roles/logging.logWriter` binding, which a build that names its own
service account needs to write the log the token's email claim is read out of (`options.logging:
CLOUD_LOGGING_ONLY`, as Fugaro's own image builds do). **Minutes at the terminal, not money**: one
build and one Cloud Run service that is idle by the time you look. A service or an account of those two
names that was **already there** is a hard stop before anything is created — this check never adopts,
grants on or deletes what it did not create — and so is a filtered **list that could not be read**: an
expired session or a transient API error is not the answer "it is not there", and read that way the
check would go on over a service or an account of its own names and then delete it.

**The assertions, and the order they are read in.** `gcloud run services get-iam-policy` is read
**before** anything is called and a public member (`allUsers` or `allAuthenticatedUsers`) in it stops
the run: a 200 from a service that answered anyone would prove nothing about the grant. An
**unauthenticated `GET`** on the service's own URL follows — a **401/403** is the pass, and anything
else ends the run before the throwaway account is created or a token is sent — because a
**project-level** public invoker does not appear in the service's own policy, so that one request is
the only thing that sees it. After the grant, the service's own policy is read **back**: it must name
the throwaway account and nobody else, so a binding that did not land is a stop rather than a 403 the
block would report as the account having been refused. The build's own record is read for its
`serviceAccount` field as well as its status, so a 200 earned by another identity cannot pass: that
field is a **resource name** (`projects/<project>/serviceAccounts/<account>`, carrying the address the
build was submitted with or the account's numeric `uniqueId`), and it is read as the account it ends in
rather than compared with the address. The step's own line — one line, `CHK195 status=… email=…` — is
read out of Cloud Logging, retried while ingestion catches up; a build whose line cannot be read is a
**failure**, not a pass, because nothing about the grant was measured.

**What you type** (the full text is in
[secrets-brokering/check195-steps.md](secrets-brokering/check195-steps.md)):

1. `bash scripts/live-checks/check195.sh --dry-run` — it prints the plan and calls **nothing at all**:
   no `gcloud`, no `fugaro`, no `curl`
2. the same without `--dry-run`; paste the `CHECK 195 RESULT` block back

**Restore.** The service (which takes the invoker binding with it), the project-level binding and the
throwaway account are all deleted, and each of the three is **read back** rather than assumed: the
project binding is removed **before** the account, because a binding that outlives its member reads
back as `deleted:serviceAccount:…` and can never be removed again. It runs from the exit trap too, so a
Ctrl-C in the middle still leaves nothing running, and the scratch directory goes at the end. What is
left is the **build's own record**, in the project's Cloud Build history: it is the project's log of
what ran rather than a resource this check made, and nothing here deletes it. **No agent runs any step
of it.**

## Check 196: a repository's image build and its daily image check through the credentials service, GitHub and Bitbucket, and the flip (installation `fugaro` only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **B4.7** of the secrets-brokering plan
([secrets-brokering/implementation-plan.md](secrets-brokering/implementation-plan.md), its "B4.7: Check
196 written"; the reconciliation's **D2076**, **D2077**, **R5**, **R6**, **G18**, **G19**, **G20**,
**F28**, **F29** and **U9**), and **run by the owner** in task **B4.8** — and again in **B4.10**, after
the flip — whose steps are [secrets-brokering/check196-steps.md](secrets-brokering/check196-steps.md) —
this section carries no steps of its own. The script is `scripts/live-checks/check196.sh`, with the
test that drives it against fake tools (`scripts/live-checks/check196_test.sh`). **No agent runs any
step of it**, and none has: what it reads is a live installation's own records — real builds, real
jobs and the service's own lines.

**What it settles.** S4 makes a repository's image build bake with a credential fetched from the
credentials service, and — once the flip lands — its daily image check re-bake the same way: before the
flip the check job keeps the mount of its own git credential, because the accessor that mount needs is
the build account's and leaves only with the flip, so the switch mode reads that pre-flip shape and
`--after-flip` reads the served one. **What a repository builds today is the catalog entry its
`image_map` names, not a derived image of its own** — D1900 turned repository-level images off, so the
image a sandbox repository runs comes from `fugaro image build <entry>` (or from `fugaro apply`'s owed
catalog-build step, which submits the same build), and that build's shape is not the one the flip was
written for: it runs as the project's **build identity**, names no service and keeps the provider
credential its request mounts. Nothing offline settles whether the installation really behaves that way:
the build's request, the account it ran as, the job the check runs as, the service's own deployment and
the lines the service actually wrote are all facts of a live installation. So the check reads them where
they are written rather than calling the service itself — the project's own Cloud Build records, the
installation's Cloud Run jobs, the service itself and its **own** `credsvc: audit` lines — and it does so
for **two** repositories, one GitHub and one Bitbucket, because the credential a build mounts is the
provider's git credential and the two providers reach it differently (**D2076**(a): the Bitbucket
token's reach is unchanged; **D2077**(a): a workflow's build secrets come from the service too).

**The boundary it reads.** B4.3's route binds a calling email to **one** repository, so the reading is
that a build of one repository is served its **own** provider credential and its **own** record and
never another's: the service's line is compared with the account the build's own record says it ran as
(**G20**, the one field of that line a call cannot claim for itself), with the provider's credential
name, and with the repository's slug. A catalog entry's build is **not** an account that route admits —
it runs as the project's build identity, **D2301** — so it never asks the route at all: its own row is
that build's status, that identity and the mount its request carries, and the service's line for the
repository is read and compared beside it (a line that names the service must still name the build's own
account, credential and slug), while a repository whose newest build is a catalog entry's and which has
no such line is recorded **INFO** and not a FAIL — that absence is what this installation's shape
predicts, and calling it a failure would end the switch mode on a correct installation. The service's own IAM policy is read beside it — build accounts
of this installation admitted, **no** `allUsers` and **no** `allAuthenticatedUsers` — which is the front
door B4.4's grant is. The plan's "another repository's build account is refused" is read as those two
and not as a cross-repository call: a call that names another repository can only be made by a build
**running as** that other account, which is a throwaway build rather than a reading of the
installation, and a caller-identity reading is what **Check 195** already makes. A **FAIL stops S4** and
comes back to the owner as a decision: a build served another repository's credential, or a service
answering anyone, is a design answer and not a bug to work around. The owner's gate is task **B4.8**:
the dry run, then the run, then the block pasted back.

**Prerequisites.** Installation `fugaro` only: the project (`fugaro-dev`) and the region (`us-east5`)
are hard-coded in the script and never read from `gcloud config`, and `fugaro doctor --project fugaro
--all` must print its `project: … (GCP fugaro-dev,` line, so the check cannot be pointed at another
one. Never `belong`. `bash`, `mktemp`, `python3`, `gcloud` and `fugaro` on PATH, with `gcloud`
authenticated as an account that can list the project's builds, list Cloud Run jobs, list one job's
executions, read the service's own IAM policy and read the service's own lines out of Cloud Logging — a
project Owner can. Two **sandbox** repositories already switched to the credentials service and built —
one GitHub (`CHECK196_REPO`) and one Bitbucket (`CHECK196_BITBUCKET`), both required — each with its
catalog entry's build submitted from its own checkout (**`fugaro image build <entry>`**, or `fugaro
apply`, which submits the same build; `fugaro image refresh` is refused under D1900 and builds
nothing). **The check submits no build of its own**: it reads the ones you submitted.

**What it creates, and what it costs.** **Nothing.** The check creates no cloud resource, submits no
build, writes no record and deletes nothing — it is a reading of the project's own records, the
installation's own jobs and the service's own lines — so the only thing its Restore removes is its own
scratch directory, which the exit trap takes even on a Ctrl-C. **Minutes at the terminal, not money.**
What it reads stays: the builds and the check executions are the project's own history, and this check
neither made them nor deletes them.

**The assertions, and the order they are read in.** The project's recent builds are read once
(`gcloud builds list`, the last `CHECK196_BUILDS`, default 50) and each repository's newest **catalog
entry** build is picked out by the entry in its `_IMAGE` substitution — the catalog image
`catalog-<entry>` under the installation's shared-images registry — so no other build can be read as
this repository's; a repository with no such build in that window is a row that **could not be
measured** (exit 2) and says so by name rather than passing, and its remedy names the command that
really submits it (`fugaro image build <entry>`, or `fugaro apply`), never `fugaro image refresh`. The
build's **status** and the **account** in its own record (`serviceAccount`, a resource name, read as the
address it ends in) are what make the build row: a build that ended anything but `SUCCESS`, or ran as
somebody other than the installation's **build identity** (`fugaro-build-identity@<project>…`, what
`gcp.CatalogBuildSpec.check` admits), is a **FAIL**. The **service** row is read **off the service
itself** (`gcloud run services describe`) and depends on no build at all: a service that is not deployed,
or that Cloud Run serves no URL, is a **FAIL**, and a read that failed is a row that could not be
measured. The **mounts** row reads the request's own `availableSecrets` (the Secret Manager
**container** ids and the env names — a container is a name and never a value, **G18**): a catalog build
mounts exactly the provider's git credential, and a build whose request carries **no** mount and names
no service holds no credential at all and is a **FAIL**. Then the service's own
`credsvc: audit` line of purpose `build` for each repository is read out of Cloud Logging — retried
while ingestion catches up, because an empty answer taken immediately is an answer about Cloud Logging
and not about the service, and a **read that failed** is a row that could not be measured rather than
the answer "there is no line". The **caller**, the **credential** and the **repository** on that line
are each compared with what the build's own record says, and any `credsvc: refused` line for the
repository is printed **redacted** in the failure's reason; where the newest build names no service — as
every catalog entry's build does — a repository with no `build` line at all reads **INFO** with the
reason that absence is the installation's own shape (with any refused line printed beside it), and only
a build that *does* name the service with no line to show for it is a **FAIL**. The repository's daily check job is found by
the slug label the installation writes: before the flip it must run as the repository's build account,
**mount** the repository's git credential (the platform's own reserved variable for the provider's git
secret, `FUGARO_GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` or `FUGARO_BITBUCKET_TOKEN`) and carry **no**
`FUGARO_CREDENTIALS_SERVICE_URL` — the address is written only where the mount has been taken away, so a
job that carries it in this mode has the flip already landed and reads **INFO**, pointing at
`--after-flip`, and a job that carries the address *beside* a mount is a shape the installation never
plans and a **FAIL** — and its **newest execution** must have ended completed. A job with neither a
mount nor an address holds no credential at all and is a **FAIL**. Last, the service's own IAM policy: a
public member is a **FAIL**.

**The flip (`--after-flip`).** The same script's second half reads the state B4.9 leaves. A repository
whose newest build is a **derived image's** carries **no** `availableSecrets` and **no** `secretEnv` and
does name the service — a build with neither a mount nor a service has no credential at all and could
only fail — and the service's own line is still there for it. A repository whose newest build is a
**catalog entry's** is read for what the flip does and does not reach: that build runs as the project's
build identity, which the build-credentials route does not admit (**D2301**), so it **keeps** the
provider credential its request mounts and names no service, before and after the flip — a row that says
so, and a **FAIL** only if the build carries neither a mount nor a service. Its daily check job mounts
**no** Secret Manager container and **is handed the service's address instead** — the flip writes the
two together, so a job that mounts nothing and names no service is a **FAIL** — and the build still
ended `SUCCESS`, which is what says the mounts being gone did not break the path. Its block has its own rows — it does not print the switch mode's rows as
`not reached`, which would read as a reading this mode never takes.

**What you type** (the full text is in
[secrets-brokering/check196-steps.md](secrets-brokering/check196-steps.md)):

1. `bash scripts/live-checks/check196.sh --dry-run` — it prints the plan and calls **nothing at all**:
   no `gcloud`, no `fugaro`
2. the same without `--dry-run`, with `CHECK196_REPO` and `CHECK196_BITBUCKET` set; paste the
   `CHECK 196 RESULT` block back
3. after the flip, `bash scripts/live-checks/check196.sh --after-flip`; paste that block back

**Restore.** The scratch directory, and nothing else: this check has no cloud resource to delete, no
build to cancel and no binding to remove. It runs from the exit trap too, so a Ctrl-C leaves nothing
behind, and `CHECK196_KEEP_SCRATCH` keeps the directory when you want to read what the check wrote.
**No agent runs any step of it.**

## Check 197: coding runs on the profile's shared project jobs through the credentials service, GitHub and Bitbucket, and the flip (installation `fugaro` only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **B5.5** of the secrets-brokering plan
([secrets-brokering/implementation-plan.md](secrets-brokering/implementation-plan.md), its "B5.5: Check
197 written"; the reconciliation's **D2071**, **D2072**, **D2078**, **D2079**, **D2080**, **G21**,
**F40** and **U9**), and **run by the owner** in task **B5.6** — the switch mode, the gate S5 stops on —
and again in task **B5.8** after **B5.7**'s flip. The owner's own steps are
[secrets-brokering/check197-steps.md](secrets-brokering/check197-steps.md) — this section carries no
steps of its own — and the script is `scripts/live-checks/check197.sh`, with the test that drives it
against fake tools (`scripts/live-checks/check197_test.sh`). **No agent runs any step of it**, and none
has: what it measures is a live installation, real runs, a **shared** job serving several repositories,
and the credentials service's own answers about them.

**What it settles.** S5 is the shape in which one project job serves every repository of a profile, and
nothing offline settles it: whether a launch lands a run on that shared job at all, whether the service
serves it from the job's **own verified identity** rather than from something the run could claim,
whether a repository the profile does not admit is refused, and whether the flip really took the mounts
away while a run already going still finished, are all answers of a live installation. So the check
launches throwaway runs in **sandbox** repositories and reads the service's own `credsvc: audit` lines
back for them: the credential, the tier, a **model** call served (`forward`), and the **caller** — the
identity the service verified, `AuditEvent.Caller`, the account Cloud Run minted the shared job's ID
token for, read off the job's own spec — which is the one field of those lines a run cannot forge
(**G21**). The job the run landed on is read out of the run's own row (the execution path is the only
place that job is written down), and it must be one of the profile's `fugaro-p-<profile>-github…` jobs,
each carrying `FUGARO_CREDENTIALS_SERVICE_URL`: that variable is the switch a launcher writes and
nothing else can (**D2072**), and a job off it holds whatever it mounts and reaches nothing. The
Bitbucket half (**D2079**) reads the same three things of a shared Bitbucket job whose profile the
published block proxies — and reads **INFO**, not FAIL, while no such job is deployed, which is the
plan's own "(after D2079)": a run that measures the GitHub half perfectly ends `0`, and a **FAIL stops
S5** and comes back to the owner as a decision rather than as something to work around.

**One thing this check does not measure, and says so in its own block.** The credentials service's own
half of the outside-profile gate — a call from a shared job for a repository its profile does not admit
— **cannot be made from the owner's machine at all**: a shared caller's call needs **both** the job's
Google ID token and a run identity, and neither can be minted outside the job (**F40**). So the row
measures the installation's refusal of the **launch** of that repository (the launcher's own sentence,
`the job profile "…" does not admit …`, and no row in that repository's listing), which the same
published policy decides, and records the service-side half as not measured rather than reading the
launcher's refusal as the service's.

**Prerequisites.** Installation `fugaro` only: the project (`fugaro-dev`) and the region (`us-east5`)
are hard-coded in the script and never read from `gcloud config`; `fugaro doctor --project fugaro --all`
must print its `project: … (GCP fugaro-dev,` line (the check reads that line, not doctor's exit status,
which is `1` whenever any check of its own failed), and `fugaro version` must not print `dev`, because a
build from a checkout resolves no released credentials-service image to deploy, and this whole reading is
about what that image does. Never `belong`. `bash`, `mktemp`, `python3`, `gcloud` (authenticated as
you, to read a job list, a job, an execution and Cloud Logging) and `fugaro` on PATH. **No `curl`, no
access token and no Realtime Database read**: a shared job's credential is the service's own bundle, and
the one record this path could read — `creds/repoauth`, Check 193's subject — belongs to a
per-repository job. The owner names a sandbox repository whose own `fugaro.yaml` selects a job profile
(`CHECK197_REPO`), a second one the project admits and that profile's own `allow_repos` does not
(`CHECK197_OUTSIDE`), and optionally a proxied sandbox Bitbucket repository (`CHECK197_BITBUCKET`); the
flip mode additionally needs `CHECK197_INFLIGHT`, a run of that repository that was **already going**
when the re-apply happened and that finished with a pull request, because a run this check picked itself
could be one that ended hours before the re-apply and would say nothing about **U9**.

**What it creates, and what it costs.** Throwaway runs in the sandbox repositories — one in the switch
mode, one more with `--after-flip` — each writing one line to `CHK197.md`, committing it, pushing a
branch and opening a pull request, plus one **refused** launch in the repository outside the profile
(which leaves nothing). No cloud resource is created, no record is written, no node is read and no
credential is minted or printed: a shared job's credential is the service's own, which is the subject.
**Wall clock, not money: a run each, about 30–40 minutes.** The one destructive reading is the flip
mode's, and it is a reading and not a write: `gcloud run jobs executions describe` on the in-flight
run's own execution shows it still holding the mount it was **created** with while the job template the
re-apply wrote holds none.

**The two modes, and what each reads.** Without an argument the check runs **Check 197** — the policy
(the repository admitted to exactly one profile, and a budget mode that is not `off`, since a mode of
`off` is no gateway and the gateway is what reaches the service, **D2071**), the profile's shared jobs
and their switch, the run on the shared job, and the outside-profile refusal — and the Bitbucket rows.
`bash scripts/live-checks/check197.sh --after-flip` runs the flip's half: **no** shared job of the
profile mounts `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, or is fed from the `anthropic-api-key`
or `claude-oauth-token*` Secret Manager IDs (the **derived** id a job mounts, so the logical name is its
last readable segment); no shared Bitbucket job carries `FUGARO_BITBUCKET_TOKEN` (**D2079**); the
in-flight run's own execution kept its mount (**U9**); and one more run on the flipped job still
succeeds. Provider keys left on a job are **counted** and are **not** a finding: **R6** keeps every
provider route a repository's stages go out on.

**What you type** (the full text is in
[secrets-brokering/check197-steps.md](secrets-brokering/check197-steps.md)):

1. `CHECK197_REPO=<owner>/<repository> CHECK197_OUTSIDE=<owner>/<outside> bash scripts/live-checks/check197.sh --dry-run`
   — it prints the plan and calls **nothing at all**: no `gcloud`, no `fugaro`
2. the same without `--dry-run`; paste the `CHECK 197 RESULT` block back
3. after B5.7's flip, with a run of the repository going across the re-apply:
   `CHECK197_REPO=… CHECK197_OUTSIDE=… CHECK197_INFLIGHT=<that run id> bash scripts/live-checks/check197.sh --after-flip --dry-run`,
   then the same without `--dry-run`, and that block back too

**Restore.** The scratch directory, and nothing else: this check creates no cloud resource, writes no
record and deletes nothing. The runs it launches open a branch and a pull request each, and the block
names every run id and pull request number it saw — they stay on the sandbox repositories, and they are
the owner's to settle, since the check holds no credential to close them. **No agent runs any step of
it.**

## Check 290: the mixed-credentials run — the coder on its provider route through the gateway, the senior review inside the same loop on a Claude OAuth account (sandbox installation and sandbox repository only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **B6** of the mixed-credentials work (design `docs/mixed-credentials/spec.md` §5 and §11; the owner's ruling **B0** of 2026-11-04). The rule is **built** — the tasks B1–B6 shipped in 0.19.0 — and no run of it has met a real installation yet: this check is the evidence the design's §9 and `docs/multi-model.md` still name as missing. It is **OWNER-RUN**: **no agent runs any step of it**, every step is yours, and **no step types, prints or pastes a token or a key value** — the two variable names step 5 reads are read as *presence in a record*, never as values.

**What the check confirms.** One `api-key` run of the sandbox repository, on a trivial task, in which

- the **coder** stays where it was: a provider-routed model (a DeepSeek ID on your own provider route) whose calls are **priced through the budget gateway** — `budget.mode: enforce`, the only mode that routes a call to a provider at all (`config.CheckProviderGateway`) — so its stage carries the gateway's routing and the gateway's own call count;
- the **senior review** runs **inside that same loop**, direct to Anthropic on ONE stage-scoped Claude OAuth account, on an **Opus** model: `stage_accounts.review` names the account, the `review` stage's `credential` is `oauth`, and its calls never reach the gateway;
- the review's **verdict** is `ship`, and nothing anywhere reads `Invalid API key`: a stage that silently fell back would be answered with a refusal, and the run's own text is where that shows;
- the **accounting** is the shipped one: the account's dollars are inside `cost.model_usd` (the stage's `model_usd` equals its `model_notional_usd`) and **outside** `cost.total_usd`, with `sum(stages[].model_usd) + cost.model_by["unattributed"] == cost.model_usd`; and
- the coder's **own stage environment holds no token**: the runner's own environment holds the account's token (the job mounts it — the exposure the ruling **B0** accepted), and every stage the account does not serve is given an environment with no `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` in it.

**The last point's two halves, and why its live half is read off the run and not off a print.** Nothing a run publishes holds a stage's environment keys, and this check does not pretend otherwise: the exact key set of a gateway stage's environment — the gateway's `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, a gateway-minted `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, and **no** `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` — is pinned hermetically, on every build, by `TestMixedRunStageEnvKeys` (`internal/runner/agentenv_internal_test.go`), and so is the account stage's own (the account's token, and neither gateway variable). What the live run adds is the same fact from the outside: a coder stage that held the account's token would not be priced by the gateway at all — it would carry `credential: oauth`, appear in `stage_accounts`, and leave no `model call` line — so the coder's `model call` lines, its `calls` count and its absent `stage_accounts` entry are this check's live witnesses that its environment was the gateway's. Step 5 asks for both halves.

1. **Cleanup first, and the state step 7 puts back.** In the sandbox checkout record: the repository's `agent` block (`auth`, `models.coder`, the senior review's model) and the branch it is committed on, the project's `default_claude_account` and its `stages:` keys in **your local project config** (`internal/localcfg`'s file — the stage keys are the machine's, not the repository's `fugaro.yaml`'s), the published policy node as it stands now (`fugaro project policy show`), which account names exist and which each one's `allow_data_to` lists, the budget mode and caps, and the deployed job variants (`gcloud run jobs list --region <region>`). **FACT:** that state, and the job variant's name that step 2's `fugaro update --repo` creates for this repository and account.

2. **The configuration, its publish, and the refusals the mix depends on.** In the sandbox checkout: `agent.auth: api-key`; the coder on a provider-routed model of your choosing; the senior review's model an **Anthropic Opus** model; and the account named for that stage alone — `stages.review.claude_account: <name>` in your local project config, or the project's `default_claude_account` there, which a review stage on an Anthropic model picks up on its own. **Commit the `fugaro.yaml` change and push it to the branch the run will read**: the run fetches the ref from the remote (`CheckoutNewBranch` → `git fetch origin <ref>`), so an edit sitting uncommitted in your checkout is not the configuration it runs under. Then **publish the policy**: the runner reads the stage keys from the **published policy node** (`resolveMixedStages` and `mixedDefaultAccount` read `p.ClaudeAccountStages` / `p.DefaultClaudeAccount`, `internal/runner/agentenv.go`), and `fugaro update`'s policy stage compares both keys (`policyConfigDrift`, `internal/cli/init_policy_publish.go`, B7) and publishes them: setting or changing an account is a widening, so the publish asks for the project's typed name and no flag stands in for it. **Check this first: whether that stage will publish from your file at all.** Where your local file records a `policy_generation` the node has moved past, it refuses to publish from the file (D854), offers to re-seed the file from the node instead, and the re-seed **refuses the account keys by name** — so running the update again does not publish them either; the command that does is **`fugaro project policy publish`, run at your own terminal**, which builds the node from the file and never consults the generation — and, because it builds the node **from the file**, it goes only after the file states the node's own values: the re-seed has already written every member it could splice, its refusal names the members it could not, and those go in by hand first — or the publish writes this file's older values for them over the newer node's (the overwrite D854 refuses). `fugaro settings get default_claude_account` reading `unpublished` after an update is that state. Then `fugaro validate`, whose stage-account judgement is `config.CheckStageAccountMix` alone (`stageAccountProblems`, `internal/cli/validate.go`): the stage vocabulary, the one-account rule and the auth. **FACT:** the clean result verbatim. Then, one at a time and restoring each, **with the command that refuses it named**:
   - **the review stage's model on a provider model, the account named by a stage key** — `fugaro validate` passes (it judges no model at all), and the refusal is the **runner's**, at bootstrap, so it is a log line of the run itself and not a launch refusal: `the review stage is served by the Claude account <name> and its model <id> is served by the provider route <route>`. **FACT:** that line from the log. **And the other reading of the same edit, which is the ruling's:** with the account named by `default_claude_account` instead, the stage's own model being a provider's is **no mix and no error** at all — rung 4 applies only where that stage's model is an Anthropic one (the owner's ruling of 2026-11-05) — so the run reviews on the gateway exactly as it did before. Say which of the two you saw;
   - **a different account named on the other mixed stage while the project default names one** — refused by **`fugaro run`**, before anything is launched (`mixedStageAccount`, `internal/cli/run.go`), and again by the runner at bootstrap: `default_claude_account is <a> and stages.<stage>.claude_account is <b>: an api-key run holds one Claude account beside the provider key the gateway holds`. **FACT:** the launch's message verbatim, and that nothing was launched;
   - **`budget.mode: off` (or `observe`) with the account still declared** — also refused by **`fugaro run`** (`config.CheckMixBudget`): the account exists because the gateway holds the provider key and routes the coder's calls to it, and only `enforce` routes a call to a provider at all. **FACT:** that message verbatim.

   Then `fugaro update --repo`, which publishes the two keys to the policy node (type the project's name when it asks) and puts the account's token on this repository's job — or, where the check above found your file's recorded generation behind the node, `fugaro project policy publish` is the one that publishes them (once the file states the node's own values, as step 2 says: it builds the node from the file), and the update behind it has nothing left to change. **FACT:** the output of whichever of the two published them, naming the account keys, the job variant's name, and that the job's container carries the account's token as a **mount** — `gcloud run jobs describe` prints the variable's name and its secret reference and never a value. **Never paste a value.**

3. **The run.** `budget.mode: enforce` for the run, so the gateway is the cap and the coder's every call is priced by it (the account's subscription dollars are not capped by anything — design §5, and the reason the check reads the split in step 5). One trivial task on the sandbox's own base branch, making **one line of change** — the run commits it, pushes its branch and opens a pull request, and all three are the Restore's to undo: `Create the file CHECK290.md at the repository root, containing the single line "check 290", and change no other file.` A **no-change** task is not the cleaner choice here: a run whose agent makes no commit fails with `the agent made no commits`, records an empty commit, pushes its branch and opens a **draft** pull request all the same (`internal/runner/runner.go`), so the branch and the pull request appear either way. `fugaro run --ref <the sandbox's base branch> '<task>'`. **FACT:** `launched` and the run reference it prints, the model the coder was pinned to, and the review level the run resolved — a `standard` launch reviews at L2, and the senior review is the stage this check is about.

4. **The log.** `fugaro logs RUN`. **FACT:** the coder's stage lines reading `msg="model call"` with `stage=implement` (and `stage=plan`) naming the provider model and the provider route the call went to — the coder's calls were priced through the gateway. **FACT:** that **no** `model call` line carries `stage=review`: the senior review's calls never reached the gateway (a first-line round, `stage=review_first`, is the gateway's and its lines are expected — say if the level you ran does not have one). **FACT:** that nothing in the log reads `Invalid API key`, and that no line prints a token or a key value.
