what that row is worth comes from the **design**, not from a reading of code: R12's own text says which prefixes the
reports job lists — R10's loop lists `runs/<slug>/` for a repository's records and writes
`reports/<slug>/<YYYY>/<key>.md` with the aggregate at `reports/<YYYY>/<key>.md`, and the stored reader R11 is
designed to list `reports/<slug>/` for the year folders and `reports/<slug>/<YYYY>/` under each, the way
`internal/cli/runs_digest.go:662` and `:690` read a checkout's folder today
([periodic-reviews/implementation-plan.md](periodic-reviews/implementation-plan.md) §R12, §R10, §R11) — so the
job's own listing set is **`runs/<slug>/`, `reports/<slug>/`, `reports/<slug>/<YYYY>/` and `reports/<YYYY>/`, and
never the bare `reports/` or the bucket root**. **R11 does not exist in this tree** (R12 lands before R7 and R11 by
the plan's own order), so this is the design's statement of what the job will list and not a measurement of a built
job: the check reads those four prefixes because that is what R12's Terraform and R11's reader are being built to
do, and a refusal of the bare `reports/` prefix is a request the design never makes, which is why it must not gate
R12. That design statement is why the revision this run's reading produced reads the four prefixes the job lists,
drops the second form, and asks the bare prefix as a **DIAGNOSTIC** that gates nothing. The revision had not itself
been run then, so the row above stayed **NOT RUN**: what it needed was **one more run of the same command**, on a
fresh sandbox bucket, whose `list-prefix` row is `PASS` and whose Restore confirms the teardown — and that is
exactly what the fourth run below did.

**Fourth run: 2026-11-13, exit `0` — the run that answers the check.** The owner ran the revision once more, on
`fugaro-dev` and a fresh sandbox bucket, and it **PASSED**: under the one relative form the throwaway account
**LISTED** `runs/<slug>/`, `reports/<slug>/`, `reports/<slug>/<YYYY>/` and `reports/<YYYY>/`, **READ** a `runs/`
object, and was **refused** the bucket root listing and a `tokens/` read and a `tokens/` and a `cache/` listing,
each refusal naming the permission the missing clause would have carried — every criterion held — and its
**Restore was clean**, so nothing the run made was left behind. **The bucket had to have uniform bucket-level
access enabled first**: the two conditioned bindings this check grants are refused on a bucket that lacks it (HTTP
`412`), and the first attempt at this run failed on exactly that until the guard of #2584 (`872a5a32a`) was added —
since then the script reads the bucket's own access mode back before creating anything and stops, naming
`gcloud storage buckets update gs://<bucket> --project=<project> --uniform-bucket-level-access`, rather than
reading a bucket's configuration as a refusal of the grant. **The reading is the value form, and it is what R12's
builder writes: the attribute carries the request's own prefix — `runs/` for the runs binding and `reports/` for
the reports binding, each written `api.getAttribute('storage.googleapis.com/objectListPrefix', '').startsWith("<prefix>/")`
— and the root, `tokens/` and `cache/` are refused with the permission names the missing clauses would have
carried.** The bare `reports/` diagnostic came back answered three ways, and its answer closes the question the
third run left open **without changing R12**: the plain `gcloud storage ls gs://<bucket>/reports/` is refused
naming `storage.objects.list`, while the wildcard `gcloud storage ls gs://<bucket>/reports/*` lists and the JSON
API's `objects.list` with `prefix=reports/&delimiter=/` answers `200` — so gcloud's own request, which resolves the
prefix as an object before it lists, is what was refused, and the clause itself does reach the bare prefix. R12's
job never lists the bare prefix, so **it needs no change on that account**, and the row above is a **PASS**.

**Run it:**

```bash
bash scripts/live-checks/check340.sh --project <project> --bucket <sandbox bucket>
```

**You** run it, on a **sandbox bucket** only, and **no agent runs any step of it**. A project or a bucket whose
name contains `belong` is refused before a single call, and the bucket is read back with your own identity first,
so a mistyped one is a stop rather than a reading. A bucket that is **not there** — gcloud answers `404` and its own
"bucket does not exist" — is a stop of its own, and both the `bucket-reachable` row and the stop name what to do:
`gcloud storage buckets create gs://<bucket> --project=<project> --location=us-central1 --uniform-bucket-level-access`
on a **sandbox** project. **The script never creates the bucket**: it grants IAM on one and writes five objects into
it, so the bucket has to be yours to throw away, created by you. The script is the whole check and asks you for nothing else. It
creates a throwaway service account of the run's own (`fugaro-chk340-<hex>`, and it never adopts an account that is
already there); grants it R12's two conditioned bindings — `roles/storage.objectViewer` under the `runs/` clause
and `roles/storage.objectUser` under the `reports/` clause, each carrying the `resource.name` read half and the
listing half joined by `||`, the listing half written with the **relative** value the third run settled (`runs/` and
`reports/`) through `--condition-from-file` so the expression's own bytes survive
gcloud's comma-splitting; seeds five small objects of its own under `runs/<slug>/`, `reports/<slug>/`,
`reports/<slug>/<YYYY>/` (the year level the job writes to), `tokens/<slug>/` and `cache/<slug>/`; and then,
impersonating that account, reads the criteria **R12's design gives the reports job**, under that one form:
`runs/<slug>/` must list, the three reports prefixes the job lists must list — `reports/<slug>/`,
`reports/<slug>/<YYYY>/` and `reports/<YYYY>/` — **each URL with its own answer in the row**, so a clause that
matches one level and not another is visible instead of folded into one `FAIL`, one `runs/` object must read, and
the root listing and a `tokens/` read and a `tokens/`
and a `cache/` listing must all be refused. The two prefixed listings are asked as **wildcards**
(`gs://<bucket>/tokens/*`, `gs://<bucket>/cache/*`), which is what makes the **List** request the one that goes out —
see the paragraph below — and their rows are criteria only when the denial names the permission the missing **listing**
clause would have carried. The **four listings and the read** that must succeed are **retried** for
`CHECK340_PROPAGATION_SECONDS` (150 seconds by default) before a failure is recorded, and the four refusals are
read only once one of those five has held — if none did, they are recorded as **not read**, because
a refusal then could be the fresh grant simply not being in effect yet. IAM propagates a fresh grant and its
condition asynchronously (V7's neighbour, §11 item **V5**), and reading one as a refusal would record a grant that
had simply not arrived. A refusal that is **allowed** instead is a grant wider than R12's two prefixes,
and it fails the check. And a refusal has to **be** a refusal: the four calls are criteria only when the failure is
the refusal itself, **for this account** and about **a resource inside this check's own bucket**, naming a permission
the missing clause could have carried: `storage.objects.list` for the root listing, **either** permission for the
`tokens/` **read** (a read is an object request, so the denial names the object permission the missing clause would
have carried, and either name is the refusal itself), and `storage.objects.list` again for the `tokens/` and `cache/`
**listings**. Those two are the reason the check does not ask them the plain way: `ls gs://<bucket>/tokens/` names a
prefix, gcloud resolves it as an object **before** it lists, and since no clause of R12's grant covers a `tokens/`
object that request is refused whatever the listing clause says — the List request would never go out, and the row
could not measure the clause it exists for (this is the reading the second run died on, and the one a wider listing
clause would hide behind: such a clause would still leave the probe refused, so the row would hold while the veto it
guards was gone). A **wildcard** names a pattern, so gcloud goes straight to listing with prefix `tokens/`, and a
denial naming `storage.objects.get` after that says the List request did not go out after all: the row says
**NOT OBSERVED**, neither a criterion that held nor one that failed, and the check does not pass — the run ends exit
`2` rather than exit `0` with R12's string, so the string is only ever handed over off a run that measured
the pair. A listing that WAS allowed is the opposite reading and fails the check. A call that did not answer instead — a 5xx
gcloud did not retry, an expired session, a killed request, a denial naming **another** permission or **another**
bucket's resource — stops the run, because recorded as a refusal it would be a criterion nobody observed passing.
A **grant the bucket refuses**, and a **removal it refuses**, are a
third thing again: the run stops there, with exit `2` and an `aborted` row naming the binding, rather than reading a
permission error as "the grant does not list". The removal comes after the criteria, and the flag that says a binding
of this run's is on the bucket stays set, so the Restore tries the removal again and reads the bucket policy back
into its own row either way.

**The bare `reports/` prefix is a DIAGNOSTIC row, and it gates nothing.** R12's design never has the reports job
list it — that design's listings are the four the criteria above hold — so it is asked with no criterion attached to it, three ways, each
answer recorded in the one `reports-bare-diagnostic` row: (1) `gcloud storage ls gs://<bucket>/reports/`, the plain
form the third run was refused; (2) `gcloud storage ls gs://<bucket>/reports/*`, the wildcard form, which makes the
**List** request the one that goes out instead of the object request gcloud makes when it resolves a prefix; and (3)
a delimiter-style `objects.list` (`?prefix=reports/&delimiter=/`) through the JSON API with this account's own access
token, which is the request a delimiter listing itself makes — a `200` there beside a gcloud refusal says gcloud's
own call is what failed rather than the clause, while a `403` naming `storage.objects.list` says the grant really does
not reach the bare prefix. Each answer is recorded with the permission the denial names, so the row says which of the
two requests was refused and not merely that one was. The row changes no `PASS`, no `FAIL` and no exit code, and
**pasting it back is the whole point of it**: it is what the next revision of this check reads, because the third
run's refusal of it is still unexplained. The one credential-shaped value the script ever touches is the access token
of that third probe, and it is never a value in the script: `gcloud auth print-access-token` writes it straight into
a mode-`0600` `curl` config file (in a `umask 077` subshell), the `Authorization` header is appended into that same
file, and the file is deleted before the row is written — so the token is never in a variable, never on a command
line, never in the block and never in a `bash -x` trace. `curl` is optional and is used by that probe alone: without
it the row says the probe was not made and nothing else about the check changes.

**Reading the `CHECK 340 RESULT` block.** The same shape as the other scripted checks': ONE block on stdout, a
`FACT <key>: PASS|FAIL|INFO — <detail>` line per fact, ending `CHECK 340 RESULT END (exit N)`. The rows are
`project`, `bucket`, `belong`, `bucket-reachable`, `account`, `seed`, `lists-runs`, `lists-reports`, `reads-runs`,
`root-refused`, `tokens-read-refused`, `tokens-list-refused`, `cache-list-refused`, the diagnostic's
`reports-bare-diagnostic`, then the row that matters, **`list-prefix`**, and last the teardown's own `restore`.
`PASS` on `list-prefix` says
every criterion held under the relative form, and it prints the exact string R12's builder must write, above the
block in one line to copy back: `runs/` for the runs binding and `reports/` for the reports binding, each in
`api.getAttribute('storage.googleapis.com/objectListPrefix', '').startsWith("<prefix>/")`. `FAIL` says a listing or
the read did not hold, which is the reading that stops the plan (E4) — so R12's Terraform does not land on it, and
the block's own rows say which prefix failed and whether the failure came after the full 150-second propagation
window. The bucket-wide `objectViewer` a listing would otherwise
need is deliberately **not** a fallback here, because it reads `tokens/` and `cache/` too. `INFO` is the third
reading, and it is the one no string comes with: **`list-prefix: INFO — not settled`** is what a run whose every
readable criterion held still gets when the `tokens/` or `cache/` listing came back **NOT OBSERVED**, and it ends
exit `2` — the rows above are visible, but the guard R12's two prefixes exist for was not
measured, so nothing is handed to R12's builder and the run is not the one that clears R12. Exit `0` means every
criterion passed **and** the Restore confirmed it deleted everything this run made; `1` means a criterion failed — or every
criterion held and the Restore could not confirm what it deleted, in which case the block's `restore` row names the
account and what to remove by hand — so exit `1` reads as **E4** only when that row passed; and `2` means the
run could not tell (a guard stopped it, a tool is missing, a grant or a removal the bucket refused, a refusal that
came back as a call that did not answer, a listing that never answered,
a **`tokens/` or `cache/` listing that came back as the object request** rather than as the List (so the guard was
never measured), an internal error ended it) — `2` is not an answer about
the attribute, and the block's `aborted` row says so. `project`, `bucket`, `belong`, `bucket-reachable`, `account` and `seed` say what the run was reading, and `restore` is last.

**Cost.** Nothing billable and no model call: one throwaway service account, two bucket bindings, one impersonation
grant of yours on that account alone, and five small objects. It never prints a credential, holds none, and the
`tokens/` object it seeds is a marker this check wrote itself.

**Restore.** The script runs it itself, **from the exit trap too**, so a failed assertion or a Ctrl-C still leaves
nothing behind: the four slug prefixes are removed, both bucket bindings go with `remove-iam-policy-binding --all`
(no condition named, so it does not matter which binding was granted when the run stopped), your impersonation grant
goes, and the account is deleted — bindings first, because a deleted account's members read
`deleted:serviceAccount:…` and the removes then fail. The year-level object is deleted **by name**
(`reports/<YYYY>/chk340-<slug>.md`), **never as the `reports/<YYYY>/` prefix**: that prefix holds the owner's own
reports, and a recursive delete there would take them. It reads the four prefixes and the year object back
afterwards, and — whenever it
made an account — the bucket policy and the account too, and says what it found: the policy read is what the PASS
row's own sentence ("the policy no longer names the account") rests on, so it is made on every run that created the
account, not only on the runs where the removals had not already been done. The account's presence is read from a
`iam service-accounts list` filter and **never** from a `describe` or from the delete's own status: IAM answers both
a describe and a delete of a service account that is not there with `PERMISSION_DENIED` ("denied on resource (or it
may not exist)"), even to a project owner, so a refused delete is not by itself an error — the row says the account is
`gone (confirmed by list)`, or `still present` and names the account and the delete command to run. Anything that did
not go is a FAILed `restore` row that names the slug and the account to delete by hand, never a silent pass. A
read-back that cannot be **read** — a refused listing, a policy the operator's identity may no longer read, an account
list that does not answer, a dropped call — is a FAILed row too, naming what could not be confirmed: only the empty
listing and the list answering no email count as gone, because an error read as "deleted" is the same silent pass from
the other side.

**Paste back:** the whole block into row 340 above and to the coordinator, with the `list-prefix` row's string —
that string is the `<list prefix>` R12's builder writes into the two listing clauses, and it is the only thing
this check exists to produce — **and the `reports-bare-diagnostic` row with it**, whose three answers are what
explain the bare `reports/` refusal the third run left open.

**What it answered.** R12, and behind R12 the reports job's first firing (Check 341) and `fugaro runs digest`'s
own writing to `reports/` (R10, Open item 5 of [periodic-reviews/implementation-plan.md](periodic-reviews/implementation-plan.md)):
the check answered on 2026-11-13, so the Terraform and what it enables may land on the two prefix forms this
section records, and the plan's **E4** no longer holds anything back.

## Check 360: the managed screens show what the CLI says, on a managed project (your own machine, an installation and a managed project; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **CM12** of the console-managed-screens plan
([console-managed-screens/implementation-plan.md](console-managed-screens/implementation-plan.md), its
§6 and its "Checks" — **F3**, the owner's ask of 2026-11-07, **D1489**). There is no script: the
check is three steps the owner does by hand in the console and the reading they take from them, and
**no agent runs any step of it**. It is the live half of a work whose hermetic half is
`console/test/e2e/managed.spec.ts`: that spec walks the same tab against the stub and asserts the
argv of every read, and this is the reading that says the tab draws the same thing when the
documents come from a real CLI on a real managed project.

**What the check confirms.** The Project tab's five later sections — the managed state, the
retirements, the account keys, the credentials service and the policy panel — show **what the CLI
says**: each within its own read, from the document that read answers with, the marks and the trail
agreeing with `fugaro managed status --json`, the account keys with `fugaro settings --json`, the
policy notes with `fugaro project policy show --json` and with `fugaro doctor`'s policy lines, and
the retirements with what `fugaro update` printed. **No section offers a control that changes
anything**, and no token appears anywhere: **D1471** puts no write on these screens, and this is the
reading that says so of a screen rather than of a test.

**What you do.**

1. On a machine with an installation and a managed project, run `fugaro update` once and let it
   finish. Record what it prints for the retirements and for the runs in flight.
2. Run `fugaro managed status --json` and `fugaro project policy show --json`, and keep both
   documents.
3. Open the console, select the project, and open the Project tab.

**Expected.** The five sections appear, each within its own read; the marks and the trail agree with
the first document, the account keys with `fugaro settings --json`, the policy notes with the second
document and with `fugaro doctor`'s policy lines, and the retirements with what step 1 printed.
**No section offers a control that changes anything**, and no token appears anywhere.

**Refutation.** Any figure that disagrees with the document it came from, any section that waits for
a sibling before drawing, or any control that writes — the last of which fails the check outright
rather than being noted.

**Restore.** Nothing to undo beyond the `fugaro update` you would have run anyway: two reads and one
window. No run is launched, no credential is minted and no project is written by the check itself,
and the console holds no secret to paste back.

## Check 361: the workspace's own Firebase's sign-in providers — one script you run (the workspace's own project only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by the task that implemented Check 361 of [workspaces/implementation-plan.md](workspaces/implementation-plan.md)
**W3** — that plan's §7 names the workspace's owner-run checks and numbers none of them, and the design's own
reconciliation claims none either (its **F22**), so the number is the first free above the register's written
sections — and **no step of it has been run, and nothing here is a claim that it works.** It settles the half of
the workspace's Firebase that no hermetic test can hold: the **provider pin** of [workspaces/spec.md](workspaces/spec.md)
§3. A workspace has a Firebase project of its own (D1290), and it is the one Firebase in this design where a person
signs in with a real provider, so the workspace's signer endpoint accepts only the pinned set of
`firebase.sign_in_provider` values — **`google.com` and `password`** — and refuses `custom` and `anonymous` (anyone
holding `signBlob` on any service account in the project can mint a custom token with whatever `email` and
`email_verified` they like, and an anonymous sign-in proves no address at all). The project, its rules and its
database come from the installation path — your `fugaro setup` for the workspace root, then `fugaro update` — but
Identity Platform is initialized there with **no sign-in provider**: that is right for a member's project and wrong
for the workspace's (`IdentityPlatformStep`, `internal/infra/identityplatform.go`). `refusePublicSignUp`
(`internal/cli/init_firebase.go`) holds a workspace's own project to the pin in ONE direction: the pinned entries
pass — refusing them would fail `fugaro update` on exactly the project this work converges (the HARD RULE) — and an
off-pin path (anonymous, a phone number, a second IdP) is refused by name, because this project is an installation
too, and its own sign-in reads a token's claim rather than the provider that signed the person in. What it never
does is *require* the pinned pair: a workspace whose providers you have not enabled yet converges as usual. So the
providers are enabled by **you**, and this check is the read-back that the pin is what the project actually carries.

**Run it:**

```bash
bash scripts/live-checks/check361.sh --project <the workspace's own project>
```

`--project` is the project the workspace is **named after** — the one `fugaro setup --name <workspace>` created —
and it is required: the check never reads a project from a config that may name another, and a value that is not a
project id is refused before any call. **You** run it, and **no agent runs any step of it**. A project whose name
contains `belong` is refused before a single call, even though the check is read-only: a check pointed at the
owner's own installation by a mistyped id would be a reading nobody asked for. You need an account that may read
the project's Identity Platform configuration (the project's owner, or Firebase Admin); a refused read stops the
run with exit `2` rather than reading as drift.

**What it reads, and what the pin is.** ONE GET — `https://identitytoolkit.googleapis.com/admin/v2/projects/<project>/config`,
the same document `infra.PublicSignUp` parses — with your own credentials, so nothing is created, granted, written
or deleted and the check is idempotent. From that document: the password provider (`signIn.email.enabled`), every
**enabled** entry of `defaultSupportedIdpConfigs` and `oauthIdpConfigs`, `signIn.anonymous.enabled`,
`signIn.phoneNumber.enabled` and `client.permissions.disabledUserSignup`. The pin holds when **password and
`google.com` are the only two enabled**, no other provider is enabled, anonymous and phone-number sign-in are off,
and public sign-up is **not** disabled — the workspace's Firebase is the one that does not refuse public sign-up
(spec §3), which is what lets a person who does not already hold a password create one and reach the workspace at
all. `custom` is the half of the pin no configuration carries: it is not a toggle in this document, and what
refuses it is the signer endpoint's own pin on the `firebase.sign_in_provider` claim (spec §3, **W4**) — so the
block records it as an **INFO** row and never as a criterion this read settled.

**Reading the `CHECK 361 RESULT` block.** The same shape as the other scripted checks': ONE block on stdout, a
`FACT <key>: PASS|FAIL|INFO — <detail>` line per fact, ending `CHECK 361 RESULT END (exit N)`. `project`, `belong`
and `xtrace` say what the run was reading, `token` and `config` say whether the one read happened and what it
answered, and the criteria are their own rows — `password`, `google`, `anonymous`, `phone`, `other-providers` and
`public-signup` — followed by `custom` (**INFO**, never a criterion) and the verdict row **`pin`**, whose detail
names every row that failed. Exit `0` means the pin holds exactly; `1` means it does not — a provider the pin admits
is off or absent, one it refuses is on, public sign-up is disabled, or Identity Platform is not initialized in the
project at all, which is the reading where nobody can sign in — and each row of that kind says what to change and
where; `2` means the run could not tell (a guard stopped it, no token could be minted, the read did not answer or
was refused, the document could not be parsed, a tool is missing, an internal error ended it) — `2` is not an
answer about the providers, and the block's `aborted` row says so.

**No credential is printed, logged or put on a command line.** The access token is minted with
`gcloud auth print-access-token --quiet` into a `0600` config file inside a `0700` scratch directory, and curl
reads it with `--config` — the pattern Check 91 uses, and for the same reason, `ps` shows a process's argv to every
user on the machine. The file is removed whether the run passes, fails or is interrupted, and the block's
`auth-conf` row reads that removal back. A shell that was started tracing (`-x`) is refused before anything is
minted, because a trace would print that line, and the scratch directory is removed at the end either way.

**Cost.** Nothing billable and no model call: one GET.

**What waits on it.** The workspace's own signer (**W4**, and every member behind it) at its first run: the
exchange is only as good as the claim it verifies, and the pinned set is what turns "the workspace's Firebase said
so" into a statement a member can hold. It is also named in the release note's `### For operators` section
(**W9**), which is where the enablement step itself is written down.

## Check 350: the failure classes an owner can see — one script you run (the sandbox installation and the sandbox repository only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by the task that implemented Check 350 of
[failure-classes/implementation-plan.md](failure-classes/implementation-plan.md) §6, and
**no step of it has been run, and nothing here is a claim that it works.** It settles the claim the
redesign exists to make true and that no hermetic test of **FC1–FC8** can hold: that the **owner** can
see why the runs failed — the class a run carries, the window's grouping, the week's digest — and that
the reader which classes a record written before the field shipped **writes nothing back into it**.
[failure-classes/design.md](failure-classes/design.md) §3 carries the closed vocabulary, §4.1 the one
call that writes a record's ending, §5 the claim that a read never writes one back, and §6 the report
the digest commits; what the design cannot settle from a test fixture is what a person sees on their
own sandbox, and that is this check.

**The plan's §6 is six steps, and the script runs the first four and step 5's read.** It, and not this
section, is where the reasoning is; what follows is what each step reads and which of them the script
measures:

1. **One run that fails for a cause the classifier can name on purpose**, and the two commands a person
   reads it with. The script cuts a **throwaway reference** on the sandbox repository — by plumbing, so
   your work tree is never switched and your branch is never moved — whose `fugaro.yaml` is your HEAD's
   with **one unknown key** added, which the strict decoder refuses: the runner ends the run at
   **bootstrap**, before its first stage, with `failure_class` **`config_invalid`** and no model call.
   It then reads `fugaro runs ls --json` and `fugaro diagnose <run>` and compares: **the row and the
   diagnosis carry the same class, and the class is the one the cause deserves** — not `unclassified`,
   which is the reading where the classifier answers nothing.
2. **`fugaro runs ls --group-by failure_class`**, over a window the owner recognises (the listing's
   window reaches back past the week the digest reports and has room for a run minted before that week
   and finished inside it; `--since <Nd>` moves it): the groups' runs **add up to the window's failed
   rows** and to no other run, `share` **follows the runs and not the spend**, and the totals line's two
   figures are the ones the plain listing prints.
3. **`fugaro runs digest --period week`**: the week's Failures table is there, the summary block carries
   `failures`, and — the half that matters — **an old record of the same week lands in the class its
   `reason` maps to**. The script looks that record up in the **bucket**, before any `fugaro` read of the
   window, and it must be one whose own bytes carry **no** `failure_class` at all: a record written
   before the field shipped. A class counted for it in the week beside the runs written after it is what
   says the week is **not** split into before and after.
4. **The read-only step, and it is the one a code review cannot settle.** That same old record is read
   **twice** through `runs ls --json` and **once** through `diagnose`, and against those reads: its
   object in the bucket is hashed **before the first** of them and again after the last, and its own
   listing line — the size and the object's own time, not its url — is taken at both ends too. **The
   bytes and the line are unchanged.** §5's claim is that nothing is written back, and a class that
   arrived in the record between the two readings is what falsifies it. A record rewritten with the
   **same** bytes (a reserialisation, a copy) is what the listing line catches, which is why the script
   compares both.
5. **The refutation step, which is YOURS to make and the check's to read.** A job image whose agent call
   the account's own limit refuses must carry `stage_error_unexplained` and **no class of its own** —
   which is **O6** unanswered, and reading it is what tells the owner what the report looks like
   meanwhile. **The script never fakes this run**: without `--step5-run <run id>` its row is the prompt
   it is, an **INFO** that decides nothing, and with that argument the class your run carries **is** a
   criterion and a class other than `stage_error_unexplained` fails the check as a finding about the
   classifier.
6. **The HARD RULE, on a real installation at the previous version: `brew upgrade`, and then `fugaro
   update` ALONE.** No second command, no prompt beyond the ones `update` already asks, and `fugaro
   doctor` clean afterwards. **The script prints this prompt and measures nothing of it** — a step a
   release needs here that the plan did not name is a defect in the release, not in this check (F29).

**Run it:**

```bash
bash scripts/live-checks/check350.sh --repo <a sandbox repository checkout> \
  --project <the installation's project> --bucket <its runs bucket>
```

`--repo` is a checkout of the **sandbox** repository — every `fugaro` command runs in it, and the
throwaway reference is cut in it — and it is required; a directory that is not a git work tree, or one
whose `origin` does not answer, is refused before anything is created. `--project` is the installation's
Fugaro project and `--bucket` its runs bucket, where the records of steps 1, 3 and 4 are read; both are
required, and the check reads neither out of a config that may name another. `--gcp-project` is the GCP
project the bucket lives in (default: the same value as `--project`), `--since <Nd>` moves the window the listing
reads and the bucket scan steps 3 and 4 choose the old record from, `--step5-run <run id>` is the run **you** made for step 5, and `--dry-run` prints the guards and
every command a real run would make — **and makes no call at all**: no gcloud call, no `fugaro` call, no
object read, and no verdict.

**You** run it, and **no agent runs any step of it**. A project, GCP project, bucket or checkout that
names the owner's own installation (`belong`) is refused **before a single call**, and so is a coding
agent's session and a shell started tracing (`-x`), which would print every command this check makes and
the run's own output with it. It is read-only against everything that is yours: it **writes no secret
and mints no token**, every read is made with your own identity, and the only text it prints is what the
tools printed.

**Reading the `CHECK 350 RESULT` block.** The same shape as the other scripted checks': ONE block on
stdout, a `FACT <key>: PASS|FAIL|INFO — <detail>` line per fact, ending `CHECK 350 RESULT END (exit N)`.
The keys are printed in the same order whatever happened, so one block can be diffed against another,
and a row that was never reached reads `FAIL — not reached`. What the run was reading is `project`,
`gcp-project`, `bucket`, `repo`, `belong`, `agent-session` and `xtrace`; the run of step 1 is `branch`,
`run`, `settled` and `class` (with `cancelled` when a run that would not end had to be stopped); the
window is `window`, the diagnosis is `agree`, and the old record and the read-only step are `target`,
`old-record` and `readonly`; the grouping is `groups`, `share` and `totals`; the week is `digest`; and
`step5` and `step6` are the owner's own two steps. The last line of the block is the verdict, and its
exit status is what decides: **`0`** when every criterion of steps 1 to 4 held — and step 5's read too, when you passed `--step5-run` — **`1`** when one
of them FAILED, or when they all held and the **Restore** could not confirm that the reference it made is
gone (the `restore` row names it, and that is the one case where a block of PASSing criteria still exits
non-zero), and **`2`** when the run could not tell — a guard stopped it, a tool is missing, the launch
named no run, the run never ended, a read did not answer, or the window holds no record old enough for
steps 3 and 4. **`2` is not an answer about the classes**, and the block's `aborted` row says so.

**What it creates, and the Restore.** ONE throwaway branch on the sandbox repository's origin
(`chk350-<hex>`, cut at your checkout's HEAD with `fugaro.yaml` plus an unknown key) and ONE run of that
repository cut from it, plus that run's own objects under the repository's slug. **The branch is deleted
from the origin and from the checkout by the Restore, which runs from the exit trap too** — an
interrupted run still cleans up after itself — and the `restore` row reads the deletion back from both
places rather than assuming it. **The run's own record is LEFT in the bucket on purpose**: it is the
evidence step 1 read, it costs nothing, and the bucket's lifecycle ages it out.

**Cost.** Nothing billable and no model call: the run is refused at bootstrap, before its first stage, so
no stage's work is paid for and the budget is not touched. It does start **one Cloud Run job execution**,
and nothing it launches outlives it — a run still going after `CHECK350_RUN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` is cancelled
with `fugaro cancel --now`, from the step that gives up on it and from the script's own exit trap.

**What waits on it.** The owner's own reading of the redesign:
[failure-classes/README.md](failure-classes/README.md) holds this check as that work's owner-run live
check, the plan's §6 is where its six steps are argued, and the design's §1 is the state the redesign
exists to leave behind — a record whose *why* is free text, nothing that groups failures, and a person
who has to open one run at a time to find out what went wrong. It is **NOT RUN**: until it is,
this register carries no reading about a class, a grouping or a digest on a real installation, and **no
`PASS` is recorded anywhere here for any of them**.

## Check 370: the security escalation — a matching diff runs level 3, and the record names the row (sandbox installation and sandbox repository only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by the task that implemented the behaviour it reads,
[security-classification/implementation-plan.md](security-classification/implementation-plan.md) **SC6**
(that plan's §6; reconciliation **D1507**, **D1508**, **D1509** and **D1519**) — §6 names the number and
leaves the row and this section to that task, which is the register's own rule for a work that reserved
none — **no step of it has been run to a reading, and nothing here is a claim that it works.**

**What no test can prove, and what this check is for.** `internal/runner/security_test.go` proves, off a
fixture repository, that a diff matching a row of the list in force turns review level 3 on, puts the
adversarial step in the plan, leaves the rigor mode where it was and records the row that decided it —
and that a diff matching nothing does none of it. What it cannot prove is that a **real** run spends the
step: the fixture's plan is a slice in memory, and only a run whose loop walks it to the adversarial
stage shows the level is not merely recorded. That is the second part below, and it is the part that
costs money.

**Part 1 — the reader, on a project with no key.** `fugaro security paths` is on this tree: it is the
same work's task **SC3**, in slice 1, landed as `cb69f1754` (#1979) and an ancestor of this checkout, so
every reading below is a step you can take now. `fugaro security paths --json` prints the floor's 43
rows on a project that has published no `security` list, each with its source layer.
`--check internal/creds/state.go` answers `sensitive: true` from the `credentials` floor row;
`--check docs/recipes.md` answers `sensitive: false`; `--check docs/pending-workflows/console-tests.yml`
answers `true` from `pending-workflows`. The pair is the point: `docs/` is a routine tree, and the five
`docs/` rows on the floor are exactly the ones the routing text's own exceptions name —
`pending-workflows` (`docs/pending-workflows/**`), `release-streams` (`docs/release-streams.yaml`),
`plan-graphs` (`docs/**/*.graph.json`) and the two redesign scripts
(`docs/website/redesign/capture-screenshots.mjs`, `docs/website/redesign/sample-logo-hue.py`) — so the
list is a **positive list and not the classifier's complement** (F1, F22). The third path is the
interesting case in between — a routine tree with a listed exception — which is the shape a project's
own list will have.

**Part 2 — the escalation, on a real run.** Two runs on the sandbox repository, each launched with a
task that says which paths to touch. The first touches a floor path: a task that creates
`internal/creds/state.go` is enough, because the floor row is a doublestar glob and needs no tree to
exist under it. It must run the **adversarial** step — the run's last review round carries
`tier: "adversarial"` in the record — and its record's `security` member must read
`{"at": "implement", "pattern": "credentials", "category": "credentials"}`. The second touches nothing
on the list, and must do neither: no adversarial round, and **no `security` member at all**, which is
the difference between "no escalation" and "an escalation with an empty row". The two runs are the whole
of the claim — that the list in force decides what a run spends, and that the record says why.

**Part 3 — the base-branch property.** With a working tree whose `fugaro.yaml` carries a `security` row
and a base branch that does not, `fugaro security paths --json` prints the **base's** list, and the
working tree's row is nowhere in it. This is the property D1518 exists for — a change that carries its
own pattern list must not also carry its own exemption from it — and it is the one part a reviewer
cannot check by reading either side.

**Run it:**

```bash
fugaro security paths --json
fugaro security paths --check internal/creds/state.go --check docs/recipes.md \
  --check docs/pending-workflows/console-tests.yml --json

fugaro run --repo <sandbox repo> "create internal/creds/state.go with a package clause and one comment"
fugaro run --repo <sandbox repo> "add a line to docs/recipes.md"
gcloud storage cat gs://<runs bucket>/runs/<slug>/<run-id>/result.json   # each run's record
```

Parts 1 and 3 are the three `fugaro security paths` commands at the top of that block — free, offline,
and runnable here; part 2 is the two runs below them, and it is the part that spends money.

**You** run it, on the sandbox installation and the sandbox repository only, and **no agent runs any
step of it**. A project or a repository naming `belong` is out of bounds for every step. The record is
read back from the runs bucket because **no `fugaro` command prints the `security` member yet**: the
member lands with the escalation, and the reader that draws it is a later slice's. `result.json`'s
`security` block and its `reviews[].tier` are what the run itself wrote, and reading them is the whole
of the check — nothing is edited, and no run is asked to do anything a person would not.

**Cost.** Two sandbox runs: model calls, and whatever the sandbox's per-run cap allows — this is the
only part of the check that is billable. The three reader commands are free and make no cloud call
beyond the policy read a `fugaro` command already makes.

**What waits on it.** Nothing in the release: the escalation ships whether or not this has been run, and
**D1519**'s slice 2 is what it proves rather than what it gates. What it settles is the claim the whole
work rests on — that the list in force changes what a run spends, and that a person can read out of the
record why it did.

## Check 510: the name-prefix IAM condition, and the grants IAM may not be able to fence (sandbox project only, never `belong`; run by you; RUN 2026-11-12, create fenced by name)

**RUN 2026-11-12 on 0.23.0; the result is below.** Written by task **DS0.2** of
[secrets-brokering/dynamic-delivery/implementation-plan.md](secrets-brokering/dynamic-delivery/implementation-plan.md)
and **run by you, its DS0.3**. The check is `scripts/live-checks/check510.sh` (its sibling test
`scripts/live-checks/check510_test.sh` drives it against fake tools only, and never a real project),
the steps are [secrets-brokering/dynamic-delivery/check510-steps.md](secrets-brokering/dynamic-delivery/check510-steps.md),
and **no agent runs any step of it**: what it measures is a live project's IAM and Secret Manager.

**The owner ran it once, on 2026-11-11**, and its `create-conditioned` row came back ADMITTED — a
conditioned `secrets.create` **was** admitted for a `fugaro_u_` name, contradicting the create half of
**F30** — and that run probed only a name inside the prefix, so whether a create outside both prefixes
is refused is unmeasured. The re-run of 2026-11-12 asked it, and its
result is the next paragraph.

**The re-run, 2026-11-12.** The owner ran it on 0.23.0 in fugaro-dev and it exited 0. The version row
read `fugaro-version` PASS 0.23.0, and the test account `chk510-20261112033246` was created and deleted.
`bindings` PASS: `roles/secretmanager.admin` and the viewer role are bound under one condition that
names `fugaro_u_` and `fugaro_p_`. `condition-version-add-allow` PASS (a `fugaro_u_` name admitted),
`condition-prefix-allow` PASS (a `fugaro_p_` name admitted: one expression, not two bindings),
`condition-version-add-deny` PASS (a `fugaro-<slug>-...` name refused with 403),
`condition-delete-allow` PASS and `condition-delete-deny` PASS (refused, the container still there).
The create rows are readings: `create-conditioned` admitted for a `fugaro_u_` name;
`create-conditioned-outside` REFUSED with 403 for a name outside both prefixes under the same grant, so
**create is fenced by name in both directions**; `create-unconditioned` admitted for any name (the
project-wide control). `list-condition-admits-nothing` PASS: `secrets.list` was refused under the
condition, so list is granted unconditioned. `secret-id-length` PASS: 255 characters admitted, 256
refused. `restore` PASS: the account, every binding and the 14 containers created were deleted and read
back, and `scratch-removed` PASS.

**Owner ruling, 2026-11-12:** DS2.2 conditions the intake's create by name (the conditioned create
grant), not unconditioned.

**What it settles, and what it gates.** The reconciliation's **U3** and **F30**, which **DS2.2**'s
Terraform is written against:

- whether an IAM condition on `resource.name` applies to `secretmanager.versions.add` and to
  `secretmanager.secrets.delete` at all. If it does not, the prefix-conditioned grants R3 and D1931
  give the intake and the credentials service are not the fence they are written as;
- whether **one** condition naming both prefixes (`fugaro_u_` and `fugaro_p_`) admits each of them and
  refuses a name outside them. The refusal is measured against **F6**'s collision class — a
  repository's own mounted secret, `fugaro-<slug>-<logical>-<hash>` — and not against a name the check
  invented: a refusal measured on the wrong shape settles nothing;
- **the create rows, where F30's create half is already known to be wrong.** F30 said a conditioned
  `secretmanager.secrets.create` admits nothing, not even the prefix it names, because the permission
  is checked on the **project** — which is why the intake grants create unconditioned. The 2026-11-11
  reading is the opposite for a `fugaro_u_` name, so the check **reports** its three create rows
  (`create-conditioned`, `create-conditioned-outside`, `create-unconditioned`) rather than passing or
  failing them, and what is open is the pair: a create **outside** both prefixes under the same
  conditioned grant. Refused beside an admitted create inside means create is fenced by name in both
  directions, so **DS2.2** may condition the intake's create; admitted outside means there is no name
  fence and the unconditioned create stays as the plan has it. An unconditioned create of a name
  outside the prefixes succeeds either way, and the row records that as the reading it is.
  `secretmanager.secrets.list` is still the project-checked case F30 states, and the check reads it
  the same way;
- the **maximum secret ID length** (R1), read by bisection — a name over the limit is refused with a
  sentence naming the limit — rather than a number assumed from the plan.

**What a run costs.** Nothing billable and no model call: no job, no build and no container of the
installation's. It creates one throwaway service account (`chk510-<stamp>`), the project IAM bindings
its own rows need — the two conditioned grants, and the one **unconditioned**
`roles/secretmanager.admin` grant the create rows' control is measured on — the same role with no
condition on it, which is what the conditioned create rows are read against — and the probe containers
they are measured on — five under the `fugaro_u_`, `fugaro_p_` and `fugaro-<slug>-…` shapes, whatever
the two conditioned create rows make if IAM
admits the create, plus the containers the length bisection makes, about a dozen. The slow part
is IAM propagation: a fresh binding can take a minute to be seen, and the rows that depend on it are
read only once it is.

**Restore.** Every binding it wrote, the account it made and every container it created are deleted
**and read back** — by your own credentials, never by the conditioned account — and the `restore` row
is that reading. It runs from the check's exit trap, so a Ctrl-C in the middle still deletes them. A
`restore: FAIL` row names what to delete by hand.

**The commands.** Read the plan's DS0.3 and the steps file, then:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check510.sh --dry-run
bash scripts/live-checks/check510.sh
```

Progress goes to stderr and one `CHECK 510 RESULT` block goes to stdout at the end: paste that whole
block here and nothing else. **Exit `0`** is every criterion that was measured holding **and every
reading taken — a create reading that contradicts F30 is one of these, printed and reported rather
than failed**; **`1`** is a measured criterion that did not hold; **`2`** is the check not being able
to measure (a tool missing, a probe of its own that could not be set up, a create answered something
other than `200` or `403`, a length probe refused for a reason that is not the ID limit — a name
already taken, say, which must never be read as the limit itself — or a fresh binding that never
became visible). A key the run never reached reads `FAIL — not reached`.

**What waits on it.** Nothing now: 510 passed, and **DS2.2** (the intake and the prefix-conditioned reader
in Terraform) is written against it. Its **create** grant is conditioned by name, because
`create-conditioned-outside` was refused; the unconditioned create the plan once had is not used.

## Check 511: a request every N seconds keeps one service instance up (sandbox installation only, never `belong`; run by you; RUN 2026-11-12, exit 2, the beat kept it warm)

**RUN 2026-11-12 in fugaro-dev; the result is below.** Written by task **DS0.2** of
[secrets-brokering/dynamic-delivery/implementation-plan.md](secrets-brokering/dynamic-delivery/implementation-plan.md)
and **run by you, its DS0.3**. The check
is `scripts/live-checks/check511.sh` (its sibling test `scripts/live-checks/check511_test.sh` drives it
against fake tools only), the steps are
[secrets-brokering/dynamic-delivery/check511-steps.md](secrets-brokering/dynamic-delivery/check511-steps.md),
and **no agent runs any step of it**: what it measures is a live Cloud Run service's own instance
behaviour, which nothing in this tree can answer.

**The run, 2026-11-12.** The owner ran it on the sandbox installation, against the credentials service
as the platform holds it. `scale-to-zero` PASS: `min_instance_count` was 0, so no instance was kept up
by configuration and whatever the window saw was the requests'. `container-answers` PASS: the unserved
route was answered by the container's own 404, so the window below reached an instance and not only the
front end. `heartbeat-answered` PASS and `heartbeat-warm` PASS: 20 requests, one every 15 s for 300 s,
were each answered by the container, and **none of them paid a cold start** — min 109 ms, mean 165 ms,
max 293 ms. `idle-cost`, the opening request, read 1511 ms: that is the one request of the run that
could pay a cold start, and it did. `instance-ids` came back **empty**: the log entries the check read
carried no instance id it could use, so this run cannot say how many instances answered, and the owner
ruled that row not part of the decision. The run's own verdict is therefore **exit 2** — the code for a
row the check could not measure, and not the `0` of every criterion holding — and what it settled is
U4's **timing**: a request every 15 s keeps an instance **answering**, with no cold start, at the
interval D1934 and **DS1.5** are written against. U4's one-instance reading, which needs the
`instance-ids` row, is not settled by this run.

**What it settles, and what it gates.** The reconciliation's **U4**, which **DS1.5**'s keep-warm
heartbeat rests on. D1934 answers U4's cold start with a heartbeat from the runner, at the interval the
runner's budget session already keeps — 15 seconds (`internal/budget/session.go`'s `HeartbeatEvery`) —
so the question this check exists for is whether a request at that interval really keeps **one**
instance up between runs.

- **The premise is a row.** The credentials service `fugaro-credentials` scales to zero (D501) as the
  **platform** holds it — `min_instance_count` read from the service, not from the Terraform in this
  tree. If the platform reports a minimum above zero, the check says so and reads its own warmth as the
  **configuration's**: an instance kept up by configuration says nothing about a heartbeat.
- **The window.** A request every 15 seconds for five minutes, each to a route the service does not
  serve. The container itself answers 404 there, with its own route list — so an answer that is not
  that one is the front end refusing, not an instance serving, and the check stops rather than reading
  it as an instance. Every request is read for whether the **container** answered and for what it cost:
  a cold start inside the window is the instance having been reaped **despite** the beat. A request
  that never completed at all — curl's own failure, with no HTTP status — is neither: it says nothing
  about an instance, so the window's rows read as ones the check could not measure rather than as U4
  answered no.
- **The instances.** The same window is read again from Cloud Logging, by the stamp the check's own
  requests carry: **one** instance id across those entries is U4's reading rather than only its timing,
  and several are the beat having measured nothing about a single instance. A log that has not caught
  up, or entries that carry no instance id, is a row the check could not measure.
- **The contrast** — what the same request costs after an idle gap — is a reading and is not asked for
  by default (`CHECK511_IDLE_GAP_SECONDS`).

**What a run costs.** Five minutes of wall clock and **nothing billable**: no job, no build, no
container, no binding and no account. The requests go to a route the service does not serve, so no
credential is read, no model is called and no budget is spent; every other call is a `describe` or a
log listing, and the instance ids row needs `roles/logging.viewer` (set `CHECK511_INSTANCE_IDS=0` to
leave that row out). The platform's own request log entries for the check's requests stay, and are not
the check's to delete — which is why its `restore` row says "nothing was created" rather than being
missing.

**The commands.** Read the plan's DS0.3 and the steps file, then:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check511.sh --dry-run
bash scripts/live-checks/check511.sh
```

Progress goes to stderr (one line per beat) and one `CHECK 511 RESULT` block goes to stdout at the end:
paste that whole block here and nothing else. **Exit `0`** is every criterion that was measured
holding; **`1`** is a measured criterion that did not hold — a cold start inside the window, a request
the container did not answer, or two instances named by the log; **`2`** is the check not being able to
measure (a tool missing, the service or its logs unreadable, the token refused, or a row with no
reading). A key the run never reached reads `FAIL — not reached`.

**What it settled.** **DS1.5** (the keep-warm heartbeat in the runner) is written against it: the
interval that task reuses — 15 s, the one `internal/budget/session.go` names — is the interval this run
measured holding the service warm, an instance answering with no cold start. The one row the run could
not read, `instance-ids`, is why the run exited `2` and why the claim recorded here is about the beat's
**timing** and not about a single instance being named.

## Check 500: the image setup skill end to end (sandbox project `fugaro-dev` and the sandbox repository only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **IS13** of
[docs/image-setup-skill/implementation-plan.md](image-setup-skill/implementation-plan.md) — its "Checks
(reserved 500-509)" — and **run by you**: what it measures is a skill run in your own session and the
images Cloud Build makes of what that skill proposed, and neither is something an offline run can answer.
The check is `scripts/live-checks/check-500.sh` (its sibling test
`scripts/live-checks/check-500_test.sh` drives it against fake `gcloud` and `fugaro` only), the owner
types `bash scripts/live-checks/check-500.sh --sandbox <a sandbox repository checkout>`, and **no agent
runs any step of it** — the skill is yours to run, and a check that ran it for you would be proposing the
thing it measures. Nothing here goes near the dev installation: a project or region naming `belong` is
refused by name before a single call, which is what **never `belong`** means on this row.

**What it settles.** **D1900** — a repository's own `image:` key is ignored once the project's catalog
decides the job's image, and a repository that carries a stale one is told so rather than refused — and
**D1903** — the cap of four images is the skill's, which nothing in the CLI enforces. Both are read from
the outside: the catalog the skill left, the builds the cloud makes of it, and one run that starts on the
result.

- **The proposal, read back rather than assumed.** `fugaro image ls --json` is the catalog as it stands —
  the entries, their tags, the default and the digest each entry's last build recorded — and `fugaro image
  survey --json` is the other half of the skill's own loop: the repositories, their signals and the
  mapping. The check reads both and proposes nothing: it builds the entries the catalog already lists, and
  it invents no entry of its own.
- **The cap is a reading, not an assumption.** At most four entries. The skill stops grouping at four, the
  catalog does not care, and nothing in the CLI refuses a fifth — so the count is kept here, and a project
  whose catalog holds five is the finding D1903 says no code will make for you.
- **The builds are the cloud's.** `fugaro image build` for each entry the check covers, through
  **Cloud Build**: a local Docker build proves nothing about the entry's runtime contract or the account it
  is built as, which is the whole reason the skill never builds locally. A catalog entry's Dockerfile is
  built from the repository it belongs to and the CLI refuses a build from another repository by name, so
  the check needs one checkout per entry: `CHECK500_CHECKOUT_<entry>` names them, every other entry is
  built from `--sandbox`, and an entry with no checkout is a row the check could not measure rather than a
  finding about the entry.
- **The run is the reading.** One run is launched from the checkout of a repository the catalog covers, and
  it is a run on a baked image: the record's `baked_commit` is the baked checkout's HEAD when the job
  started, so a non-empty one is the outside evidence that the image carried the repository, which is what
  makes the build worth paying for. It is read only where the project bakes at all — a project that bakes
  nothing has nothing to show here — and the run has to reach its own `result.json`, because a launch on
  its own says nothing about the image it started on.
- **The stale block is a warning, not a refusal.** A second repository whose own `image:` block is stale is
  where **D1900** is read: `fugaro update --repo <that checkout> --plan-only` prints one `warning:` line per
  ignored key and names the entry that decides the job instead, and it writes nothing and changes nothing.
  The check points at that repository with `--stale-repo`, which is the sandbox checkout unless you name
  another one — a repository whose own `image:` block is stale is the subject, and the sandbox is only the
  convenient default. A launch or an update that refuses such a repository instead of warning is the
  finding: D1900's whole point is that it keeps working.

**What a run costs.** One Cloud Build per catalog entry the check covers — at most four, each billable,
and the build leases its own cost from the project's budget where the installation has one — plus one
sandbox run and what its task costs, which is a real run with a real pull request. The check writes no
catalog entry, no mapping and no switch: those are the skill's writes and yours, made in your own session.
On disk it is one scratch directory, removed at the end. `CHECK500_SKIP_BUILDS=1` reads the catalog and
launches the run without spending a build, which is what to use for a second pass.

**The commands.**

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check-500.sh --dry-run
bash scripts/live-checks/check-500.sh --sandbox <a sandbox repository checkout>
bash scripts/live-checks/check-500.sh --sandbox <a sandbox repository checkout> --stale-repo <another checkout>
```

Progress goes to stderr and one `CHECK 500 RESULT` block goes to stdout at the end: paste that block here
and nothing else. **Exit `0`** is every criterion that was measured holding; **`1`** is a measured
criterion that did not hold, or a guard that stopped the check — a catalog holding more than four entries,
an entry whose build recorded no digest, a run that refused, a stale repository told nothing; **`2`** is the
check not being able to measure (a tool missing, the checkout not being one, the catalog or the record
unreadable, the run never ending). A key the run never reached reads `FAIL — not reached`. The knobs are
`CHECK500_DRY_RUN`, `CHECK500_KEEP_SCRATCH`, `CHECK500_SANDBOX`, `CHECK500_STALE_REPO`,
`CHECK500_CHECKOUT_<entry>`, `CHECK500_TASK`, `CHECK500_RECIPE`, `CHECK500_SKIP_BUILDS`,
`CHECK500_REGION` (us-east5: the guard that refuses a project or region naming `belong` reads it),
`CHECK500_MAX_BUILDS` (4: the most Cloud Builds the check will spend, one per entry — an entry past it is
not built and its build row fails, which is the same count as the skill's own cap),
`CHECK500_BUILD_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (1800), `CHECK500_RUN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (3600),
`CHECK500_UPDATE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (900), `CHECK500_POLL_SECONDS` (15),
`CHECK500_DOCTOR_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (180), `CHECK500_CLI_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (180) and
`CHECK500_LAUNCH_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (600).

**What waits on it.** IS2 and IS8b — the two tasks of the folder that are still open pull requests — and
the removal work the same reconciliation parked (R2-R10, D1900): this check is the first outside reading of
the skill's own proposal on a project that is not the author's, and a finding here is what reopens either.

## Check 501: the slim base, reached by the one command that is the whole upgrade (sandbox project `fugaro-dev` and the sandbox repository only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **IS13** of
[docs/image-setup-skill/implementation-plan.md](image-setup-skill/implementation-plan.md) — its "Checks
(reserved 500-509)" — and **run by you**: nothing below is a claim that the upgrade moves a base and a run
starts on it, and what it measures is a real `fugaro update` at your own terminal followed by a real
sandbox run. The check is `scripts/live-checks/check-501.sh` (its sibling test
`scripts/live-checks/check-501_test.sh` drives it against fake `gcloud` and `fugaro` only), the owner types
`bash scripts/live-checks/check-501.sh --sandbox <a sandbox repository checkout>`, and what it runs is the
owner's own two commands in the owner's own session: run `fugaro update` in the sandbox checkout, then
`fugaro run` from it, with the update's questions answered by you and by nobody else — **no agent runs any
step of it**, and the check passes no `--yes` precisely so that you are the person it asks. A project or
region naming `belong` is refused by name, and the update is refused in such a checkout — **never `belong`**
is the first thing this row says.

**What it settles.** That the slim base of this release is what an installation actually runs on, read in
two steps rather than one: the base pin `fugaro update` leaves in the local config, and then a run whose
own record says its image was built by the upgrade. The first alone is a claim about a config file;
the second is the reading that a job starts on it.

- **The pin, before and after.** `fugaro doctor --json` reports the installation the checkout belongs to
  and the base pin it records (`project.base_images.base`). It is read twice — once as the check starts and
  once after the update — because the one command is the whole upgrade: what it leaves is what the
  installation is on. An installation whose config records no base pin is a finding here too, and it is the
  same one doctor's own `local-config-base` check makes.
- **The update is yours to answer.** `fugaro update`, run in the checkout the check was pointed at, with no
  `--yes` and its output echoed to your terminal as it is written: its review, its Terraform and the
  rebuild of the checkout's workflow images are answered by you in its own confirmation, and the check
  never answers one for you. It keeps the transcript in the scratch directory and reads the exit status —
  that is all. A failed update is a finding, and the rows below still say what the installation it left is
  on, because that is the state a reader has to know about.
- **The pin the update left.** Read again with the same command, and the row says which of the two happened:
  the ref moved to this release's base, or the installation was already on it and there was nothing to move.
  Neither is a finding; a config that records no base at all after the update is.
- **The run is what proves it.** One sandbox run launched from the checkout the update converged, followed
  with `fugaro runs ls --repo <the repository the launch named> --json` until the run is terminal — a record
  read while a run is still working is whatever was there before — and then its `result.json`, read from
  the runs bucket at the key that listing's own row gives (`runs/<the repository's slug>/<run>/result.json`,
  where the slug is **one path segment** and not the `owner/name` the launch names) and checked against the
  run id this check launched, because a record read by listing alone could be another run's.
- **The image's own build time.** The record's `image.built_at` against the moment the update **started**:
  at or after it, the job started on an image the upgrade built, which is the outside evidence that the base
  pin the update left is what a run really starts on. Before it, the job ran the image the installation
  already had — usually because the rebuild the update offered was declined — and that is the row that says
  so. The start and not the end, because `fugaro update` waits for its own rebuilds before it returns: a
  rebuilt image's build time is always inside the update's own window, so a comparison against the end would
  read a run on the rebuilt image as a declined rebuild — failing exactly when the upgrade worked. A
  record that carries no build time at all (an image built before the field existed, or a job running the
  base image directly) is reported as a row the check could not date rather than as a finding.

**What a run costs.** What `fugaro update` costs on your installation — among its steps, the rebuild of the
checkout's base-derived workflow images (each is built FROM the installation's base), billable and asked for
on its own — plus one sandbox run and what its task costs, with the pull request it opens. The check writes
no pin, no config and no policy of its own: the only
write is the update, whose steps you answer. On disk it is one scratch directory, removed at the end.
`CHECK501_SKIP_UPDATE=1` measures the pin and the run without running the upgrade, which is what to use on
a machine that has just been updated.

**The commands.**

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check-501.sh --dry-run
bash scripts/live-checks/check-501.sh --sandbox <a sandbox repository checkout>
```

The update runs in the foreground, so its questions and Ctrl-C reach it: that is the bound an interactive
command should have, and there is no timeout knob for it. Progress goes to stderr and one `CHECK 501 RESULT`
block goes to stdout at the end: paste that block here and nothing else. **Exit `0`** is every criterion
that was measured holding; **`1`** is a measured criterion that did not hold, or a guard that stopped the
check — a failed update, an installation with no base pin, a record that is not this run's, an image built
before the update; **`2`** is the check not being able to measure (a tool missing, the checkout not being
one, a read that did not answer, the run never ending). A key the run never reached reads `FAIL — not
reached`. The knobs are `CHECK501_DRY_RUN`, `CHECK501_KEEP_SCRATCH`, `CHECK501_SANDBOX`, `CHECK501_TASK`,
`CHECK501_RECIPE`, `CHECK501_SKIP_UPDATE`, `CHECK501_DOCTOR_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (180),
`CHECK501_RUN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (3600), `CHECK501_POLL_SECONDS` (15), `CHECK501_CLI_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (180),
`CHECK501_LAUNCH_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (600) and `CHECK501_REGION` (us-east5).

**What waits on it.** Nothing gates on it: it is the outside reading of the release's own upgrade path, and
the one to take again whenever `fugaro update` changes what it pins or what it rebuilds — the rebuild the
check dates the run's image against is the step an installation notices by hand.

## Check 520: a text-only coder reads a screenshot on the vision model — the stage timings and the cost split (sandbox project and sandbox repository only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **V8** of

the sandbox repository, on a real model, over a task whose own text names a console `__screenshots__` PNG —
the issue's own case, run `20261107-104613-b2af`. The check is `scripts/live-checks/check520.sh` (its
sibling test `scripts/live-checks/check520_test.sh` drives it against fake `gcloud` and `fugaro` only, and
launches nothing), what it starts is **one sandbox run, which is billable**, and **no agent runs any step of
it**: a project or region naming `belong` is refused by name, and so is a coding agent's session.

**The state it measures, and the plan's slip.** The plan's sentence for 520 reads "a repository whose
`agent.models.coder` is a provider model with an image rate and `agent.models.vision` set". Those are two
different states, and only one of them is this work's: **D2016** means a coder whose own price row carries an
image rate reads the picture itself and keeps its own model, so V7's rewrite never reaches the slot. The
state V7 rewrites — and the one doctor's own `vision-coder` sentence names, "the coder model X is priced
without an image rate, and Y, which a stage that reads a picture runs instead" — is the coder priced
**without** an image rate with the slot set. That is what this check reads, and its `premise` row says so in
as many words when the sandbox is configured the other way: a coder with an image rate of its own, or a slot
that is unset (which is Check 521's state), is a reading of a different repository than this check is about,
and the check stops before it launches anything.

**What it settles.** The issue's own case, at the places it can be read:

- **The release.** `fugaro version` and the usage line `fugaro models use --help` prints: the work ships in
  **0.24.0**, so a build that predates it, or one whose `models use` does not name the `vision` slot, stops
  with the release named rather than measuring a run that cannot carry the feature. A build that reports no
  release number at all (a dev build or a commit) is decided by the feature probe, not by a guess at how
  `dev` sorts.
- **The premise, from `doctor`.** `fugaro doctor --json`, read in the sandbox checkout: its `vision-coder`
  check's own sentence has the coder priced without an image rate and `agent.models.vision` set. The two
  model IDs come from `fugaro models ls --json` — the project configuration's row for the sandbox
  repository — and the vision model's ID is what every row below looks for in the run's own record. Two IDs
  that name the same model are a finding here: a stage timing naming it then says nothing about the rewrite.
- **The run.** One sandbox run whose task names a `.png`, launched with `fugaro run --json` from the
  checkout and followed with `fugaro runs ls --json --limit 1` until it is terminal — a record read while a
  run is still working is whatever was there before. Its `result.json` is read from the runs bucket at the
  key that listing's own row gives (`runs/<the repository's slug>/<run>/result.json`, where the slug is
  **one path segment** and not the `owner/name` the launch names) and checked against the run id this check
  launched, because a record read by listing alone could be another run's.
- **The reading the issue is about.** The run ended `succeeded`; every coder-role stage it ran —
  `implement`, and `fix` where the recipe ran one — names the **vision** model's ID in its stage timing, so
  the picture was read on the slot's model rather than by the coder; and `cost.model_by` carries that model,
  so the spend is split the way the record says rather than the way the configuration suggests. A record
  whose coder-role stages ran on the coder's own model is the failure the issue reports, and the row names
  the stages that did it.
- **The same split, through the command an owner reads a run with.** `fugaro diagnose <run> --json`, read
  for the vision model's ID in its own split. The two readings are separate rows: the record is what the run
  wrote, and the diagnosis is what the command an owner reaches for makes of it.

**What a run costs.** ONE sandbox run and what its task costs — the model spend of its coder-role stages,
on the sandbox's own budget — plus the pull request that run opens. **Billable, and the check requires
`--yes`**: without it the check prints the plan, changes nothing and exits. Every other call is a read (a
`doctor`, a `models ls`, the run record, a `diagnose`), and `CHECK520_MAX_MODEL_USD` turns the run's own
figure into a criterion when you set it. On disk it is one scratch directory, removed at the end. The run's
pull request and its branch are **not** closed by the check: the `restore` row names them, because a pull

## Check 521: the early refusal — a task naming a `.png`, no vision slot, and a run that never reaches a stage (sandbox project and sandbox repository only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **V8** of
[docs/vision-model/implementation-plan.md](vision-model/implementation-plan.md) — its "Checks 520–521" —
and **run by you**: nothing below is a claim that the refusal happens. What it measures is a real run of the
sandbox repository, refused by its own bootstrap, over a task whose text names a `.png`. The check is
`scripts/live-checks/check521.sh` (its sibling test `scripts/live-checks/check521_test.sh` drives it against
fake `gcloud` and `fugaro` only, and launches nothing), and **no agent runs any step of it**: a project or
region naming `belong` is refused by name, and so is a coding agent's session.

**What it settles.** **V5**'s early check and the two decisions that write its sentence — **D2005** (the
refusal is at bootstrap, not mid-run) and **D2006** (the sentence names the price member, or an owner who
sets the slot meets the same refusal on the gateway). The failure it removes is the issue's own: without the
refusal the run reaches `implement`, reads the picture, and dies on the gateway's image refusal with the
stage's work already paid for.

- **The release.** `fugaro version` and the usage line `fugaro models use --help` prints, the same gate
  Check 520 carries: a build without `agent.models.vision` has no bootstrap refusal to measure, and it stops
  with **0.24.0** named.
- **The premise, from `doctor`.** `fugaro doctor --json` in the sandbox checkout: its `vision-coder`
  sentence has the coder priced without an image rate and `agent.models.vision` **unset**. The slot set is
  Check 520's state and the check says so rather than launching: a run with the slot set would run the
  picture on that model instead of being refused, and this check's cost is nothing only because the refusal
  comes first. A coder that reads images itself (**D2016**) is the same kind of finding. The task must name
  an image file, by name or by the kind's own word — the two spellings the run's own check matches — and a
  `--task` that names neither is refused before anything is launched, because the refusal this measures is
  the one the task's text triggers.
- **The run.** One sandbox run launched with `fugaro run --json` from the checkout and followed with
  `fugaro runs ls --json` until it is terminal. It ends in seconds: the refusal is at bootstrap and no stage
  starts. **Nothing it launches outlives it** — a run that has not ended within `CHECK521_RUN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`
  is cancelled with `fugaro cancel <run> --now` from the step that gives up on it **and** from the script's
  exit trap, so a Ctrl-C in the middle cancels it too, and the `cancelled` row (or its `FAIL`, with the
  command to run by hand) is in the block rather than only in the log.
- **The refusal, from the record.** `result.json`, read from the runs bucket at the key the listing's row
  gives and checked against the run id this check launched: the run did not succeed, its `failure_class` is
  `config_invalid` — the class a bootstrap refusal of the resolved configuration is recorded under, so
  another class is a different ending and is reported as such — and its `reason` is the refusal's own
  sentence.
- **The sentence an owner acts on.** The `reason` has to name the refusal's own opening ("the coder can't
  read an image the task names"), the slot to set (`agent.models.vision`), the file the task names, and the
  price member that gives the slot's model an image rate (`model_prices`' `image_tokens`). A sentence missing
  any of the four is the finding: an owner who meets this needs the model that cannot read, the file that
  made the check refuse, the slot to set and the member to price — **D2006** and **D2001** — and a sentence
  naming the slot alone sends them to a key whose model the gateway then refuses for the same reason.
- **Early, and free.** The record holds **no stage at all** and its `cost.model_usd` is **zero** with an
  empty `cost.model_by`. A stage in the record is a stage whose work was paid for, which is the failure V5
  exists to remove; money spent is the owner paying to be told no.

**What a run costs.** **NOTHING billable and no model call.** The run is refused at bootstrap, before its
first stage, so no stage's work is paid for and the budget is not touched — which is why this check passes
no `--yes` and asks for nothing but a terminal and a few minutes. It does start one Cloud Run job execution,
which the check cancels if it has not ended. It creates nothing else: no job of its own, no build, no
binding, no account and no pull request. On disk it is one scratch directory, removed at the end.

**Run it:**

```sh

bash scripts/live-checks/check521.sh --sandbox <a sandbox repository checkout>
```

Progress goes to stderr and one `CHECK 521 RESULT` block goes to stdout at the end: paste that whole block
here and nothing else. **Exit `0`** is every criterion that was measured holding; **`1`** is a measured
criterion that did not hold, or a guard that stopped the run — among them a build older than the release,
a premise that is not the state this measures, a run that succeeded, and a refusal under another failure
class; **`2`** is the check not being able to measure (a tool missing, the checkout not being one, a record
that could not be read, or a run that never ended and had to be cancelled). A key the run never reached

`CHECK521_TASK` (what the run is launched with; it must name an image file) and `CHECK521_RECIPE`,
`CHECK521_RELEASE` (0.24.0), `CHECK521_REGION` (us-east5), `CHECK521_RUN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (900),

## Check 550: a repoint with a run in flight — the run keeps its own account, and the next launch gets the new one (sandbox installation and sandbox repository only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **AL3** of
