is on, so the check reads the switch rather than assuming it. **D1629** and **MC8** are the record's half:
the additive `craft_credentials` names the member that served. All of it is read from outside — the
installation's own crafts, the published node, the service's bundle and a real run's record.

- **The premise, from the installation's own words rather than assumed.** `fugaro craft ls --json` names
  the coder craft's effective access; it must be a pool, and `fugaro project policy show --json` — the node
  the credentials service itself reads — must say that pool is a **failover** pool of two or more members.
  Every member must be in the service's bundle (`fugaro creds ls --json`, names only and never a value),
  and a pool that lists a Claude OAuth subscription must have `subscription_spread` on. A build without
  the four verbs stops on the `features` row instead of measuring a pool that cannot exist.
- **The pool is yours to declare.** No command of this release stores a key under a credential's own name —
  `fugaro accounts add --type` takes `claude-oauth` alone — so the two API-key credentials Check 420's own
  sentence names are entries in your project configuration with their keys stored under their own names,
  and the pool that lists them is yours too. The check adds no credential, writes no config and publishes
  no node; its FAIL rows name exactly which piece is missing.
- **The exhaustion is at the provider, and it is deliberate.** One member is at a deliberately tiny cap
  there, so the provider refuses it and the credentials service's failover steps to the next member of the
  pool. That refusal is what the check is buying: a pool whose members are all healthy never fails over,
  and a run on it says nothing about the feature.
- **The run is the reading.** One sandbox run with a small task, launched with `fugaro run --json` from the
  checkout, followed with `fugaro runs ls --json` until it is terminal (a record read while a run is still
  working is whatever was there before), and then its `result.json` from the runs bucket at the key that
  listing's own row gives — read against the run id this check launched, because a record read by listing
  alone could be another run's. The run must end **succeeded**.
- **The switch, and the member the record names.** The record's `switches` log must carry the move from the
  pool's first member onto another: that is the failover, and it is the credentials service's own record
  (**C1.16**, **D140**) rather than a reading this script made up. The credential the record names —
  `stage_accounts`/`oauth_account`, and the additive `craft_credentials` of **D1629** — must be a member of
  that pool. **This build's record carries no `craft_credentials`**, so that one row is a finding until
  MC8's record half lands; it is reported rather than hidden, because Check 420's own sentence is that the
  field names the member that served.

**What a run costs.** ONE sandbox run and what its task costs, on the sandbox's own budget, plus the pull
request it opens: **billable, and `--yes` is required** before anything is launched — a dry run prints the
same sentence and asks for nothing. Every other call is a read (`doctor`, `craft ls`, `accounts pool ls`,
`project policy show`, `creds ls` and the run's own record), and `CHECK420_MAX_MODEL_USD` turns the run's
own figure into a criterion when you set it. On disk it is one scratch directory, removed at the end; the
pull request and its branch are **not** closed by the script and the Restore row names them.

**The commands.**

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check420.sh --dry-run
bash scripts/live-checks/check420.sh --sandbox <a sandbox repository checkout> --yes
```

Progress goes to stderr and one `CHECK 420 RESULT` block goes to stdout at the end: paste that block here
and nothing else. **Exit `0`** is every criterion that was measured holding; **`1`** is a measured criterion
that did not hold, or a guard that stopped the check — a build without the vocabulary, a craft that names no
pool, a pool that is not a failover pool, a member the bundle does not hold, `subscription_spread` off on a
mixed pool, a run that did not end succeeded, no switch in the log, a credential the record names that is
not a member, the missing `craft_credentials`; **`2`** is the check not being able to measure (a tool
missing, the checkout not being one, a `--json` document unreadable, the run never ending). A key the run
never reached reads `FAIL — not reached`. The block's keys, in order, are `fugaro-version`, `features`,
`xtrace`, `agent-session`, `belong`, `bound`, `sandbox`, `crafts`, `pool`, `bundle`, `run-launched`,
`terminal`, `result-json`, `run-succeeded`, `budget`, `failover`, `served`, `craft-credentials`, `restore`
and `scratch-removed`. The knobs are `CHECK420_DRY_RUN`, `CHECK420_KEEP_SCRATCH`, `CHECK420_SANDBOX`,
`CHECK420_YES`, `CHECK420_REPO`, `CHECK420_TASK`, `CHECK420_RECIPE`, `CHECK420_REGION` (us-east5: the guard
that refuses a project or region naming `belong` reads it), `CHECK420_RUN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (3600),
`CHECK420_POLL_SECONDS` (15), `CHECK420_CLI_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (180),
`CHECK420_LAUNCH_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (600), `CHECK420_DOCTOR_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (300) and
`CHECK420_MAX_MODEL_USD` (unset: the run's figure is read and not graded). No credential value reaches the
script's stdout, stderr, block or scratch directory.

**What waits on it.** MC8's record half — the `craft_credentials` this build's record does not yet carry —
and MC9's surfaces, which read the same record; a finding here that is about the record rather than the
build is what MC8 and MC9 answer. Nothing gates on it: it is the outside reading of the failover the
folder's own tests can only fake.

## Check 421: round-robin spread over N runs — at least two members served, or the pool is not rotating (sandbox project and sandbox repository only, never `belong`; run by you; RAN 2026-11-15, premise not met)

**RAN 2026-11-15: premise not met, no run launched, nothing spent; blocked on publishing crafts and pools into the policy node** (`check421.sh`, sandbox checkout ~/git/fugarosandbox, exit 1). The crafts and pool rows FAILED (no round-robin pool the node holds) and the runs were not launched. Same cause as Check 420: no command yet writes the crafts, credentials and pools into the published policy node.

Written as follows, before that run: Written by task **MC10** of
[docs/model-crafts/implementation-plan.md](model-crafts/implementation-plan.md) and **run by you**: the
rotation is a property of N real runs on a real installation, and no offline test can make the credentials
service take it up. The check is `scripts/live-checks/check421.sh` (its sibling test
`scripts/live-checks/check421_test.sh` drives it against fake `gcloud`, `fugaro` and `curl` only), the
owner types `bash scripts/live-checks/check421.sh --sandbox <a sandbox repository checkout> --yes`, and
**no agent runs any step of it**. A project or region naming `belong` is refused by name, and so is a
coding agent's session — **never `belong`**, as on the row.

**What it settles.** That **MC7**'s rotation is really taken up by the service, on an installation rather
than in a unit test. MC7's own red step is this check's reading — "three selections must not all pick
member 1" — and what the check reports is the live form of it: over N runs, **at least two different
members of the pool served one run each**. **D154** is the per-run stickiness the reading depends on (one
member serves a whole run, and the rotation is between runs), and **D1625** is the counter behind it.

- **The premise, including the part that is easy to get wrong.** The coder craft's effective access must
  name a pool whose strategy is `round-robin`, of two or more members, every one of them in the service's
  bundle (`fugaro creds ls --json`). And **no craft the service serves may be pinned** — to a credential,
  to an OpenRouter key or to the built-in `vertex` — because one call hands the service one candidate list,
  so the rotation is only taken up when every craft that contributes to that list goes out on a pool asking
  for it. A craft on `vertex` or on an OpenRouter key contributes nothing to the list, and the check names
  it as such rather than reading a spread that could not have happened.
- **The pool is yours to declare.** This check writes no config and no credential: it reads the
  installation's own crafts, published node and bundle, and launches the N runs. The FAIL rows say exactly
  which piece is missing.
- **The runs are the reading.** N sandbox runs (two by default, `--runs` 2 or more) with a small task, each
  launched with `fugaro run --json`, each followed to its terminal state with `fugaro runs ls --json`, and
  each one's `result.json` read from the runs bucket against its own run id.
- **The credential each run names.** `craft_credentials` where the build writes it (D1629, MC8 — this build
  does not), else `oauth_account`, `stage_accounts` or the switch log: the per-run member is read however
  the build records it.
- **THE reading: the spread.** Over the N runs, at least two different members of the pool served one run
  each. One member serving every run is the pool **not** rotating — the state MC7 exists to remove — and the
  `spread` row is the FAIL that says so. Two runs are the fewest that can show a spread at all, which is
  why the check refuses `--runs 1`.

**What a run costs.** N sandbox runs (two by default) and what their tasks cost, on the sandbox's own
budget, plus the pull requests they open: **billable, and `--yes` is required** before anything is
launched. Every other call is a read, and `CHECK421_MAX_MODEL_USD` turns the **total** figure into a
criterion when you set it. On disk it is one scratch directory, removed at the end; the runs' pull requests
and branches are **not** closed by the script and the Restore row names them.

**The commands.**

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check421.sh --dry-run
bash scripts/live-checks/check421.sh --sandbox <a sandbox repository checkout> --yes
bash scripts/live-checks/check421.sh --sandbox <a sandbox repository checkout> --runs 3 --yes
```

Progress goes to stderr and one `CHECK 421 RESULT` block goes to stdout at the end: paste that block here
and nothing else. **Exit `0`** is every criterion that was measured holding; **`1`** is a measured criterion
that did not hold, or a guard that stopped the check — a build without the vocabulary, a craft that names no
pool, a pool that is not round-robin or holds fewer than two members, a member the bundle does not hold, a
craft the service serves that is pinned, a run that did not end succeeded, a credential the record names
that is not a member, one member serving every run; **`2`** is the check not being able to measure (a tool
missing, the checkout not being one, a `--json` document unreadable, a run never ending). A key the run
never reached reads `FAIL — not reached`. The block's keys, in order, are `fugaro-version`, `features`,
`xtrace`, `agent-session`, `belong`, `bound`, `sandbox`, `crafts`, `pool`, `bundle`, `runs-launched`,
`runs-ended`, `records`, `succeeded`, `budget`, `spread`, `restore` and `scratch-removed`. The knobs are
`CHECK421_DRY_RUN`, `CHECK421_KEEP_SCRATCH`, `CHECK421_SANDBOX`, `CHECK421_YES`, `CHECK421_REPO`,
`CHECK421_TASK`, `CHECK421_RECIPE`, `CHECK421_RUNS` (2; two or more, and a smaller count is refused before
anything is launched), `CHECK421_REGION` (us-east5), `CHECK421_RUN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (3600),
`CHECK421_POLL_SECONDS` (15), `CHECK421_CLI_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (180),
`CHECK421_LAUNCH_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (600), `CHECK421_DOCTOR_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (300) and
`CHECK421_MAX_MODEL_USD` (unset: the total is read and not graded). No credential value reaches the
script's stdout, stderr, block or scratch directory.

**What waits on it.** Nothing gates on it: it is the outside reading of MC7's rotation, and the one to take
again whenever the candidate list, the pool shape or the counter behind the rotation changes — the three
things a unit test can pin and a real service's answer cannot be inferred from.

## Check 422: `fugaro update` on an installation at the previous version converges with no manual step (a sandbox installation; never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **MC10** of
[docs/model-crafts/implementation-plan.md](model-crafts/implementation-plan.md) — its "Checks 420, 421,
422" — and **run by you**: no test in this tree runs Terraform, the rules deploy and a policy publish
against a project, and that is exactly what the check's first converge is. The check is
`scripts/live-checks/check422.sh` (its sibling test `scripts/live-checks/check422_test.sh` drives it
against a fake `fugaro` whose converge **really** migrates the case's own local config the way the release
does, a fake `gcloud` that prints an access token and a fake `curl` that serves the published policy node
before and after), the owner types `bash scripts/live-checks/check422.sh` and nothing else, and **no agent
runs any step of it**. A name or a config path naming `belong` is refused, whether you typed it or `fugaro
doctor` answers it, and so is a coding agent's session — **never `belong`**, as on the row.

**What it settles.** **MC4**'s migration and the reconciliation's **F17** and **D1621**, on one installation
whose local config is still at the previous version: `claude_accounts`, `default_claude_account` and
`stages` are converted **in place** into the craft vocabulary, and the converge finishes with nothing left
for the person. The hermetic halves of the same claim are two tests in this tree —
`TestUpdateConvergesPreviousInstallation` (`internal/cli/init_craft_migrate_test.go`), which drives the
migration on a config in a temp directory, and `TestUpdateIsIdempotent` (same file), which pins the second
converge — and the check is what they cannot be: the same claim against a real project.

- **The migration, read from the config rather than from the CLI's account of itself.** The local config's
  shape is read before the converge (`claude_accounts`, `default_claude_account`, `stages` — the accounts
  design's keys — and the typed `credentials` and `crafts` the migration writes) and again after it. What
  is asserted is what **MC4** does: one typed `claude-oauth` credential per named account, and one craft
  access per craft whose stages all run on one of those accounts.
- **The older keys stay.** The migration only **ADDS** — the launch, the runner and `fugaro models` still
  read the account keys until MC5 moves them — so a converge that emptied them would be the finding, not
  the success: an installation whose runs resolve no model and no credential at all.
- **Nothing left for the person.** Exit 0, no `left_for_you`, no failed stage. That is the row the task's
  own sentence is about ("converges with no manual step"), and it is read from the converge's own `--json`
  document, which the check refuses to proceed without.
- **The unconvertible key is reported, not refused.** MC4 reports a key it cannot convert as a `note:` line
  on **every** write, so the check reads the note rather than assuming silence, and an account left
  unconverted **with** its note is a different row from one left unconverted **without** it.
- **The idempotence is a second converge of the same installation.** The migrated keys must be left byte for
  byte as the first converge left them; a second converge that re-appends or rewrites them is the FAIL, and
  the check compares the two documents rather than re-reading the file for a substring.
- **The crafts resolve.** `fugaro craft ls --json` must resolve the crafts the migrated config states.
- **The published policy node did NOT move.** No command of this release writes the crafts members of the
  published policy — `fugaro project policy publish` keeps whatever the node holds — so the check reads the
  node `config/policy/shared` **outside the CLI**, with your own credentials (`gcloud auth print-access-token`
  and the Realtime Database REST endpoint), before and after the converge. A release that started rewriting
  the operator's published crafts from a local file would be the silent loosening this row exists to catch,
  and MC5 is where the node's writer is decided.

**What it costs.** TWO converges of the sandbox installation — the whole of what `fugaro update` does: the
Terraform plan and apply, the rules deploy, the published policy, the job images behind their own
confirmation and the local config — the second being the idempotence reading. Nothing here is billable on
its own (no run is launched and no model call is made) and `--yes` is passed to each converge, so run it
where an image rebuild, a deploy or a first policy publish that an unrelated stage decides it wants is
acceptable. The plugin stage writes your own Claude Code plugin at user scope, outside every checkout. Two
reads of the published policy node with your own credentials are the only other call. On disk it is one
scratch directory, removed at the end — and **the migration STAYS**: it is the installation's own state,
`fugaro update --forget` is your own rollback and the check never runs it.

**The commands.**

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check422.sh --dry-run
bash scripts/live-checks/check422.sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check422.sh --installation <a sandbox project> --config <its local config>
```

Nothing is required but the script's own path: the installation is the one `fugaro doctor --json` answers
(run it from a checkout of the sandbox project, or with `$FUGARO_PROJECT`/`$FUGARO_CONFIG` naming it), and
the config is that installation's own local config as the CLI's own `--config` default documents it
(`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/<name>.yaml`, else under `~/.config`). `--installation` and `--config`
are both compared against doctor and against the config's own `name` and `gcp_project`, and a disagreement
is a STOP before anything runs. Run it on an installation you have **not** yet converged with this CLI;
on one whose config already holds the typed credentials and the crafts, the check says so and asserts the
end state and the idempotence alone. Progress goes to stderr and the plan of a dry run, then one
`CHECK 422 RESULT` block, go to stdout: paste that block here and nothing else. **Exit `0`** is every
criterion that was measured holding; **`1`** is a measured criterion that did not hold, or a guard that
stopped the check — a converge that failed, one that left a step for the person, a key migrated with no
note, a second converge that moved the keys, crafts that do not resolve, a policy node that moved; **`2`**
is the check not being able to measure (a tool missing, the installation or the config unreadable or
disagreeing, the converge's `--json` document unreadable, the node unreadable). A key the run never
reached reads `FAIL — not reached`. The block's keys, in order, are `fugaro-version`, `features`, `xtrace`,
`agent-session`, `belong`, `bound`, `installation`, `config-before`, `update`, `no-step-left`, `crafts`,
`policy`, `config-after`, `second-update`, `restore` and `scratch-removed`. The knobs are
`CHECK422_DRY_RUN`, `CHECK422_KEEP_SCRATCH`, `CHECK422_INSTALLATION`, `CHECK422_CONFIG` (the config path;
`$FUGARO_CONFIG` is honoured when neither is set) and `CHECK422_TIMEOUT` (3600: how long **one** converge
may take).

**What waits on it.** MC5 — the task that moves the readers off the account keys and onto the crafts — which
is why the migration only adds today; when MC5 lands, the older keys' row here is the one to re-read. And
the release's own `### For operators`: MC4's PR carries the entry that says `fugaro update` converges
accounts, the auto list and model keys to credentials, pools and crafts in place, which is the step this
check takes twice.

## Check C0: the console-coordinator page's reads, timed and sized — one script you run (an installation you name, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN, and it takes no check number.** C0 is a task of
[docs/console-coordinator-v2/implementation-plan.md](console-coordinator-v2/implementation-plan.md) rather
than a check, so this section carries the task's own name: the register's numbering paragraph above is
untouched, no number is spent on it, and the census sentence that reads the register's highest written
`## Check` section is unaffected — this heading carries no number for it to find. What it produces is the
readings [docs/console-coordinator-v2/spec.md](console-coordinator-v2/spec.md) §2.2's cells are waiting for,
the ones that say **`(unmeasured)`**, and **you** paste them: the script edits no document and never
decides a number, and filling the table is the plan's C0 itself.

**The one command.**

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check-c0.sh --project <name> [--project <name>...] [--checkout <path>...]
```

`--project` names the installation the reads are made against, and it is required and repeatable: the
`coordinator status` read is made **once per name**, which is how the spec's `~724 KB` — read on a
four-repository installation — gets a second point on the size-versus-repository-count curve. `--checkout`
names a checkout whose `plan status` is timed; without it the current directory is used when it is a
checkout (it has a `docs/`), and when it is not, that row says so and the run ends `2`. `--dry-run` prints
every command a real run would make and runs none of them: no fugaro command, no read, no verdict. A name
carrying `belong` — in `--project` or in `--checkout` — is refused before any read is made.

**What it measures, and how.** `fugaro runs ls --json` at `--since 24h`, `--since 7d` and `--since 0`, and
the same window with `--limit 50` and with `--limit 20`; `fugaro coordinator status --from-store --all
--json` once per installation named; `fugaro plan status --json --all` once per checkout named, run from
that checkout (the read walks `docs/` there); and `fugaro budget show --json`. The installation travels in
the read's own environment (`FUGARO_PROJECT=<name>`), so the argv stays the console's own words, and the
reads that do not need a checkout are made from the check's scratch directory — outside every checkout, the
way the console's own working directory is the app's — so no checkout's `fugaro.yaml` decides which
installation answers. The bytes are the document's own length on stdout and the seconds are the whole
spawn's wall clock, taken with bash's own `TIMEFORMAT` so no GNU `date` is needed. Each document is counted
by one `python3` reader that prints counts and never a document, and scanned for credential-shaped text
before any of its own words is echoed.

**Both page sizes, because the plan and the spec disagree.** The plan's C0 row names
`fugaro runs ls --json --since 24h --limit 50` (D818's first page, spec §2.6), while the `(unmeasured)`
size cell in spec §2.2 — the halted-or-failed-job item — reads `--limit 20` (D810's bounded read). The
check measures both and settles neither: a number for a flag combination the spec does not use, and none
for the one it does, would send you back for a second run. **Which limit the queue uses is a product
decision, and the reading does not make it.**

**What it prints.** Progress on stderr and ONE block on stdout: a `FACT` row per read, `PASS` when it
answered with the shape the check reads and `FAIL` when it did not, plus a `C0 READINGS` table — read,
bytes, human size, seconds, and what the document held — and a `CELLS` section with one line per read in
the wording the spec's cells need (`size about 1.1 KB, time about 5.8 s`). Exit `0` when every read
answered, `1` when every read answered and one came back a document this check does not read, and `2` when
a read did not answer or a guard stopped the run: a run that could not measure a read ends `2` even if
another read also came back the wrong shape, because the table has a hole in it.

**Why nothing has to be undone.** Every command it runs is a read — a listing of the runs bucket, the
stored view out of the project's database, the plan walk over a checkout, and the budget document — so the
check creates nothing, writes nothing, launches no run, mints no credential and changes no cloud state.
There is therefore nothing for a teardown to put back, and the block's `restore` row says exactly that;
the only thing removed is the check's own scratch directory, mode 0700, taken from its exit trap even on a
failed read or a Ctrl-C. The one read that is not a single call is `plan status`: it walks the checkout and
asks the forge about the pull requests its tasks carry, one `gh` per joined pull request, at most 32.

**What it costs.** Nothing billable and no model call. It is `USER-RUN, NOT RUN`: **no agent runs any step
of it**, and its own test (`scripts/live-checks/check-c0_test.sh`, wired into `scripts/live_checks_test.go`)
drives it against a fake `fugaro` on `PATH` alone — no network, no project, no bucket and no credential.

**What waits on it.** The page's own work (C1 to C4 and the console release) reads these numbers: the
action queue's page size, the decision between the stored view as it stands and one narrowed per
repository, and whether `plan status` may be one of four reads started together or has to be asked for on
demand. Nothing is blocked on the reading itself — the tasks are droppable and independent — but a figure
in that table which the reading contradicts is corrected by C0, and the spec's own sentence says so.

## Check 660: the service wakes on its tick and holds nothing between wakes (a sandbox installation carrying the always-on module, in its own project, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **P5.1h** of [mobile/implementation-plan.md](mobile/implementation-plan.md), from
the design of record [mobile/design/always-on-orchestrator.md](mobile/design/always-on-orchestrator.md) §4.1 and
§4.9, and its number is the first free past every claim on 2026-11-16. **No agent runs any step of it**: what it
needs is a deployed service, a real tick and a real project, and every step below is yours.

**What it settles.** That the resident orchestrator is **available rather than busy**. §4.1 chose one Cloud Run
**service** per installation, `min-instances = 0`, request-based billing and a **Cloud Scheduler** tick, and it
did not take `min-instances = 1` — the shape that buys sub-tick latency and a permanently listening socket for a
fixed monthly charge per installation. Three readings make that a check rather than a claim: the deployed
revision's own `autoscaling.knative.dev/minScale` annotation is **`0`**; the scheduler job that wakes the
service exists, is **enabled**, and carries the cadence P5.1c ships; and a tick over an **empty mailbox**
produces a pass that reads the state the previous pass left — the consumer lease (D1232's, fenced on an ETag and
stamped from the server clock) and the ledger are read from the store and not from memory — starting no
execution and writing no message. It is the reading that tells a scale-to-zero service from one that answered
out of a warm instance, and it is the premise of §4.10's idle-cost sentence: with `min-instances = 0` "the
service bills nothing between ticks" holds only while the instance really goes away. It measures the service's
**existence and shape** and not its end-to-end behaviour — a phone's message is Check 661's.

**What has to exist before it runs.** A **sandbox installation** — its own GCP project, **never `belong`** (F31:
this check changes nothing, but it reads a project's own configuration and it is not the owner's) — carrying
**P5.1b**'s `orch` account and its piecemeal grants and **P5.1c**'s service, its tick and the never-list as
code, with the module in the installation root and the opt-in switch on, **applied by `fugaro update`**
(P5.1-Q8: no release ships an operator step that is another command, so the module ships in the root the update
already applies). Your own Google credential for the reads, `gcloud`, and the service's name, region and bucket
from the module's own output. **None of P5.1b to P5.1g is built** — the tasks are approved and unbuilt — so this
section is written now and run when they land: the plan writes a check into the register **before** anyone runs
it, and writing one is not running it.

**The commands.**

```sh
gcloud run services describe <service> --project <project> --region <region> \
  --format="value(spec.template.metadata.annotations)"
gcloud scheduler jobs list --project <project> --location <region>
gcloud scheduler jobs run <job> --project <project> --location <region>   # one tick, mailbox empty
gcloud logging read 'resource.type="cloud_run_revision" AND resource.labels.service_name="<service>"' \
  --project <project> --limit 20 --format="value(timestamp,textPayload)"
gcloud run jobs executions list --project <project> --region <region> --limit 5
# the instance count between ticks, which is the annotation's own consequence. The GA `gcloud`
# carries no `monitoring time-series` group, so this is the Monitoring API's own surface, with the
# token this shell mints (paste an RFC3339 timestamp ten minutes back, and now):
TOKEN=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)
curl -s -G -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  --data-urlencode 'filter=metric.type="run.googleapis.com/container/instance_count" AND resource.labels.service_name="<service>"' \
  --data-urlencode 'interval.startTime=<rfc3339-10-minutes-ago>' \
  --data-urlencode 'interval.endTime=<rfc3339-now>' \
  "https://monitoring.googleapis.com/v3/projects/<project>/timeSeries"
unset TOKEN
```

The first command prints the revision template's annotations, and the value of `autoscaling.knative.dev/minScale`
is what this check turns on; the last read is that value's consequence — with `0` and no tick in flight, the
series' last point is `0`, which is the instance really going away rather than the annotation alone. It is the
one read above that is not a `gcloud` command (`projects.timeSeries.list`, on the Monitoring API's own endpoint,
against the metric name Cloud Run's metric list carries), and the metric's name is the only string in this
section a future Cloud Run release could move. The third forces one tick with **nothing in the mailbox**: the pass runs, writes no
message, starts no execution — the fifth command is the negative control, and the list must not have grown —
and the generations it writes are the ones a pass over an empty mailbox writes, which the fourth command's log
lines show. Record the
annotation's value, the cron, the tick's own log lines, and the execution lists **before and after** — under
Check 660 here.

**What a run costs.** One forced tick and one pass over an empty mailbox: **no model call, no run and nothing
billable**, and no job execution at all. The service's own request time is a few hundred milliseconds of a
1-vCPU instance (§4.10); the scheduler job is a Cloud Scheduler job, whose free allowance is **per billing
account and not per installation** (§11's U8 — an owner with several installations prices it once, not per
installation). Every command above is a **read** except `scheduler jobs run`, which runs the job that is already
there and creates nothing. Restore: **nothing** — the tick leaves the state as it found it, which is half of
what the check asserts.

**What waits on it.** **P5.1c**'s service and tick are what it measures, and its reading is what P5.1-Q1's
cadence is confirmed against; §4.10's idle-cost sentence and §11's U8 are the two claims it grounds. Nothing
downstream is blocked on the reading — no task consumes it — but a `minScale` of `1`, or a tick that started an
execution from an empty mailbox, is a finding to raise rather than a number to record.

## Check 661: a phone's message becomes a job execution with the laptop shut (a sandbox installation, a real paired phone and the sandbox repository, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **P5.1h** of [mobile/implementation-plan.md](mobile/implementation-plan.md), from
the design of record [mobile/design/always-on-orchestrator.md](mobile/design/always-on-orchestrator.md) §4.2 and
§3.2, and its number is the first free past every claim on 2026-11-16. It is the end-to-end check of phase 2,
and **no agent runs any step of it**: it needs a real phone, a real installation and a machine that is really
shut.

**What it settles.** That a message from a phone becomes a **job execution** while no machine of the owner's is
running anything — which is the whole of what phase 2 claims and the one thing no unit test can answer, because
every piece of it is unit-tested already. The pass the tick wakes verifies the tag (`internal/mailbox/mac.go`'s
`VerifyMAC`, over the canonical bytes of the direction), takes the launch claim, mints the budget token **after**
the claim (§4.9's duplicated-launch row: only the claim's holder mints) and starts a Cloud Run **job
execution**; the agent runs in that container and not in the resident service (§4.2's central decision: the
long-lived process holds no model credential), and the run ends as a laptop-launched run does — a run record, a
pull request, the phone's outbox answer and its presence heartbeat. Three things are read: the message is acted
on **once** and not twice (§4.9's two-consumers row: the ledger keyed `(sender, id)`, the ten-minute consumer
lease and the launch claim, in that order, at most one of which can win); the execution's own job id and
revision are the **job's**, not the service's, which is where "the agent does not run in the resident service"
is read; and the run's record and PR are the ones a laptop launch would have produced. The launch takes **no
confirmation** (D162, answered against the recommendation) and is bounded by the caps and by P5.1g's envelope —
which is why the budget must be on for this check to be runnable at all.

**What has to exist before it runs.** A **sandbox installation** — its own project, **never `belong`** — with
**P5.1b**'s account, **P5.1c**'s service and tick, **P5.1d**'s launcher half, **P5.1e**'s pairing-key copy
(the pass cannot verify a tag without the key), **P5.1f**'s consumer wiring and **P5.1g**'s launch envelope
(a per-device repository allow-list, a per-device rate and cost cap, and the named recipe an unconfirmed launch
may run). **P5.1f and P5.1g wait on P4.1** — `internal/cli/mailbox.go` and the `fugaro mailbox` command are
not in the tree, and the cloud consumer is that pass run elsewhere rather than a second implementation of it.
Also required: the **sandbox repository**, admitted to the project (`allow_repos`) so the runner's admission
check passes, and its `fugaro.yaml` carrying the workflow the launch names; a **real phone** paired with
`fugaro pair` (`internal/cli/pair.go`, merged as #2572); and the installation's **budget published, on and
enforcing** — P5.1-Q3's requirement, without which no caps sentence of the design is true and a phone-launchable
installation does not exist.

**The commands.**

```sh
# 1. on the desktop: pair the phone
fugaro pair                    # the installation is the one this checkout's config names
# 2. shut the laptop down. No `fugaro mailbox` may be running anywhere.
# 3. from the phone: send the launch message for the sandbox repository and the task
gcloud run jobs executions list --project <project> --region <region> --limit 5
gcloud run jobs executions describe <execution> --project <project> --region <region>
```

Step 3 may be run from another machine; the laptop of step 1 must be **shut and no `fugaro
mailbox` running anywhere** for the duration, which is the premise of the check and not a convenience. Record
the execution's name, job name and revision, the run id it produced, the pull request it opened, the phone's
own outbox answer and presence, and the count of executions for the same message — **under Check 661 here**.
The last reading is the one that would catch a doubled launch: one message, one execution.

**What a run costs.** One sandbox run: **billable**, on the installation's own budget, which is on and enforcing
per P5.1-Q3 — the model spend is the run's own and is what a laptop-launched run of the same task costs, and the
launch itself is a claim, a mint and a job start. The caps bound it as they bound any run: the per-run cap, the
daily cap, the kill switch. Restore, and it is part of the check: decline the pull request, delete its branch
and the run's objects the way the register's other sandbox runs are cleaned up, and `fugaro pair revoke --uid
<uid>` if you paired a device for this check alone (which is Check 662's territory, not this one's).

**What waits on it.** **P5.1f** and **P5.1g** are what make it runnable, and both wait on **P4.1**. The
reading is what phase 2's own claim rests on: §4.2's "the agent does not run in the resident service" and §3.2's
launch path are asserted in unit tests against fakes, and this is the one run that would show them against a
phone. A second execution for one message, or a run whose agent is the service's own process, is a finding to
raise and not a number to record.

## Check 662: `pair revoke` destroys the pairing key's cloud copy, and the messages stop verifying in the cloud (a sandbox installation with the module applied, a real paired phone, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **P5.1h** of [mobile/implementation-plan.md](mobile/implementation-plan.md), from
the design of record [mobile/design/always-on-orchestrator.md](mobile/design/always-on-orchestrator.md) §4.7 —
its step **2b** — and §4.6, and its number is the first free past every claim on 2026-11-16. **No agent runs
any step of it**, and **no command in it reads a secret value on any path**.

**What it settles.** That revocation reaches the **third copy** of the pairing key. Under Q8's answer of
2026-10-19 the key exists in three places — the phone's platform secure storage, the laptop's OS keychain, and a
per-installation Secret Manager copy the service reads to verify a tag — and §4.7 says plainly that step 3 (the
keychain item) no longer reaches the secret and that deleting one of two copies leaves the other verifying
perfectly. The check has **two halves and both are needed**: the **positive** half, without which "messages stop
verifying" measures nothing — with the copy in place the pass **acts on a message from the phone once** — and
the **negative** half — after `fugaro pair revoke --uid <uid>`, the Secret Manager version the service reads is
**destroyed** (*destroyed*, not merely disabled: a disabled version is still readable by any principal granted
`versions.access` on the parent, which is the design's own sentence, and rotating the value is not enough
unless the old version is destroyed), the device node and the Auth user are gone (steps 1 and 2), and the
phone's next message is **refused in the cloud, with no action taken and no execution started**. What it does
**not** settle is said in the design and repeated here so a reader does not take more from the reading than it
gives: **deleting the copy un-reads nothing** — every principal in §4.3's reader set who held the value keeps it,
and the basic Owner and Editor roles read any secret's value whatever its own policy says — so what the step
ends is the **service's** ability to verify and to forge, not a reader's.

**What has to exist before it runs.** The sandbox installation of Check 661 — **never `belong`** — with
**P5.1b**, **P5.1c**, **P5.1d** and **P5.1f** built, **P5.1e**'s cloud copy in place and its revocation written
as the command's behaviour (`fugaro pair revoke` deleting the copy is P5.1e's Files list), and **P5.1g**'s
envelope, since the positive half is a message the pass acts on. **P5.1e** also carries the note D111 and
Global Constraint 4 are owed for the third copy (P5.1-Q2), which is a prerequisite of a reader being able to
tell what changed rather than of the check running. **P5.1f and P5.1g wait on P4.1**, so this check is
runnable only once that pass exists. You need the project's own credential, the secret's name from the
module's output, and a **real phone** paired by `fugaro pair`.

**The commands.**

```sh
fugaro pair revoke --uid <uid>    # the installation is the one this checkout's config names
gcloud secrets versions list <secret> --project <project>
gcloud secrets versions describe <version> --secret <secret> --project <project> --format="value(state)"
gcloud run jobs executions list --project <project> --region <region> --limit 5
gcloud logging read 'resource.type="cloud_run_revision" AND resource.labels.service_name="<service>"' \
  --project <project> --limit 20 --format="value(timestamp,textPayload)"
# from the phone, send one more message; the pass must refuse it and start nothing
```

The first command is this work's whole revocation as **P5.1e** writes it — the device node, the Auth user, the
cloud copy and the laptop's keychain item — and the second and third read what it did: the version's state must read **`DESTROYED`**, and a
version that reads `DISABLED` still in the list is the finding this check exists for. **No command here reads a
secret's value**, and a run that prints one is not this check: if you want the strongest form of the negative
half, `gcloud secrets versions access` with its output sent to `/dev/null` is a **refusal** to record as an exit
status, never as bytes. Record the two version readings, the pass's own log lines for the phone's next message,
the execution count before and after it, and the phone's own state — **under Check 662 here**. The restore is
**re-pairing**: `fugaro pair` issues a new device uid and a new key (the old pairing stays revoked), and a new
cloud copy is written by the same path that wrote the first.

**What a run costs.** The positive half is **one message the pass acts on**, and the cheapest one is the launch
Check 661 runs — this check may be run directly after it, and then the model spend is 661's and this one adds
none. Every other step is a read or the revoke itself: **no model call, no run beyond that one, and nothing
billable**. Destroying a Secret Manager version is free; it is also **irreversible**, which is why the restore is
a re-pairing and not an un-destroy. A launch already claimed continues after the revoke — the budget token was
minted and the job started — and the caps, not the revocation, bound what it spends; that is §4.7's own
sentence and this check does not contradict it.

**What waits on it.** **P5.1e** is the copy and its revocation, and this is that task's own end-to-end reading;
the design's §4.5 E2 sentence ("the key never left the device" is false the day a cloud consumer exists) and
§4.7's step 2b are the claims it grounds. No other task waits on the reading.

## Check 663: the `orch` account is refused the grants §4.3 does not list (a sandbox installation with the module applied, your own credential, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **P5.1h** of [mobile/implementation-plan.md](mobile/implementation-plan.md), from
the design of record [mobile/design/always-on-orchestrator.md](mobile/design/always-on-orchestrator.md) §4.3, its
§4.5's **E4** and §6's never-list — rules 1, 2, 5 and 11 in particular — and its number is the first free past
every claim on 2026-11-16. **No agent runs any step of it**: it reads a real project's IAM and probes it with a
real token for that account.

**What it settles.** That the account the service runs as is **the least-privilege set §4.3 wrote and not the
list beside it**. Half of the design's envelope is what a compromise of the resident process *can* do (E4), and
the other half — the half this check reads — is what the account was **given**. Two kinds of reading, and both
are needed: **read from the project's actual IAM**, and then **probed with a token minted for that account**, so
that a grant that would be refused by the rules rather than by IAM is not mistaken for a missing binding.

*The IAM reads.*

- The `orch` account is **not a member of the installation's `var.launchers` list**, and holds none of the
  three project-level roles that list confers in `deploy/terraform/gcp/modules/firebase/iam.tf`:
  `roles/firebasedatabase.viewer` (an IAM read that **bypasses the RTDB rules entirely**, reaching every
  mailbox in the installation), `roles/datastore.viewer` and `roles/serviceusage.serviceUsageConsumer`. §6's
  rule 11 and §4.3's "what the table does not list" both turn on this, and the module must grant §4.3's rows
  **one binding at a time**.
- It holds no `setIamPolicy` on the project or on any resource and no `iam.roles.*`, and it cannot reach the
  deployer indirectly — no `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs` / `getAccessToken` on the deployer's own account — §6's
  rule 1:
  an orchestrator that could grant itself a role could widen its own envelope, and then none of E1–E4 is true.
- It holds `secretmanager.secrets.list` and `versions.list` and **no `secretAccessor` on a model, git or App
  secret** — §6's rule 5. The one exception the tag forces is the pairing key's copy (§4.7), and §4.3's reader
  table is where the rest of that set is recorded: "the `orch` account alone" is not the reader set, and the
  check does not pretend it is.

*The probes, with a token minted for the account.*

- A read of **another mailbox**, and of `config/admin/devices/**`, over the RTDB REST API is **denied by the
  rules** — a 401/403 — and **not answered with a `null` or with data**, which is exactly what the
  `firebasedatabase.viewer` role would give it: an IAM read that bypasses the rules. This is the one probe that
  distinguishes the piecemeal grant from the list.
- A **write at the runs-bucket root** is refused — the launcher's condition is `runs/`, `tokens/` and `issues/`
  only (`gcp.LauncherBucketCondition`), so the marker that permits a managed apply (D56/D57) and
  `fugaro/allow-delete.json` (D74) are unwritable — **while the read of the root is not**, which §4.3 says in
  its own words: listing needs `storage.objects.list` and a condition on an object's *name* cannot grant it, so
  the root is outside the **write** condition and not outside the read.
- The `projects:testIamPermissions` call — **no `gcloud` surface carries it**, so it travels as a `curl` against
  the Resource Manager API, the way Check 660's instance-count read travels against the Monitoring API — answers
  with **only the permissions the caller holds**, so the reading is the absence of
  `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy` and `iam.roles.create` from its answer; and
  `secretmanager.versions.access` on a model, git or App secret is **refused** on the probe that actually
  attempts it.
- **The positive controls**, because a check of nothing but refusals passes on an account that was never
  created: the same token **does** list the installation's jobs (`run.jobs.get`/`list`), **does** list secrets
  and versions by name, and **does** succeed at a write under `runs/` on a throwaway key of your own.

**What has to exist before it runs.** A **sandbox installation** with **P5.1b** built — the `orch` account, its
piecemeal bindings and the module applying them — and **never `belong`** (this check reads a project's IAM and
probes its bucket; it is not the owner's project, F31). Your own credential, with
`roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator` **on the `orch` account** so a token for it can be minted: `fugaro
update` makes that grant to the installation's operators (the module's
`fugaro_orchestrator_token_creator`, in the same apply that creates the account), so an operator needs no step
and the check makes **no change at all**. The grant lets an operator act as `orch`, which holds
`iam.serviceAccounts.signJwt` on the budget signer (the design's section 4.3 and E4), and it is there because
the daemon on an operator's own machine mints its ID token as `orch` to call the credentials service. **P5.1b is
unbuilt**, so this section is written now and run when it lands. The project's number, the account's address,
the bucket and the names of the secrets come from the module's own output.

**The commands.**

```sh
gcloud projects get-iam-policy <project> --format=json | grep -n '<orch-account>'
gcloud iam service-accounts get-iam-policy <orch-account> --project <project>
TOKEN=$(gcloud auth print-access-token --impersonate-service-account=<orch-account>)
# a read of another mailbox, and of the device node, through the RTDB rules:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "https://<project>-default-rtdb.<region>.firebasedatabase.app/config/admin/devices/<other-uid>.json"
# which permissions the account holds: the Resource Manager API's own call, since no gcloud
# surface carries it. The answer lists what it holds, so the reading is the two names' absence.
curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"permissions":["resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy","iam.roles.create","secretmanager.versions.access"]}' \
  "https://cloudresourcemanager.googleapis.com/v1/projects/<project>:testIamPermissions"
# the value read is attempted with its output thrown away: the refusal is the reading, never bytes
gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret=<model-secret> --project <project> \
  --impersonate-service-account=<orch-account> >/dev/null
# the positive control on the write reach: this one must SUCCEED, because runs/ is inside the
# launcher's condition. The object is your own throwaway, never the marker. Every storage
# command below runs as the account under test: a denial your own identity meets proves
# nothing, and a write your own identity is allowed to make would read as a failure (Check 68).
printf '' | gcloud storage cp - gs://<bucket>/runs/<throwaway-key> --impersonate-service-account=<orch-account>
# and the same throwaway at the bucket root must be REFUSED:
printf '' | gcloud storage cp - gs://<bucket>/<throwaway-key> --impersonate-service-account=<orch-account>
# the root read succeeds: the condition fences writes, and the listing under it does too
gcloud storage ls gs://<bucket>/ --impersonate-service-account=<orch-account>
gcloud storage ls gs://<bucket>/runs/ --impersonate-service-account=<orch-account>
# the restore: the one object this check creates, removed as the account that made it
gcloud storage rm gs://<bucket>/runs/<throwaway-key> --impersonate-service-account=<orch-account>
# the positive controls
gcloud run jobs list --project <project> --region <region> --impersonate-service-account=<orch-account>
gcloud secrets list --project <project> --impersonate-service-account=<orch-account>
unset TOKEN
```

The RTDB read's status code is the reading the whole check turns on: **403 or 401 is a pass**, and a `200` with
`null` is a **failure**, because a `null` is what an IAM read that bypasses the rules answers a node the caller
may not see. The two writes are **one reading, and neither half means anything alone**: the throwaway under
`runs/` must be **created** — it is the positive control that tells an account with grants from one that was
never created, and only the `runs/` prefix is inside the launcher's write condition — and the same throwaway at
the bucket root must be **refused**. Both objects are empty and named by you, and **never the marker itself**: a
probe that succeeded must not leave a marker behind. Record the status code, the two IAM readings, the
permission answers, the three storage results (the `runs/` write, the root write, the root listing) and the two
other positive controls — **under Check 663 here**.

**What a run costs.** Reads and probes: **no model call, no run and nothing billable**. Nothing is created but
the one throwaway object under `runs/`, and the block's own `gcloud storage rm gs://<bucket>/runs/<throwaway-key>`
is how the restore removes it — run it with the same impersonation flag, since it deletes what that account
wrote; the other half of the restore is removing the `serviceAccountTokenCreator` grant you added by hand. The
root write creates nothing, which is what it is there to show: run as the `orch` account it is refused, and run
as your own identity it would be a write that left an object and a failure that was never the account's. The token lives in one shell variable for the length of the
check and is unset at the end; the value read that is refused never reaches stdout, because
`>/dev/null` is what makes it a refusal with an exit status rather than bytes.

**What waits on it.** **P5.1b** is the account and its grants, and this is that task's own reading of what it
produced; §4.3's table, §6's rules 1, 2, 5 and 11, and E4's "never `var.launchers`" sentence are the claims it
grounds. A `roles/firebasedatabase.viewer` binding found here is not a number to record: it is the widening
rule 11 exists to prevent, and it is raised as a finding.

## Check 650: the one-time reconciliation — a whole window's recorded, reported and table spend beside the OpenRouter invoice (the dogfood installation `fugaro`, GCP project `fugaro-dev`, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **SA0.1** of
[spend-accuracy/implementation-plan.md](spend-accuracy/implementation-plan.md), from the plan's own Checks
section, under the block that plan reserved (**650–659**; the paragraph above the table is the reading that
took it). It runs **once the release carrying SA1.3 is installed** — `fugaro budget reconcile` is that task's
command, and until it ships there is nothing to type — and what it reads are records written **before** the
settle rule changed, which is the point of it: SA2.1 and SA3.1 need not be in the release that carries it.
**No agent runs any step of it**: the figure this output is laid beside is the owner's own OpenRouter invoice
for their own key, and the window is real spend on the owner's installation.

**What it settles.** The spec's opening figure: on the dogfood project, from 2026-10-12 to 2026-11-16,
`fugaro report --by model`'s billed spend for the DeepSeek models was **about 46% of what OpenRouter billed**
on the one API key only Fugaro runs use. Three of the reconciliation's unknowns close on this one output:

- **U1, does the endpoint report a cost at all — with O1 behind it.** OpenRouter's Anthropic-compatible
  `/messages` may return `usage.cost` only when the request asks for it, and Fugaro's routed request asks for
  nothing (`routedKeys`; **D2642** declined a body rewrite). The share of the window's runs whose record
  carries `reported_usd` is that answer, and **O1** is what turns on it: if most DeepSeek answers carry none,
  D2640 settles few calls and D2642 — the rewrite — comes back to the owner as its own decision.
- **U5, the 46% and how it splits.** The three causes the spec ranks separate here: the `cheapest` policy
  charging the minimum of each dimension, from endpoints that need not be the same one (cause 1); the dogfood
  config's `cache_read: 0.0042`, read as a **multiplier** of the input price and so pricing cache reads at
  about $0.0006 per million against an ~89% cache hit rate (cause 2; **OR1** deletes that override, and the
  check reads the records whether or not it has been deleted); and `splitModel` moving billed DeepSeek
  dollars into the notional column on a day that mixes tiers (cause 3).
- **U2, do the endpoint's `output_tokens` include reasoning tokens.** One call's token counts and its
  `reported_micros`, multiplied out at the endpoint's own price, either reproduce the reported cost or do not,
  and the difference is what OpenRouter billed outside `output_tokens`.

It is also **A5**, the one-time reconciliation note: past spend is not repriced (spec, out of scope), so this
output is the record of what the gap was, and no later command reprints it.

**What has to exist before it runs.** A release carrying **SA1.3** installed on the **dogfood installation** —
**A4**'s installation `fugaro`, whose local config is the owner's own
`~/.config/fugaro/projects/fugaro.yaml`, with route `openrouter` and `route_fee_pct: 5.5` — its runs bucket
holding the window's records, which are the records the 46% came from, and the **OpenRouter invoice for that
key** for the same window. **Never `belong`**: nothing here writes, but the read is the owner's own spend and
the check is the dogfood project's. `fugaro budget reconcile` reads only and asks nothing.

**The command.**

```sh
fugaro budget reconcile --all --from 2026-10-12 --to 2026-11-16 --json
```

The window is the spec's own and is **typed** rather than defaulted, so the reading is the one the 46% was
taken over: 2026-10-12 is the first day the records hold a DeepSeek run and 2026-11-16 the day of the
reconciliation. `--all` reads every repository's slug in the runs bucket (`--repo owner/name` would read one),
and the read is bounded to the window's newest runs — `UserStatsMaxRuns`, 5000, the bound `fugaro report`'s own
by-mode read uses — so **the output says when the window held more than that**, and that sentence is part of
what is pasted.

**What is pasted, and what passes.** Paste the whole `--json` document and, beside it, the **OpenRouter
invoice's dollar figure for the key over the same window**, with the note of whether the read truncated. Then
these three readings, each with its own pass:

1. **The share of runs carrying a report (U1, O1).** The document's own count of the window's runs whose
   record carries `reported_usd`, out of the runs it read. **It passes when** the count is stated over a window
   the bound did **not** truncate — a truncated window's share describes its newest runs and not the window —
   and the share is recorded as the fact. What follows from the number is O1's and is not this step's: present
   on most runs, D2640 settles most calls; mostly absent, D2642 goes back to the owner.
2. **Per model, the charge against the report (U5).** The output's rows — the charge (`model_by`) beside the
   report (`reported_by`), the table's band over the same calls (`table_lo_usd` and `table_hi_usd`), the
   tokens and the share of runs carrying a report — with `unattributed` a row of its own, because a call
   settled after its stage's wait lands there and it is not a model's (F19's open question), and the totals
   read **with and without the route fee**. **It passes when** the totals carry both figures, the two differ
   by the route fee, and every model row is read: a charge under the report is the gap this work exists for,
   and which of the three causes it decomposes into is recorded per model rather than assumed. **Not a failure
   here:** a report outside the band by more than 10% — that is SA5.3's alarm over the day counters, and this
   output is where its first real figures come from.
3. **One call, multiplied out (U2).** One call's `model call` entry — `in`, `out`, `cache_read`,
   `cache_write_5m`, `cache_write_1h` and `reported_micros` (`reported_micros` is written only when the cost
   is above zero, so its absence is itself a "no report" answer to U1) — against the price of the endpoint
   that served it, which is the model's row in `fugaro budget prices` (the catalog's own row, whose
   `checked_at` is recorded with the reading: past `catalog.StaleAfter` — 30 days, so from 2026-11-22 — every
   catalog-priced row charges its tier's maximum, F11). The entries are read where they are, in Cloud Logging,
   with the filter the CLI's own reader builds (`jsonPayload.message="model call"`; **Check 139**'s section
   carries the recipe, the view and the reason `fugaro logs` will not answer), and the price is the
   **endpoint's**, not the charge's. **It passes when** the arithmetic is done and recorded: the tokens at
   that price reproducing `reported_micros` answers U2 "the reported `output_tokens` include reasoning
   tokens"; a report above it answers "they do not", and **O2** says what that leaves — every call carrying a
   report is already settled on it by D2640, so only the estimated calls would under-charge.

**What a run costs.** **Nothing billable.** No run is launched, no model call is made and no image is built:
one bounded read of the runs bucket's records, one read of the owner's own invoice, and one read of one run's
log entries. Nothing is created, changed or deleted, and the Restore is nothing — which is also why the owner
can re-run it as often as they like while the window's records are still in the bucket.

**What waits on it.** **SA1.3**'s release is what makes it runnable, and nothing downstream is blocked on the
reading — no task consumes it. It is the note **A5** names, and Check 651 is read against it: 651 is a
different window under a different settle rule, so a 651 that fails is not this check's number repeated, and a
share near zero here is what would have explained it. A window the bound truncated, or a per-model gap that
does not decompose into the three ranked causes, is a finding to raise with the owner rather than a number to
file.

## Check 651: the acceptance — the week's recorded spend within ±3% of the OpenRouter invoice, and a run halted at a cap below its expected cost (the dogfood installation `fugaro`, GCP project `fugaro-dev`, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **SA0.1** of
[spend-accuracy/implementation-plan.md](spend-accuracy/implementation-plan.md), from the plan's own Checks
section, under the block that plan reserved (**650–659**). It runs **a week after the release that carries
SA2.1 and SA3.1** — SA2.1 settles a complete call on the provider's own report (D2640, floored at the tier's
cheapest end by D2651) and SA3.1 makes `highest` the default `price_policy` (D2644) — because what it compares
is a week of records written under those rules against a bill. **No agent runs any step of it**: step 2
launches a real run on the owner's own budget, and the invoice is the owner's.

**What it settles.** The spec's acceptance for the whole change — on the dogfood project, over a week after
release, recorded billed spend for OpenRouter models is **within ±3%** of the OpenRouter invoice for the key
the project uses — and the second half of that sentence, the cap promise ("halts the run at its dollar cap"),
which no hermetic test can settle because it is about money.

- **D2643, which OpenRouter figure.** The comparison is the **invoice's dollars** against the charge **with**
  the fee. The recommendation the owner did not take was the key's usage in credits against the charge without
  the fee; the daily noise of credit purchases is the cost that answer accepted, and it is the figure this
  check does **not** read.
- **F11, the catalog's date.** The row is recorded beside the totals: the catalog was checked on 2026-10-23 and
  `catalog.StaleAfter` is 30 days, so from **2026-11-22** every catalog-priced row charges its tier's maximum
  whatever `price_policy` says. Once `highest` is the default (SA3.1) staleness changes only which prices are
  read and never the end, so this is the comparison's condition and **not** a failure: a week that ran on a
  stale catalog is accepted, with its `checked_at` in the row.
- **The cap.** The spec's other half is that a run's cap halts it "measured against what the provider billed".
  With D2640 the settled charge is the provider's own figure plus the fee, so the cap counts what the provider
  bills rather than the table's guess, and one run stopped at a cap set below its expected cost is the reading
  that says so.

**What has to exist before it runs.** The release carrying **SA2.1** and **SA3.1** installed on the **dogfood
installation `fugaro`** (**A4**: route `openrouter`, `route_fee_pct: 5.5`), with **a week of runs on that
route recorded under those rules** — a window holding no OpenRouter run compares two figures that are not
about each other, and the row records that rather than passing — and **OR1 done**: the dogfood
`cache_read: 0.0042` override deleted by hand and the policy node republished by `fugaro update` (D2645),
since a config that still prices cache reads at about $0.0006 per million is the undercharge this acceptance is
about. The **OpenRouter invoice for the key** over the same week, and a **sandbox repository** for step 2's
run, so what the halt costs is a sandbox task's own spend. **Never `belong`.**

**The commands.**

```sh
fugaro budget prices                                  # the row and its checked_at, recorded with the totals
fugaro budget reconcile --all --from <the week's first UTC day> --to <its last> --json
fugaro run --repo <a sandbox repository> --max-usd <below the task's expected cost> "<a small task>"
fugaro runs show <the halted run>                     # the chain's limits: the figure, what is used, what is left
fugaro diagnose <the halted run> --json               # the halt, and reported_usd
```

The week is typed: it runs from the release's install day, and the invoice's own week is the same seven UTC
days. **Set `--max-usd` below the task's expected cost and at or below the chain's dollar limit** — a figure
above the limit is refused before any call (`--max-usd 4.5 is above the chain dollar limit this launch
resolves`) — and the plan's own rule stands here too: **do not pass `--total-timeout`**, because a shorter one
ends the run with the time budget exhausted instead of the dollar cap, which is the other reading this step
wants.

**What is pasted, and what passes.**

1. **The week against the invoice (±3%; D2643).** Paste the reconcile's totals **with the route fee** — the
   output prints both sides, and the fee-bearing one is the figure D2643 names — beside the invoice's own
   dollar figure for the key over the same week, with the catalog's `checked_at` (F11) and the window's
   truncated-or-not note beside them. **It passes when** the two figures differ by **at most 3%** of the
   invoice's. A window the read truncated is recorded as truncated and does not pass this row: the bound's
   window is not the invoice's window.
2. **The halted run (the cap promise).** Paste `fugaro diagnose <run> --json`'s `halt` and `reported_usd`,
   `fugaro runs show`'s chain block — the dimension's limit, what the chain has used and what is left, which
   is the first question a halt raises (D1055) — and, from the run's `model call` entries in Cloud Logging
   (Check 139's recipe), the largest single call's `reported_micros` beside the run's total. **It passes
   when** the run ends **`halted` with `run_cap`**, and **`cost.reported_usd` is within one call of the cap**:
   the cap minus `reported_usd` is smaller than the largest single call's `reported_micros`, so the run stopped
   on the call that would have crossed it rather than with room to spare — part of that gap is the route fee,
   which the cap counts and `reported_usd` does not, and the row records both figures. **Record, and do not
   grade:** whether the run opened a pull request and whether it is a draft (a halt before the first push opens
   none, and that is a pass), and `model_usd`, the reported-plus-fee figure, which the cap bounds.

**What a run costs.** **ONE billable run** — step 2's launch, on the installation's own budget, with whatever
the task spends before the cap halts it — plus the pull request it may open. Every other step is a read: the
reconcile over the week's records, the price table, the invoice, the run's record and its log entries.
Restore: decline that pull request if it opened one and delete its branch, and record the cap you set so the
next week's comparison is not read against it.

**What waits on it.** Nothing is blocked on the reading — no task consumes it — and it is the last word on
this spec: a 651 that holds is the change's acceptance, and a 651 that does not is the owner's decision about
which of the three causes is still open, read against Check 650's per-model figures, rather than a task this
plan adds.

## Check 127: the rigor modes on a real repository — a POC run against the same task at Critical, a Hotfix run over a sensitive path, the preview against a finished run's gateway figure, a merged Hotfix pull request's post-merge CI, two repositories of one project that differ in `rigor.default`, a `--ref` run's own revision, two matched areas, `fugaro watch` on a live run, and the two item pull requests (a sandbox repository's own project, read-only, nothing launched, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by **task T8.1** of the rigor-modes plan (its Check 127), and run by **task T8.2** —
**you**, at your own terminal. It is the eleven live steps that plan's §9 lists, and each one is a step
no container can take: every row is a reading of something only a real run, a real pull request or a
real project produces. **No agent runs any step of it.** The script refuses a coding agent's session and
a traced shell by name, refuses every value that names `belong` before it calls a tool at all, and reads
a sandbox repository's own project and nothing else.

**What it is.** One script — `bash scripts/live-checks/check127.sh` — and its sibling test
`scripts/live-checks/check127_test.sh`, which drives it against a fake `fugaro`, a fake `git` and a fake
`gh` on `PATH`, each answering out of the case's own documents and logging every call, so no network, no
project and no credential is touched by the test and every reading the check makes is one a case can
break on purpose. The check **launches nothing**: it reads the runs your installation already has
(`fugaro runs ls --json`, `fugaro diagnose --json`), the config in force in each checkout
(`fugaro config show --json`), the security list (`fugaro security paths --check`), the cost surface
(`fugaro budget preview --json`), `gh`'s own documents of a pull request and of the workflow runs on the
branch it merged into (each `gh` call naming the sandbox's own repository, so a read answers about the
project you point the check at and not about the checkout you started it in), and one
`fugaro watch --once --json` frame. Where a step needs a run that does
not exist yet, its row is **INFO** naming the command that produces it — `fugaro run --mode critical`
for step 2, and so on — rather than a FAIL: **a run that was never asked for is not a finding about the
modes**, and the block says which steps stayed yours.

**How to read the block.** The script prints one block on stdout — from `CHECK 127 RESULT` to
`CHECK 127 RESULT END (exit <s>)` — and everything else it says, including each step's progress,
goes to stderr: the block is what you paste into the `| 127 |` row above, with the date and the
verdict. Its rows are the script's own `BLOCK_KEYS`, printed in that order whatever happened, and a
step the run did not reach reads `FAIL — not reached` rather than passing silently. `exit 0` means
every row that could be measured passed; `1` means at least one row FAILed and that failure is an
answer about the modes; `2` means the run could not tell — a guard refused it, a command a step rests
on did not answer, or a step that was asked for read nothing — which is a reading about the run and
never a verdict about the modes.

**The eleven steps, and what makes each row pass.**

1. **The POC run, and its record.** The run named by `--run` resolved mode **poc**, the record says
   which layer decided it (`from`) and what the run cost; `fugaro diagnose` reads its review rounds, the
   levels the triage reached and how many findings the mode tolerated. **It passes when** the mode is
   the one the run asked for and the diagnose document parses — the row that says the modes reach a real
   record at all, and D19's default (**Critical**) is what a run that asks for nothing resolves to.
2. **The same task at Critical, diffed against step 1.** `--critical` names it. **It passes when** the
   strict run **tolerated no more** than the lenient one over the same task, and its row prints both
   counts, both round counts and both level sets — the modes' whole claim, read off two records rather
   than off the table that resolves them.
3. **A Hotfix run over a security-sensitive path.** `--hotfix` and `--path`. **It passes when** the path
   is on the security list in force (`fugaro security paths --check <path> --json`, whose row names the
   rule that matched) **and** the Hotfix run over it tolerated no finding: what kept a finding open is
   then the mode's own reading and not a guard refusing the run. **One premise is stated rather than
   assumed**: T1.5's built-in sensitive-path floors (`internal/rigor/floors.go`) are **not in the tree**
   at this section's commit — `internal/rigor/floor.go` holds the finding-score reading alone — so a path
   that no row of the list in force matches is written **FAIL**, naming T1.5 as the work that would make
   it one, rather than passing. Run step 3 in full once that task has landed; until then its FAIL is a
   reading about the tree and not about the modes.
4. **`fugaro budget preview` against a finished run's own figure.** `--recipe` and `--runs` (default: the
   run's own recipe, ten runs). **It passes when** the preview's ceiling at `--mode critical` is **not
   below** what that finished run's own gateway figure was, and its review-round knob is **not below**
   the resolution in force: a mode may only raise what a run spends, so a preview that prices fewer
   rounds than the repository resolves to is the failure this step exists to catch.
5. **A merged Hotfix pull request's post-merge CI.** `--pr`. **It passes when** the pull request is
   merged into the base branch **and** the provider ran at least one workflow on that branch at the
   merge commit itself (`gh run list --branch <base> --repo <the sandbox's owner/name> --json headSha`),
   which is the one thing a container cannot read: CI firing on the provider.
6. **Two repositories of one project that differ only in their own `rigor.default`.** `--checkout2` and
   `--run2`. **It passes when** both checkouts belong to the **same** installation (two installations
   are two projects, which is a FAIL and not this step), each repository's `rigor.default` resolves from
   its **own** file (`repo`) with a different value, and each repository's run obeyed its own key — a
   run that **named no mode**. A run that asked for one (`--mode poc`, which is how step 1's run gets
   **poc** whatever the repository's key says) is held to the mode it asked for instead, so a sandbox
   whose default is not `poc` is no failure here.
7. **A run whose mode came from the base branch's revision.** `--ref-run` and `--ref`. **It passes
   when** the record's `rigor.revision` is the base branch's tip (`origin/<base>`) and **not** the branch
   under review, and the layer that decided it is not the run's own request — the answer **D25** is
   waiting for, which is *which revision* the mode was read from. The step also reads the branch's own
   `fugaro.yaml` out of the checkout (`git show <ref>:fugaro.yaml`) and reports what it finds there; a
   branch with no config at that ref is an **INFO** row, since the record's revision above is what the
   step compares.
8. **A run whose diff matched two area rules.** `--areas-run`. **It passes when** the record carries
   **two or more** area rules with the mode each set, and its second half is an **INFO** row when one of
   them was first applied at a **round** rather than at bootstrap: a round that reached a new rule needs
   a live multi-round agent, so the row reports the moments the record carries rather than inventing one.
9. **`fugaro watch` on a live run.** No flag: it reads a frame. **It passes when** every live run in the
   frame carries a mode and the layer it came from; a run whose mode reads `-` is a **FAIL** naming the
   drop-and-warn path **F40** and the deploy that fixes it (`fugaro update --firebase-project` regenerates
   and deploys the rules the frame is read out of). A frame with no live run at all is recorded as a step
   that **could not be read** rather than passed: start a run and run this step while it is in flight.
   This is the unnumbered check §9's D24 answer proposes, written beside the check rather than as one.
10. **The pull request that fixes a filed item.** `--item-pr`. **It passes when** the pull request
    touches at least one item file under the backlog folder, that file reads `status: closed` (or
    `dropped`) **at the pull request's own revision**, the same pull request carries
    `docs/backlog/README.md`, and **one commit carries both** the flip and the regenerated index —
    **D31**'s claim, read as a diff a person would have to review. The item is read out of the sandbox
    repository at a **commit** — the merge commit, or the last commit of the pull request itself when it
    is not merged yet (`gh api repos/<repo>/contents/<path>?ref=<that commit>`) — and never at the
    pull request's head branch: GitHub deletes a merged pull request's branch, so a read at it 404s for
    exactly the pull requests this step is asked about. A pull request that is not merged yet is read
    anyway with a line on stderr rather than a second row under the same key.
11. **Two branches that filed items on the same day.** `--item-pr` and `--item-pr2`, with the sandbox
    checkout at the base branch that carries both merges. **It passes when** both pull requests are
    merged, they carry item files whose **names differ** (the rename **D26** asks for), and the
    checkout's `docs/backlog/README.md` is **current**: the folder is copied into the script's scratch
    directory, `fugaro backlog index --dir <the copy>` regenerates the index **there**, and the bytes are
    compared with the checkout's own — **D28**'s one command, read without writing anything in the
    checkout. A checkout that is not on its base branch, or an index that regenerates differently, stops
    or FAILs with the copy left in the scratch for you to diff.

**Run it:**

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check127.sh --help                 # the flags, and the plan
bash scripts/live-checks/check127.sh --sandbox <checkout> --run <slug>/<run-id> --dry-run
bash scripts/live-checks/check127.sh --sandbox <checkout> --run <slug>/<run-id> \
  --critical <slug>/<run-id> --hotfix <slug>/<run-id> --path <path> --pr <N> \
  --checkout2 <checkout> --run2 <slug>/<run-id> \
  --ref-run <slug>/<run-id> --ref <branch> --areas-run <slug>/<run-id> \
  --item-pr <N> --item-pr2 <N>
```

`--dry-run` prints the plan and calls **nothing at all** — no `fugaro`, no `git` beyond the one remote read
that names the repository, and no `gh`. Every value you type is refused at once if it names `belong`.

**What it is not.** It is not a check of the **code path**: the table that resolves a mode, the round
counts, the area rules and the floors are pinned by the tree's own tests, and this check reads what a
**real** run did with them. It does not grade whether the modes' numbers are **right** — that is the
plan's own UNVERIFIED list, **U1** (whether a cheap model scores reliably enough for a strict mode to be
worth it) and **U2** (whether a mode in fact costs less), which this check's records give figures to
rather than answers. And it is not a deployment: it deploys nothing, so step 9's frame is read on the
rules your installation already has.

**What it costs and what it restores.** **Nothing.** The script makes one scratch directory under
`TMPDIR` (mode 0700, removed at the end, with `restore` as its own row and `CHECK127_KEEP_SCRATCH=1` if
you want to keep it) and writes nowhere else: no run, no pull request, no object, no node, no config and
no file in any checkout. The runs the eleven steps read are the ones **you** launched, and the four
commands that produce a missing one are printed in the rows that stay yours rather than run for you. No
secret is read or printed by the check or by its test, and no value it reads is echoed in a way that
