  run's record, `foldPhase` turns the outcome into the item's phase, and `phaseToLabels` turns the phase
  into the label — success is signalled by the pull request becoming ready, not by a label.
- **The spec label.** The item's spec, folded to lower case and prefixed, in **D2437**'s grey: the check
  reads the spec from the daemon's own state for the item and requires the pull request to carry it.

**D2437's table is the whole of the colours**, and the check reads each one against the repository's own
table: `fugaro:running` `1d76db` (blue), `fugaro:failed` `d73a4a` (red), `spec:<name>` `6e7781` (grey). A
label the repository does not hold, or holds in another colour, is a FAIL naming which of the three it is —
and a label the daemon creates on first use is **never repainted** (**D2440**), so a colour that is already
there in another shade is a finding about the label and not about the run.

**The premise it reads first, and why it stops.** The daemon reaches the label route only when it has an
identity the service's verifier admits (**F19**): the installation's orchestrator account
(`fugaro-orch@<project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com`) holding `roles/run.invoker` on the credentials service,
and the service's own revision naming that account in the orchestrator class. **That prerequisite is not
this check's to fix: plain `fugaro update` gives the installation the account, the invoker grant and the
class (it writes the installation root's `orchestrator` block for an installation that has the credentials
service and a recorded Firebase backend), so on an installation that has been updated it is in place — and
on one that has not, `fugaro doctor`'s orchestrator-identity check warns and names `fugaro update`.** The
check reads it FIRST: with either half
missing it writes **ONE** row — *"the daemon cannot reach the label route: F19"* — and **stops** (exit 2),
rather than failing every row below it for a reason that is not about the labels. A daemon with no identity
builds no seams at all, which is a silent no-op (**R7**), and a check that went on would report the daemon's
silence as a label defect.

**Prerequisites.** Installation `fugaro` in GCP project `fugaro-dev`, region `us-east5` — hard-coded and
overridable by `CHECK640_INSTALLATION`, `CHECK640_GCP_PROJECT` and `CHECK640_REGION`; `belong` is refused by
name as the installation and as the project, both as a value you typed and as one the doctor reports. The
orchestrator daemon running **on this machine** (`fugaro orchestrator ls` must show the installation as a
local orchestrator whose cached brief is not stale and whose lease a holder holds), **one approved task in
flight** — an item whose phase is `running` and which carries the run id of the run whose pull request is
read. `fugaro` and `gh` on PATH, `gh` authenticated for the repository with pull-request read access, and
`gcloud` authenticated with permission to read the service's IAM policy, its revision and its log entries
(`roles/logging.viewer` or a role holding `logging.views.access`). The run is the one **you** launched: the
check launches nothing, and a run the daemon did not launch has no item and is never labelled.

**What a failure means, row by row.** Each row says what it read and where to look next, and the F19 row
above is the only one that stops the run:

- `installation` / `belong` — the installation read is not the one you named, or names `belong`: nothing was
  measured on any installation.
- `identity` — F19: the daemon's identity to the service is not in place, and no label can be written.
- `daemon` — the daemon is not one this machine runs and is beating, its cached brief is stale, or no lease
  holder holds it: a daemon that is not ticking holds the labels where they were, which is a finding about
  the daemon and not about the label.
- `item` / `run` — no item is in flight with a run id, more than one is (use `--run-id`), or the run's own
  row is not in `fugaro runs ls`: the pull request number and the repository are read from that row.
- `running` — the pull request never carried `fugaro:running` while the check watched it live: read the
  daemon row, the audit row, and the item's phase — a run the daemon did not launch is never labelled.
- `settled` — the label the pull request is left with is not the one this run's ending wants: read the
  item's phase against the run's record, then the audit row for a refused write.
- `spec-label` — the label the item's spec asks for is not on the pull request: read the colours row (does
  the repository hold it, and in which colour?), the audit row (a refused `ensure` is written there), and
  the item's spec — a spec whose name is not a shape Fugaro builds is skipped with one line in the daemon's
  own log.
- `colours` — a label the repository does not hold, or holds in another shade than D2437's table.
- `audit` — the service's own lines for this repository carry a **refused** act: `state_unavailable` is
  GitHub refusing the App's token (U1: raise `pull_requests: write` on the App's settings page), a bundle
  holding no App key, a provider that could not be built, or the route's own rate limit; `request_refused`
  is the call itself — a write whose pull request is not corroborated (its head branch is not exactly
  `fugaro/<run id>`, or its author is not Fugaro's own App identity).

**The knobs.** Every one of them is read from the environment and none of them is asked for:
`CHECK640_INSTALLATION`, `CHECK640_GCP_PROJECT`, `CHECK640_REGION`, `CHECK640_SERVICE_NAME`,
`CHECK640_ORCH_ACCOUNT`, `CHECK640_RUN_ID` (the run to read when more than one item is in flight),
`CHECK640_COLOUR_RUNNING`, `CHECK640_COLOUR_FAILED`, `CHECK640_COLOUR_SPEC` (D2437's table, so a repaint can
be read against what the table says today), `CHECK640_CALL_SECONDS`, `CHECK640_RUN_SECONDS`,
`CHECK640_RUN_POLL_SECONDS`, `CHECK640_SETTLE_SECONDS`, `CHECK640_SETTLE_POLL_SECONDS`,
`CHECK640_AUDIT_WAIT_SECONDS` (Cloud Logging lags the request by seconds, so the audit read is retried),
`CHECK640_AUDIT_POLL_SECONDS`, `CHECK640_AUDIT_AGE`, `CHECK640_AUDIT_LIMIT`, `CHECK640_RUNS_LIMIT`,
`CHECK640_LABEL_LIMIT` and `CHECK640_DRY_RUN`. The command line itself takes `--installation`, `--run-id`,
`--gcp-project`, `--region`, `--service`, `--dry-run` and `--help`; `--dry-run` prints the plan, makes no
call at all and touches nothing.

**Reading the `CHECK 640 RESULT` block.** One block of `FACT <key>: PASS|FAIL|UNVERIFIED — <what it read>`
lines, in this order, and the same block is what you paste back: `xtrace` (the shell was not started with
`-x`), `agent-session` (no coding agent's marker is set), `installation`, `belong`, `identity` (F19),
`daemon`, `item`, `run`, `running`, `settled`, `spec-label`, `colours`, `audit`, `restore` (the scratch
directory is gone). A row reading **UNVERIFIED** is a criterion that could **not** be measured — a reading
taken after the run had already ended, an item carrying no spec, a `gh` that never answered — and a row
reading **FAIL — not reached** is one the run stopped before. The exit status is **0** for an all-PASS
block, **1** for a measured criterion that failed, **2** for a run that could not measure (the F19 premise,
an installation that is not the one you named, a tool that is missing) and **3** for a run that reached the
end with at least one row reading UNVERIFIED. A block that carries an extra `aborted` row is one that ended
on an error rather than on an answer, and its FAIL rows say so.

**What it costs, and what it leaves.** **Nothing billable and nothing written.** The run the check reads is
the one **you** launched: the check launches no run, writes no label, creates no label, changes no policy
and publishes nothing. Every call it makes is a read — `fugaro doctor`, `fugaro orchestrator ls`, `fugaro
orchestrator state`, `fugaro runs ls`, `gh pr view`, `gh label list`, `gcloud run services get-iam-policy`,
`gcloud run services describe` and `gcloud logging read` — and the only write anywhere is its own scratch
directory, under `$TMPDIR`, mode 0700.

**Restore.** The scratch directory — the doctor's answer, the service's policy and revision, the daemon's
listing and state, the run's row, the pull request's labels, the repository's label list and the service's
audit lines — is removed on the way out, from the exit trap on a Ctrl-C as well, and the `restore` row is
that reading (a FAILed row names the directory to remove by hand). Nothing else is left, because nothing
else was made: the pull request, its branch and the run's record are the run's own, and the check neither
closes, edits nor deletes any of them. **OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.**

## Check 611: the implicit Bitbucket review-only job, end to end (a sandbox Bitbucket repository and its own installation only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **RJ10** of
[docs/review-job/implementation-plan.md](review-job/implementation-plan.md) (its "Checks the plan takes"),
which the owner approved on **2026-11-18**; its **RJ9** is the same check on a GitHub repository (**Check
610**). It is **run by you**, at your own terminal, **after Check 191's open state is closed**, and nothing
below is a claim that a review runs on the implicit Bitbucket job: what it measures is one real review of one
sandbox pull request, read back from the outside. The check is `scripts/live-checks/check611.sh` and its
sibling test is `scripts/live-checks/check611_test.sh` (which drives it against fake `fugaro`, `gh`, `curl`
and `gcloud` only, and is what `go test ./scripts` runs). **No agent runs any step of it**, and none has; it
asks you nothing, and it prints one `CHECK 611 RESULT` block for you to paste back into this section.

**What the check settles.** Five things the tree can only claim offline, all read from outside:

- **RJ8, by its behaviour.** With the credentials service on and a Bitbucket repository recorded, an
  installation with **no profiles** deploys ONE implicit review-only job for provider `bitbucket`,
  `fugaro review --pr N` resolves a review onto it — and **not** onto a per-repository job, which a review
  must never run on — the run finishes with its review recorded, and the job it ran on carries **no
  credential at all**. That last reading is the one that matters: a job that mounts no Bitbucket token can
  only have cloned the pull request's head through the service's own git route.
- **U1, the base-image review path.** The job an implicit review runs on is deployed with the installation's
  **base image** (`infra`'s `implicitReviewVariant` takes it from `lc.BaseImage`), and this is the review of
  a repository that carries an image of its own: the two readings are the doctor's `base_images.base` and
  the job's own container image, and they have to be the same name.
- **U2, a project with no profiles admits the default account to a repository** (F4). The published policy
  defines **no profile at all**, and its `accounts` block carries the default account with this repository
  in its list, so the set the service admits for the repository is not empty.
- **U3, the default account, whatever the project's model auth is** (an API key, or Vertex). The account the
  review runs as is the default one — the implicit job's account segment is fixed where it was deployed —
  and the credential that answered its **first** model call is read off the service's own `forward` line: an
  account the node admits for this repository, or one of the two names this release uses for the project's
  own key (`anthropic-api-key--project`, `provider-key--project`), which are not admitted per repository.
- **U4, a live `terraform apply` with no project jobs.** The installation holds project jobs, and **every
  one** of them is a job name this release's own derivation produces, while the published policy defines no
  profile a coding job could have been built from. The golden plan test is the offline half; this is the
  live one.

**The readings it takes.** Each of these is a command of its own, and the row it produces says which one it
read:

- **The sandbox checkout is the repository and the installation.** It is a Fugaro repository's checkout
  (`fugaro.yaml` present) whose own `origin` is a **Bitbucket** repository, and the sandbox is passed in
  (`--sandbox`/`CHECK611_SANDBOX`): the repository this check reviews is the one that origin names, and the
  installation, project, region and base image are read **from that checkout** (`fugaro doctor --json`), so
  the check measures the installation you work in rather than one it guessed. A GitHub or GitLab checkout,
  an origin naming no repository, a checkout that is not a Fugaro repository, and an origin carrying a
  credential in its userinfo are each a refusal by name — the last one before the URL is matched, recorded
  or printed.
- **The published policy** (`fugaro project policy show --json`): the **project** admits the repository,
  **no profile** of the document admits it (a profile that did would give the repository a shared project
  job, and *its* review variant is what a review of it would run on — not the implicit job this check is
  about), the budget mode is not `off` (the gateway is what reaches the service, and it exists only in
  `observe` and `enforce`), and the node's `bitbucket_token` block admits the repository with
  **`proxy: true`**. That last one is the launcher's own gate (`nodeBrokersBitbucket`) and the only way a
  job that mounts no token reaches `bitbucket.org` at all.
- **The one review**, launched with `fugaro review --pr <N> --project <the installation> --json` from the checkout. The launch document
  is held to four things: it answered `launched`, its own `job` is the installation's implicit review-only
  job of provider `bitbucket` — the name this release derives for (`config.DefaultJobProfile`, provider,
  `config.ReviewVariantAccount` + `config.ReviewVariantSuffix`) — its `account` is the default one, which is
  the only account that job serves, and the pull request the document is about is the one this check asked for
  (the rows below are read by the run id it names all the same, so a mismatch is a finding and not a stop).
- **The run's own row**, polled out of `fugaro runs ls --repo <R> --pr <N> --project <the installation> --no-cache --json` until it is terminal:
  the run ended `succeeded` with outcome `reviewed`, it pushed nothing, and it names the pull request it
  reviewed. A launch refused, a row that never appears or never ends is **not measured** (exit 2) with the
  command to read that run yourself.
- **The job itself**, out of `gcloud run jobs list`: the job the launch named carries
  `FUGARO_CREDENTIALS_SERVICE_URL` and carries **no** `FUGARO_BITBUCKET_TOKEN`, no `FUGARO_SECRET_ENVS` and
  no secret reference of any kind (**RJ8**, **CSR7**: the review-only variant mounts nothing at all). The
  same document is where the installation's project jobs are read for U4 and where the job's container image
  is read for U1.
- **The verdict**, read back with `fugaro review show <slug>/<run-id> --json`: the artifact is there, and it
  names the repository, the pull request, the head it read, and the account and model of the reviewer. A
  review run that ended `succeeded` with no artifact is a review that recorded nothing.
- **The credentials service's own lines for that run** (`gcloud logging read` over `credsvc: audit`,
  filtered by the run id, oldest-first because the run's **first** model call is what U3 is read from): at
  least one line of purpose **`git`** with status **`ok`** — the clone and the fetch of the head arriving at
  the service rather than at a token the job holds, naming a credential and never a value, with no tier (the
  purpose does not tell a fetch from a push, and a review pushes nothing) — and the earliest line of purpose
  **`forward`** with status `ok`, whose credential name is U3's model half. A read that did not answer is
  **not** the service having written no line: the rows say which it was and are left **unmeasured** (exit 2)
  when the read failed.

**What it costs, and what it leaves.** **One billable review run** of the sandbox repository: a review is
shorter than a coding run and it touches nothing, but its model calls are real, on the sandbox's own budget
(`CHECK611_RUN_SECONDS`, 2400, is how long it is waited for). What is left behind is that run's own record
and its verdict objects, which stay in the installation exactly as every run's do — and **nothing on the
repository**: a review pushes no branch, opens no pull request and writes no comment (**spec §5**), so
unlike a coding check there is no branch to delete and no pull request to decline. Everything else is a
**read** — the checkout's own `origin`, the doctor document, the published policy, the project's job list,
the run's own row, the verdict and the service's own lines — and the check writes no cloud resource, no
record, no object and no node: no `creds set`, no policy publish and no `fugaro update`. Each write it does
make is the launcher's own (the task record and the run's record), under your own `fugaro`. On disk it is one
scratch directory, removed from its exit trap whatever happened.

**The commands.**

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check611.sh --sandbox <a sandbox Bitbucket repository checkout> --pr <N> --dry-run
bash scripts/live-checks/check611.sh --sandbox <a sandbox Bitbucket repository checkout> --pr <N>
```

The dry run prints the plan and calls nothing. The real run needs `fugaro` **on PATH** (the review it drives
is the one you have), `gcloud` authenticated as **you** (it is your credential that lists the jobs and reads
the service's own lines), `git` for the one remote read that names the repository, `python3` for every
`--json` document and `mktemp`. Progress goes to stderr and one `CHECK 611 RESULT` block goes to stdout at
the end: paste that block here and nothing else. **Exit `0`** is every criterion that was measured holding;
**`1`** is a measured criterion that did not hold, or a guard that stopped the check — a value naming
`belong`, a checkout that is not a Fugaro repository, an origin that names no repository or names a host
that is not Bitbucket, a repository admitted to a profile, a budget mode of `off`, a
`bitbucket_token` block that does not admit the repository with `proxy: true`, a launch that resolved
another job or another account, a run that did not end `succeeded`/`reviewed`, a job that carries any
credential, a verdict about another repository or another pull request, no served `git` line, or a first
`forward` line naming a credential outside what the node admits, or a launch
document about another pull request; **`2`** is the check not being able to
measure (no `--sandbox` or no `--pr`, a tool missing, a sandbox that is not a directory, a repository the
published project does not admit — a launch of it would be refused, so there is nothing to measure — and a
doctor, policy, job-list, launch, listing, verdict or log read that did not answer). A key the run never reached reads
`FAIL — not reached`. The knobs are `CHECK611_SANDBOX` (or `--sandbox`), `CHECK611_PR` (or `--pr`),
`CHECK611_DRY_RUN`, `CHECK611_KEEP_SCRATCH`, `CHECK611_RUN_SECONDS` (2400), `CHECK611_POLL_SECONDS` (20),
`CHECK611_LOG_AGE` (`1h`), `CHECK611_LOG_LIMIT` (200), `CHECK611_LOG_WAIT_SECONDS` (120),
`CHECK611_LOG_POLL_SECONDS` (5), `CHECK611_DOCTOR_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (180) and
`CHECK611_CLI_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (180). None of them can point the check at another installation: the project
and the region are read from the checkout.

**Restore.** The scratch directory, including from the exit trap on a `Ctrl-C` — the `scratch-removed` row
is that reading, and a FAILed row names what to remove by hand. What is left is the review run's own record
and its verdict objects, which the block names and which stay as every run's do; **nothing is left on the
repository**, because a review pushes nothing, opens nothing and comments on nothing. **USER-RUN, NOT RUN:
no agent runs any step of it.**

## Check 730: the identity project, its non-exportable key, the signer and the JWKS, and the key ceremony (the identity project only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **T0** of
[docs/mobile-identity-pairing/implementation-plan.md](mobile-identity-pairing/implementation-plan.md) — its
"Checks the plan takes" row for **730**, "the identity project exists; the KMS key is non-exportable; the
signer and JWKS answer; the key ceremony" — and owed to that plan's task **A3**, whose Terraform root defines
the project, the key ring, the Ed25519 signing key, the signer service and the JWKS route. It is **run by
you**, at your own terminal, straight after you apply A3's root: **no agent applies it**, and **no agent runs
any step of it**. The offline half is already pinned — `ee/identitysvc/infra_test.go` holds the purpose, the
algorithm and the protection level the way the key service's own `infra_test.go` holds its ring — and this is
the half no plan can read: the key GCP really made, the service really answering, and the document the JWKS
really serves.

**What it settles.** Four things, in the order the check reads them:

- **The key is the pinned one.** The signer key's `purpose` is `ASYMMETRIC_SIGN`, its algorithm is the
  Ed25519 one the plan pins, and its protection level is the one A3's root asks for. An asymmetric signing
  key in Cloud KMS is **non-exportable** by construction — the private half never leaves the service and the
  API offers no export — so what a reading can hold is the purpose and the algorithm, and a key that is not
  the pinned one is a key that signs nothing this work will verify.
- **The signer answers.** The service A3 deploys is up, on its own narrow role, and its JWKS route returns a
  document rather than an error. A deploy that has not propagated yet is a **reading of its own** (the route
  is cold), not a failure of the key.
- **The JWKS publishes keys, and nothing else.** One `kid` per published key, `crv` `Ed25519`, and **no
  private member anywhere in the document**. A JWKS carrying a `d` member is a **STOP**: it is the half that
  must never leave the KMS project, and nothing else this check reads matters beside it.
- **The ceremony is recorded.** The KMS key version in use, the `kid` the set names, the not-after date of
  the newest signed set and the alert A3's root defines 30 days before it. Task **P8** pins the first two
  numbers into the build, so the reading is what a release is pinned from rather than a fact that lives here
  alone.

**What has to exist before it runs.** `ee/identitysvc/terraform/` merged and **applied by you** (Check 730 is
named in the plan's after-deploy order ahead of everything else), the provider configuration the plan's A3
task defines, an account that may read KMS metadata and the service in the project, and — for the ceremony's
half — task **A4**'s root key project, whose first signed key set is Check 737's. Run it after the apply and
again after 737's first set, because the second reading is the one P8 pins.

**The command.** It is **one command**, and it only reads:

```sh
gcloud kms keys describe <the signer key> --keyring=<the identity key ring> --location=<the ring location> --project=<the identity project> --format='value(purpose,versionTemplate.algorithm,versionTemplate.protectionLevel)' && curl -fsS <the pinned JWKS URL> | jq -c '.keys[] | {kid, crv, private: has("d")}'
```

**What it reads, and what a run costs.** The first half prints three values — purpose, algorithm, protection
level — and the second prints one object per published key with its `kid`, its curve and whether it carries a
private member. `private: false` on every line is the pass; a `true` is the STOP above. Nothing is created,
granted, written or deleted: two reads with your own credentials, **nothing billable and no model call**, so
the check is safe to run again after any change. There is no script behind it and there is deliberately no
scratch state: the command's output is what the section's own numbers are written from.

**What waits on it.** **A3**'s apply is what the whole signer half of this work waits on, **P8** pins the
issuer, the JWKS URL and the keys this reading produces, and **Check 735** — the live sequence after
`fugaro update` — is run against the pair. The apply itself also carries the plan's release-actions entry
(**F26**), which is where the number this reading produced is written down.

**Restore.** Nothing to restore: the check reads two documents and writes none. It creates no resource, no
object and no file, and a re-run after a rotation is expected — the ceremony moves and the reading is taken
again.

## Check 731: the provider consoles, one email under several providers, and a Microsoft tenant-verified email flag (the identity project only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **T0** of
[docs/mobile-identity-pairing/implementation-plan.md](mobile-identity-pairing/implementation-plan.md) — its
row for **731** — and owed to task **A3** on the tree's side and to **you** on the consoles' side: the app's
own OAuth clients live in Google Cloud, Microsoft Entra and Apple's developer portal, and no agent may create
one. It settles the reconciliation's **U8** and **U9** and the finding **F28** that put them here. **No agent
runs any step of it**, and it is **never `belong`**: the identity project is the owner-only one A3 creates,
not the installation you work in.

**What it settles.**

- **The consoles are set up, and the project agrees.** Google, Microsoft and Apple are enabled in the
  identity project's Identity Platform configuration, email and password sign-in is enabled with
  verification, and no provider the plan does not name is on. The console half is yours — an OAuth client in
  each provider's own portal, its redirect URI, its client id and secret into the project — and the read
  below is the half that says the project agrees with what you did.
- **U8: one email under several providers.** Sign one address in with two providers and read whether the
  project links them onto one user or makes two. The plan's identity records are read under that answer —
  the app's record is the provider's subject, not the address — so the reading is written into this section
  and into the plan's own answer, and the tree is read against it rather than assumed.
- **U9: whether a Microsoft ID token carries a tenant-verified email flag.** Read the claims of a token a
  real Microsoft sign-in produced — **the claims, never the token** — and record whether the flag the plan's
  fallback is about is there. If it is not, the plan's fallback (the app treats the address as unverified
  unless the tenant claim says otherwise) is what the implementation is read against; the reading, not the
  check, decides it.
- **The exchange the app depends on.** The provider tokens these consoles yield are the ones the app hands
  to Firebase's REST `signInWithIdp`; that the exchange accepts them is **Check 733**'s, on two real phones,
  and this check stops at what the project carries.

**What has to exist before it runs.** The identity project applied (Check 730), your accounts on the three
providers, and two sign-in addresses you may use — one of them under two providers for U8, one of them a
Microsoft work or school account for U9 if you want the tenant flag's positive reading (a personal account
answers the other half and is worth recording as such).

**The command.** It is **one command**, and it only reads:

```sh
curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth print-access-token --quiet)" https://identitytoolkit.googleapis.com/admin/v2/projects/<the identity project>/config | jq -c '{password: (.signIn.email.enabled // false), idps: [.defaultSupportedIdpConfigs[]? | select(.enabled) | (.name | split("/") | last)], idpsFieldPresent: has("defaultSupportedIdpConfigs")}'
```

**What it reads.** The same document `infra.PublicSignUp` parses and Check 361 reads for a workspace's own
project — one GET with your own credentials, nothing written, idempotent — and from it the enabled providers
and whether password sign-in is on. The field is the **list** the tree reads it as: entries of `name` and
`enabled`, where `name` is the full resource path and the provider id (`google.com`, `microsoft.com`,
`apple.com`) is its last segment, which is what the `jq` above prints — never the list's indices, which is
what reading it as an object's keys would print. **`idpsFieldPresent` is read with the list**: a `false`
there means the project's answer carries no such field at all, which is a different finding from an empty
`idps` with the field present, and the one reading this check must not lose — a field that is absent is not
"no provider enabled", it is a configuration the console has not written. **No model call and nothing
billable.** The U8 and U9 halves are not in this document: they are real sign-ins you make, and what they
produce goes into this section as the claims and the account shape, never as a token.

**What waits on it.** The app's sign-in path (**M1** to **M3**) and the plan's release: the provider set is
what the app may offer, and U8's answer is what its identity records are keyed by. A provider enabled here
that the app does not offer, or one the app offers that is not enabled, is the mismatch this check exists to
find.

**Restore.** Nothing to restore: one read with your credentials. The console work — clients, redirect URIs,
secrets — is yours and stays; a client you created only to answer U9 is yours to delete in that console, and
the check neither creates nor removes one.

## Check 732: the operator's Claude Code session — context fullness, an injected `/compact` and the usage limits (the machine you operate from, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **T0** of
[docs/mobile-identity-pairing/implementation-plan.md](mobile-identity-pairing/implementation-plan.md) — its
row for **732** — and owed to task **Z0**, the context spike whose result document
(`docs/mobile-identity-pairing/context-spike.md`) is what the context module (**Z1** to **Z3**) waits on. It
settles the reconciliation's **U1**, **U2** and **U3**, and **no agent runs any step of it**: the session it
reads is the operator's own, and half of what it settles is a question about Claude Code rather than about
this tree.

**What it settles.**

- **U1: context fullness, and an injected `/compact`.** Whether the session exposes how full its context is
  to a hook or a status line, and honours a `/compact` — or another slash command — while it is idle. Read in
  the session itself: note what the screen shows, inject the command while nothing is running, and record
  whether it was honoured. Z1's gauge and Z2's compaction are built on the answer, so a "no" here is what
  makes them draw a message instead of a control.
- **U2: the auto-compact threshold.** Whether the built-in threshold is configurable at all, and where that
  setting lives. A threshold nobody can move is a fact Z2 has to design around.
- **U3: the five-hour and weekly limits per token.** Whether the limits that the usage meter would draw are
  readable by code for the session's own token, and whether reading them is within Anthropic's terms. The
  command below is the machine half; a refusal or an undocumented answer is **the answer**, and it is written
  into Z0's document as such — a meter drawn from a read the terms do not allow is the outcome this check
  exists to prevent.

**What has to exist before it runs.** Your own Claude Code session on the machine you operate from, an OAuth
login whose token the read may use (a subscription login, as the plan assumes) with that token exported in
the shell you run the command from as `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` (the variable it reads, and the only place
the value is), and — for U1's second half — a session idle enough that an injected command can be seen to be
honoured rather than queued behind output.

**The command.** It is **one command**, the machine-read half, and it only reads:

```sh
curl -fsS --config <(printf 'header = "Authorization: Bearer %s"\n' "$CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN") https://api.anthropic.com/api/oauth/usage | jq -c '{five_hour, seven_day}'
```

**The script is that command.** `scripts/live-checks/check732.sh` (its sibling test is
`scripts/live-checks/check732_test.sh`, which drives it against a fake `curl` only and is what `go test
./scripts` runs) is THE command you run, with `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` exported in your own shell: `bash scripts/live-checks/check732.sh [--out PATH]`.

It refuses a coding agent's session, does the one read above (the token goes to `curl` through a `--config`
file of mode 0600 that is removed on exit, and is never printed, logged or put on a command line), records a
`401`, a `403` or a missing window as **not readable by this route**, prints the exact U1 and U2 steps, and
writes `context-spike-DRAFT.md` (never over a file that exists): a skeleton of `context-spike.md` with the
machine reading filled in and U1 and U2 as `OWNER: FILL IN` fields, **UNVERIFIED** until you fill them. It
asks nothing and waits for nothing. Send the draft back so an agent can write `context-spike.md`.

**What it reads.** Two windows for the token, if the answer carries them: the five-hour one and the weekly
one. A `401`, a `403` or a document without them is recorded as **not readable by this route** — which is
U3's finding rather than a failure of the check — and what the session itself shows is then the only reading
the meter could use. **No model call and nothing billable.** Nothing is written; the token is read from your
own session and is **never printed, logged, written to a file or put on a command line** — it is taken from
`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` in your own shell and handed to `curl` through a `--config` process substitution,
the register's own rule for a credential at your terminal, so the value is never in `curl`'s argv where `ps`
would show it to every user of the machine, and the block here carries the variable's name, never a value.

**What waits on it.** Z0's result document, and through it **Z1 to Z3**: the gauge's source, the compaction's
mechanism and the meter's route are each chosen from this reading, and the plan's U-items are answered by it
and by nothing else.

**Restore.** Nothing to restore: one read with your own session's credential.

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **T0** of
[docs/mobile-identity-pairing/implementation-plan.md](mobile-identity-pairing/implementation-plan.md) — its

(`docs/mobile-identity-pairing/app-spike.md`) is what tasks **M1**, **M2** and **X3** wait on. It settles the

taken on **two real phones**, an **iPhone** and an **Android** one, and nothing on a laptop can stand in for
them.

**What it settles.**

- **U4: provider tokens, and two identities at once.** Whether the Google, Microsoft and Apple sign-ins the

- **U10: the synced keychain.** Whether the platform's synced **keychain** works with the secure-store

**What has to exist before it runs.** The app built and installed on both phones (task **M0**'s spike build;

```

with the paired devices named and, for the iPhone and for the Android phone, a table for **U4**, **U5**, **U7**

`mobile-vX.Y.Z`), your developer accounts with their review consoles open, and the two phones with the store

```

## Check 735: the live sequence after `fugaro update` (a sandbox installation with your own two phones, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **T0** of
[docs/mobile-identity-pairing/implementation-plan.md](mobile-identity-pairing/implementation-plan.md) — its
row for **735** — and owed to task **UP1**, the update that converges an installation paired the old way. It
settles the reconciliation's **U11** and **U12** and the whole of the live behaviour the plan describes, and
**no agent runs any step of it**: it is the owner's own phones, the owner's own installation, and a sequence
that has to be watched rather than asserted.

**What it settles.**

- **`fugaro update` converges.** After `brew upgrade` and `fugaro update`, an installation paired the old way
  still works: the phone keeps its D171 MAC, the consumer accepts it during the transition, and the app is
  offered identity pairing. **Refresh** after an hour answers with a new token rather than a refusal.
- **Revocation, both kinds.** Revoking a device ends its access on its next request; revoking a person's
  roster grant ends that person's mobile access; and the phone's own state after each is recorded.
- **Restore.** A restore from the synced list brings the pairing back on a phone that lost it, and the
  keychain item it reads is the one Check 733 settled.
- **The strict switch, and an outage.** With the project's strict mode on, a new device without a QR is
  refused; with the identity project unreachable, the old-way phone keeps working through its MAC rather than
  being locked out — the two states the plan's transition exists for.
- **U11: a custom token from outside the project.** Firebase refuses a custom token signed by a service
  account that is not in the Firebase project, which is why the signer is created there. Read it as the
  refusal it is, with the error's own words in this section.
- **U12: whether the owner's own role can sign with the consumer key.** The command below is that reading:
  your own login against the consumer KMS key. If it **cannot sign**, the grant the plan asks for is the
  finding and is recorded as the step U12 says it is; if it **can**, the plan's J6 grant is unnecessary and
  that too is recorded, because a grant nobody needs is a grant to remove.
- **The replies verify.** The consumer's replies verify with its own KMS consumer key (**J6**) — the
  assertion path end to end rather than a unit test's fake signer.

**What has to exist before it runs.** A **sandbox installation** (never `belong`, never your working one)
brought to the previous version, upgraded with `fugaro update`, with the consumer key applied and its public
half published; two phones, one of them paired the old way before the upgrade; the roster with a second
person in it for the roster revoke; and one person's address you may revoke.

**The command.** It is **one command**, the U12 half, and it only reads what KMS answers. Two things about
the flags, because on either one `gcloud` would exit before it calls KMS and the branch below would print
**refused** for every login — including the role that can sign, which is the whole reading: `--signature-file`
is the flag `gcloud` writes the signature into and it is **required**, and there is **no
`--digest-algorithm`**, because this key is **Ed25519** (O17: one Ed25519 key per project, in the
installation project): gcloud passes the file's bytes to KMS as the message
and KMS refuses a digest for an Ed25519 version, which is why the tree's own signer
(`ee/licence/mint/kms.go`) runs `asymmetric-sign` with the flags below and its test refuses a
`--digest-algorithm` in the argv — "a digest algorithm is not what a raw Ed25519 signature takes":

```sh
gcloud kms asymmetric-sign --project=<your installation project> --location=<the consumer key location> --keyring=<the consumer key ring> --key=<the consumer key> --version=1 --input-file=<a small file of your own> --signature-file=<a scratch path of your own> && echo 'SIGNED: your own role can sign, so J6 needs no grant' || echo 'refused, as U12 assumes'
```

**What it reads.** Whether your own login is refused by the consumer key — and it is KMS's own refusal, the
`PERMISSION_DENIED` the role is read from, that answers: a `gcloud` or KMS error about the flags settles
nothing and must not be read as either. **The sequence itself is yours**,
step by step on the two phones, and each step's reading goes into this section: **pair** (the phone ends
paired), **refresh** (a new token after the hour), **revoke** (access ends on the next request), the **roster
revoke** (the person's mobile access ends), **restore** (the synced list brings the pairing back), **strict
mode** (a device without a QR is refused), and the **outage** (the old-way phone keeps working). The
simulated outage is the identity project's route made unreachable for the duration — on a sandbox project
only, and restored in the step below.

**What a run costs, and what waits on it.** Nothing billable and no model call: the phones talk to the
project and the CLI reads, and no run is launched. What waits on it is the release itself: **UP1**'s
`### For operators` entry sends every installation to this sequence, and the mobile release's own notes
point here.

**Restore.** The outage's change is undone — the route is reachable again and a pairing after it succeeds —
the second phone is unpaired, and the roster grant you revoked is restored if the person needs it. On disk
there is nothing to undo: the command writes only the signature file you named, and you delete it with the
input file you made; the sandbox's own state is what the sequence changed, step by step.

## Check 736: the Firebase Auth, KMS and Cloud Run quotas at the stated scale (the identity project only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **T0** of
[docs/mobile-identity-pairing/implementation-plan.md](mobile-identity-pairing/implementation-plan.md) — its
row for **736** — and it settles the reconciliation's **U6**: the quotas that decide whether the planned
fleet can pair, refresh and sign at all. It is **run by you**, on the identity project, with your own
credentials, and **no agent runs any step of it**.

**What it settles.** Three services' limits beside one another, read against the plan's own scale:

- **Firebase Auth** — the Identity Platform sign-in operations per second and the daily limits, against the
  refresh-on-the-hour the spec describes: every paired phone refreshing inside the same minute is the peak
  this reading is about.
- **Cloud KMS** — the asymmetric **sign** operations per second for the project, against every assertion and
  every signed reply the fleet can want at once.
- **Cloud Run** — the request and instance quotas of the signer service's region, against the same peak, and
  the concurrency the service is deployed with.

**What has to exist before it runs.** The identity project applied (Check 730) and **the plan's stated
scale** to hand: the number of phones and the request rate per phone that the check is read against. Without
that figure the reading has no denominator, and the check says so rather than passing.

**The command.** It is **one command**, and it only reads:

```sh
gcloud alpha services quota list --service=cloudkms.googleapis.com --consumer=projects/<the identity project> --format='value(quotaId,limit)' && gcloud alpha services quota list --service=identitytoolkit.googleapis.com --consumer=projects/<the identity project> --format='value(quotaId,limit)' && gcloud alpha services quota list --service=run.googleapis.com --consumer=projects/<the identity project> --format='value(quotaId,limit)'
```

**What it reads.** The quota ids and their limits for the three services. **No model call, nothing billable,
nothing written.** Where a limit is not in this listing — a console-only quota, or one the API answers in
another shape — the reading is the console page instead, and the section names which of the two it used,
because a quota that cannot be pointed at is a number nobody can re-check.

**What waits on it.** The plan's capacity assumption and **A3**'s deployment shape: a quota below the stated
scale is a project limit to raise (a console act, yours) before the fleet reaches it, and the reading is what
makes that a planned step rather than an incident. It is also where **U6** is closed.

**Restore.** Nothing to restore: three reads with your own credentials. A quota you raise in the console is
yours and stays; the check raises none.

## Check 737: the root key project, the first signed key set and a rotation rehearsal (the root key project only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **T0** of
[docs/mobile-identity-pairing/implementation-plan.md](mobile-identity-pairing/implementation-plan.md) — its
row for **737** — and owed to task **A4**, whose Terraform root defines the separate owner-only project, its
Ed25519 **root key** and the key-set signing command. It settles the owner's **O7** and **O15** (a root key
only the owner can use, and a separate owner identity as a variable), and the failure it is built around is
the worst one this work can produce: a root key any default login can sign with. **No agent applies, signs or
holds the key**, and **no agent runs any step of it**.

**What it settles.**

- **The root key project exists, and the key is the pinned one.** Its purpose is `ASYMMETRIC_SIGN`, its
  algorithm is the Ed25519 one the plan pins, it is **non-exportable** as every asymmetric KMS key is, and
  signing is granted to **exactly one member** — the separate owner identity given as a variable (O15) — and
  to **no service account**.
- **Your own login cannot sign.** The command below is the reading O7 is about: the laptop's default login
  against the **root key**. A sign that succeeds is the **worst finding this check can produce**, because a
  key the default login can use signs key sets no client should trust.
- **The first key set is signed and served.** The signing command has wrapped the JWKS in the envelope (a JWS
  over it with `seq`, `iat` and `exp` 180 days on, O18), the root key has signed it, and A2 serves it
  unchanged at the pinned URL. The set verifies against the root public key, its `seq` is above every set
  before it, and its not-after date is the one the envelope carries. **P8** pins the root public key and the
  signing keys from this reading.
- **A rotation rehearsal has run.** A new KMS key version, added and published in a rehearsal, is read back:
  the new `kid`, the set that carries both keys during the overlap, and the command that signed it. A
  rotation rehearsed once is a rotation someone can do under pressure — which is the point of doing it before
  the 180-day expiry is real.

**What has to exist before it runs.** `ee/identitysvc/rootkey/` merged and **applied by you**, the owner
identity (O15) in place with its one signing grant, the signing command built, and the bucket A3's root
defines for the signed document — which only the owner writes and the signer service reads.

**The command.** It is **one command**, and it is the refusal that matters. Two things about the flags,
because on either one `gcloud` would exit before it calls KMS and the branch below would print **refused** for
every login — including the one that can sign, which is the whole finding this check exists to catch:
`--signature-file` is the flag `gcloud` writes the signature into and it is **required**, and there is **no
`--digest-algorithm`**, because the root key is the **Ed25519** one A4's root defines (D2792, O7): gcloud
passes the file's bytes to KMS as the message and KMS refuses a digest for an Ed25519 version. The tree's own
signer (`ee/licence/mint/kms.go`) runs `asymmetric-sign` the same way, and its test refuses a
`--digest-algorithm` in the argv — "a digest algorithm is not what a raw Ed25519 signature takes":

```sh
gcloud kms asymmetric-sign --project=<the root key project> --location=<the root key location> --keyring=<the root key ring> --key=<the root key> --version=1 --input-file=<a small file of your own> --signature-file=<a scratch path of your own> && echo 'SIGNED: your own login signed with the root key, which O7 forbids' || echo 'refused, as O7 asks'
```

**What it reads.** Whether your own login can sign with the root key — and the reading is KMS's answer: a
`PERMISSION_DENIED` is the refusal O7 asks for, while a signature written into the file you named is the
finding. A `gcloud` or KMS error about the flags settles nothing and must not be read as either. The rest —
the ceremony, the first signed **key set** and the rehearsal — is the signing command you run in your own
terminal: the command prints the root public key and no private material, refuses a `seq` not above the last
signed one, and refuses inside an agent session. The readings this section carries are the root public key,
the `seq` and dates of the first set, and the rehearsal's new version's `kid` — **public values only, never a
key**.

**What waits on it.** **P8** (the production root key, the signing keys and the `seq` floor pinned into the
build), and through it **P1** and the verifier every client trusts; the alert A3's root defines 30 days before
the set expires is what makes the next ceremony a planned one. It is also the check the plan's after-deploy
order puts beside Check 730, before the release and before every operator's `fugaro update`.

**Restore.** The apply's resources stay — the project, the ring, the key and the bucket are the work's, not
the check's — and the signature files the rehearsal wrote are yours to delete. What must not be left is a
second signing grant: the reading's own criterion is that exactly one member can sign, so a rehearsal that
granted anyone else must have that grant removed before the section is written.

**USER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.**

## Check 770: the load — 100 concurrent runs across at least two members, on the workspace's credentials service (the workspace's own installation only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **WS20** of
[docs/workspace-service/implementation-plan.md](workspace-service/implementation-plan.md) — its row for
**770** — and owed to the release that carries the workspace's credentials service. It settles **O1** and
**D2986** of [docs/workspace-service/reconciliation.md](workspace-service/reconciliation.md): R9's first
values (a maximum of **10 instances** and a **concurrency of 40** per instance) are a guess until a real
load is read against the platform, and a value the load corrects is a change to R9 rather than a release
note. **No agent runs any step of it**, and the load itself is yours: 100 concurrent runs is a billable act
no script may start.

**What it settles.**

- **R9's values, as the platform holds them.** The deployed revision's `max_instance_count` and its
  container concurrency are read from Cloud Run and compared with R9's 10 and 40. A different value is the
  reading O1 asks for — either the Terraform moved them and R9's sentence is stale, or this is another
  service — and the row says which.
- **What the load left.** The service's own request log over the window holds at least the number of
  requests the load implies, over **distinct instances** no greater than the maximum the service states,
  with the statuses the platform answered: a **429** or a **503** is the platform having no capacity for the
  call, which is what the load exists to find, and it fails the row. The read is filtered to the log's
  **request entries**, and only an entry carrying an `httpRequest` counts: the service writes its own lines
  into the same revision log, and an application line read as a call would make a window with no load in it
  pass this row. A read that comes back at its own `CHECK770_LOG_LIMIT` is **truncated** — whatever the
  service logged older than the newest entries was never read, and a refusal there is what a pass would be
  hiding — so it is **not measured** rather than a pass.
- **What the load left behind.** The workspace's own meter node — `meter/workspace/<name>/<month>`
  (`budget.PathWorkspaceSpend`) — holds the reservations the load's calls took. A reservation older than
  `budget.WorkspaceReservationTTL` (6h) is room no settle will ever find, and it fails the row.
- **Git traffic rides the same service.** Pushes and clones go through the workspace's service from the
  first release (D2984), so the load is model calls **and** forge traffic on one deployment.

**What has to exist before it runs.** The workspace's credentials service deployed in the workspace's own
installation, at least two members declared with their job accounts, and the load itself launched by you:
`CHECK770_RUNS` concurrent `fugaro run`s (100 by default) across `CHECK770_MEMBERS` members (2 by default),
each on a repository whose kind the route sends to the workspace (`fugaro workspace show <workspace>` names
the members and their repositories).

**The command.**

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check770.sh
```

`--dry-run` prints the plan and measures nothing, and `--help` prints the whole definition. The knobs are
`CHECK770_*`: `SERVICE`, `INSTALLATION`, `WINDOW_MINUTES` (60), `LOG_LIMIT` (1000, the most request entries
the window is read at), `RUNS` (100), `MEMBERS` (2), `MAX_INSTANCES` (10), `CONCURRENCY` (40),
`DATABASE_URL` and `WORKSPACE` (unset, the reservations row is not measured), `KEEP_SCRATCH`.

**What it reads.** `gcloud run services describe <service> --format=json` for the revision and its limits,
`gcloud logging read` for the last `CHECK770_WINDOW_MINUTES` of requests, `fugaro config show` for the
workspace's database address, and a Realtime Database GET of the meter node with a token from
`gcloud auth print-access-token`. The check **makes no call to the service at all** — the load's own traffic
is the reading — and it creates and deletes nothing.

**What waits on it.** O1's ruling on R9's values (the reconciliation's own sentence is written from this
reading), and any later load the owner runs at 200 or 500 runs: the instance quota the project holds is
where a bigger load meets its first wall, and the row says so as an INFO line rather than a check.

**Restore.** Nothing to restore: the check creates nothing and deletes nothing. The load's runs, their
branches and their pull requests are yours and are cleaned up the way any of your runs is.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.**

## Check 771: a member's job account on a real deployment — admitted, reading with `fugaroWorkspaceRead` alone, refused at the ceiling, and refused within a minute of removal (the member's own installation, reading the workspace's own project for the service and its log, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **WS20** of
[docs/workspace-service/implementation-plan.md](workspace-service/implementation-plan.md) — its row for
**771** — and owed to the release that carries the workspace's credentials service. It settles **U3** of
[docs/workspace-service/reconciliation.md](workspace-service/reconciliation.md) — whether
`firebasedatabase.instances.get` **alone** is enough for the service to read a member's policy and its run
state on a real deployment, which is the workspaces design's own **U1** — and R13's one minute: the service
re-reads its own node when it is older than 60 seconds, so a member removed is refused inside that minute.
**No agent runs any step of it**: the three calls it reads are yours.

**What it settles.**

- **The role is the narrow one, and somebody holds it.** `fugaroWorkspaceRead` carries exactly
  `firebasedatabase.instances.get` and nothing else
  (`deploy/terraform/gcp/modules/firebase/workspace_access.tf` creates it), and it is bound to the account
  the service **revision runs as** — not to another account in the project.
- **A member's call is admitted.** The service's log holds an admission (`credsvc: audit`) naming a member's
  job account, with the repository and the tier beside it.
- **U3 is answered.** A refusal whose read label is the member's policy or state (`read=policy_shared`) is
  the get-only role **not** being enough to read what the service reads: U3 answered **NO**, and the row
  says which read failed.
- **The ceiling refuses, and a removal takes effect inside the minute.** A call made at the workspace's own
  ceiling leaves a refusal whose own words **name the ceiling** (`budget.ErrWorkspaceCeilingReached`): every
  refusal the service writes looks alike, so a refusal for any other reason — an unverified identity, a
  removed member, a read the role did not carry — is **not measured** at this row rather than read as the
  ceiling having been checked. A call from a member removed `CHECK771_REMOVED_AT` leaves a 4xx inside
  `CHECK771_GRACE_SECONDS` (60 by default) that is **not** the ceiling's own refusal — the ceiling would
  refuse the call whether the member was still on the workspace or not, so its status is excluded by its
  moment — which is R13 read live.

**Two projects, one check.** This is the only check of the four that reads two GCP projects, because the
feature is two-sided: the Cloud Run service and its log are the **workspace's own** project's (the one its
own root deploys, `deploy/terraform/gcp/roots/workspace/main.tf`), and the `fugaroWorkspaceRead` role and
the binding that holds it are the **member's** (`fugaro-dev` for the dogfood installation, created by
`deploy/terraform/gcp/modules/firebase/workspace_access.tf`). The workspace's project has **no default** —
the member's project carries no such service, so reading the service there would describe a deployment that
is not this check's subject — and a run without it refuses at once, naming the knob.

**What has to exist before it runs.** The workspace's credentials service deployed, a member declared whose
job account has run a repository the route sends to the workspace, the workspace's cap set at its own
ceiling for the one call, and the member removed for the last one. Three acts, all yours: the member's run,
the call at the ceiling, and the call after the removal — each with the moment you made it.

**The command.**

```sh
CHECK771_WORKSPACE_PROJECT=<the workspace's GCP project> \
  CHECK771_CEILING_AT=<epoch or RFC 3339> CHECK771_REMOVED_AT=<epoch or RFC 3339> \
  bash scripts/live-checks/check771.sh
```

`--dry-run` prints the plan and measures nothing, and `--help` prints the whole definition. The knobs are
`CHECK771_*`: `WORKSPACE_PROJECT` (the workspace's own project, **required**, no default),
`MEMBER_PROJECT` (`fugaro-dev`), `SERVICE`, `INSTALLATION`, `WINDOW_MINUTES` (60), `ROLE`
(`fugaroWorkspaceRead`), `JOB_ACCOUNT` (unset, any job account will do), `CEILING_AT`, `REMOVED_AT`,
`GRACE_SECONDS` (60), `KEEP_SCRATCH`.

**What it reads.** `gcloud iam roles describe` and `gcloud projects get-iam-policy` for the binding, in the
**member's** project; `gcloud run services describe` for the account the revision runs as and
`gcloud logging read` for the service's own `credsvc:` lines and the httpRequest statuses beside them, in
the **workspace's** project. It creates and deletes nothing.

**What waits on it.** The workspaces design's **U1** (whether the narrow role the design chose is
sufficient), and through it any plan that would widen it; R13's minute is read here rather than assumed
in R13's own sentence.

**Restore.** The check creates nothing and deletes nothing. Put the workspace's cap back where it was, and
re-declare the member you removed, before you write the section.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.**

## Check 772: the workspace's service cold — the beat on and off — and a run across a forced outage shorter and longer than the bound (the workspace's own installation only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **WS20** of
[docs/workspace-service/implementation-plan.md](workspace-service/implementation-plan.md) — its row for
**772** — and owed to the release that carries the workspace's credentials service. It settles **U4** of
[docs/workspace-service/reconciliation.md](workspace-service/reconciliation.md) — the service's real
cold-start time, and with it the owner's own doubt in **D2985** (*"I'm not sure we actually need it"* about
the keep-warm beat) — and **D2983**: a client that cannot reach the workspace's service waits and retries
for a bounded time and then halts with a reason that names that service, which is why an outage **shorter**
than the bound must end no run and one **longer** must end one. **No agent runs any step of it**: forcing
the outage, running the two runs and turning the beat are yours.

**What it settles.**

- **The beat's setting, and what it is worth.** `agent.workspace_beat` (the key C2 reserves) is read from
  the project's resolved config — absent means ON, which is R10's default — and read against the
  deployment's warm floor, its minimum instance count: the beat ON with a floor of zero is a beat that
  keeps nothing warm (**FAIL**), and the beat ON with a cold start still in the log is a beat not holding
  what it claims (**FAIL**).
- **The cold start, in the configuration U4 has to be taken in.** With the beat OFF and a floor of zero,
  the request log must hold a request that followed an idle gap of at least `CHECK772_IDLE_GAP_SECONDS`
  (600 by default): its latency beside the steady median is U4's figure. A window with no such silence is
  **not measured** rather than a pass, and the row says how to produce the reading.
- **The bound, from both sides.** The run that met the outage **shorter** than the retry bound must be
  terminal with **no halt** — a halt there means the bound is shorter than its name, and the row says so.
  The run that met the outage **longer** must halt with **no workspace refusal marker**: a marker is
  written from the header the service puts on a refusal it **answered** (`workspace_refusal.go`: stop, cap
  or settle), and an outage is the service not answering at all. The wait from the moment the second
  outage began (`CHECK772_OUTAGE_AT`) to the halt is the bound this check records.

**What has to exist before it runs.** The workspace's credentials service deployed, the beat turned the way
the reading needs it (`fugaro config` / the project layer), a window long enough to hold an idle gap, and
two runs the owner forced an outage across — one shorter than the bound, one longer — with the moment the
second began written down.

**The command.**

```sh
CHECK772_SHORT_RUN=<run id or its last 4> CHECK772_LONG_RUN=<run id or its last 4> \
CHECK772_OUTAGE_AT=<epoch or RFC 3339> bash scripts/live-checks/check772.sh
```

`--dry-run` prints the plan and measures nothing, and `--help` prints the whole definition. The knobs are
`CHECK772_*`: `SERVICE`, `INSTALLATION`, `WINDOW_MINUTES` (180 — a cold start needs an idle gap, and a
window shorter than the gap holds none), `BEAT_SETTING` (`agent.workspace_beat`), `IDLE_GAP_SECONDS` (600),
`PROJECT` (`fugaro`), `SHORT_RUN`, `LONG_RUN`, `OUTAGE_AT`, `KEEP_SCRATCH`.

**What it reads.** `gcloud run services describe` for the revision and the warm floor, `gcloud logging read`
for the requests and the gaps between them, `fugaro config show --json` for the beat, and
`fugaro runs ls --json` for the two runs. The check forces no outage, scales nothing, starts nothing and
stops nothing, and it creates and deletes nothing.

**What waits on it.** U4's answer — whether the real cold start is small enough that the beat is not needed
(and the beat is switched off, or its value stated) or large enough that it is — and D2983's bound, which
is read from the wait the second run measured rather than from the design's estimate.

**Restore.** Put the beat back where the installation wants it (`fugaro update` applies the config), and
leave the service's revision as you found it. The check itself restores nothing, because it changed
nothing.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.**

## Check 773: `fugaro update` on a workspace and on a member at the previous release, with a run in flight on each (a sandbox installation with your own credential, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **WS20** of
[docs/workspace-service/implementation-plan.md](workspace-service/implementation-plan.md) — its row for
**773** — and owed to the release that carries the workspace's credentials service. It settles **R11** of
[docs/workspace-service/reconciliation.md](workspace-service/reconciliation.md), and through it the HARD
RULE in [CLAUDE.md](../CLAUDE.md): `fugaro update` is the whole upgrade and it works perfectly, and it is
safe while runs are in flight, always. **No agent runs any step of it**, and no agent runs an update here:
the two updates and the two runs are yours, and the check reads what they left.

**What it settles.**

- **Both sides converge with no other step.** `fugaro doctor --all --json` on the workspace and on the
  member reports **no warning** afterwards. An update that leaves a warning is an update with another step
  behind it — a `fugaro update-skills`, a manual repair, a `policy publish --delete` — which is exactly what
  the HARD RULE forbids; the fix belongs in the same release's update.
- **The update says the one line, and lands every step.** Both logs must carry the HARD RULE's own sentence
  (`internal/cli/update_in_flight.go`: `<N> in flight: update waits for none and changes nothing they hold`)
  and **no** line naming a step that did not land (`refused`, `failed`, `could not`, `not applied`,
  `permission denied`).
- **The run finishes.** Each run in flight is **terminal** in `fugaro runs ls --json`, and no halt of it
  falls inside the update's own window (`CHECK773_WORKSPACE_UPDATE_AT` plus
  `CHECK773_UPDATE_WINDOW_SECONDS`, one hour by default): a run whose halt falls there is a run the update
  stopped, which R11 forbids. Two things may still reach a run, and the update names each in one short line
  rather than denying it: a membership or an entry that changed, which the service refuses from its next
  read of the node (R13), and a new revision of the service, which drains the old one.

**What has to exist before it runs.** A sandbox installation with its own repository, at the **previous
release** — a checkout at the previous tag, or the older installed CLI — with the workspace's service on
one side and a member on the other; one run launched on each, before the update, with its run id kept; the
two updates run with their output saved; and the moment the update began written down.

**The command.**

```sh
CHECK773_WORKSPACE_PROJECT=<workspace's Fugaro project> \
CHECK773_WORKSPACE_UPDATE_LOG=/tmp/ws-update.log CHECK773_MEMBER_UPDATE_LOG=/tmp/member-update.log \
CHECK773_WORKSPACE_RUN=<run id or its last 4> CHECK773_MEMBER_RUN=<run id or its last 4> \
CHECK773_WORKSPACE_UPDATE_AT=<epoch or RFC 3339> bash scripts/live-checks/check773.sh
```

`--dry-run` prints the plan and measures nothing, and `--help` prints the whole definition. The knobs are
`CHECK773_*`: `WORKSPACE_PROJECT`, `MEMBER_PROJECT` (`fugaro`), `INSTALLATION` (`fugaro`),
`WORKSPACE_UPDATE_LOG`, `MEMBER_UPDATE_LOG`, `WORKSPACE_RUN`, `MEMBER_RUN`, `WORKSPACE_UPDATE_AT`,
`UPDATE_WINDOW_SECONDS` (3600), `KEEP_SCRATCH`.

**What it reads.** `fugaro doctor --project <p> --all --json` on each side, the two update logs you saved,
and `fugaro runs ls --json` for the two runs. It runs no update, writes nothing anywhere and creates and
deletes nothing; the copies it reads sit in a scratch directory (mode 0700) it removes.

**What waits on it.** R11's own sentence, and the release notes of the first release that ships the
service: this is the check that says the release converged a previous installation with runs in flight —
which is the promise the `### For operators` section of that release ("run `fugaro update`") is read
against.

**Restore.** Nothing to restore: the two runs, their branches and their pull requests are yours, and the
check changed nothing. Bring the sandbox back to the current release when you are done, and delete the two
logs if you kept them only for this reading.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.**

## Check 780: one project owner's `fugaro update` across a run in flight (a sandbox installation, project and repository, your own credential, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **KS17** of
[docs/keys-through-service/implementation-plan.md](keys-through-service/implementation-plan.md) — its row
for **780**, out of that plan's §8 — and owed to the release that carries **KS15** (the one that stops
mounting a model key and starts serving it from the credentials service). It answers the reconciliation's
**R4**, **R7** and **U3**, and **U3** is the whole reason it is a check rather than an assumption: the
owner's requirement of 2026-11-09 is that `fugaro update` is safe **while runs are in flight**, always, and
what makes that a measurement rather than a claim is a run that was launched before the update and finishes
after it. **No agent runs any step of it**, and none can: what it measures is a live installation and an
update that changes it.

**What it settles.**

- **The premise, first, because everything below depends on it.** The repository's Cloud Run jobs still
  **mount** a model credential and the Secret Manager containers behind those mounts are still there — the
  state of an installation that was at the release before **Release A** and that no project owner has
  updated since. An installation whose jobs mount nothing is not this check's subject, and it ends the run
  as one that could **not measure** before launching anything or spending anything.
- **The run in flight.** One sandbox run is launched and its own row read **before** the update starts; a
  run that is already terminal there is not the run U3 is about.
- **The copy (KS12, D3001).** The installation's ONE bundle container
  (`fugaro-project-<project>-creds-bundle-<hash>`, the name `internal/backend/gcp` derives) holds a version
  created **inside the update's own window** — the copy landing. Nothing of the bundle is read as a value:
  the reading is that a version of it was written while the update ran.
- **The mounts dropped (KS13).** After the update, no job of the repository is fed from a model credential
  of any kind — no `credential-<name>-key` container, no `anthropic-api-key`, no `claude-oauth-token*`, no
  `FUGARO_PROVIDER_KEY_*` variable with a value.
- **The old containers deleted (KS15, R7, D3005).** Every model container the repository's jobs mounted
  before the update that **no job of the installation mounts any more** is gone; one another job still
  mounts is **kept** by KS15's own rule and recorded as kept rather than as a finding. Each deletion is
  **named** in the update's transcript — one line each, never a value — and the transcript is scanned for
  long credential-shaped runs, which is reported rather than asserted, because this check never reads a
  value and so cannot compare one.
- **The run finishing (U3).** The run launched above is terminal, it **succeeded**, and its `started_at` is
  before the repository's jobs were last updated — the moment `fugaro update --repo` re-applied that
  repository, which is what says the update ran **across** a run rather than after one.
- **The operator's update (U3, and the other half of the owner's requirement).** An operator's
  `fugaro update` — an account that is **not** a project owner — copies nothing, deletes nothing, and its
  copy stage says it was skipped and **who** must run it. That transcript is yours to make **before** you run
  the check, with `--operator-transcript <file>`; with none handed, the row is one the check could **not
  measure** and its text is the instruction for making one.

**The command.** It is **one command**, run from the sandbox checkout at your own terminal, as a **project
owner** of the installation:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check780.sh --sandbox <the sandbox repository checkout> --operator-transcript <the operator's update transcript>
```

`--operator-transcript` is optional and its absence costs one row, not the run. `--dry-run` makes every
guard and prints every command it would run, calling nothing; `--help` prints the header above. The script
prints progress on stderr, the update's own output on your terminal (that output **is** this check's
transcript), and ONE block on **stdout** headed `CHECK 780 RESULT`, ending `CHECK 780 RESULT END (exit N)`:
exit **0** when every criterion held, **1** when one did not or a guard stopped the run, **2** when the
check could not measure — a tool is missing, the checkout is not one, the installation is not in the state
this check is about, a read did not answer, or no operator's transcript was handed. Paste that block back
for the row; a key the run never reached reads `FAIL — not reached`. The block's keys are
`fugaro-version`, `xtrace`, `agent-session`, `belong`, `installation`, `state-before`, `run-in-flight`,
`update`, `bundle-version`, `mounts-dropped`, `secrets-deleted`, `deletions-named`, `transcript-scan`,
`run-finished`, `operator-update`, `restore` and `scratch-removed`.

**What it reads, and what it never reads.** Names, refs, counts, windows and exit codes: secret container
NAMES, job NAMES, the bundle version's creation time, the update's own timestamped transcript. **No secret
value is read by any step**, and none can reach the block — a container's name appears, its value never
does.

**What it does not put back.** This check's update is **not** reversible by it and is not meant to be: the
copy into the bundle, the dropped mounts and the deleted containers are the release's own migration, and
the run's branch and pull request are left as the run left them. The `restore` row says exactly that, and
the scratch directory is removed from the exit trap even on a failed assertion or a Ctrl-C. Run it only
where that is acceptable: a **sandbox installation, project and repository**, and **never `belong`**.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** Its own automated proof is
`scripts/live-checks/check780_test.sh`, which drives every step of it against fake tools — no cloud, no
installation, no update and no run — and is run by `go test ./scripts`.

## Check 781: a non-Claude provider model served through the credentials service, end to end (a sandbox installation, project and repository, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **KS17** of
[docs/keys-through-service/implementation-plan.md](keys-through-service/implementation-plan.md) — its row
for **781**, out of that plan's §8 — and run **after Release A**. It answers the reconciliation's **R6**
and **F13**, and the pair of facts it settles is **D3005**'s: the provider key is **not** in the job — the
job carries the credentials service's address instead — so a provider call that reaches the endpoint was
served **from the bundle**, and what it cost is the **provider's own reported figure**. **No agent runs any
step of it**, and none can: it launches a real run on the owner's own installation.

**What it settles.**

- **The bundle exists.** `gcloud secrets list` carries the installation's ONE bundle
  (`fugaro-project-<project>-creds-bundle-<hash>`), matched by the logical name and the hash the backend
  derives rather than by a prefix a rename would move.
- **The key is not in the job.** The job the run's execution names is fed from **no** model credential of
  any kind — no `credential-<name>-key` container, no `anthropic-api-key`, no `claude-oauth-token*`, no
  `FUGARO_PROVIDER_KEY_*` variable with a value — while the credentials service's URL **is** in its
  environment. That pair is what says the call had to be served rather than carried.
- **The call went to a provider.** The gateway's own `model call` lines for that execution are read for the
  ones carrying `route`, which the gateway emits **only** for a call it forwarded to a provider
  (`internal/gateway/forward.go`, `internal/gateway/log.go`), with their `serving_model`, their `priced_as`
  and the provider's own `reported_micros`.
- **The cost is the provider's.** `result.json`'s `cost.reported_usd`, `cost.route_by` and
  `cost.model_usd` — read from the runs bucket at the key the listing's own `run` ref gives, and checked
  against the run id this check launched — agree with the lines above, so the money charged is the figure
  the provider reported and not a price table's guess.
- **The service said so.** The credentials service's own audit line for the run (`credsvc: audit`,
  `internal/credsvc/audit.go`) carries this run, the purpose `forward`, the status `ok`, and the **name**,
  tier and purpose of the credential it served — never a value. That line is the service's record of the
  act, and it is what makes the row a reading rather than an inference.

**The command.** It is **one command**, run from the sandbox checkout at your own terminal:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check781.sh --sandbox <the sandbox repository checkout>
```

`--dry-run` makes every guard and prints every command it would run, calling nothing; `--help` prints the
header above. The script launches **one** sandbox run, follows it to a terminal state, and prints ONE block
on **stdout** headed `CHECK 781 RESULT`, ending `CHECK 781 RESULT END (exit N)`: exit **0** when every
criterion held, **1** when one did not or a guard stopped the run, **2** when the check could not measure —
a tool is missing, the checkout is not one, the bundle is missing, a read did not answer, or the run never
ended. Paste that block back for the row; a key the run never reached reads `FAIL — not reached`. The
block's keys are `fugaro-version`, `xtrace`, `agent-session`, `belong`, `installation`, `bundle`,
`run-launched`, `terminal`, `result-json`, `job-env`, `calls`, `charged`, `key-from-bundle`, `restore` and
`scratch-removed`.

**What it reads, and what it never reads.** Names, refs, counts, model IDs, purposes, tiers, statuses and
money: the bundle's name, the job's environment keys, the credential's name, the calls' own attributes. **No
credential value is read by any step**, and none can reach the block.

**What it does not put back.** The run's branch and the draft pull request it leaves are yours to decline
and delete; this check does not, and neither is it a change to the installation — it writes nothing. The
