## Check 630: the crossing, on a real installation — one pool per half, and the update that gets you there (a sandbox installation, project and repository, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **MC26** of
[docs/model-crafts/activation-plan.md](model-crafts/activation-plan.md) — its row for **630**, the third of
that task's five owner-run checks — and it answers the plan's third input: a pool's members must be served
by one half of a run, because a pool's order means nothing across the two. **No agent runs any step of it**,
and none can: it writes a pool on the owner's own installation and converges it with `fugaro update`.

**What it settles.**

- **The write door refuses a crossing pool, by name.** `fugaro accounts pool add <pool> <member> <member>`
  is handed the acceptance's own pair — one OpenRouter member and one Anthropic-key member, taken from the
  credentials the installation declares — and must refuse it with the **one sentence** ("name two pools, one
  per half") naming **both** members. The listing is read back afterwards: a refusal that wrote the pool is
  a finding in its own right, because that door (`internal/config`'s `ValidatePoolPaths`) is the one place a
  new member list is written through.
- **The published node's own read is the crossing's second door.** `fugaro project policy show --json` runs
  `projectpolicy.Decode`, which runs `config.ValidatePublishedPools`: a node that already carries a crossing
  pool is refused with the same sentence, naming the same two members. That is the door `doctor`, the
  runner's `Read`, the credentials service's per-call re-read and `update` all go through, and a node that
  crossed without being refused here is a finding.
- **`fugaro update` converges it.** Run from the checkout, with the config's own crossing pool read before
  and after: what was one pool is **two** — `<pool>-claude` and `<pool>-provider` — each carrying the members
  of its own path **in the order the crossed pool listed them**, and the node reading back with no crossing
  pool and a version that did not go down.
- **Both clauses this build does not hold are reported, not passed.** `fugaro validate` reads a
  repository's `fugaro.yaml` (its `--project-layer` is that repository's own layer, and a config's pools are
  not in it): the acceptance names it as the crossing's second door, and in this build it is not one — the
  row runs it, prints what it read, and names the door that is. And the plan's *"whose policy version the
  update moves to 8"* is the version **step** `migrateV8ToV9` — 8 is the version a node of that vintage
  starts from, and the chain is at **10** today (`internal/projectpolicy/version.go`) — so the section, the
  script and the row say the step's own name rather than a number that would read as this release's.


`--dry-run` makes every guard and prints every command it would run, calling nothing; `--help` prints the
header above. The script asks the write door for **one** pool, which must refuse it, and then runs
`fugaro update`, which is the acceptance's own verb. It prints ONE block on **stdout** headed

one did not or a guard stopped the run, **2** when the check could not measure — a tool is missing, the
checkout is not one, a read did not answer, or the update did not finish. Paste that block back for the row;
a key the run never reached reads `FAIL — not reached`.

is asked to declare), `CHECK630_OPENROUTER_MEMBER` and `CHECK630_ANTHROPIC_MEMBER` (the pair it hands it,
each defaulting to the first credential of that kind the installation declares),
`CHECK630_CLI_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (180), `CHECK630_DOCTOR_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (300),
`CHECK630_UPDATE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (1800), `CHECK630_DRY_RUN` and `CHECK630_KEEP_SCRATCH`.

## Check 632: convergence and the run in flight, on a real installation — one `fugaro update` over all four halves, and the run it does not disturb (a sandbox installation, project and repository, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **MC26** of
[docs/model-crafts/activation-plan.md](model-crafts/activation-plan.md) — its row for **632**, the last of
that task's five owner-run checks — and it is the plan's own last input: the four halves converge in **one
command**, and a run launched before it finishes undisturbed. **No agent runs any step of it**, and none can:
it updates the owner's own installation and launches a real run.

**What it settles.**

- **The installation is behind this CLI.** `fugaro doctor --json` carrying a check whose `fix` names
  `fugaro update` is the acceptance's own premise — an installation the update has something to converge. A
  doctor with no such check says it is already current, and the update then converges nothing; the row says
  which of the two it read, so the reading below is never mistaken for a convergence that had nothing to do.
- **What it held before, read only.** The policy node's version and its three blocks
  (`fugaro project policy show --json`), the coder craft's model (`fugaro craft ls --json`), the pools and
  their members (`fugaro accounts pool ls`) and the credentials and their serving paths
  (`fugaro accounts ls --json`).
- **One run is in flight when the update starts.** A sandbox run launched from the checkout with
  `fugaro run --json`, still going (`fugaro runs ls --json`) when `fugaro update` begins — the state the
  acceptance is about, and the state no run of this check may be asked to leave first.
- **The update converges, in one command.** `fugaro update` exits 0, its own output carries the **one**
  in-flight line (`N runs in flight: update waits for none and changes nothing they hold`) whose count is the
  runs this check knows are in flight, and **no line of it** sends the owner to another `fugaro` command — a
  release that shipped an operator step beside `update` is the HARD RULE's own failure.
- **The four halves converged, each read back with a read alone.** The coder craft's model; the node carrying
  its crafts blocks with a version that did not go down; no pool naming members of both halves (the listing
  and the config's own pools); and every credential with its type and serving path.
- **The run is undisturbed.** It reached a terminal state after the update, its ledger still accounts for the
  same run (`fugaro runs show --json`), its counters never went backwards (money, tokens and time), and its
  record (`result.json`, read at the key the listing's own ref gives) carries the same run id, task and
  repository with an outcome. That is the acceptance's *"the run it does not disturb"*, read as the three
  things a run holds: its ledger, its counters and its record.

**The command.** It is **one command**, run from the sandbox checkout at your own terminal:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check632.sh --sandbox <the sandbox repository checkout>
```

`--dry-run` makes every guard and prints every command it would run, calling nothing; `--help` prints the
header above. The script launches **one** sandbox run, runs `fugaro update` over the installation while that
run is in flight, and prints ONE block on **stdout** headed `CHECK 632 RESULT`, ending
`CHECK 632 RESULT END (exit N)`: exit **0** when every criterion held, **1** when one did not or a guard
stopped the run, **2** when the check could not measure — a tool is missing, the checkout is not one, a read
did not answer, the update did not finish, or the run never ended. Paste that block back for the row; a key
the run never reached reads `FAIL — not reached`.

**The knobs.** Every one of them is read from the environment and none of them is asked for:
`CHECK632_SANDBOX` and `CHECK632_PROJECT`, `CHECK632_TASK` and `CHECK632_RECIPE` (what the run is launched
with), `CHECK632_REGION` (us-east5), `CHECK632_LOG_VIEW`, `CHECK632_RUN_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (3600),
`CHECK632_POLL_SECONDS` (15), `CHECK632_CLI_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (180),
`CHECK632_DOCTOR_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (300), `CHECK632_LAUNCH_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (600),
`CHECK632_UPDATE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (1800), `CHECK632_DRY_RUN` and `CHECK632_KEEP_SCRATCH`.

**Reading the `CHECK 632 RESULT` block.** One block of `FACT <key>: PASS|FAIL|INFO — <what it read>` lines,
in this order, one per criterion above: `fugaro-version`, `xtrace`, `agent-session`, `belong`,
`installation`, `version-before`, `before`, `run-launched`, `run-in-flight`, `update`, `update-notes-runs`,
`no-operator-step`, `converge-model`, `converge-publish`, `converge-crossing`, `converge-key`,
`run-terminal`, `ledger-intact`, `counters-intact`, `record-intact`, `restore` and `scratch-removed`. A
`FAIL` under `run-launched` or `run-in-flight` means the update ran with no run to disturb, and the rows that
read the run below it read `FAIL — not reached`.

**What it reads, and what it never reads.** Names, members, paths, versions, counts, statuses, money, tokens,
durations and the words of the update's own note: the node's blocks and version, the crafts' models, the
pools' members and their order, the credentials' types and serving paths, the run's id, stage, ledger and
counters. **No credential value is read by any step**, and none can reach the block.

**What it does not put back.** The update is the acceptance's own convergence and is **not** undone: a config
or node the update converged stays converged, and the `restore` row names exactly what moved. The run's own
branch and the draft pull request it opens are yours to decline and delete. The scratch directory is removed
from the exit trap even on a failed assertion or a Ctrl-C. It costs one sandbox run and what its task spends,
plus the wall clock of the update.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** Its own automated proof is
`scripts/live-checks/check632_test.sh`, which drives every step of it against fake tools — a fake `fugaro`
and a fake `gcloud`, no cloud, no installation, no update and no run — and is run by `go test ./scripts`.

## Check 560: the installation renews its key by itself — one fire of the deployed Scheduler job (a sandbox installation holding a short-lived auto key, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **K7.4** of
[docs/licence-key-v2/implementation-plan.md](licence-key-v2/implementation-plan.md) — its row for **560**,
out of that plan's "Checks this plan takes (560–569)", on the owner's instruction of 2026-11-21 — and run on a
**sandbox** installation first. It answers **K4.2** with **K2.3** and **K2.4**, read end to end on a real
installation and from the outside only: the tick Terraform applies is the one that renews a key nobody is
watching, the key it renews is an auto one whose successor the licence server issues, and the installation ends
up holding that successor **beside** the key it replaces. It is the opposite half of `fugaro licence refresh`:
that command renews the key a person is watching, and this check measures the path where nobody is. **No agent
runs any step of it**, and none can: the fire writes the installation's own key, and `fugaro licence renew
--job` refuses an agent's session for that reason.

**What it settles.**

- **The tick is the one Terraform applies.** The Scheduler job `fugaro-licence-renew`, in the installation's
  Scheduler region, is there, is **ENABLED** (K4.2's module says it ships RUNNING, because a paused schedule is
  a licence that quietly stops renewing), and its target is Scheduler's own POST to the Cloud Run job's `:run`
  endpoint, authorised with an OAuth token of the installation's scheduler account. Its cron and time zone are
  printed and are **not** a FAIL: `23 4 * * *` UTC is the module's own pin, and a difference is drift the row
  shows rather than a licence the check calls broken.
- **The job is this installation's licence job.** `fugarolicence` in the installation's region carries the two
  `fugaro` labels, argv `licence renew --job`, the 600s timeout, no retries, the licence service account, and
  the two names K4.2's own preconditions pin (`FUGARO_PROJECT` is the Fugaro project doctor read,
  `FUGARO_GCP_PROJECT` the GCP project).
- **The premise of a renewal.** `fugaro licence status --json` in the sandbox reads the **project's** own key
  (source `project`, never a machine's: the job renews the project's and only the project's, D2137) with
  `renewal_mode: auto` — a manual key is checked and never renewed — and a state of active or grace. A
  **short-lived** auto key is what makes the renewal window open now; the window itself is not in that document,
  so a window that is not open is read where the job says it.
- **The fire, and the execution it starts.** One `gcloud scheduler jobs run` of that Scheduler job — the same
  call the daily tick makes — and then the newest execution of `fugarolicence` created at or after it, with its
  terminal condition. Nothing else in this check starts a Cloud Run execution, so an execution created after the
  call is that call's.
- **The renewal itself.** The job's own lines for that execution, read back with `gcloud logging read`
  filtered by the execution's own `run.googleapis.com/execution_name` (a line an earlier execution wrote is
  not this fire's answer):
  `checked: the licence server answered that key … is good` where a check was due, and `renewed: key
  <successor> is installed in project <name> beside the key it replaces (fugaro/licence.json)`. The successor's
  key **ID** is the support handle the specification says is not a secret, and it is the one thing about the
  key the block carries. A window that is not open is that same read: `nothing to do: key … is paid through …,
  its renewal window opens …` is a row that could **not be measured**, naming the short-lived key the check
  needs.
- **The state after.** `fugaro licence status --json` again: the term is **strictly later** than the premise's,
  the source is still the project's, the renewal mode still `auto`, the state still active or grace. The check
  record is reported and is not required to have moved — a window that opens between two checks renews without
  asking one, K4.1's order being the check first and the renewal after.

**The command.** It is **one command**, run at your own terminal:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check560.sh --sandbox <the checkout>
```

`--dry-run` makes every guard and prints every command it would run, calling nothing; `--help` prints the header
above. `--project`, `--region` and `--scheduler-region` default to what `fugaro doctor --json` and K4.2's module
name, so an unset shell runs it as written. `--project fugaro-prod` is refused unless `--production` is given, a
value naming `belong` is refused **by name**, and a coding agent's session is refused too. The check prints ONE
block on **stdout** headed `CHECK 560 RESULT`, ending `CHECK 560 RESULT END (exit N)`: exit **0** when every
criterion held, **1** when one did not, **2** when it could not measure — no `gcloud`, no `fugaro`, a key whose
`renewal_mode` is not auto, a renewal window that is not open. Paste the block back for the row; a key the run
never reached reads `FAIL — not reached`. The block's keys are `xtrace`, `agent-session`, `belong`, `sandbox`,
`project`, `scheduler`, `job`, `premise`, `execution`, `renewed`, `status`, `restore` and `scratch`.

**What it creates, and what it leaves behind.** ONE Cloud Run execution of the installation's own licence job —
one container run at the job's 600s ceiling, 1 vCPU and 512 MiB — which writes what the licence server issues:
the successor key and its secret version, in the installation's own project. **That write is the
installation's licence and is kept on purpose**; the `restore` row says so, and says the check wrote no object
of the runs bucket itself, read the licence object's bytes nowhere and deleted nothing at all. The scratch
directory is removed from the exit trap even on a failed assertion or a Ctrl-C.

**What it reads, and what it never prints.** No licence key and no renewal secret: names, IDs, states and terms
only. The licence bucket's object is not read at all — `licence status --json` carries no key — and the only
thing about the key in the block is its **ID**, which the specification calls a support handle.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** Its own automated proof is
`scripts/live-checks/check560_test.sh`, which drives every step of it against fake tools — a fake `gcloud`
serving the Scheduler job, the licence job, the fire, the execution and the job's own log lines — with no cloud
and no installation, and is run by `go test ./scripts`.

## Check 561: a revocation recorded at the next check, and an unreachable server revoking nothing (a sandbox installation whose key is auto, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **K7.4** of
[docs/licence-key-v2/implementation-plan.md](licence-key-v2/implementation-plan.md) — its row for **561** — and
run on a **sandbox** installation first. It answers **K2.6** with **K4.1** and **D2140**, from the outside: a
revocation the owner makes on the portal's operations screens (**P5.3**) is recorded at the next tick, and a
licence server that cannot be reached revokes **nothing**. The revocation itself is the owner's, made on the
page before the command; the check makes no call to the operations API and revokes nothing. **No agent runs any
step of it.**

**Two halves, one command each way.** A revoked key is not the good key the other half needs, so `--part
revoke` (the default) and `--part unreachable` are two runs, each with the owner's own change made **before**
it: `revoke` needs the key already revoked on the portal's operations screens, `unreachable` needs the licence
job's route to the licence server gone (D2140's block — the job ships no network switch of its own and the
server's address is a constant of the build, so this is a change at the network or at the server).

**What it settles.**

- **The premise, both halves.** `fugaro licence status --json` reads the project's own key, `revoked: false`,
  a state of active or grace, and a check record whose `key_id` is that key — the name the job's own line is
  held against.
- **`--part revoke`.** The tick's own line — read from the execution **this fire** started, filtered by its own
  `run.googleapis.com/execution_name`, so yesterday's answer cannot be read as this fire's — is `the licence
  server answered that key <id> is revoked: project <name> runs on Free from now on, nothing has been deleted,
  and a new key restores everything (fugaro licence set)`; a line naming a key the installation does **not**
  hold is a **FAIL**, because a revocation is about the key it names. After the tick the installation reads
  `revoked: true` with state **expired**, its tier, seats and `paid_through` **still readable** (D436's read-only: a revocation records an answer and deletes nothing), the
  installation's own key still installed, and the check record's status `revoked` about the same key.
- **`--part unreachable`.** The tick's own line is `note: the check of key <id> did not complete, so the key
  keeps its state and nothing was renewed (only an explicit answer revokes, D2140)`. After it: the state is the
  one read before the tick, `revoked` is still false, the **failure count is up**, the last-ok time has **not
  moved** (last-ok is when a check last reached the server, and it is what the 30-day warning counts from), and
  the record's status is `unreachable`. A `revoked: true` there, a state that moved, a count that did not
  move, a moved last-ok or a record that says anything else is a **FAIL** — each one is the failure D2140
  exists for.
- **The step the owner has not made** is never a silent FAIL: a tick that reached the server with the key still
  good, or a job that records no check at all, is a row that could **not be measured**, and its sentence names
  the step to make and run the check again.

**The command.** It is **one command per part**, run at your own terminal:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check561.sh --sandbox <the checkout>                       # the key is revoked on the operations screens first
bash scripts/live-checks/check561.sh --sandbox <the checkout> --part unreachable    # the route to the licence server is gone first
```

The `MANUAL:` line the block prints is the owner's own part, with the page or the change it names. `--dry-run`
makes every guard and prints every command it would run; `--help` prints the header above. `--project`,
`--region` and `--scheduler-region` default as Check 560's do; `--project fugaro-prod` is refused unless
`--production` is given, a value naming `belong` is refused **by name**, and a coding agent's session is refused
too. The block is headed `CHECK 561 RESULT`, ends `CHECK 561 RESULT END (exit N)`, and exits **0** when the
half's criteria held, **1** when one did not, **2** when a row could not be measured (the premise holds no key
the tick checked, the tick recorded no check, the key is manual or offline — a key that contacts no server can
never see a revocation — or the tick reached a server that was supposed to be gone). Its keys are `xtrace`,
`agent-session`, `belong`, `sandbox`, `project`, `scheduler`, `job`, `premise`, `manual`, `execution`, `answer`,
`state`, `restore` and `scratch`, plus a `warning` row when the installation's own D2140 window is open.

**What it creates, and what it leaves behind.** Its one write of any kind is the fire, which makes the
installation's own check and records the licence server's answer. Under `--part revoke` the installation is
**Free** until a key is installed again (`fugaro licence set` with the key the licence server issues in the
revoked one's place) and the revoked key is the owner's own test key; under `--part unreachable` the key was
never touched and the route is the owner's own change, theirs to put back. Either way the check deleted nothing,
wrote no object of the runs bucket itself, revoked nothing and read the licence object's bytes nowhere, and its
scratch directory goes with the exit trap.

**What it reads, and what it never prints.** No licence key and no renewal secret: the key's **ID**, states,
counts and times only. The licence bucket's object is never read — it holds every key — and a log line this
check does not recognise is counted and **not printed**: a line it cannot name is a line it cannot vouch for,
and the row names the `gcloud logging read` command instead.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** Its own automated proof is
`scripts/live-checks/check561_test.sh`, which drives both parts against fake tools — a fake `gcloud` for the
Scheduler job, the fire, the execution and the job's lines, and a fake `fugaro` answering `doctor --json` and
two `licence status --json` reads — with no cloud and no account, and is run by `go test ./scripts`.

## Check 562: the browser sign-in, and the callback whose `state` is not the flow's own (the staging site first, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **K7.4** of
[docs/licence-key-v2/implementation-plan.md](licence-key-v2/implementation-plan.md) — its row for **562** — and
run on **staging** first. It answers **K3.3** and **K2.4**: `fugaro licence login` opens the licence site, takes
ONE callback on a listener bound to the literal `127.0.0.1`, exchanges the code for a key and installs it; and a
callback whose `state` is not the flow's own is refused **and does not end the flow** (RFC 8252 §7.3). **No
agent runs any step of it**: the browser half is a person's own account.

**What it settles.**

- **The origin is the licence site.** One read carries no sign-in at all: `GET <site>/cli/authorize` with no
  query answers **403** with the site's own refusal sentence ("This sign-in could not be verified. …"), which is
  what says the host in front of the check is the licence site and not a marketing page. Anything else and every
  row below is off-target, so it is a row the check could **not** measure.
- **The address the CLI prints.** `<site>/cli/authorize` over **https**, carrying the flow's own `state` and a
  PKCE S256 `code_challenge`, with a callback of `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback` — the literal loopback and
  the port the kernel gave. The site the CLI talks to is a **constant** of the build
  (`licenceServerURL = "https://keys.fugaro.dev"` in `ee/register/licence.go`), which nothing can repoint: `--site`
  only holds that address against the origin you expect, it never moves the CLI.
- **The wrong-`state` refusal.** `GET <callback>?state=…&code=…` with values the **check made up** — so nothing
  a person's sign-in holds ever travels — answers **400** with the page headed "This is not the sign-in's own
  callback", and the login command is **still running** afterwards. A **200**, or a login that ended, is a
  **FAIL**: a local process that guessed the port must not be able to spend the person's sign-in.
- **The sign-in itself.** One `MANUAL:` line says what to do in the browser; the command then ends, and
  `fugaro licence status --json` in the checkout reads `source: project` with a non-empty `tier` and
  `renewal_mode` and a state of active or grace — the key the sign-in installed is the installation's own
  licence. No key is read: the status document carries none, and no line of the command's output may carry a
  key-shaped string (that check is a row of its own).

**The command.** It is **one command**, run at your own terminal:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check562.sh --sandbox <the checkout>
```

`--site` names the origin when the deployment is not the CLI's own constant; `--dry-run` makes every guard and
prints every command it would run, calling nothing; `--help` prints the header above. `--project fugaro-prod`
is refused unless `--production` is given, a value naming `belong` is refused **by name**, and a coding agent's
session is refused too. The block is headed `CHECK 562 RESULT`, ends `CHECK 562 RESULT END (exit N)`, and exits
**0** when every criterion held, **1** when the wrong-state callback was accepted or ended the flow, **2** when
it could not measure — the origin is not the licence site, the installation has no Firebase project, the browser
sign-in was not finished, or `licence status` does not answer. Its keys are `xtrace`, `agent-session`, `belong`,
`project`, `site`, `sandbox`, `address`, `wrong-state`, `signin`, `restore` and `scratch`.

**What it creates, and what it leaves behind.** The key the sign-in installs — this installation's own licence —
and nothing else: every other call is a read, plus the callback the check makes up, which is refused. **The key
is kept on purpose**: it is the object of the whole check, and a check does not delete a person's licence. The
scratch directory is removed from the exit trap, and the login process is killed if the check ends before it
does.

**What it reads, and what it never prints.** No licence key, no renewal secret and no authorize code, in whole
or in part. The `state` and `code` the check sends are its own and non-secret; the CLI prints no code at all;
and the block reads only `source`, `tier`, `state` and `renewal_mode`.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** Its own automated proof is
`scripts/live-checks/check562_test.sh`, which drives every step against fakes — a fake `curl` serving the site's
own 403 and the loopback refusal page, and a fake `fugaro` whose `licence login` prints an authorize address and
holds a listener — with no cloud and no site, and is run by `go test ./scripts`.

## Check 563: the device code, from a machine with no browser (the staging site first, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **K7.4** of
[docs/licence-key-v2/implementation-plan.md](licence-key-v2/implementation-plan.md) — its row for **563** — and
run on **staging** first. It answers **K3.3**'s device half: a machine that cannot open a browser prints an
address and a short code and waits, a person opens the address on **any** machine that has one, signs in and
types the code, and the terminal is signed in with no browser ever opening on it. **No agent runs any step of
it.**

**Two halves, one command each way.** An approved code is not an expired one, so `--approve` (the default)
measures the sign-in and `--expiry` measures the deadline and the poll's stop. The half a run did not take reads
`INFO — not this run's half`.

**What it settles.**

- **The address.** The site's own approve page, `<site>/cli/device`, over https, printed by the command — and the
  block says **no browser was opened on this machine**, which is the whole point of the flow.
- **The code.** Eight characters of K2.4's alphabet — `A`–`H`, `J`–`N`, `P`–`Z` and `2`–`9`, so **no `I`, no
  `O`, no `0` and no `1`** — grouped four and four with one `-`, and the command's own line names its life:
  `The code is worth 10m0s.`
- **`--approve`.** One `MANUAL:` line says to open the address on any machine with a browser, sign in, type the
  code and pick the licence; the login then ends **0** and `fugaro licence status --json` reads `source:
  project` with a non-empty `tier` and a state of active or grace — the sign-in installed the installation's own
  key. The key is never read or printed.
- **`--expiry`.** Nothing is approved: the check waits out the code's ten minutes and holds that the login ended
  with the client's own refusal, `the sign-in was not finished before its code expired`, that the installation's
  licence is **unchanged** from the read taken before the flow started, and that the address and code held above
  were live while it waited. This is the half that proves the code is worth ten minutes and that the poll
  **stops** at the expiry rather than hanging.

**The command.** It is **one command per half**, run at your own terminal:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check563.sh --sandbox <the checkout>            # approve the code from a browser elsewhere
bash scripts/live-checks/check563.sh --sandbox <the checkout> --expiry   # approve nothing; wait the code out
```

`--site` names the origin when the deployment is not the CLI's own constant; `--wait` bounds the sign-in;
`--dry-run` makes every guard and prints every command it would run, calling nothing; `--help` prints the header
above. The project under test is the checkout's own installation — this check has **no `--project` flag**, and
reads `fugaro doctor --json`'s `project.gcp_project` — so an installation whose project is `fugaro-prod` is
refused unless `--production` is given; a value naming `belong` is refused **by name**, and a coding agent's
session is refused too. The block is headed `CHECK 563 RESULT`, ends
`CHECK 563 RESULT END (exit N)`, and exits **0** when the half's criteria held, **1** when one did not, **2**
when it could not measure — no approve page, an installation with no Firebase project, a sign-in not finished
inside `--wait`. Its keys are `xtrace`, `agent-session`, `belong`, `project`, `site`, `sandbox`, `address`,
`code`, `signin`, `expiry`, `restore` and `scratch`.

**What it creates, and what it leaves behind.** Under `--approve`, the key `fugaro licence login` installs — the
installation's own licence, written to the project's store and the renewal secret to its own container (D2137) —
**kept on purpose**. Under `--expiry`, nothing at all: the flow writes nothing and the row says so. Either way
the scratch directory goes from the exit trap, and the background login with it.

**What it reads, and what it never prints.** No licence key, no renewal secret and no device token: the address,
the **user code** (K2.4's own short code, which the site's page asks a person to type and is not a secret), and
`source`, `tier`, `state` — `licence status --json` carries no key.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** Its own automated proof is
`scripts/live-checks/check563_test.sh`, which drives both halves against a fake `fugaro` whose
`licence login --device` prints an address and a code and then ends approved or expired — no browser, no site
and no account — and is run by `go test ./scripts`.

## Check 564: a Paddle sandbox purchase, its renewal and its refund, end to end (a throwaway installation and a staging deployment, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **K7.4** of
[docs/licence-key-v2/implementation-plan.md](licence-key-v2/implementation-plan.md) — its row for **564** — and
run on **staging** first. It answers **K2.5**: Paddle's events reach v1 and mean what the licence says they
mean. A card buys a licence in the Paddle **sandbox**, the licence is granted, the term renews, and a refund
withdraws the **whole** licence rather than merely the key the event happened to name (**D2147**) — the row a
refund stream gets wrong most often, and the reason the check exists. Two rows are about the installation as
much as the portal: after the refund `fugaro licence status --json` must read `revoked: true` with the tier and
the seats **still readable** and the key **still installed**, because a withdrawal deletes nothing
(**D436**). **The Paddle sandbox account is subscriptions S8.5's**, an owner-run task: without it the check
**refuses at once, naming it**, and builds the sandbox catalogue first. **No agent runs any step of it.**

**What it settles.**

- **The origin is the API's.** One read carries no sign-in: `GET /api/workspaces` answers **401
  `unauthenticated`**, which is what says the origin in front of the check is the portal's API and not a
  marketing page or somebody else's host.
- **The sandbox account.** `GET /prices?status=active` against `https://sandbox-api.paddle.com` is printed as a
  count of active prices and the first price id — **never the key**, which travels in a `0600` curl config file
  and reaches neither a command line nor the block. A **401** or a **403** is a row that could **not be
  measured**, and its sentence names S8.5.
- **The purchase.** `POST /api/checkout` with your token, the workspace and the licence terms you accepted
  answers **201** with a Paddle `transaction_id`, and that transaction is read back from the **SANDBOX**
  (`GET /transactions/{id}`): a transaction the sandbox does not hold was minted by a **LIVE** merchant, which
  is the finding that row exists for.
- **The entitlement.** The purchase appears at `GET /api/entitlements` for the workspace with source `purchase`
  and status `active`, and the workspace's own mirror (`GET /api/workspaces/{workspace}/subscription`) names
  Paddle's subscription. A purchase whose workspace names none is a **FAIL**.
- **The binding.** A purchase mints no key of its own (**F25**): it is a licence of the **account** you sign in
  as. So the check asks for **ONE browser sign-in** in the middle of the run — `fugaro licence login` in the
  sandbox, as the account that bought — and holds the installation's own read against the purchase's own tier.
  A key of the per-machine store rather than the project's own is a **FAIL**; a sign-in for a licence whose
  tier is not the purchase's is a row that could **not be measured** (nothing below it would be about this
  purchase). The key is never read.
- **The renewal.** Paddle's own period end (`GET /subscriptions/{id}`) and the entitlement's own end **agree**,
  and after you bill the renewal the term has **moved**. A renewal that did not move the term is a row that
  could **not be measured** rather than a finding, because it may mean the sandbox did not bill. The check
  fires the deployed Scheduler job `fugaro-licence-renew` through `gcloud scheduler jobs run` to make the
  installation re-read its licence, and it fires it in the job's **own** location: Scheduler is not offered in
  every Cloud Run region (**K4.2**), so the job's location is read from the installation's project (and
  `--scheduler-region` names it when there is nothing to read) rather than taken to be the installation's own
  region. A job in no location the project serves, or a fire that fails, is a row that could **not be
  measured**, and the check says so **before** anything is bought.
- **The refund.** The entitlement reads **`revoked`** — every key it ever minted, and not only the key the event
  named (**D2147**, **F29**) — and it is the portal's own record that says so.
- **The tick after the refund.** The installation hears about a withdrawal only from its **own** check
  (**K4.1**): the portal's record and the local store say nothing to it until then. So after the refund the
  check fires `fugaro-licence-renew` **once more** and waits for a completed execution of the Cloud Run job
  `fugarolicence` that was **created after that fire** — an execution that ran earlier is never read as this
  fire's answer, and a tick whose fire started no execution is a row that could **not be measured**.
- **The installation.** `fugaro licence status --json` in the sandbox reads `revoked: true` with
  `last_check.status` `revoked` and a `last_check.at` **after** the instant the check saw the refund land at the
  portal, while the tier, the seats and the key itself are **still there** (D436). A key still **serving** after
  the refund is the **FAIL**; an installation that has recorded **no check since the refund** has not heard
  about the withdrawal, which is a row that could **not be measured** — never a FAIL, however the local store
  reads.

**The command.** It is **one command**, run at your own terminal:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check564.sh --sandbox <the checkout> --workspace-id <the portal workspace> \
  --token-file <a 0600 file holding your ID token> \
  --paddle-key-file <a 0600 file holding the Paddle SANDBOX API key S8.5 minted>
```

`--workspace-id` names the portal workspace the purchase is for (one workspace has one subscription, D2192) and is
required; `--api` names the portal's own origin, `--terms` the licence terms **version** you accepted and
`--scheduler-region` the location the licence renewal Scheduler job lives in (read from the installation's
project when it is not given, since Scheduler does not serve every Cloud Run region); `--dry-run` makes every guard and prints every
command it would run, calling nothing; `--help` prints the header above. The **LIVE** Paddle host is refused
**by name** — no live purchase is ever made — a value naming `fugaro-prod`, and the GCP project the
installation's own `fugaro doctor` names, are refused unless `--production` is given, a value naming `belong`
is refused by name, and a coding agent's session is refused too. The block is headed
`CHECK 564 RESULT`, ends `CHECK 564 RESULT END (exit N)`, and exits **0** when every criterion held, **1** when
one did not, **2** when it could not measure — a token file that is not `0600`, the sandbox account missing or
refusing its key, a transaction the sandbox does not hold, a renewal the sandbox did not bill, a sign-in that
did not come back, a renewal job in no location the project serves or a fire that failed, and an installation
that has recorded no check since the refund. Its keys are
`xtrace`, `agent-session`, `belong`, `project`, `paddle-sandbox`, `api`, `token`, `sandbox`, `scheduler`,
`checkout`, `entitlement`, `bind`, `renewal`, `refund`, `tick`, `install`, `restore` and `scratch`.

**What it creates, and what it leaves behind.** A Paddle **SANDBOX** transaction, its subscription and its
refund — real objects in the sandbox and nothing at all in the live merchant — plus one withdrawn entitlement in
the portal deployment you point at, and one revoked key in the throwaway installation. The `restore` row names
each by id rather than hiding it: the sandbox objects and the withdrawn entitlement are **left as they are**
(they are the sandbox's), and the revoked key is replaced by the `MANUAL:` line the block prints — a fresh key
for the installation, which is the owner's own step. The scratch directory is removed from the exit trap.

**What it reads, and what it never prints.** No Paddle API key, no ID token and no licence key: ids, statuses,
counts, amounts and dates only. The ID token travels in a `0600` curl config file and the Paddle key in a `0600`
file of its own; neither reaches a command line or the block.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** Its own automated proof is
`scripts/live-checks/check564_test.sh`, which drives every step against fakes — a fake `curl` over the portal's
API and the Paddle sandbox API, a fake `fugaro` (its `licence login` prints an address; its `licence status
--json` holds a check the case places before or after the refund) and a fake `gcloud` (the Scheduler job in a
location the installation's region is not, both fires, and the licence job's executions, the fire's own and an
older one) — with no cloud, no purchase and no account, and is run by `go test ./scripts`.

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **P9.4** of

answers the reconciliation's **F25/D2197**, **D2205**, **D2196** and **D2200/K3.4**: a purchase creates an
entitlement and never a key, so a customer pays before their project exists and the term runs from the
payment; binding needs an installation and is refused rather than done unchecked; binding is the act that

## Check 571: every identity that reaches signing in the project, printed as a census (the staging project first, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **P9.4** of
[docs/portal/implementation-plan.md](portal/implementation-plan.md) — its row for **571** — and run on
**staging** first, which is the plan's **P0.6**. It is the row of the reconciliation's **F18/D2194**: the
portal lives in **one** project and not a dedicated one, round 1 of that review found what that costs, and
the owner re-asked on 2026-11-12 and **kept** the one project with those facts in hand. This check is the
half that remains: it prints the list, so the accepted risk is one the owner **reads** rather than one they
were told about once. **No agent runs any step of it**; it reads IAM policies with your own credential.

**What it settles.**

- **The census.** Every binding in the project's IAM policy whose role carries a permission that reaches
  signing — `useToSign`, `signBlob`, `actAs`, `getAccessToken`, `run.services.update`, the store's
  entities, a Hosting site's update, `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy` — is printed, one line per
  binding, above the block, beside a row that counts it. **Nothing in the census is a FAIL**: it is
  D2194's accepted exposure, and printing it is the whole point. The two examples the review found are
  named in the section rather than assumed: Firebase Hosting's IAM is project-wide, so the website's CI
  deployer can replace the portal's JavaScript and with it take a fresh operations sign-in and mint; and a
  project-level `datastore.user` or `run.services.update` reaches signing too.
- **The minter's invokers.** Exactly **one**, the API's account — D2194's own fence, and the fence D450(a)
  rests on — and never `allUsers`.
- **The signing ring.** The signer role on the ring holds exactly the minter's account, and **no other
  member** sits on a role that can sign: a second identity there signs licence keys for workspaces it does
  not serve.
- **The handover ring.** The sealer role holds exactly the API's account and no other member: a second
  identity there opens every sealed reveal in the store (**D2182**).
- **The two accounts' own policies** are **empty**. `actAs` on the minter's account is impersonating the
  one identity that signs; `actAs` on the API's is wearing the identity the minter trusts.

**The command.** It is **one command**, run at your own terminal:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check571.sh --project fugaro-staging
```

`--environment staging|production` picks which key id this deployment signed for and so which ring's policy
is read (production for `fugaro-prod`, staging otherwise); `--minter-service`, `--minter-account`,
`--api-service`, `--api-account`, `--ring`, `--signer-role`, `--handover-ring` and `--handover-role`
default to `ee/keyservice/terraform/services/variables.tf`'s own names, so an unset shell runs it as
written. `--dry-run` makes every guard and prints every command it would run; `--help` prints the header
above. `--project` is refused for `fugaro-prod` unless `--production` is given, a value naming `belong` is
refused by name, and a coding agent's session is refused too. The check prints the census and ONE block on
**stdout** headed `CHECK 571 RESULT`: exit **0** when every reading held, **1** when one did not — a second
invoker, a second member where the plan states one — and **2** when it could not measure (no `gcloud`, or
an account that cannot read the project's policies). The block's keys are `gcloud`, `xtrace`,
`agent-session`, `project`, `belong`, `census`, `invokers`, `signer`, `handover`, `actas`, `restore` and
`scratch`.

**What it reads, and what it never prints.** A policy read here is a list of **names** — addresses, service
accounts, roles. No permission is asked for, no secret is read, no key material is touched and no token is
minted: this check **is** the list, and a list of names is what the owner pastes back.

**What it leaves behind.** Nothing: every call is a `get-iam-policy`, a `describe` or a `list`, and the
`restore` row says so. The scratch directory is removed from the exit trap even on a failed assertion or a
Ctrl-C.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** Its own automated proof is
`scripts/live-checks/check571_test.sh`, which drives every step of it against a fake `gcloud` — no cloud
and no project — and is run by `go test ./scripts`.

## Check 573: a redelivered sandbox event, a replayed one and the five-minute window (the staging deployment first, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **P9.4** of
[docs/portal/implementation-plan.md](portal/implementation-plan.md) — its row for **573** — and run on
**staging** first, which is the plan's **P0.6**. It answers the reconciliation's **F16/D2192** and F16's
window: a delivery is verified, then stored, then processed; a redelivery of an event the ledger already
holds does not unmake it nor is it applied twice; and `VerifyDelivery` (`ee/keyservice/paddleevents.go`)
refuses a delivery whose own `ts` is more than five minutes (`DeliveryWindow`) from the service's clock,
while a body that failed verification never reaches the store at all. **No agent runs any step of it**, and
none should: the check holds the deployment's sandbox webhook secret and posts signed deliveries at it.

**How it makes a redelivery happen.** Paddle sandbox cannot be made to redeliver on command, so the check
signs its own deliveries: it takes the deployment's sandbox webhook secret from the file you hand it,
writes two Paddle-shaped `transaction.completed` bodies, and signs each the way Paddle does — HMAC-SHA256
of `ts:<body>` under that secret — then posts them at the webhook route. Every id it uses carries the
instant this run started, so a second run's deliveries are its own events and not the first run's.

**What it settles.**

- **The ledger it compares against.** `GET /api/ops/events?state=parked`, read with the operations
  member's own token, is read **before** anything is delivered. A body whose transaction did not begin with
  a checkout this API created is **parked** there (F15); an invented transaction is exactly that, so
  parking is the state the check's own events have.
- **The delivery.** Body A, signed with a `ts` of now, answers `200` with no body, and the queue then holds
  exactly **one** record for A, in state `parked`.
- **The redelivery (D2192).** The same bytes and the **same signature** again — one second later, so the
  two instants are told apart — answer `200` with no body, and the queue still holds exactly **one** record
  for A: its **state did not move**, and its `received_at` did. One record and an unchanged state is the
  whole of what "the ledger is unchanged" means here.
- **The window.** Body B, signed with a `ts` half an hour old, answers the same `200` with no body that a
  forger gets (§5.2), and the queue holds **no record for B at all** — the difference a refused delivery
  makes, because it never reaches the store.
- **The control that makes that reading the window's and not the signature's.** The **same body B** signed
  with a `ts` of now is stored, and the queue then holds exactly one record for it. Same body, same secret,
  same scheme: the only difference between the two deliveries is the age of the timestamps, so the
  five-minute window is what refused the first.
- **The origin is the API's.** `GET /api/workspaces` with no sign-in answers `401 unauthenticated`.

**The command, and the one secret it needs.** It is **one command**, run at your own terminal, and it needs
a file only you can write — the deployment's sandbox webhook secret, whose name P1.5's variables give as
`fugaro-portal-paddle-webhook-secret`:

```sh
gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret=fugaro-portal-paddle-webhook-secret \
  --project=fugaro-staging > /tmp/paddle-webhook-secret && chmod 600 /tmp/paddle-webhook-secret

bash scripts/live-checks/check573.sh --project fugaro-staging \
  --token-file <a 0600 file holding the operations member's ID token> \
  --webhook-secret-file /tmp/paddle-webhook-secret
```

That `gcloud` line is **yours** and is the only place the secret is read: the check itself runs no `gcloud`
and no `fugaro`. `--dry-run` makes every guard and prints every command it would run; `--help` prints the
header above. `--project` is refused for `fugaro-prod` unless `--production` is given, a value naming
`belong` is refused by name, and a coding agent's session is refused too. The check prints ONE block on
**stdout** headed `CHECK 573 RESULT`: exit **0** when every criterion held, **1** when one did not — a
ledger that moved under a redelivery, a stale delivery that was stored — and **2** when it could not
measure (a secret file that is not 0600, a token that is not an operations member's, a body this service
parked as something else). Paste the block back for the row; a key the run never reached reads `FAIL — not
reached`. The block's keys are `xtrace`, `agent-session`, `project`, `belong`, `api`, `token`, `secret`,
`queue`, `delivery`, `redelivery`, `window`, `replay`, `restore` and `scratch`.

**What it leaves behind, and what it does not.** **Two parked events per run**, one for A and one for B,
whose ids the `restore` row names: they are the check's own evidence and are left in the operations queue
on purpose. Ending one is a WRITE with a sign-in from the last five minutes, which the check does not make
on your behalf — `POST /api/ops/events/resolutions` with `{"id":"<id>","decision":"dismiss"}` — so parse
the two ids from the `restore` row and dismiss them when you are done reading them. The scratch directory,
which holds the signature configs and the two bodies, is removed from the exit trap even on a failed
assertion or a Ctrl-C.

**What it never prints.** Not the webhook secret, not one byte of a signature over a body, and not the ID
token. The secret is read from its file into `python3`'s own stdin, never onto a command line; each
signature travels in a `0600` curl config file; and the block carries names and numbers only — event ids
this check minted, states, a received instant, an HTTP status. It costs nothing billable.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** Its own automated proof is
`scripts/live-checks/check573_test.sh`, which drives every step of it against a fake `curl` — no cloud, no
project and no secret — and is run by `go test ./scripts`.

## Check 574: a staging-signed key in a production build (the staging deployment and a throwaway installation, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **P9.4** of
[docs/portal/implementation-plan.md](portal/implementation-plan.md) — its row for **574** — and run on
**staging** first, which is the plan's **P0.6**. It answers the reconciliation's **F17/D459** as the code
holds it: a verifier trusts the key ids of **one** environment, so a staging-signed licence key is refused
by a production build for its **id** alone — before the signature is read, before the claim set is decoded
and before anything is written (`ee/licence/key.go`'s first rule, and `ErrUnknownKeyID`). **No agent runs
any step of it**: it runs the released CLI against a real keyring and would install a key if the build were
wrong.

**Why the build is the released CLI.** The production build this check drives is the released `fugaro`, the
verifier a person's own installation really runs (`ee/register`'s `licenceRing`, the ring `licence set` and
`licence status` both verify with). Its ring is empty in a build of P9.4 and stays empty until the release that
creates the renewal secret container publishes it (K4.2; the production half itself is published in
`ee/licence/keys/production.pub`, S2.9) — which is why every key is refused by its id today, and why
the check **reads the state of that ring rather than assuming it**.

**What it settles.**

- **The key.** The file you hand it is one line and mode `0600`, and it decodes here, without the build: a
  v1 key whose `kid` is the staging id the ring below holds, with its tier, kind, renewal mode, term and
  its renewal secret's digest **named**. The key's text is never printed.
- **The ring.** `--project`'s signing key for that id — `ASYMMETRIC_SIGN`, `EC_SIGN_ED25519`, at least one
  ENABLED version (`ee/keyservice/terraform/keyring`) — which is the key this staging key was signed with
  and the public half a production build must **not** hold. `--project` is the project the key service is
  deployed in (P1.5, one project per environment), never the installation's.
- **The refusal.** The released build, handed the key the way a console hands one to the CLI it spawns
  (`FUGARO_LICENCE_KEY`, never a word on a command line), refuses it: `fugaro licence status --json`
  answers the verifier's own refusal — `licence: the key id is not in the keyring`, inside the sentence
  about `fugaro/licence.json` — and `fugaro licence set --file`, the one command here that **could** install
  a key, refuses it too, with `the key was not accepted, and nothing was written: …`. Both sentences carry
  the id's sentinel, which is the row.
- **The control, and what it says about the ring.** The same key with its `kid` rewritten to the **other**
  environment's id re-encodes the payload and so breaks the signature over its raw bytes. Refused for the
  **signature** means the ring holds that id, so the fence the refusal above rests on is the **id** and not
  an empty ring; refused for the **id** again means the ring holds neither, so today's refusal cannot be
  told apart from a ring that refuses everything. The row says **which of the two** this deployment is in
  rather than picking the convenient one.
- **Nothing was written.** The installation's own licence is read before and after and the two reads have
  to be the **same**. The check refuses a checkout whose licence does not read free, because the row it
  drives is `licence set`: on a correct build that command stops before its first write, and a working
  installation's licence is not what this check is for.
- **The digest is not a fence here**, and the block says so rather than leans on it: `licenceSecretMatches`
  (`ee/register/licence.go`) answers true whenever no secret was read, so a build that wrongly held this id
  would write line 1 alone. That is what the `before`/`after` pair exists for.

**The command.** It is **one command**, run at your own terminal:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check574.sh --project fugaro-staging \
  --sandbox <a throwaway installation's checkout, its licence free> \
  --key-file <a 0600 file holding one line: the staging-signed key>
```

The key is an artifact you produce — a key minted by the staging portal for a workspace you own, written to
a file with no trailing comment and nothing else on the line. `--fugaro` names the released build (PATH by
default); `--location`, `--ring`, `--kms-key` and `--other-key-id` default to
`ee/keyservice/terraform/keyring`'s own spellings. `--dry-run` makes every guard and prints every command it
would run; `--help` prints the header above. `--project` is refused for `fugaro-prod` unless `--production`
is given, a value naming `belong` is refused by name, and a coding agent's session is refused too. The
check prints ONE block on **stdout** headed `CHECK 574 RESULT`: exit **0** when every criterion held, **1**
when one did not — a build that **accepted** the staging key, one that refused it for something other than
its id, an installation whose licence moved — and **2** when it could not measure (a key file that is not
0600 or not one line, a ring the project does not hold, a checkout that is not an installation's or whose
licence is not free). Paste the block back for the row; a key the run never reached reads `FAIL — not
reached`. The block's keys are `xtrace`, `agent-session`, `project`, `belong`, `ambient`, `gcloud`, `ring`,
`key`, `sandbox`, `version`, `before`, `refusal`, `install`, `control`, `after`, `restore` and `scratch`.

**What it reads, and what it never prints.** Not the licence key's text, not its signature and not one byte
of the payload as it arrived. The key is read from its file into this shell and handed to the one child that
needs it as a variable in **that child's own environment** — never as a word on a command line, where `ps`
would show it — and the CLI takes that variable out of its environment as its first step
(`ee/licence/store.go`, F41). The block carries names and numbers only: the key id, the claims, the ring,
states and exit codes.

**What it leaves behind.** Nothing, on a correct build: three `gcloud` reads and four CLI runs, of which
the only one that is not a read is `licence set`, and it writes nothing. The scratch directory — the check's
copy of the rewritten key and the tools' output — is removed from the exit trap even on a failed assertion
or a Ctrl-C.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** Its own automated proof is
`scripts/live-checks/check574_test.sh`, which drives every step of it against fake `gcloud` and `fugaro`
binaries — no cloud, no project and no key — and is run by `go test ./scripts`.

## Check 575: a staging reseller's month — the accrual, the statement's mail and the refusal over the limit (the staging deployment first, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **P9.4** of
[docs/portal/implementation-plan.md](portal/implementation-plan.md) — its row for **575** — and run on
**staging** first, which is the plan's **P0.6**. It answers **D2189** against P6.2 and P6.3 as the deployed
portal runs them: a reseller's accrual is days × seats × the wholesale rate; a sale that would pass the
credit limit operations set is refused with `over_credit_limit`; the month's statement carries one line per
customer and the sum of the part of each term inside a UTC month; and the run that issues and mails it is
P1.5's Cloud Scheduler job, with F33's OIDC token and `api_statements.go`'s own line for what the run did.
**No agent runs any step of it**: it signs in as a reseller, fires the statement job and reads a real
reseller's money.

**What it settles.**

- **The origin is the API's.** `GET /api/workspaces` with no sign-in answers `401 unauthenticated`.
- **The sign-in is a reseller's.** The token's provider has to be an SSO one (`google.com` or
  `microsoft.com`): a reseller organisation's members sign in that way and an email-link account is refused
  at its routes (that refusal is **Check 572**'s row, and this check is the other side of the same rule), so
  a token of the other kind would make every row below say nothing about a reseller.
- **The terms.** `GET /api/resellers/terms` gives the credit limit and the wholesale price per row that
  operations set; they are what the sale below is composed against, and a row this reseller is not priced
  for is a row it cannot sell (`resellers.schema.json`).
- **The customers and their keys.** `GET /api/resellers/customers` and `GET
  /api/resellers/customers/{id}/keys` give one customer and the newest key it holds, which is bound to the
  Firebase project the sale below is composed for. **F5** is why this is all of the key a reseller sees:
  metadata and never a key.
- **The workspace the sale names.** The key's own `workspace_id` is the Firebase **project** id it is bound
  to (TN2), while the mint reads the sale's `workspace_id` as a portal workspace **document** id
  (`mintResellerLicence` loads `workspaces/{workspace_id}`; a workspace that is not there, or is another
  organisation's, is answered `404 not_found` **before** anything is compared against the credit limit). No
  reseller route answers a portal workspace id, so the check reads the operations area's own list of the
  customer's workspaces (`GET /api/ops/workspaces?organisation_id={customer}`) and takes the one whose
  `project_id` is the key's project id. That read needs an account that is a member of the operations
  organisation — on staging the owner's own is, seeded by P0.5 — and it writes the operations log's own line
  (`D456`), so `--workspace-id` names the workspace instead for a token that is a reseller's and nothing
  else.
- **The job.** `gcloud scheduler jobs describe` reads P1.5's monthly statement job: its method and path, the
  account its OIDC token is minted for, the audience that token carries, and whether the deployment has
  lifted the pause the apply creates it under. Those are held against the API revision's **own**
  `FUGARO_SCHEDULER_ACCOUNT` and `FUGARO_SCHEDULER_AUDIENCE`, which is the comparison
  `ee/keyservice/portalauth.go`'s `SchedulerVerifier` makes: an audience that is the job's own target URI is
  the misconfiguration `scheduler.tf` documents, and the row names it as that.
- **The run and its mail.** The check **fires** that job and then reads the API's own log line for it —
  `the statement run as <account> issued N statement(s) and mailed M message(s)`, which is what
  `api_statements.go` says an operator reads of a run, since the run route answers `204` with no body. The
  account in that line has to be the job's own token's, which is what makes the line **this** fire's and not
  an earlier run's; the counts are the run's own.
- **The month.** `GET /api/statements` gives the reseller's newest statement, held to the arithmetic the
  schema promises: every line positive, the lines' sum equal to the statement's `accrued_micros`, `state`
  following the two amounts, the month a whole UTC month that is **over**, and every line a customer this
  reseller holds. That is the accrual read as the month it was billed in rather than recomputed here.
- **The refused sale.** `POST /api/resellers/customers/{id}/keys`, naming the workspace resolved above, a
  row, a seat count and a span whose cost is **strictly greater than the whole credit limit**, so that no
  state of the accrual can admit it, has to answer `409 over_credit_limit` with the sentence "This sale
  would pass the credit limit operations set for this reseller. The licences it already holds are
  unchanged." The customer's keys are read before and after it: the sentence's own claim, **measured**
  rather than believed. A `404 not_found` here is the workspace the sale named and not the ceiling — the
  row says so and names `--workspace-id`.

**What creates, and what it does not.** Firing P1.5's job is the **one** act here, and it is the act the
deployment does by itself once a month (the first of the month, 03:00 UTC). The run is idempotent per month
(`issueStatement` reads a month it already holds), so a second fire states no month twice, and a month it
does state is mailed to that reseller's owners — on staging through the merchant's and the mail provider's
test modes (P0.2). **If the deployment's job is still PAUSED** (the apply creates it paused), the check
fires it by hand and says so, and the pause is a row that could **not be measured** naming
`statements_paused=false` rather than a FAIL: a job left paused is a month nobody is billed for, which is
worth knowing and is not this check's criterion. Beside the fire, the read of the customer's workspaces
writes the operations log's own line for it (`D456`; `--workspace-id` skips even that), which is the
deployment's record of a read rather than a thing this check leaves behind. The refused sale writes
nothing, and the check writes no customer, no term and no licence of its own.

**The command.** It is **one command**, run at your own terminal:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check575.sh --project fugaro-staging --token-file <a 0600 file holding a reseller member's ID token>
```

`--customer`, `--workspace-id` (read from the customer's own workspaces through the operations read when it
is not given), `--row` (`team-annual` by default), `--days` (29), `--seats` (computed from the limit and the
rate), `--api-service` (`fugaro-portal-api`), `--statement-job` (`fugaro-portal-statements`), `--region`
(`us-east5`) and `--statement-path` (`/api/statements/run`) all default to P1.5's own names. `--dry-run`
makes every guard and prints every command it would run; `--help` prints the header above. `--project` is
refused for `fugaro-prod` unless `--production` is given — whoever reads a production reseller's month is
reading real money — a value naming `belong` is refused by name, and a coding agent's session is refused
too. The check prints ONE block on **stdout** headed `CHECK 575 RESULT`: exit **0** when every criterion
held, **1** when one did not — a sale beyond the limit that was **admitted**, a month whose lines do not sum
to what it says it accrued, a job whose token is minted for the wrong account or audience — and **2** when
it could not measure (a token file that is not 0600, an account that is not a member of a reseller
organisation, a token whose account may not read the operations area — which is when `--workspace-id`
is the way in — a customer that holds no key, a job the deployment does not have). Paste the block back for
the row; a key the run never reached reads `FAIL — not reached`. The block's keys are `xtrace`,
`agent-session`, `project`, `belong`, `api`, `token`, `signin`, `terms`, `customers`, `keys`, `workspace`,
`service`, `job`, `run`, `statements`, `limit`, `restore` and `scratch`.

**What it reads, and what it never prints.** No ID token, in whole or in part, and no address, uid or name
of the account: the token travels in a `0600` curl config file, its payload is decoded in the scratch
directory to read three claims, and what the block carries of it is the provider spelling, the `aud` project
id and an expiry state. Organisation ids, key ids and the scheduler account **are** named, which is what a
register row is read against. The read of the customer's workspaces writes the deployment's own operations
log line, which names the account that made it (`D456`); the block carries nothing of that line. It costs
nothing billable: a handful of reads, one refused sale and one scheduler fire.

**What it leaves behind.** The run it fires and nothing else; the scratch directory — the check's copy of
the composed sale and the tools' output — is removed from the exit trap even on a failed assertion or a
Ctrl-C.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** Its own automated proof is
`scripts/live-checks/check575_test.sh`, which drives every step of it against fake `curl` and `gcloud` —
no cloud, no project and no reseller — and is run by `go test ./scripts`.

## Check 760: how long `runs ls` takes on a real installation (the installation you name, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **RL6** of [docs/runs-ls-speed/implementation-plan.md](runs-ls-speed/implementation-plan.md) — its row for **Check 760** — and run **after the release and `fugaro update`**, which is what backfills the pull-request index (RL2B). It answers the one question no offline test can: whether the `runs ls` that RL1, RL2W, RL2B and RL3 built is **fast enough on a real runs bucket**, and its figures are read against your own readings of 2026-11-19. **No agent runs any step of it**, and none can: it times a real installation's listing with the credentials on your machine, and the numbers are meant to be pasted back by the person who ran it.

**What it settles.**

- **The four queries**, three times each with the run cache warm, plotted beside the 2026-11-19 baseline: `runs ls --state running` (20 s, 0 rows), `runs ls --pr N` (23 s, 1 row), the same read with `--no-cache` (32 s, 1 row) and the default `runs ls --since 7d` (15 s, 991 rows). Each row carries its three samples and its **median**, the median being the figure the row reads. The plan sets a target for two of them — `--state running` and `--pr N` **under 5 s** — and the `--pr --no-cache` read and the default listing have none: their figures are read against their own baselines and nothing else.
- **The one decision: RL4.** The plan's **D2966** gates the optional follow-up — the task that would make the default listing itself faster — on a single reading, and the `rl4-gate` row is it: a default listing **over 8 s** WANTS RL4, and **under 8 seconds means never**. A reading under the gate is the whole of the decision: the optional task is not built.
- **The sanity reading.** Two pull requests' rows are compared by **count and run ids only**, never by a row's content: the one this check timed, and a second — the oldest other the 7-day window names, or the one you name with `--old-pr N`, which is the interesting case when its runs are older than the backfill, so its answer comes from the fallback scan. The `pr-rows` row says, for each of the two, which path its read took, read off the CLI's own note on stderr: the **pull-request index**, or the **fallback scan** (its note that there is no pull-request index entry for that pull request, or that the index could not be read). Nothing here is a criterion: it is the reading that would catch a `--pr` answer coming from somewhere you did not expect.
- **A slow figure is a reading.** Nothing in this check fails on a duration: it exits 0 having printed the numbers, whatever they are. Its exit 2 is a reading it could **not** take.

**The command.** It is one command, at your own terminal, on the installation you name:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check-760-runs-ls-speed.sh --installation <installation> --pr <N>
```

`--repo OWNER/NAME` scopes the pull-request reads (give it with `--pr N` for a pull request the 7-day window does not name, where no row of the timed pull request can name the repository); `--old-pr N` picks the second pull request of the sanity reading; `--dry-run` prints the plan and touches nothing — no call, no read, no file of yours is opened; `--help` prints the header. The block is ONE block on **stdout** headed `CHECK 760 RESULT`, its last line the verdict, and the verdict is the exit status: **0** the readings were taken and are printed, **2** the run could not measure — a guard stopped it, a tool is missing, a call was refused or never answered. There is no exit 1: this check has no criterion a figure could fail, and the three timed runs default to three, so a single sample is never the reading. Paste the block back for the row.

**Reading the `CHECK 760 RESULT` block.** Each line is `LEVEL: STATE — words`, one per step, in the order the check runs them: `xtrace`, `agent-session`, `installation`, `belong`, `warmup`, `query-state-running`, `query-pr`, `query-pr-no-cache`, `query-since-7d`, `rl4-gate`, `pr-rows`, `restore` — and a step the run never reached reads `FAIL — not reached` rather than going missing, so the block names all twelve whatever happened.

**What it writes, and what it reads.** Nothing on the installation, in the project or in the runs bucket: every call is a read (`fugaro doctor`, `fugaro runs ls`), no run is launched, no model is called, no bucket object is written, no credential value is read — the CLI uses the credentials already on the machine, inside its own process — and nothing billable is spent. It costs wall clock: minutes on an installation whose listing is as slow as the baselines' own 15 s to 32 s a read.

**What it puts back.** The only thing the check writes is a scratch directory of its own (`mktemp -d`, mode 0700, with a marker file the exit trap checks before it removes anything), and the exit trap removes it however the run ends — a failed step, a refused call, a Ctrl-C. The `restore` row says whether it really went, and `CHECK760_KEEP_SCRATCH=yes` keeps it and names where for you to look through.

**Worked from where.** `belong` is refused: an installation, a repository or a `doctor` answer that names it ends the run before the first `runs ls` — refused whatever a knob or a flag says — and a coding agent's own session is refused the same way. The knobs are `CHECK760_FUGARO`, `CHECK760_INSTALLATION`, `CHECK760_REPO`, `CHECK760_PR`, `CHECK760_OLD_PR`, `CHECK760_RUNS`, `CHECK760_CALL_SECONDS`, `CHECK760_TARGET_MS`, `CHECK760_GATE_MS`, `CHECK760_BASELINE_STATE_RUNNING_MS`, `CHECK760_BASELINE_PR_MS`, `CHECK760_BASELINE_PR_NO_CACHE_MS`, `CHECK760_BASELINE_SINCE_7D_MS`, `CHECK760_KEEP_SCRATCH` and `CHECK760_DRY_RUN`; the four baseline knobs move the figure a reading is compared against, the two threshold knobs move the words MET/OVER, and `CHECK760_CALL_SECONDS` is the deadline a single read is held to before it is killed with its process group.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** Its own automated proof is `scripts/live-checks/check-760-runs-ls-speed_test.sh`, which drives every step of it against fake tools — a fake `fugaro` and a fake `git`, no cloud, no bucket and no installation — including the median each row prints (the fake sleeps a plan, so the figure has to be the middle of the three samples it also prints), a read that never answers and is killed at the deadline, and the dry run that makes no call at all. It is run by `go test ./scripts`.

## Check 790: the upgrade that gives an installation its budget database, watched across a run already in flight (an installation at the previous release, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **AB14** of
[always-a-budget/implementation-plan.md](always-a-budget/implementation-plan.md), its "### AB14: the live
checks, as scripts" and its "Checks 790 and 791"; the three questions it answers are **U1**, **U2** and
**U4** of [always-a-budget/reconciliation.md](always-a-budget/reconciliation.md) §7, and the behaviour it reads
back is **D3023**'s (the release stops an installation with no budget database from launching anything until a
**project owner** runs `fugaro update`). It is **run by the owner** at their own terminal. The script is
`scripts/live-checks/check790.sh`, with the test that drives it against fakes
(`scripts/live-checks/check790_test.sh`, run by `go test ./scripts`). **No agent runs any step of it** — the
script refuses a coding agent's session by name (`CLAUDECODE` and the four other markers that say an agent,
and not a person, is driving the shell) and refuses a shell started with `-x` — and the whole of its
registration is this one command:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check790.sh --installation <name> \
  --sandbox <a sandbox repository checkout> --job <that repository's Cloud Run job> \
  --gcp-project <project> --region <region> [--operator-config <a second installation's local config>]
```

**What the check settles.** `always-a-budget` removes budget mode off (**D3009**), so every run of every
repository opens a budget session and is metered by a gateway (**R3**). An installation that predates that
release has **no budget database at all**: the release stops such an installation launching anything until a
**project owner** runs `fugaro update`, which creates the database, migrates the config and the published
policy, and re-applies the repositories it is run for (**D3023**). Nothing offline can settle what that
upgrade does to a real installation, and this check settles the three questions the reconciliation leaves
open, plus the two readings that depend on them:

- **U1 — do an OPERATOR's roles suffice to apply the Firebase root?** A second installation at the previous
  release is updated with the operator's own credential, through `--operator-config`: the command must **exit
  0**, must **change nothing** — no job of that installation's **own** project, the `gcp_project` its local
  config names, may carry a database address — and must **say that a project owner has to run it**. An operator's update that fails, that changes the installation, or that
  exits 0 in silence is a FAIL naming which of the three it was.
- **U2 — what does a run IN FLIGHT do when the database's rules are deployed for the first time underneath
  it?** It holds no session, so nothing is expected of it. The check launches **one** run before the update
  and follows its own row across the upgrade: a run the new rules killed is the finding this row exists for.
- **U4 — does a runner from BEFORE the release behave as any observe run?** The check reads the job's own
  image reference and compares it with the checkout's `HEAD`: when the image still predates the release it is
  a pre-release runner, and two readings follow, both of the world **after** the update. First the mode the
  re-applied **job** names, `FUGARO_BUDGET_MODE` — a job that carries its database and names **no** mode is a
  FAIL, because a runner from before the release reads its mode from exactly that variable and would resolve
  the off the release removed. Then the **run's own record**, read from the runs bucket
  (`gcloud storage cat gs://fugaro-runs-<project>/runs/<slug>/<run-id>/result.json`, the key `fugaro runs ls`
  names as the row's own `run`), which must read budget mode **`observe`** — its budget session's mode
  (`runstore.Record.Budget`), or the policy block's effective mode when the record carries the mode there
  instead; no JSON view the CLI prints carries a run's mode at all. An unset mode IS observe (**C1**), a
  record that names no mode and a record that could not be read both leave the row UNVERIFIED, and an image
  carrying this checkout's own `HEAD` is not a pre-release one, and the row
  says so rather than measuring nothing.
- **The gateway.** A run launched **after** the update must land on an execution whose own environment
  carries the database address and **mounts no model key**: the agent's environment holds no API key for want
  of a gateway (**AB1b**, **D3009**), and a container that still mounts one is a run that can reach the model
  without it.
- **The database itself.** The upgrade is the plan's after-deploy pair, run by the check as the project owner:
  `fugaro update --project <installation>` (which creates the database and migrates the local config and the
  published policy) and then `fugaro update --repo --project <installation>` in the checkout, which is what
  re-applies the repository's own root (**F20**). The same job, read back after both, must carry
  `FUGARO_RTDB_URL`, and the installation's own output must name the database it created. A job that was not re-applied is a FAIL; a job that
  carries the address while the output names no database is UNVERIFIED, because the row that says *which*
  database a run will spend against was not read.

**The premise it reads first, and why it stops.** This check is about an installation the release has **not
reached**. So the first thing it reads is the opposite, in two legs. The repository's job must carry **no**
`FUGARO_RTDB_URL`. And the installation's **own state** must refuse: `fugaro project policy show --project
<installation> --json`, run in the checkout, is the command that reads the installation's **published node**,
