and an installation with **no budget backend has no node to read**, so the command refuses and names the
missing backend — an **exit 0** means the release has already been here and is a FAIL. Either leg failing is
a row reading FAIL and a **STOP (exit 2)** — the rows below would all be rows about nothing — and the job's
`describe` failing is a stop too, because nothing can be read about an installation whose job is not there.
A refusal that exits non-zero **without** naming a missing budget backend (an unreachable project, a typo in
`--installation`) is a row reading **UNVERIFIED** and a stop as well, deliberately: the check launches two
**billable** runs, and a premise nobody settled is not a state to spend on — a changed wording of the
refusal, then, costs a person nothing but the run of this check.
The check launches **no run** before the premise holds: a check that launched first and asked later would
spend two runs' budget on an installation it cannot learn anything from.

**Prerequisites.** An installation **at the previous release** that you may upgrade — no budget database, and
after the upgrade its mode is the **`observe`** the release writes for one that had none, so a run of its
project may still resolve a mode other than `observe` if you deliberately set one, and `old-image` says so
rather than reading it as a pass — its GCP project and
Cloud Run region, and the Cloud Run job that the **sandbox repository's** runs land on, named as the
installation names it. `--sandbox` is a **git checkout** of a sandbox repository you may spend on — both
launched runs commit to it and open pull requests. `fugaro`, `gcloud` (authenticated as the installation's
**project owner** for the update half, and for the `gcloud storage cat` that reads the post-update run's
record out of the runs bucket) and `git` on PATH, with `python3` for the readers. For the operator
half, `--operator-config` is the **local config file of a second installation** at the previous release, whose
`gcp_project` and `region` are what the check reads its jobs with; the operator's own default credential is
used for it and an owner's for the first. Without `--operator-config`
that row reads UNVERIFIED rather than being skipped silently.

**What a failure means, row by row.** Each row says what it read and where to look next:

- `premise` — the installation already carries a database (its job's environment names one, or
  `fugaro project policy show` answered instead of refusing): this is the wrong installation, and every row
  below would be a row about nothing. A refusal that names no missing backend is UNVERIFIED, and both
  **stop the check**.
- `in-flight` — the run that has to be in flight across the update could not be launched: read the
  launcher's own refusal in the detail. Only a launch that **failed** stops the check — the upgrade is not
  run without the run it watches. A run that was launched but whose answer carries no run id the check can
  read leaves the row UNVERIFIED, and `in-flight-2` says there is nothing to follow.
- `update` — the project owner's `fugaro update --project <installation>` or the repository's own
  `fugaro update --repo` did not exit 0, so the upgrade did not finish and nothing below can be read.
  **Stops the check.**
- `database` — both updates exited 0 and the job still carries no database address (the re-apply did not
  reach this repository): re-apply it with `fugaro update` run for that repository. A job that carries the
  address while the update's output names no database is UNVERIFIED.
- `in-flight-2` — the run that was in flight ended `failed` or `cancelled`, which is the database's rules
  having killed a run that started with no session (**U2**, and the stop **R1** accepts only for runs that
  have **not** started). A run still not terminal after the check's own wait is UNVERIFIED: read it yourself
  with `fugaro runs ls`.
- `gateway` — the post-update run's execution carries no database address (a run with no database is refused
  at its start, and the gateway that reaches the credentials service **is** the database's own session), or it
  still carries a model credential in the container's own environment, so a run on it can reach the model
  **without** the gateway.
- `old-image` — the re-applied job carries its database but names **no** `FUGARO_BUDGET_MODE` (a runner
  from before the release reads its mode from that variable, so it would resolve the off the release
  removed), or the run launched on a pre-release image recorded a budget mode that is not `observe` (a
  runner resolving a mode of its own, which **C1** does not allow). An image carrying this checkout's `HEAD`,
  a job image that could not be read, a record that names no mode at all and a record that could not be read
  each leave the row UNVERIFIED with what it read.
- `operator` — the operator's `fugaro update --config <file>` did not exit 0 (it must skip the stage and say
  who must run it, never fail), **changed** the second installation (a job of the project its own config
  names now carries a database address, which an operator's roles must not be able to create), or exited 0
  **without naming a project owner** (an installation that launches nothing until an owner acts, with an
  update that says nothing about it). A config that names no `gcp_project` leaves the changed-nothing half
  UNVERIFIED rather than unread.
- `aborted` — an extra row, present only when the script ended on an error rather than on an answer; the
  rows it did not reach were **not** measured.

**The knobs.** Every one of them is read from the environment and none of them is asked for:
`CHECK790_INSTALLATION`, `CHECK790_SANDBOX`, `CHECK790_JOB`, `CHECK790_GCP_PROJECT`, `CHECK790_REGION`,
`CHECK790_OPERATOR_CONFIG`, `CHECK790_POLL_SECONDS` (how long each `fugaro runs ls` poll waits) and
`CHECK790_DRY_RUN`. The command line itself takes `--installation`, `--sandbox`, `--job`, `--gcp-project`,
`--region`, `--operator-config`, `--dry-run` and `--help`; `--dry-run` prints the plan, makes **no call at
all** — no `gcloud`, no `fugaro`, no run, no update — and touches nothing.

**Reading the `CHECK 790 RESULT` block.** One block of `FACT`-shaped lines, in this order, and the same block
is what you paste back: `premise`, `in-flight`, `update`, `database`, `in-flight-2`, `gateway`, `old-image`,
`operator`, then `aborted` when the script ended on an error rather than on an answer, and `restore` (the
scratch directory is gone) last. Each line is the key,
`PASS`/`FAIL`/`UNVERIFIED` and the sentence saying what was read. The exit status is **0** for an all-PASS
block, **1** for a criterion that was measured and failed, **2** for a run that stopped before it could
measure everything (the premise, a missing tool, a failed update — and any run that ended before its last
step) and **3** for a run that reached the end with at least one row reading UNVERIFIED. **ONLY an all-PASS
block is a PASS.**

**What it costs, and what it leaves.** **Two billable runs** — the one left in flight across the update and
the one launched after it, each an ordinary run of the sandbox repository on its own budget — plus the budget
database the update creates, at the design's own estimate of about two dollars a month (**F18**). Everything
else the check does is a read: the job's own `describe`, the installation's own refusal, `fugaro runs ls`,
the post-update run's own record out of the runs bucket, the newest
execution of the job and the update's own output. **No secret is read**, so none can be printed: the check
reads a job's environment **names** — never a value that could be one — a refusal, a run's own record
and an update's output, and the one value it writes is a task file of its own making, in its scratch
directory.

**Restore.** The scratch directory — the job's describe before and after, the installation's own refusal, the two
task files, both runs' documents, the runs listing, the post-update run's record, the newest execution, the two updates' own outputs and the
second installation's job list — is removed
on the way out, from the exit trap on a Ctrl-C as well, and the `restore` row is that reading (a FAILed row
names the directory to remove by hand). The **two runs are left to end on their own**, as any run is, and
their pull requests and branches are the runs' own: the check closes, edits and deletes none of them. Nothing
else was created. **OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.**

## Check 791: the two refusals the release adds under `observe`, read on a sandbox repository (never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **AB14** of
[always-a-budget/implementation-plan.md](always-a-budget/implementation-plan.md), its "### AB14: the live
checks, as scripts" and its "Checks 790 and 791"; the two statements it reads back are **D3020** (a model with
no price is refused **in every mode**, with the `model_prices` entry named as the fix) and **D3022** (a
repository's committed `fugaro.yaml` that says `budget.mode: off` is rejected **at once**, with the removal
named as the fix), both read under **D3010**'s `observe` — the mode every installation lands on and the one
that refuses nothing. It is **run by the owner** at their own terminal. The script is
`scripts/live-checks/check791.sh`, with the test that drives it against a fake `fugaro` and a real local git
repository in a temp directory (`scripts/live-checks/check791_test.sh`, run by `go test ./scripts`). **No agent
runs any step of it** — the script refuses a coding agent's session by name (`CLAUDECODE` and the four other
markers that say an agent, and not a person, is driving the shell), refuses a shell started with `-x`, and the
refusals it reads are meant to be read by a person, because the fix each one names is a person's to make — and
the whole of its registration is this one command:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check791.sh --sandbox <a sandbox repository checkout> [--installation <name>]
```

**What the check settles.** Both statements are about refusals a **person** meets, and both name a fix only a
person can perform: an entry to add to `model_prices`, and a key to remove from a repository's own file.
Nothing offline can settle that the refusal a **real** installation prints is the one the plan wrote, that the
fix it names is the fix that clears it, or that the refusal really happens under a mode that refuses nothing:

- **`unpriced` — D3020.** `fugaro validate fugaro.yaml`, run in the checkout, must **refuse**, and its refusal
  must name `model_prices`. The model it is about is the one the repository's own committed file carries (the first
  `model:` under `agent:`, or the top-level one a file may carry). The **exit status** is what says the
  validation refused: a message that names the fix and exits **0** is a warning, and the row reads **FAIL** —
  a run that goes on to spend a model nobody priced. A checkout whose model **is** priced has no subject for
  this row and reads UNVERIFIED, naming the model it read.
- **`mode-off` — D3022.** The repository's **COMMITTED** `fugaro.yaml` is read with `git show HEAD:fugaro.yaml`
  — never the working tree, because the file a **run** reads is the one on the branch, and the two differ
  exactly when a task is half-written. When that file says `budget.mode: off`, a launch from that checkout
  (`fugaro run --task-file <a task the check writes> --json`) must be **refused** and its refusal must name
  the word **`off`**. Off is accepted nowhere (**AB2**), and the refusal is a config load's, so it happens
  **at once**: nothing is spent. A launch the release does **not** refuse is the finding — it is a real,
  billable run then, and the row names it and the command that stops it (`fugaro cancel --now <run id>`) —
  and a refusal that never names `off` leaves the person guessing which key to remove. A committed file that
  does not say off leaves this row UNVERIFIED — the check names what to commit rather than inventing a
  reading.

**The premise it reads first.** Both rows are statements about what happens under **`observe`**, so the mode
in force is read first, from the published policy (`fugaro project policy show --project <installation>
--json`). A mode of `observe` is the premise and the two
rows follow. A mode that is **not** observe is a FAIL: a refusal read under another mode measures a different
thing. A policy read that did not answer with a mode is **UNVERIFIED, never a PASS** — a refusal read under an
unknown mode is a refusal about nothing. The same step reads the committed file and refuses to go on when the
working tree **differs from its HEAD**: the committed file and the file `fugaro validate` reads would then not
be the same document, and the rows below would read one file and name the other.

**Prerequisites.** `--sandbox` is a **git checkout** of a sandbox repository whose model has **no price** and,
for the second row, whose **committed** file says `budget.mode: off` — the state the release rejects, so commit
it on a sandbox branch. The repository must be one the installation's published policy puts in **`observe`**,
which is what `--installation` names. `fugaro` and `git` on PATH, with `python3` for the readers. The check
reads a checkout and a published policy and touches nothing else; run it on a sandbox you are happy to see
named.

**What a failure means, row by row.**

- `premise` — the mode in force is not `observe` (a refusal read under another mode measures a different
  thing), the policy read answered with no mode at all (UNVERIFIED), the committed file could not be read, or
  the working tree differs from its HEAD (UNVERIFIED: commit or stash the change and run it again).
- `unpriced` — the validation named `model_prices` **and exited 0** (a warning is not the refusal **D3020**
  writes), or it refused **without naming** `model_prices` (the person meeting it is told which entry clears
  it, and a refusal that does not name it leaves them with nothing to do). A clean validation is UNVERIFIED:
  this repository's model is priced here, and the row has no subject.
- `mode-off` — a launch from a checkout whose committed file says off was **not** refused (a real run the
  release should never have started: the row names it and the `fugaro cancel --now <run id>` that stops it),
  or it was refused **without the refusal naming `off`**. A committed file that does not say off is
  UNVERIFIED.
- `aborted` — an extra row, present only when the script ended on an error rather than on an answer.

**The knobs.** Every one of them is read from the environment and none of them is asked for:
`CHECK791_SANDBOX`, `CHECK791_INSTALLATION` and `CHECK791_DRY_RUN`. The command line itself takes `--sandbox`,
`--installation`, `--dry-run` and `--help`; `--dry-run` prints the plan, makes **no call at all** — no `git`,
no `fugaro`, nothing spent — and touches nothing.

**Reading the `CHECK 791 RESULT` block.** One block of `FACT`-shaped lines, in this order, and the same block
is what you paste back: `premise`, `unpriced`, `mode-off`, then `aborted` when the script ended on an error
rather than on an answer, and `restore` (the scratch directory is gone) last. Each line is the key,
`PASS`/`FAIL`/`UNVERIFIED` and the sentence saying what was read. The exit status is **0** for an all-PASS
block, **1** for a criterion that was measured and failed, **2** for a run that stopped before it could
measure everything (a missing tool, a missing `--sandbox`, a path that is not a checkout) and **3** for a run
that reached the end with at least one row reading UNVERIFIED. **ONLY an all-PASS block is a PASS.**

**What it costs, and what it leaves.** **Nothing, as long as the release holds.** No model is called, no build
is made and no write is made anywhere: `fugaro validate` spends nothing, and the one launch spends nothing when
the refusal happens — the refusal is a config load's, made before anything is built or run, which is exactly
the reading **D3022** is about. The other side of
that coin is honest to state: a launch the release does **not** refuse is a **real, billable run**, and the
`mode-off` row then names it and the `fugaro cancel --now <run id>` that stops it. Every row is otherwise a read
of a document the repository or the installation already wrote — its committed `fugaro.yaml`, its HEAD's own
tree, the published policy, and the refusals themselves. **No secret is read**, so none can be printed.

**Restore.** The scratch directory — the committed `fugaro.yaml`, the published policy, the validation's
output, the launch's own answer and the task file the check wrote — is removed on the way out, from the exit trap
on a Ctrl-C as well, and the `restore` row is that reading (a FAILed row names the directory to remove by
hand). Nothing else was created and nothing was changed: the checkout, its branches and the installation are
exactly as they were. **OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.**

## Check 830: what links a Batch VM to its job, and what a launcher can put on one (the sandbox project `fugaro-dev` only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **BR0** of
[docs/batch-run-identity/implementation-plan.md](batch-run-identity/implementation-plan.md) — its
row for **830** — as the probe the plan blocks **BR3** (the VM-to-job link the credentials service
releases a job's blob on), **BR5** and **BR12** on (**R4**). It settles the owner's **O1** (which
fact links a VM to its job and which permission reads it) and the four UNVERIFIED questions the
reconciliation carries. **No agent runs any step of it**, and **BR3 starts only after this result is
recorded**.

**What it settles.**

- **U1 — the link, and its forge.** Which Google-made fact ties a Batch VM to its job: a field of
  the instance's own object (readable only with `compute.instances.get` on the VM — the second read
  **D3102** asks about, and one that cannot be scoped to Fugaro's VMs), a field of the job's own
  object (read with the `batch.jobs.get` the service already holds, **F26**), something visible
  **inside** the VM only, or nothing at all. The row names the field and the read it costs, because
  **BR3** is written against exactly that. A second job then tries to **forge** it: it carries the
  probe job's uid and name in every field a launcher controls — its own labels, the labels Batch
  puts on the VMs, and the task's variables — and its VM is read for the field the probe's own VM
  carries the probe's identity in. **A field a launcher can write there must not be the link**
  (**R1**, **D3108**): a launcher who can name another job's uid in it would be handed that job's
  release. The same attempt is made against a **plain Compute Engine VM** named after the probe job
  (**O8**): anyone holding `compute.instances.create` and `actAs` on a run account can make one.
  Each avenue carries a **control** — how many of the written keys reached that VM at all — so an
  attempt Batch copies nowhere reads as inert rather than as a pass.
- **U2 — the identity token.** Whether a task's container can reach the metadata server at all, and
  whether the token in **full** format carries the instance's **id**, **name**, **project** and
  **zone**. Those claims are what **D3101** matches a VM to its job with, so a claim that is not
  there cannot be matched on. The token itself is a bearer credential for that VM and is never
  printed, here or in the container's own lines.
- **U3 — where a job's variable reaches.** Whether the value of a variable the job carries — the
  wrapped key's own variable (**R5**) with a generated stand-in value — appears in the probe job's
  own log entries, anywhere in the project's Cloud Logging, in the instance metadata or the
  instance's own object, or in the **`CreateJob` audit record**. The row is **fail-closed**: it
  passes only when the value reached the container's own environment (the positive control, so the
  job carried it) **and** every reading was taken and saw nothing, including the audit record,
  which is waited for within a bound. The value is compared and never printed — a block that
  printed it would be a block that had to be treated as secret — so the row names the readings
  instead.
- **U8 — reusing a deleted job's name.** The probe job is deleted, the same name is submitted again
  in a bounded loop, and the seconds to acceptance are printed, with the first refusal's own
  message. The re-created job is deleted at once; it existed to hold a name, not to run. **D3108**'s
  registration does not depend on this answer.

**What has to exist before it runs.** Nothing of the work: the check creates its own job and is
built to run before a line of **C1**'s sides is written. It reads the tree it lives in — the log
filter out of `internal/backend/batch/logs.go`, the managed label pair out of
`internal/backend/gcp/names.go` and the wrapped variable's name out of `docs/batch-run-identity/` —
so it must be run from the checkout whose commit you record. It needs `gcloud`, `bash`, `python3`
and `git` on PATH, and nothing is installed or fetched.

**The command.** It is **one command**, and the owner marker is the whole of the ceremony:

```sh
CHK830_OWNER_RUN=yes bash scripts/live-checks/check-830.sh
```

It names GCP project `fugaro-dev` and region `us-east5` itself: there is no `--project` flag and no
variable that could point another project at it, and `belong`, EdgeWeb and EdgeServer are refused by
name. `--dry-run` runs the guards and the tree reads, prints every command a real run would run, and
touches no cloud project. A traced shell (`bash -x`) is refused, because a trace would print the
commands into the log you paste back. Every bound is a knob — `CHK830_WAIT_LINES`, `CHK830_WAIT_AUDIT`,
`CHK830_REUSE_BOUND`, `CHK830_LINGER_A`, `CHK830_LINGER_B` — because a slow project should be given
longer rather than read as a `FAIL`.

**What it reads, and what the block says.** One block on stdout headed `CHECK 830 RESULT`, whose last
line is `CHECK 830 RESULT: PASS|FAIL`, with **one row per fact**: `u1-link` (the field, and the
permission that reads it), `u1-forge` (whether a second job reproduced it, with the per-avenue
control), `u1-handmade` (`O8`'s plain VM), `u2-token` (the four claims), `u3-marker` (the three
readings, fail-closed), `u8-name` (the seconds) — beside the rows that say what ran: the probe job,
the container's own readings, the VM, the guards and `restore`. Paste the **whole block** into this
section, with the date and `fugaro version`. If `u1-link` is `FAIL`, or `u1-forge` is `FAIL`, or
`u1-handmade` is `FAIL`, the work returns to **you** rather than falling back to **K1** (**R4**):
that is the answer, and it is the reason this probe runs before **BR3** is written.

**Restore.** The check deletes everything it made — the probe job, the forging job, the re-created
job and the plain VM — and its `restore` row names anything an interrupted run left behind with the
one command that removes it. Two small `e2-standard-4` jobs alive for their linger (300 s and 120 s by
default), one VM alive for seconds, and a dozen `gcloud` reads: no model call, no build, no run of
the backend, no image built. The scratch directory always goes, including on a Ctrl-C.

**What waits on it.** **BR3** (**R4**), and through the owner's **O1** answer also **BR5** and
**BR12**; the plan's critical path starts here, and the row **830** in the implementation plan's
table says "after BR0 merges, before `R-C1-link-permission`, BR3, BR5 and BR12 start".

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** The script's own test,
`scripts/live-checks/check-830_test.sh`, drives it entirely against a fake `gcloud` on PATH — no
network, no project, no resource — and is run by `go test ./scripts` like every other check's.

## Check 831: a Batch run's identity end to end, and four attacks on the claim (the sandbox project `fugaro-dev` only, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **BR13** of
[docs/batch-run-identity/implementation-plan.md](batch-run-identity/implementation-plan.md) — its row for
**831** — as the proof **R11** asks for: the requirement that a run's identity is served to that run's
own VM and to nothing else, measured on a real run rather than argued from the code. It is run **after**
the release that ships the launcher's ticket and the credentials service's claim, and on an updated
`fugaro-dev`, because the readings it takes are of that release's launcher and of that release's
service. **No agent runs any step of it.**

**What it proves.**

- **The run exists, and its job is the run's.** One real sandbox run is launched with `fugaro run`,
  and the job the launch answered is read back. The check does not take a name on trust: it reads the
  job's own `FUGARO_RUN` variable (`internal/backend/batch/env.go`), which the backend writes as the
  repository's **slug** and the run id joined by a slash, and holds the job to the run only when the
  uid matches the launch's answer and that variable's run half is the run. The slug is the same
  derivation the record and the ledger are keyed by (`task.Slug`), so a second job carrying another
  job's name cannot pass for the run's own. A **second** sandbox run is launched later, for the third
  attack only; it is read the same way, and deleted while its job is still queued.
- **It opened its session, and it was metered.** The ledger at
  `<rtdb>/runs/<slug>/<run>.json` is read with the owner's own access token, waited for within a
  bound, and both readings are taken: the run's session was opened, and the run was **metered** (a
  spend or a token count above zero). A run whose job never appears, or never reaches the ledger, is
  a `FAIL` on its own row rather than a silent pass.
- **Where Batch printed the ticket (D3115, U3 as re-cut).** The ticket is one of the job's variables
  — Batch prints variables, and **D3115** accepts that because a ticket alone claims nothing. The
  check reads the three places the plan names: the job's own document, the task logs, and the
  **`CreateJob` audit record** (waited for within a bound). Its `launch-ticket` row names the
  variable and **never its value**: the value goes to a mode-0600 file of its own and never into the
  block, the progress log, a command line or the facts the block is printed from, so a block that
  was pasted back could not be read as a secret.
- **Four attacks, made as a second launcher.** `--second-launcher <account>` names an account that
  is **not** the run's, and every attack is made through it (`--impersonate-service-account`). All
  four attack jobs are submitted to run as the run's **own job account** (the account the run's job
  runs as, read off the job's `allocationPolicy`), so a refusal is about the **VM** the claim comes
  from and not about the account it is made with:
  - **`attack-replay`** — the run's ticket, read out of its job as the second launcher, replayed
    into a job of the second launcher's own, claiming from **its own VM**. The attestation must
    refuse it: that VM is not the recorded job's. A **token** coming back is the finding, and this
    is the row the check exists for. A `PASS` here is the service's own decision **about the VM**,
    and the row reads the refusal's own sentence to know it: the two refusals this route answers
    **before it asks the link** — the ticket already spent by the run's own bootstrap, which is
    what a replay of a metered run's ticket meets, and the ticket's own life — are a `FAIL` of this
    row and not a `PASS`, because a service that never asks whether the VM is the job's answers
    exactly those. So is `not_served` (the installation's link is not wired: nothing is judged) and
    any refusal that is not the claim route's own.
  - **`attack-noticket`** — the same job with **no ticket** at all, the control: it must be refused
    too, so that the replay's refusal is about the attestation rather than about a job that could
    never have claimed.
  - **`attack-rename`** — a **second sandbox run** is launched for this attack and **its** job is
    deleted while it is still `QUEUED` — before its VM exists, so before its bootstrap has spent its
    ticket — and **re-created under the same name** carrying that run's ticket (**D3108**, **F30**):
    the record's **id** must refuse the claim, because a name is not an identity, and nothing else is
    left to refuse it — the ticket is unspent and the name is the same. This is why the job is a
    second launch's and not the run's own: the run whose identity every other row reads has been
    metered by the time the check reaches here, so its ticket is spent and a re-creation carrying it
    would be refused for being spent rather than by the record. The row names the state the job was in
    when it was deleted and **`FAIL`s when that state is not `QUEUED`** (the window had passed and the
    attack was not made), and the second run never comes up: it is deleted while queued, so it is
    never metered and spends nothing. A Batch delete is **asynchronous** — the name stays the
    platform's, in `DELETION_IN_PROGRESS`, until it has finished with the job — so the re-creation is
    retried within its own bound rather than reading the platform's `ALREADY_EXISTS` as the attack's
    refusal, and its row is judged by the same rule as the replay's.
  - **`attack-record`** — the issuance record is read **straight out of the database** with the
    second launcher's own token. The database's rules must refuse it; a `200` is the finding.

  Each attack's job is deleted by the step that made it, and the check refuses to judge an attack
  whose container reported no reading at all rather than reading silence as a pass.

**What has to exist before it runs.** The release (the launcher's ticket and the service's claim),
`fugaro update` on `fugaro-dev`, a sandbox repository to launch into, and a **second launcher
account** in the installation's launcher roster. It reads the tree it lives in — the ticket's
variable and the claim's route out of `internal/identitywire/wire.go`, the record's path family and
`budget.Key`'s escaping out of `internal/budget/`, the run's own variable and the credentials
service's variable out of `internal/backend/batch/env.go`, the run label out of
`internal/backend/batch/names.go`, and the database URL's variable out of
`internal/runner/budget_session.go` — so it must be run from the checkout whose commit you record.
It needs `gcloud`, `bash`, `python3` and `git` on PATH, and nothing is installed or fetched.

**The command.** It is **one command**, and the owner marker plus the second launcher are the whole
of the ceremony:

```sh
CHK831_OWNER_RUN=yes bash scripts/live-checks/check-831.sh --second-launcher <account>
```

It names GCP project `fugaro-dev` and region `us-east5` itself: there is no `--project` flag and no
variable that could point another project at it, and `belong`, EdgeWeb and EdgeServer are refused by
name. `--dry-run` runs the guards and the tree reads, prints every command a real run would run, and
touches no cloud project. A traced shell (`bash -x`) is refused, because a trace would print the
ticket into the log you paste back. Every bound is a knob — `CHK831_WAIT_JOB`, `CHK831_WAIT_SESSION`,
`CHK831_WAIT_METERED`, `CHK831_WAIT_ATTACK`, `CHK831_WAIT_AUDIT`, `CHK831_WAIT_RENAME`,
`CHK831_RENAME_POLL`, `CHK831_WAIT_QUEUED`, `CHK831_QUEUE_POLL`, `CHK831_SWEEP_BOUND`,
`CHK831_SWEEP_POLL`, `CHK831_MAX_USD` — because a slow project (or a platform slow to let a deleted
job's name go, or slow to publish the second launch's job) should be given longer rather than read
as a `FAIL`.

**What it reads, and what the block says.** One block on stdout headed `CHECK 831 RESULT`, whose last
line is `CHECK 831 RESULT: PASS|FAIL`, with **one row per fact**: `installation`, `launch`,
`job-found`, `session`, `metered`, `launch-ticket`, `ticket-printed`, `attack-replay`,
`attack-noticket`, `attack-rename`, `attack-record` and `cost` — beside the rows that say what ran
and what was left behind: `xtrace`, `owner`, `tree`, `belong` and `restore`. A row that no step
reached is a `FAIL` of its own, so a run that ended early cannot print a `PASS` block. The exit
status is `0` when every row passed, `1` when a row failed, `2` when the run could not tell (an
internal error, or a run that ended before its last step), and `130` when it was interrupted. Paste
the **whole block** into this section, with the date and `fugaro version`. **A `FAIL` on
`attack-replay`, `attack-rename` or `attack-record` is the answer R11 was asked for**: the identity
of a Batch run can be obtained by a VM that is not its job's, and the work returns to the plan
rather than being recorded as a pass.

**Restore, and what it costs.** The check deletes every job it made — the run's job, the second
launch's job, the replayed job, the control and the re-created one — by the label it puts on them and
by the label the backend writes on a run's job, and its `restore` row names anything an interrupted
run left behind with the one command that removes it. **Two sandbox runs**: the run whose identity
the attacks are about, model calls included (the `cost` row prints the spend and the tokens the run's
own ledger recorded), and the second launch of the third attack, which never comes up — its job is
deleted while it is queued — and so is never metered and spends nothing. Three short-lived
`e2-standard-4` jobs: no build, no image, no change to any installation. The scratch directory
always goes, including on a Ctrl-C.

**What waits on it.** Nothing: **R11**'s acceptance is the result itself, and the plan's row **831**
puts it after the release rather than on the critical path. Check 124 stays as it is — 831 does not
replace its preemption.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** The script's own test,
`scripts/live-checks/check-831_test.sh`, drives it entirely against a fake `gcloud`, `curl` and
`fugaro` on PATH — no network, no project, no resource — and is run by `go test ./scripts` like
every other check's. It fails when the replay step is removed from the script, which is the proof
that the replay row is what the row measures; and it fails when the row is made to accept any
refusal the service answers, the once-only fence's *the ticket was already claimed* among them,
which is the difference between a row that measures the VM-to-job link and one that would pass on a
tree with no link at all.

## Check 840: what a Cloud Run execution can prove — its identity token, the override read back, and one custom token exchanged twice (your own development installation, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **LM0** of
[docs/launcher-does-not-mint/implementation-plan.md](launcher-does-not-mint/implementation-plan.md), and it
is that work's register row for the three things its
[reconciliation.md](launcher-does-not-mint/reconciliation.md) lists as **UNVERIFIED**: **U1**, **U2** and
**U3**. It changes nothing it does not remove, it launches no Fugaro run, it calls no model, and **no agent
runs any step of it**.

**What it settles.** Three readings, and each of them is a question about the platform rather than about
this installation, so an answer against the design is a **finding** and not a fault of the project it ran
against.

- **U1 — what the execution's identity token carries.** Every Cloud Run job execution has a metadata
  server, and `internal/runner/gateway.go` mints an ID token from it for a fixed audience
  (`…/service-accounts/default/identity?audience=…&format=full`). The check creates one throwaway job whose
  only command prints the **claims** of that token — every claim's **name**, and the values of only four
  of them — never the token, with the execution's own name **and** the **uid** of its own document known
  from the platform's answers rather than from the container. **F11** reads the platform as
  unable to tell two executions of one job apart, and this is where that reading is checked: if a claim
  **carries the execution** — its name, its full resource name, or that uid, the row naming which — that is
  the finding **R15** and its **R-C1-execution** exist for, and the residual **R5** leaves closes for Cloud
  Run; if nothing does, the claim set is the account and the audience, and a claim by a run proves the
  **job**. The block's claim row also says how many claims the probe printed, because Cloud Logging ingests
  a container's lines one at a time: a block the log holds only in part is a claim set with claims missing,
  and it is not read as one (the check waits for the probe's own closing line and compares its count).
- **U2 — whether `run.executions.get` returns the override.** The launch puts a marker variable on the
  execution as an **execution-level override** (the shape the launcher writes, and the one
  `gcloud run jobs execute` has no flag for), and the check then reads the execution's own document back at
  `GET https://run.googleapis.com/v2/<the execution's name>` — the call `run.executions.get` admits. The
  reading is whether that document carries the marker with the value the launch set. **F9** rests on it: a
  second launcher reads a peer's sealed token out of the execution's own override this way. The role is read
  beside it, because "the owner's own credential can" and "a launcher can" are different claims: if
  `fugaroLauncher` does not carry `run.executions.get`, F9's premise does not hold on this installation, and
  that is a finding too.
- **U3 — whether one custom token exchanges twice.** The check mints one Firebase custom token the way the
  launcher does (`internal/budget/token/mint.go`'s claims, signed as `fugaro-token-signer` through IAM
  Credentials `signJwt`), with a **run-shaped uid that names no run** (`r~chk840~<random>`), and posts it at
  `accounts:signInWithCustomToken` **twice**. **F9** assumes a second exchange inside the hour works, which
  is what makes the copy it describes a race; a refusal is a **finding** and means that copy was never the
  race it is written as.

**What has to exist before it runs.** An installation with a Cloud Run job (`--job`), your own `gcloud`
login (`gcloud auth login`), and — for U3 — the right to sign as the installation's signer
(`fugaroTokenMinter` on `fugaro-token-signer@<project>.iam.gserviceaccount.com`, which the installation
granting you its deployer role gives). Nothing is installed and nothing is built: the probe job runs a
public Cloud SDK image, and the check needs only `bash`, `gcloud`, `curl`, `python3`, `sed` and `mktemp`.

**The command.**

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check-840.sh --project <project> --region <region> --job <a job the installation already runs>
```

`--job` is a job the installation already runs — a repository job, a shared job or the review job. The
check reads exactly two things off it and changes nothing on it: the service account it runs as (which the
probe job is created with, so that the identity token U1 reads names the account the installation's own jobs
use) and the Firebase web API key in its environment (`FUGARO_FIREBASE_API_KEY`, a plain value, not a secret
reference), which is what the U3 exchange is addressed with. `--signer <email>` overrides the signing
account, and `--dry-run` prints every call it would make and makes none. **Any typed value containing
`belong` is refused before any call** — the project, the region and the job alike — because the owner's own
installation is never the subject of a check that creates a Cloud Run job.

**What it reads, and what it never prints.** The access token this check carries is minted into a **0600
curl config file** inside a 0700 scratch directory and curl reads it with `--config`; the Firebase web API
key travels the same way, inside that file's URL; the custom token U3 mints, and the ID token Firebase
answers with, are written to 0600 files and are never printed at all. `ps` shows a process's argv to every
user of the machine, which is why none of the three is ever an argument of a command, and why a shell that
arrived tracing (`-x`) is refused: a trace would print the credentials into the log you would paste back.

**The three answers, and what each one moves.** A **PASS** on all three is the design's assumption holding,
and the block says so in one verdict line. A **FAIL** on any of them is an answer against it, and the row
names which: **U1** moves the reconciliation's **U1** and **R15** (**R-C1-execution** binds the run's claim
to the claim that names the execution, and R5's residual closes for Cloud Run); **U2** moves its **U2** and
**F9** (the launcher's read of a peer's override is not the way it is described); a launcher role without
`run.executions.get` moves **F9** and the role's own permission list; **U3** moves its **U3** and **F9** (the
copy was never a race). The `override-echo` row is U2's control: the launch's marker either reached the
container or did not, and a row that carries some other value is a **FAIL** too, because the execution's own
document is then not a read of an override that took effect. Exit 0 is all three as assumed, **1** is an
answer against one of them (or that control failing), and **2** is **not measured** — a guard stopped it, a
read did not answer, a credential minted nothing, or the job name was already taken — with the block's rows
saying which.

**Restore.** The check creates **one** Cloud Run job (`fugaro-chk840-probe`) and **one** execution of it,
both its own, and deletes the job at the end — including on a Ctrl-C — then reads the deletion back with a
describe that must answer `NOT_FOUND`. If a job of that name is **already** there, the check refuses before
creating anything and deletes nothing: it never adopts a job it did not make. **U3's exchange creates a
Firebase Auth user too**: signing in with a custom token is what makes the account, under the run-shaped
uid the check minted. The check deletes it through the project's own Identity Toolkit (`accounts:delete`)
and reads it back with an `accounts:lookup` whose own answer must hold no user for that uid; an `auth-user`
row FAIL is that account still there, and the row names the uid to delete by hand. What stays in the
project is the executions' own log lines, which are the project's record of what ran rather than a resource
this check made, and the scratch directory and every credential file in it are removed and read back as
gone.

**What waits on it.** The launcher work's own items read against these three: **U1** against **R15** and
**R-C1-execution**, **U2** and the launcher role's permission against **F9**, and **U3** against **F9**'s
copy. Nothing here is a prerequisite for another task; the three are read when the owner runs the script.

**USER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.**

## Check 810: the auth retirement's first release, watched across four repositories and a run in flight (an installation at the previous release, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **CM22** of
[credentials-belong-to-models/implementation-plan.md](credentials-belong-to-models/implementation-plan.md), its
"### CM22: the live checks, as scripts" and the plan's own **Check 810, after release 1** (§8); what it reads
back is **U5** and the owner's **O1** of
[credentials-belong-to-models/reconciliation.md](credentials-belong-to-models/reconciliation.md), and the
record it reads them against is **C1**'s (a repository's crafts resolve to a credential, written at
`creds/repoaccess/<slug>`, **C1** (d); a file that still writes `agent.auth` is read as the same answer it
always meant, **C1** (c); a refusal of a craft a record does not name writes exactly **one** audit line,
**C1.13**). It is **run by the owner** at their own terminal. The script is
`scripts/live-checks/check810.sh`, with the test that drives it against fake `gcloud`, `fugaro` and `curl` on
PATH and **four real local git repositories** in a temp directory (`scripts/live-checks/check810_test.sh`, run
by `go test ./scripts`). **No agent runs any step of it** — the script refuses a coding agent's session by name
(`CLAUDECODE` and the four other markers that say an agent, and not a person, is driving the shell) and refuses
a shell started with `-x` — and the whole of its registration is this one command:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check810.sh --installation <name> --oauth <checkout> --api-key <checkout> \
  --cascade <checkout> --vertex <checkout> --job <the subscription repository's Cloud Run job> \
  --gcp-project <project> --region <region> [--rtdb-url <url>] [--access-header <name>]
```

**What the check settles.** Release 1 of `credentials-belong-to-models` takes a repository's auth mode away:
a run stops saying how it goes out, and the installation records, per repository, which credential its crafts
resolve to. Nothing offline can settle what that migration does to a real installation, so the check watches
one, and the clauses it reads are these:

- **The migration reaches every repository.** A project owner's `fugaro update` is run once for the
  installation (which migrates the local config and the published policy) and once with `--repo` in each of the
  four checkouts. All five must exit 0: the whole upgrade is that one command (CLAUDE.md's HARD RULE), and an
  update that did not finish is not the migration this check is about.
- **Each craft resolves to what the old file meant.** Every repository's **new** record out of the database's
  `creds` node (`creds/repoaccess/<slug>`) names the credential its old `agent.auth` meant: `vertex` for the
  Vertex repository and **never** for the other three, the account the subscription repository's own old record
  carries for that one, a credential that is neither for the key and cascade repositories, and a version of 1
  where it names one at all. The old `agent.auth` is read as the answer "what did it mean" — **C1** (c).
- **The update says what it did.** Its own output names each of the four repositories **and** a credential its
  crafts resolve to: the plan's after-deploy step for this release is that the update tells the owner what each
  craft resolves to (§9), and an owner who is not told cannot tell a migration from a stop.
- **A run in flight survives it.** One run of the subscription repository is launched **before** the update and
  followed across it: the migration must not kill a run that started on the release behind (**U5**).
- **The four runs afterwards go out the same way.** A run of each repository is launched **after** the update,
  ends, has a **served line** in the service's own log (`credsvc: audit` with status `ok`, so its calls went
  through its gateway) and carries in its own record out of the runs bucket the **same `model_basis`** the
  subscription repository's runs carried before the update — the subscription for the subscription repository,
  the API list for the other three (**F25**).
- **A craft the record does not name is refused, and recorded once.** A call the check builds **by hand**,
  carrying a live run's own identity (a Google ID token for the job's own account, over a run identity minted
  the way the launcher mints it: the runs' signer, a Firebase custom token, the identity toolkit exchange) and
  declaring a craft no repository's record names, must be **refused**, with **exactly one** audit line for that
  run in the service's log (**U5**, **O1**, **C1.13**). The four runs above are launched **first** and read
  afterwards, so the call is made while one of them is going and the identity it presents is one the service
  can verify.

**The premise it reads first, and why it stops.** This check is about an installation the release has **not**
reached, and the first thing it reads is the opposite. Each of the four checkouts' **committed** `fugaro.yaml`
writes its own old `agent.auth` (`oauth`, `api-key`, `cascade`, `vertex`); the database's `creds` node carries
the four old records (`creds/repoauth/<slug>`) and **no** access record (`creds/repoaccess`) at all. Any leg
failing is a row reading FAIL and a **STOP (exit 2)** — the check launches **five billable runs**, and every
row below would be a row about nothing. The database's URL comes out of the installation's own local project
config (`${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/fugaro/projects/<installation>.yaml`, key `budget.rtdb_url`), or from
`--rtdb-url` when that file names none — `fugaro doctor --json` carries no database address, so it is not a
source. An installation whose records cannot be read is a stop too, because no row below can be measured
without them. The check launches **no run** before the premise holds.

**Prerequisites.** An installation **at the previous release** that you may upgrade, and four **git checkouts**
of its repositories — one on a subscription, one on an Anthropic key, one on the cascade, one on Vertex — each
whose committed `fugaro.yaml` still writes its own `agent.auth`. `--job` is the subscription repository's own
Cloud Run job: the `audit` row reads it for the account and the Firebase web API key the identity toolkit is
addressed with. `--gcp-project` and `--region` name where that job and the service live. `--access-header` is
the header the new narrowing declares a craft in (**C1** (e), the headers a new runner declares its craft in):
this script was written before that contract, so it is an argument and never a guess, and without it the
`audit` row reads **UNVERIFIED** rather than making a call whose header the check made up. `--signer` overrides
the account the custom tokens are signed as. `fugaro`, `gcloud` (authenticated as the installation's **project
owner**), `curl`, `git`, `python3` and `mktemp` on PATH; nothing is installed and nothing is fetched.

**What a failure means, row by row.** Each row says what it read and where to look next:

- `premise` — the leg that failed is named: a checkout that does not write the `agent.auth` the flag naming it
  claims, a database that cannot be read, an access record that is already there (the installation has already
  been reached) or an old record that is not. **Stops the check** before anything is launched.
- `in-flight` — the run that has to be in flight across the update could not be launched; read the launcher's
  own refusal in the detail. A run launched whose answer carries no run id the check can read leaves the row
  UNVERIFIED, and `in-flight-2` then says there is nothing to follow.
- `update` — the installation's own `fugaro update --project`, or one repository's `fugaro update --repo`, did
  not exit 0; the failing checkout is named, and each run's own output is in the scratch directory's
  `update-*.out`.
- `crafts` — a new record names no credential, names `vertex` for a repository whose old auth did not mean it,
  does not name the account the subscription repository's own old record carries, is missing altogether, or
  names a version that is not 1. The records themselves are at `creds/repoaccess.json`.
- `says` — the update's own output names no repository, or names none of the credentials its crafts resolve to.
- `in-flight-2` — the run that was in flight when the migration was applied underneath it ended `failed` or
  `cancelled` (**U5**). A run still not terminal after the check's own wait leaves the row UNVERIFIED; read it
  yourself with `fugaro runs ls`.
- `runs-launched` — how many of the four repositories' runs were launched after the update. A launch that
  failed has its own row above; this row is the count, and it is a reading rather than a criterion.
- `oauth-run`, `key-run`, `cascade-run`, `vertex-run` — the run did not end, ended `failed` or `cancelled`,
  has **no served line** in the service's log (its model calls did not go through its gateway, **F25**),
  carries no `cost.model_basis` (UNVERIFIED), or is recorded with a `model_basis` other than the one its
  repository's runs carried before the migration.
- `audit` — no `--access-header` was given, no run of the subscription repository is going, the job or the
  service could not be read, or the identity could not be minted: UNVERIFIED, with what was read. A call that
  was **served** is a FAIL (a repository offered a credential its record does not name, **O1**). A refusal with
  **no** audit line is a FAIL (an operator cannot see it). A refusal with **two**, or one the check cannot tell
  from the run's own traffic, or a refusal whose words name neither the craft nor a repository, is UNVERIFIED —
  as is the shape of a refusal taken **before** the identity was verified.
- `aborted` — an extra row, present only when the script ended on an error rather than on an answer; the rows
  it did not reach were **not** measured.

**The knobs.** Every one of them is read from the environment and none of them is asked for:
`CHECK810_INSTALLATION`, `CHECK810_OAUTH`, `CHECK810_API_KEY`, `CHECK810_CASCADE`, `CHECK810_VERTEX`,
`CHECK810_JOB`, `CHECK810_GCP_PROJECT`, `CHECK810_REGION`, `CHECK810_RTDB_URL`, `CHECK810_ACCESS_HEADER`,
`CHECK810_SIGNER`, `CHECK810_SERVICE` (the credentials service's name, `fugaro-credentials` by default),
`CHECK810_CONFIG` (the installation's local project config file, when it does not sit at the path the premise
paragraph names), `CHECK810_DRY_RUN`, and the polling, logging and curl knobs the test uses to keep a case
short (`CHECK810_POLLS`, `CHECK810_POLL_SECONDS`, `CHECK810_LOG_AGE`, `CHECK810_LOG_LIMIT`,
`CHECK810_LOG_POLL_SECONDS`, `CHECK810_LOG_WAIT_SECONDS`, `CHECK810_CURL_SECONDS`). The command line itself
takes `--installation`, `--oauth`, `--api-key`, `--cascade`, `--vertex`, `--job`, `--gcp-project`, `--region`,
`--rtdb-url`, `--access-header`, `--signer`, `--service`, `--dry-run` and `--help`; `--dry-run` prints the
plan, makes **no call at all** — no `gcloud`, no `fugaro`, no run, no update, nothing spent — and touches
nothing.

**Reading the `CHECK 810 RESULT` block.** One block of `FACT`-shaped lines, in this order, and the same block
is what you paste back: `premise`, `in-flight`, `update`, `crafts`, `says`, `in-flight-2`, `runs-launched`,
`audit`, `oauth-run`, `key-run`, `cascade-run`, `vertex-run`, then `aborted` when the script ended on an error
rather than on an answer, and `restore` (the scratch directory is gone) last. Each line is the key,
`PASS`/`FAIL`/`UNVERIFIED` and the sentence saying what was read. The exit status is **0** for an all-PASS
block, **1** for a criterion that was measured and failed, **2** for a run that stopped before it could
measure everything (the premise, a missing tool, an update that did not finish — and any run that ended before
its last step) and **3** for a run that reached the end with at least one row reading UNVERIFIED. **ONLY an
all-PASS block is a PASS.**

**What it costs, and what it leaves.** **FIVE billable runs** — the one in flight across the update and the
four launched after it, each an ordinary run of its own repository on that repository's budget — plus a project
owner's `fugaro update` five times over. Everything else is a read: the four checkouts' committed
`fugaro.yaml`, the database's `creds` node before and after, the job's and the service's own documents, the
five updates' own outputs, `fugaro runs ls`, the five runs' rows and records out of the runs bucket and the
service's own log lines. **No credential is printed**: the job's own document is read for the **names** of what
its container holds, for its account and for the Firebase **web** API key the toolkit is addressed with (a
public key, written only into a `0600` file inside the check's `0700` scratch directory and never into the
block), and the one value the check writes elsewhere is a task file of its own making. The premise row **stops
the check (exit 2)** on an installation release 1 has already reached, **before any run is launched**.

**Restore.** The scratch directory — the four checkouts' committed files' `agent.auth` readings, the
database's `creds` node before and after, the five updates' own outputs, the five runs' rows and their records,
the job's and the service's documents, the service's own log lines, the identity documents and the task file
the check wrote — is removed on the way out, from the exit trap on a Ctrl-C as well, and the `restore` row is
that reading (a FAILed row names the directory to remove by hand). The identity the `audit` row mints is signed
in as the run the check launched, whose Auth user that run's own launch already made, so the exchange creates
**no** user and none is deleted. The five runs are left to end on their own, as any run is. **OWNER-RUN, NOT
RUN: no agent runs any step of it.**

## Check 811: the auth retirement's second release — the token out of the agent's environment, the image gate, the retired key and the old record (an installation release 2 is reaching, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **CM22** of
[credentials-belong-to-models/implementation-plan.md](credentials-belong-to-models/implementation-plan.md), its
"### CM22: the live checks, as scripts" and the plan's own **Check 811, after release 2** (§8). It is the
second half of the retirement: release 2 takes the subscription token out of the agent's environment
(**CM28**), rejects a file that still writes a retired key (**CM29**) and stops writing the repository's old
record, deleting it only where the repository has no run in flight (**CM31**); the run's own record naming no
subscription credential for any stage is **CM9**'s and **D3067**'s reading of the flip. It is **run by the
owner** at their own terminal, after release 2. The script is `scripts/live-checks/check811.sh`, with the test
that drives it against fake `gcloud`, `fugaro` and `curl` on PATH and **three real local git checkouts** in a
temp directory (`scripts/live-checks/check811_test.sh`, run by `go test ./scripts`). **No agent runs any step
of it** — the script refuses a coding agent's session by name (`CLAUDECODE` and the four other markers) and
refuses a shell started with `-x` — and the whole of its registration is this one command:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check811.sh --installation <name> --subscription <checkout> \
  --job <the subscription repository's Cloud Run job> --gcp-project <project> --region <region> \
  [--rtdb-url <url>] [--retired-key <checkout>] [--old-image <checkout>]
```

**What the check settles.** Four statements about a release's second half, each of which needs a **real**
installation, and one of which — the old record — is a statement about **when** the update runs rather than
about what it writes:

- **A run on a subscription has no token in its agent's environment.** Three places are read together: the
  repository's **job document**, whose container environment must carry no `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`
  (**CM28**'s flip takes the mount that variable comes from away); the **service's own log**, which must hold a
  **served line** for the run (`credsvc: audit` with status `ok`, so its calls went through its gateway); and
  the run's **own record**, which must name no subscription credential (`oauth`) for any of its stages — a
  stage's `credential`/`served_by` names a credential the **job itself** holds (**CM10**), so a record that
  names one is a run that went out on a token of its own rather than on the service alone (**CM9**, **D3067**,
  **F25**).
- **A file that still writes a retired key is rejected with the fix.** `fugaro validate` in the checkout you
  point `--retired-key` at must **reject** its file, **naming** the retired key it writes (`agent.auth`,
  `agent.oauth_token`, a craft's `access`, a grade's `access`) **and** the command that fixes it — the removal
  `fugaro update` offers as a diff (**CM29**). The check's own scan of the file is only the **premise** (the
  file must write one, or the row would be about nothing): the refusal is what the row measures.
- **A launch on an image older than release 1 is refused with the rebuild command.** A launch in the checkout
  you point `--old-image` at must be **refused**, naming the command that rebuilds the image (`fugaro update`,
  or `fugaro image build`) **and** the release it needs (**CM28**). A launch that is **not** refused is the
  finding, and the run it started is left to end on its own.
- **An old record is kept while a run is in flight, and gone after.** `fugaro update --repo` is run in the
  subscription checkout **while** the run is going: the repository's old record (`creds/repoauth/<slug>`) must
  still be there afterwards, and the update's own output is read for the line that says so. The same update is
  then run again with no run of the repository going — read off `fugaro runs ls`, this check's own run
  included — and the old record must be **gone** (**CM31**, **D3063**). Where the installation carries **no**
  old record at all, both record rows read **UNVERIFIED** and say how to measure them; a record the update
  **writes** where there was none is a FAIL, because release 2's update no longer writes that record.

**The premise it reads first, and why it stops.** The subscription checkout must be a git checkout whose
repository can be matched (its origin's slug), whose **committed** and **working** `fugaro.yaml` write **no**
retired key — release 2 refuses a launch from a file that does, so every row below would be about a launch
that cannot happen — and whose repository the installation's `creds` node carries an **access** record for
(`creds/repoaccess/<slug>`), which is the state release 1 left. The database's URL comes out of the
installation's own local project config (`${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/fugaro/projects/<installation>.yaml`,
key `budget.rtdb_url`), or from `--rtdb-url` when that file names none — `fugaro doctor --json` carries no
database address, so it is not a source. A leg failing is a row reading FAIL, and a database that cannot be
read is UNVERIFIED; both **stop the check (exit 2)** before the one paid run is launched.

**Prerequisites.** An installation release 1 has reached and release 2 is reaching, with `creds/repoaccess`
written for the repository whose checkout you name, and a run of it you may spend on. `--job` is that
repository's own Cloud Run job: the `token` row reads **its** container environment, because that is where the
token would be. `--retired-key` needs a checkout whose `fugaro.yaml` still writes a retired key, and
`--old-image` a checkout whose repository's job image is older than release 1; without either flag that row
reads **UNVERIFIED** rather than being skipped silently. `fugaro`, `gcloud` (authenticated as the installation's
**project owner**), `curl`, `git`, `python3` and `mktemp` on PATH; nothing is installed and nothing is fetched.

**What a failure means, row by row.** Each row says what it read and where to look next:

- `premise` — a committed or working `fugaro.yaml` that still writes a retired key, a checkout whose origin
  names no repository, or a repository with no access record. A database that cannot be read is UNVERIFIED.
  Both **stop the check** before anything is launched.
- `launch` — the run could not be launched; read the launcher's own refusal in the detail. A refusal here may
  be one of release 2's own (a subscription the service does not serve, an image older than release 1), and the
  message names the command that fixes it. A launch whose answer carries no run id leaves the row UNVERIFIED,
  and the rows below say there is nothing to follow.
- `old-record` — the update did not exit 0; the update **wrote** an old record where the installation had none
  (release 2 no longer writes one, **CM31**); or the old record is **gone** after an update run while the run's
  own row was live, which takes the narrowing a run in flight holds away from it
  (`docs/design/update-in-flight.md`). An installation with no old record, a run that had already ended, and a
  run whose row could not be read all leave the row UNVERIFIED, naming which of the three it measured.
- `token` — the job's container environment carries `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` (**CM28**), or the run's own
  record names a subscription credential (`oauth`) for one of its stages, so the agent had something of its own
  to go out on (**CM9**). An unreadable job document, a run still not terminal, a log with no served line, a
  record that cannot be read and a record that names no stage each leave the row UNVERIFIED with what it read.
  The job's document is read **first** and its finding kept, so a job that still mounts the token is the FAIL
  it is even where the run cannot be followed.
- `record-gone` — the old record is **still there** after an update run with no run of the repository going, or
  the update did not exit 0. A run that had not ended when the row was reached, an installation with no old
  record to delete, and a row that could not establish that no other run of the repository is going all leave
  it UNVERIFIED, because an update that kept the record under those conditions did the right thing by its own
  rule.
- `retired-key` — `fugaro validate` **accepted** the file (exit 0), or it refused it **without naming a fix**.
  A refusal that names none of the retired keys the file writes is UNVERIFIED: a refusal whose words are not
  the key's is not the refusal **CM29** is about.
- `old-image` — the launch was **not** refused (a run was launched on a job image older than release 1), or it
  was refused without naming a command that rebuilds the image, or without naming the release the image has to
  be at or past — both UNVERIFIED, with the refusal's own words.
- `aborted` — an extra row, present only when the script ended on an error rather than on an answer; the rows
  it did not reach were **not** measured.

**The knobs.** Every one of them is read from the environment and none of them is asked for:
`CHECK811_INSTALLATION`, `CHECK811_SUBSCRIPTION`, `CHECK811_JOB`, `CHECK811_GCP_PROJECT`, `CHECK811_REGION`,
`CHECK811_RTDB_URL`, `CHECK811_RETIRED_KEY`, `CHECK811_OLD_IMAGE`, `CHECK811_SERVICE` (the credentials
service's name, `fugaro-credentials` by default), `CHECK811_CONFIG` (the installation's local project config
file, when it does not sit at the path the premise paragraph names), `CHECK811_DRY_RUN`, and the polling,
logging, retry and curl knobs the test uses to keep a case short (`CHECK811_LIVE_TRIES`, `CHECK811_POLLS`,
`CHECK811_POLL_SECONDS`, `CHECK811_LOG_AGE`, `CHECK811_LOG_LIMIT`, `CHECK811_LOG_POLL_SECONDS`,
`CHECK811_LOG_WAIT_SECONDS`, `CHECK811_CURL_SECONDS`). The command line itself takes `--installation`,
`--subscription`, `--job`, `--gcp-project`, `--region`, `--rtdb-url`, `--retired-key`, `--old-image`,
`--service`, `--dry-run` and `--help`; `--dry-run` prints the plan, makes **no call at all** — no `gcloud`,
no `fugaro`, no run, no update, nothing spent — and touches nothing.

**Reading the `CHECK 811 RESULT` block.** One block of `FACT`-shaped lines, in this order, and the same block
is what you paste back: `premise`, `launch`, `old-record`, `token`, `record-gone`, `retired-key`, `old-image`,
then `aborted` when the script ended on an error rather than on an answer, and `restore` (the scratch directory
is gone) last. Each line is the key, `PASS`/`FAIL`/`UNVERIFIED` and the sentence saying what was read. The exit
status is **0** for an all-PASS block, **1** for a criterion that was measured and failed, **2** for a run that
stopped before it could measure everything (a premise that failed, a missing tool, a path that is not a
checkout — and any run that ended before its last step) and **3** for a run that reached the end with at least
one row reading UNVERIFIED. **ONLY an all-PASS block is a PASS.**

**When to run it, and the one reading that depends on it.** Release 2's own after-deploy step is "run `fugaro
update`", and its update is the one that deletes a repository's old record. So **the two record rows are the
reading that depends on the order**: run Check 811 on a repository **no update has reached yet** and
`old-record` measures the record being kept across an update that finds a run in flight; run it after your own
`fugaro update` and that record is already gone, so both record rows read **UNVERIFIED** and say so, rather
than passing on a state release 2 has already changed. The other four rows — the token, the retired key, the
image gate and the record never being written — measure either way.

**What it costs, and what it leaves.** **ONE billable run** — the subscription repository's own model spend,
bounded by its cap — plus a second launch that costs **nothing** when the row is right, since an image older
than release 1 is refused before anything is built or run, and **two** `fugaro update --repo` calls in the
subscription checkout. The other side of that coin is honest to state: an old-image launch the release does
**not** refuse is a **real, billable run**, and the row names it. Every other row is a read of a document the
repository or the installation already wrote: the checkout's committed and working `fugaro.yaml`, the
database's `creds` node before, between and after the two updates, the two updates' own outputs, `fugaro runs
ls`, the run's own record out of the runs bucket, the job's own document and the service's own log lines. **No
secret is read at all**, so none can be printed: the job's own document is read for the **names** of its
container's environment and the **ids** of the secrets it mounts, and never for a value.

**Restore.** The scratch directory — the checkout's committed file's retired keys, the database's `creds` node
before, between and after the two updates, the two updates' own outputs, the run's own row and record, the
job's own document, the service's own log lines, and the task files the check wrote — is removed on the way
out, from the exit trap on a Ctrl-C as well, and the `restore` row is that reading (a FAILed row names the
directory to remove by hand). Nothing else was created: the run it launched is left to end on its own, and the
two updates are the ones the owner would run anyway. **OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.**

## Check 740: messaging a run that is going (a scratch installation you name, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **RM8** of
[docs/run-messages/implementation-plan.md](run-messages/implementation-plan.md) — its "### RM8: Check 740,
the owner's live check" — and **run by the owner**, at their own terminal, **after the release and after
`fugaro update`**, on a scratch installation they name (**never `belong`**, the owner's own development
installation). It is the live half of the run-messages work: **D2940** to **D2947** ship in the release the
check names, RM1, RM4 and RM6 are merged, and every offline test of them runs against a fake agent, a fake
store or `terraform test`. **No agent runs any step of it** — it launches a real run on the owner's
installation — and the script refuses a coding agent's session by name (`CLAUDECODE` and the four other
markers that say an agent, and not a person, is driving the shell; the editor extension's own marker is
dropped rather than refused).

**What it settles.** Four readings, and nothing else in this repository takes any of them:

- **A plain message is delivered at the next coder stage** (step 1). `fugaro tell <run> "…"` writes one
  object under `tokens/<slug>/<run>/messages/NNNN.msg.json` — the one prefix a job account may only read
  (**D2941**) — and the run's runner reads it at its next coder stage's boundary. The check reads the fate
  the **run's own record** writes for that message (the `messages` block in `result.json`): `delivered` at
  a coder stage is the message having reached the agent, and a message whose run ended before it did is
  `undelivered`.
- **U2 and U3 — does a `--now` stop find a quiet point, and does the same session go on from it?** The
  check sends the plain message first and a `--now` message second, a few seconds later, **while implement
  is going**: the stop drains both into the stage it stopped, so the second message's fate is read at
  `stage=implement` and its **reason** is the answer. The runner writes a reason only where the stop did
  **not** land as the rule reads it — `no quiet point in 10m` when its own ten-minute bound was reached
  (`agent.YieldAtBound`) and `session lost at forced stop` when a forced stop left a session that could not
  be resumed (`internal/runner/yield.go`) — so an **empty** reason on a `delivered` fate at that stage, in a
  run whose own record went **past** implement (its `stage` and `status`, read from the same record), is the
  runner's own statement that a quiet point **was** found and that the turn after it ran in the **same**
  session. Either reason is this row failing, and the row quotes it. The ending is read with the fate
  because an empty reason alone is not that statement: the entry is written before the turn it resumes runs
  (`claimYield`), and `session lost at forced stop` is written afterwards by `retagYield` for a **forced**
  stop only — so a quiet-point stop whose resume failed with `agent.ErrNoSession`, which a first run's
  implement has no recovery for, leaves `delivered`/`implement` with no reason and ends the run there. A
  record that ends in implement is therefore written **not measured** (the block is INCOMPLETE), never read
  as U2 and U3 holding.
- **D2941's fence, asked about the real accounts** (step 3). The check takes the account the run really ran
  as — the record's own `execution` (`projects/<project>/locations/<location>/jobs/<job>/executions/<execution>`),
  then `gcloud run jobs describe` for `spec.template.spec.template.spec.serviceAccountName` — and, where
  the installation deploys one, the account of its shared **project job** (`gcloud run jobs list`, matched
  by the `fugaro_profile` label). It asks the **IAM Policy Troubleshooter** whether each of those accounts
  holds `storage.objects.create` on the runs bucket
  (`gcloud policy-troubleshoot iam //storage.googleapis.com/projects/_/buckets/<bucket> --permission=storage.objects.create --principal-email=<account> --project=<project> --format=json --quiet`),
  and **denied** is the pass: both accounts hold `roles/storage.objectViewer` on `tokens/`, which carries no
  write at all. The `troubleshoot` verb takes its resource as a **positional** argument — there is no
  `--resource=` flag — and the resource asked is the **bucket**, because the Troubleshooter refuses an
  object-level full resource name (`INVALID_ARGUMENT INVALID_RESOURCE_NAME`). The object-name condition, the
  `tokens/` prefix fence, is therefore **not evaluated** by the decision; the check reads the condition the
  answer explains (`explainedPolicies[].bindingExplanations[].condition`, and v1's `policy.bindings`) and the
  row reports that text rather than a verdict about an object, saying so where the answer explains none.
  The decision itself is read the way the v3 Explainer the command asks states it: `overallAccessState`,
  where `CAN_ACCESS` is a pass and `CANNOT_ACCESS` — the older `accessDecision` spelling of the same
  answer is **NOT_GRANTED** — is the denial D2941 needs, and any `UNKNOWN_*` means the
  answer settled nothing and the row is **not measured**, never a pass. An answer that is not a denial but
  **also** explains a **conditional** binding whose role **includes** `storage.objects.create`
  (`rolePermission: ROLE_PERMISSION_INCLUDED`, for the account asked about) is **not measured** too, and the
  row prints that role and its condition: the condition is exactly what a bucket-level answer does not
  evaluate, so a role carrying the permission behind it could still write the message object, and reading
  `CANNOT_ACCESS` there as the fence would hide precisely the change D2941 exists to catch. A refusal naming
  `SERVICE_DISABLED` (the API not enabled on the project) is written **not measured** with the one command
  that fixes it, `gcloud services enable policytroubleshooter.googleapis.com --project=<project>`.
  A throwaway account given only `objectViewer` would prove nothing — the role cannot write **by definition**
  — which is why the accounts this check asks about are the installation's own, and a grant of
  `storage.objects.create` on the bucket at all is a failure naming the account and the bucket.
- **U4 — the bucket's rule for the message objects** (step 4). `gcloud storage buckets describe` reads the
  runs bucket's lifecycle configuration, and the check requires a rule whose action is **Delete**, whose
  `age` is the installation's `messages_days`, and which carries `matches_prefix = ["tokens/"]` with
  `matches_suffix = [".msg.json"]`. RM6's `terraform test` is the offline half of that rule; this is the
  **applied** bucket, and the rule it reads must leave the sealed `budget-token` beside the messages alone
  — GCS matches a prefix and a suffix and never a middle segment, which is what keeps a `.msg.json` suffix
  off the token. A bucket with no such rule is a failure, because a message object is a person's own words
  and a bucket with no rule for it keeps them until something else deletes them.

**The command.** It is **one command**, run at your own terminal, with `--repo` naming the repository the
small run is launched in:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check-740-run-messages.sh --installation <name> --repo <owner/name>
```

`--repo` takes the `owner/name` form `fugaro run --repo` takes from anywhere, so no checkout of it is
needed; a value without a slash is refused. `--recipe <name>` runs the launched run under a named recipe
(the repository's own otherwise), `--dry-run` makes every guard and prints every command it would run,
calling nothing, and `--help` prints the script's header. **Prerequisites.** `fugaro`, `gcloud`, `bash`,
`mktemp` and `python3` on PATH (a missing one stops the run with one line naming it); a `gcloud` login that
may read Cloud Run jobs on the installation's project (`roles/run.viewer` or better), the runs bucket's
metadata (`roles/storage.objectViewer` on it, or the bucket's own describe permission) and the IAM Policy
Troubleshooter; and the installation at the release or later. `fugaro version` and `fugaro tell --help` are
probed **first**: a build carrying no run-messages channel is stopped before anything is launched, because
the messages below could not be sent at all, and the `release` row says so rather than failing every row
after it. The repository you name is a **real** launch of it: the run pushes a branch and opens a pull
request, and its task asks for one small file at the repository root, so pick a repository whose pull
requests you do not mind seeing.

**Reading the `CHECK 740 RESULT` block.** Progress goes to stderr; ONE block on stdout, headed
`CHECK 740 RESULT` and ending `CHECK 740 RESULT: <verdict> (exit N)`, is what you copy back. Its keys, in
the order it prints them, are `installation`, `belong`, `release`, `bound`, `run-launched`,
`message-plain`, `message-now`, `run-ended`, `record`, `iam-workflow-job`, `iam-project-job`, `lifecycle`,
`agent-session`, `xtrace` and `restore`, followed by `fugaro-version` and — if an internal error ended the
run — `aborted`. A criterion the check never reached prints `FAIL — not reached` with the reason, so a
block is never short and a key missing from it is a key the version you ran does not know. The last line is
the verdict and it is the exit status: **0** when every criterion passed; **1** when a criterion was
measured and failed; **2** when the check stopped before it could measure everything (a guard stopped it, a
tool is missing, an error ended it); **3** when it ran to the end with at least one row **UNVERIFIED**.
Only an all-PASS block is a PASS: a check that measured most of its criteria and left one unmeasured is
INCOMPLETE, not a pass.
