**What it reads, and what it never reads.** Names, ids, stages, status words, a reason, a decision word and
a count: the installation and its project, the accounts it asks about, a run id and its slug, the two
message sequence numbers and the fate of each, the job the run landed on, the troubleshooter's decision,
and the lifecycle rules' fields. **No credential value is read by any step**, and no message **text** is
printed: the record reader prints a fixed vocabulary — a name, an id, a stage, a status word, a yes/no, a
number and the record's own reason for a fate — and every value is clipped to that vocabulary with
`[A-Za-z0-9 ._/@:+-]`, so a document that echoed back something else (a token in an error body, a message
a service wrote) cannot reach the block. And no trace: `bash -x` prints every command as it runs, so the
check **refuses** a run whose shell arrived with tracing on rather than printing the installation's own
names.

**What it does not put back.** It launches **one real run** of the repository you name: that run's own
model spend (its implement stage, its review rounds and whatever fixes follow, under the repository's and
the installation's own caps), one branch and one pull request in that repository, and the two small objects
`fugaro tell` writes under `tokens/`, which expire by the bucket's own message rule. Everything else it
does is a read — `fugaro doctor`, `fugaro version`, `fugaro runs ls`, `gcloud run jobs describe`/`list`,
`gcloud storage cat`/`buckets describe`, the troubleshooter — and the check **writes nothing anywhere
else**: the run it launched stays, because the run is what the check is a reading of, and the `restore` row
says whether its scratch directory (holding the task file and every document it read) really was removed
from the exit trap, on a failed assertion and on a Ctrl-C as well.

**The knobs.** `CHECK740_INSTALLATION`, `CHECK740_REPO`, `CHECK740_RECIPE` and `CHECK740_DRY_RUN` are the
inputs, beside the bindings this check's own test and an owner's own patience use:
`CHECK740_CALL_SECONDS`, `CHECK740_LAUNCH_SECONDS`, `CHECK740_RUN_SECONDS`, `CHECK740_POLL_SECONDS`,
`CHECK740_IMPLEMENT_SECONDS`, `CHECK740_SEND_GAP_SECONDS`, `CHECK740_RUNS_LIMIT` and
`CHECK740_JOBS_LIMIT`. None of them can point a call at another project or another host, and none is
needed to run the check as the register writes it.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** Its own automated proof is
`scripts/live-checks/check-740-run-messages_test.sh`, which drives every step of it against fake tools — a
fake `fugaro` and a fake `gcloud`, no cloud, no installation and no run — and is run by
`go test ./scripts`.

## Check 670: the sandbox enrolment and the removal under a run in flight (a throwaway installation and the GitHub sandbox, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **RE6** of
[docs/repos-management/implementation-plan.md](repos-management/implementation-plan.md) — its "## RE6. Check 670,
enrol the sandbox end to end and remove it" — and **run by the owner**, at their own terminal, on a **throwaway
installation** and the GitHub sandbox repository (`dimipaun/fugarosandbox`), after the release and `fugaro update`.
It is the live half of the repos-management work: RE1 to RE4 (the four verbs) are merged, and every offline test of
them runs against a fake backend, `internal/gcpfake` and `t.TempDir()`. **No agent runs any step of it** — it
enrols and removes a repository on a real installation and launches two real runs — and the script refuses a coding
agent's session by name (`CLAUDECODE` and the four other markers that say an agent, and not a person, is driving
the shell) as well as a traced shell, because `bash -x` would print a document's contents a second time.

**The number is this work's own, and it was renumbered.** The check was written as Check 620; **620 to 627 are the
mobile-auth work's** (the register's own paragraph and `docs/status.md` both say so), so the owner ruled on
2026-11-21 that this plan's one check is **Check 670**. The plan, the reconciliation, the README, the script's own
name, the register row above and this section all read **670**; **621 to 629 stay reserved and unused**, and no
number is reused.

**What it settles.** Six readings of the four verbs as shipped, each taken from the outside and nowhere else:

- **The enrolment's six steps, in the order it printed them** (step 1). `fugaro project repos add <repo>
  --project <installation>` is run on a **fresh throwaway checkout** and the check reads its own output: one
  numbered line per step — the repository's own `fugaro.yaml`, this machine's config entry, its image map, the
  allow-list, the publish and the job with its `roles/run.invoker` grant — the sentence that names the first image
  build as **billable and not part of it**, the question it asks for the project's name, and the closing
  `enrolled ... is ready` line (**D2400**). A converge that ran fewer steps than it printed is what this row is
  for.
- **F11: the empty `github-app-key` container** (step 2). The container is left **empty** on the first attempt —
  the state Terraform leaves, and the check refuses to measure the failure if a version is already stored, because
  then there is no empty container to read. `fugaro project repos status <repo>` must name that row
  (`credential-version`), say the container holds no enabled version, **name `fugaro secrets set` as the fix** and
  **exit nonzero** (**F11** with **D2411**): an enrolment that reads as complete while the readiness gate plans no
  job for the repository. The screen clips a long row at 160 columns, so the fix is read from the same command's
  `--json` document — the document is where it survives whole, and it is the document the console reads.
- **The fill, and the same read the other way** (step 3). `fugaro secrets set github-app-key --repo <repo>` takes
  the App's private key **by redirection from a `0600` file** (never on a command line, never in a fact), the
  converge is run again, and `status` then exits **zero** with a **green** row.
- **A run starts** (step 4). `fugaro run --repo <repo> --json` names a run, and the project's own listing holds
  its row. This is the first of the check's **two billable runs**.
- **D2407: the removal under a run in flight takes the strict confirmation, and the run finishes** (step 5). A
  **second** run is launched and watched until it is going; `fugaro project repos rm <repo>` is then run **while
  it goes**. The typed project name is the **only** thing that confirms a removal while a run is in flight, and
  the sentence that says so is printed in the command's own **refusal** and nowhere else — so the check runs the
  removal once with **no terminal at all**, requires the refusal to name the run and to write nothing before the
  question, and then runs the same command at your terminal, where the question the CLI prints is read (the
  project whose name it asks for, and **the run it is about**). What the row is really about is the other half:
  the run must **end anyway**, because a removal is never allowed to rewrite what a run in flight holds.
- **D2406: the six things `rm` leaves** (step 6), each read from the outside after the removal — the provider's
  **App installation** (`gh api /repos/<repo>/installation`, the one fact only the provider holds, which is why
  this check's fakes include `gh`), the **built image** (the shared lock's entry through `fugaro image ls --shared
  --json`, then Artifact Registry through `gcloud`), the **secret and its version** (`gcloud secrets describe` and
  the enabled versions), the **run history** in the runs bucket, the **pull request** the run opened (`gh pr
  view`) and the **remote branch** (`git ls-remote --heads`). And then that **`fugaro update` writes nothing
  new**: it exits 0, fails no stage, leaves nothing for the owner, and the allow-list and the enrolment read
  afterwards are the ones read before.

**The command.** It is **one command**, run at your own terminal, against an installation you may throw away and
the GitHub sandbox repository:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check670.sh --installation <name> --app-key-file <the App's .pem>
```

`--installation` is the installation's own name (what `fugaro doctor --json` prints as `project.name`, not the GCP
project id); `--app-key-file` is the GitHub App's private key, written to a file of its own at **mode 0600**.
`--repo <owner/name>` names another repository (the default is `dimipaun/fugarosandbox`, and the name must contain
`sandbox` on purpose), `--task <file>` is the brief the two runs are launched with, `--base <branch>` the `--ref`
they are launched on, `--gcp-project <id>` and `--production` are the escape hatches a project not named by the
checkout's own `doctor` needs, `--dry-run` makes every guard and prints every command it would run while calling
nothing, and `--help` prints the script's header. **Prerequisites.** `fugaro`, `gcloud`, `gh`, `git`, `bash`,
`mktemp` and `python3` on PATH (a missing one stops the run with one line naming it); a `gcloud` login that may
read the installation's project (Artifact Registry, Secret Manager, Cloud Run) and the runs bucket; a `gh` login
that may read the repository's installation and pull requests; and the installation at the release or later. **The
script asks you nothing of its own**: the two confirmations are the CLI's own (`add` and `rm` each ask for the
project's name) and their output is printed on your terminal as it happens.

**Reading the `CHECK 670 RESULT` block.** Progress goes to stderr; ONE block on stdout, headed `CHECK 670 RESULT`
and ending `CHECK 670 RESULT END (exit N)`, is what you copy back. Its keys, in the order it prints them, are
`fugaro-version`, `installation`, `sandbox`, `app-key`, `checkout`, `xtrace`, `agent-session`, `belong`, `enrol`,
`empty-container`, `status-screen`, `status-fix`, `status-exit`, `filled`, `status-green`, `run-started`,
`strict-confirmation`, `confirmation`, `removal`, `run-finished`, `kept-app`, `kept-image`, `kept-secret`,
`kept-history`, `kept-pull-request`, `kept-branch`, `kept-update`, `restore` and `scratch`, followed by `aborted`
if an internal error ended the run. A criterion the check never reached prints `FAIL — not reached` with the
reason, so a block is never short and a key missing from it is a key the version you ran does not know. **The
exit status is the verdict:** **0** when every criterion that was measured held; **1** when a measured criterion
did not hold, or a guard stopped the check before it could run; **2** when a row could not be measured for a
reason that is this check's own setup rather than a break — a missing tool, a container that already holds a
version (so F11 has nothing to read), a run that ended before the removal could be run under it, an image nothing
built, a run that opened no pull request. Only an all-PASS block is a PASS: a check that measured most of its
criteria and left one unmeasured is INCOMPLETE, not a pass.

**What it reads, and what it never reads.** Names, ids, versions, states, stages, a status word and a count: the
installation and its project, the repository's slug, the six steps' own lines, the container's id and version
count, the runs' ids and their rows, the App's installation id, the image ref, the secret's id and latest version,
the pull request's URL and the branch's name. **No credential value is read by any step**, and the App's private
key never reaches the block, a command line or a fact: it is redirected out of a 0600 file into `fugaro secrets
set`, and every read here is metadata. And no trace: `bash -x` prints every command as it runs, so the check
**refuses** a shell that arrived with tracing on rather than printing what it read. `belong` is refused by name
wherever it appears — the installation, the repository, the project or a path — before anything is cloned or run.

**What it leaves, and what it costs.** It launches **two real runs** of the sandbox repository: the one it only
watches start, and the one the removal is run under (that second one is what makes the strict confirmation the
confirmation that fires). Both are the repository's own model spend under the installation's caps, the repository
ends up with a branch and a pull request from each, and the enrolment itself drives a deployment (the repository's
job set, the allow-list's publish and the policy node). The first image build is **not** part of any of it: `add`
says so itself and leaves the build to `fugaro image build <entry>` — and the `kept-image` row is measured only
when the installation's shared lock already serves the repository, and says so rather than failing when nothing
has built it. Everything else the check does is a read (`fugaro doctor`, `fugaro version`, `fugaro project repos
status`, `fugaro secrets ls`, `fugaro runs ls`, `fugaro project show --json`, `fugaro image ls --shared --json`,
`gh api`, `gh pr view`, `git ls-remote`, `gcloud secrets describe`, `gcloud storage ls`) or a config write the
enrolment itself makes.

**Restore.** Nothing this check did to the installation's own base image goes back, and there is nothing to undo
that the check could undo itself: the removal **is** this check's own point, so the repository ends up removed
from the installation, and the six things `rm` leaves are left on purpose. The `restore` row names exactly what is
still there and what you may want to take away by hand — the branch (`git push <remote> --delete <branch>`), the
pull request it opened (`gh pr close <url>`) and the App's **installation** on the repository, which is a
person's step on the provider's side and not something this check may do. The **scratch directory and the
throwaway checkout** in it are removed from the exit trap, on a failed assertion and on a Ctrl-C as well;
`CHECK670_KEEP_SCRATCH=yes` keeps the scratch directory and the `scratch` row then says where it is rather than
that it went. The installation itself is a throwaway one, so the rest goes with it.

**The knobs.** `CHECK670_INSTALLATION`, `CHECK670_REPO`, `CHECK670_APP_KEY_FILE`, `CHECK670_TASK`,
`CHECK670_BASE`, `CHECK670_GCP_PROJECT`, `CHECK670_RUNS_BUCKET`, `CHECK670_PRODUCTION`, `CHECK670_DRY_RUN` and
`CHECK670_KEEP_SCRATCH` are the inputs, beside the bindings this check's own test and an owner's own patience use:
`CHECK670_RUN_SECONDS`, `CHECK670_POLL_SECONDS`, `CHECK670_LAUNCH_SECONDS`, `CHECK670_CLI_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`,
`CHECK670_CLONE_SECONDS` and `CHECK670_LOG_LIMIT`. None of them can point a call at another project or another
host, and none is needed to run the check as the register writes it. A project named `fugaro-prod` is refused
outright unless `CHECK670_PRODUCTION` says otherwise, and every knob is read with a default so an unset shell runs
the check as written.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** Its own automated proof is
`scripts/live-checks/check670_test.sh`, which drives every step of it against fake tools — fake `gcloud`, `fugaro`,
`gh` and `git` on PATH, no network, no cloud, no installation and no run — with every row read in a passing,
failing and unmeasurable form. Its registration and its description are in `scripts/live_checks_test.go`
(`liveCheckScripts`), and it is run by `go test ./scripts`.

## Check 680: the cloud tier of `fugaro troubleshoot`, end to end (the sandbox installation and its `checkout: clone` checkout, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by task **T-TC10** of
[docs/troubleshoot-cloud/implementation-plan.md](troubleshoot-cloud/implementation-plan.md) — its "### T-TC10: Check 680,
the live check (OWNER-RUN)" — and the owner renumbered it from Check 620 on 2026-11-21, because 620 is
mobile-auth's and 670 is repos-management's RE6. **Run by the owner**, at their own terminal, from the
sandbox checkout, on the sandbox installation, **never `belong`**. It is the live half of the
troubleshoot-cloud work: **D2408**'s three parts, which no hermetic test can read, because every one of them
is about a machine with **no local login**, a **real installation's own config** and a **real job**.
**No agent runs any step of it**: it rolls an installation's base image back, rewrites its project config and
launches one job on the project's own account. Its own automated proof is
`scripts/live-checks/check680_test.sh`, which drives every step against fake tools — fake `fugaro`, `gcloud`
and `git` on PATH, a fake installation's project config, a mini object store and an execution counter, no
cloud and no run — and is run by `go test ./scripts`.

**What it settles.** Three parts, and nothing else in this repository takes any of them:

- **(a) A broken launch path declines the tier instead of launching** (spec acceptance 3, F8, D2401). The
  check rolls the installation's **own base image** back — `base_images.base` in the installation's own
  project config, the ONE file it writes — to a release **older than the one this release's policy requires**
  (default `0.1.0`), and then runs `fugaro troubleshoot <run>` with **no local login**. What it requires is
  the **gate's own sentence**: `the cloud diagnosis is not available: <repo> needs a job image whose runner
  knows <…> (fugaro <release> or later), but the checkout: clone job image of <repo> workflow <workflow> is
  <ref>, release <rel>. Run fugaro update --base base …`, read from **tier 4** (`evidence`, `offline: true`,
  exit 1) — `troubleshootDeclineCloud`, produced by the **pre-flight**, which runs **before** the bundle is
  uploaded and **before** any execution exists — and **no execution created** against the count it read
  first.
  The **deliberately refused launch** is a real `fugaro run`, and `fugaro run` has **no dry run**: a launch
  that is not refused starts a billable run. So the check launches **only after** the decline has read which
  gate judges that repository's image. The two gates are told apart by their own sentences: the one whose
  image is judged by the **local config** says `the checkout: clone job image of …` (and its fix is `fugaro
  update --base base`), the one judged by the **runs bucket's build record** does not. A repository whose
  workflow is judged from the build record is left **entirely alone** — this check does not doctor the bucket
  — and parts (b) and (c) then read **NOT MEASURED**, never a pass. When the judge **is** the local config,
  the launch is made and must be refused by **the same gate the decline quoted**: the same required release,
  the same workflow, the same fix, and **no execution** — a launch that exits 0 is a FAIL that names the run
  it may have started, and the row says so.
- **(b) The cloud tier made unavailable answers from tier 4 with the reason** (D2400's fourth tier, D2401).
  A part is measured by making the tier's **own** reads impossible rather than by reading someone else's
  outage. The roll-back of (a) is put back **first** — the image gate is the first question the pre-flight
  asks, and leaving it broken would make this row read (a)'s sentence a second time — and then the config's
  `gcp_project`, `budget.firebase_project` and `budget.rtdb_url` are pointed at a project that
  `gcloud projects describe` confirms is **not there**. The row requires tier 4, `offline: true`, a non-zero
  exit and the pre-flight's own sentence, and it names **which lever** answered: the **budget/database read**
  in a project that is not there, or the **credentials service's own switch** (`checkReviewService`, which
  refuses a review-only job's account when the installation publishes no credentials service) —
  T-TC10(b)'s two levers. A reason that is neither is **not measured**, and a reason that is still (a)'s
  sentence is **not measured** too: the part proved nothing about the project it moved.
- **(c) On a healthy sandbox the cloud diagnosis answers, costs, records, reads back and cleans up** (D2403,
  D2404, D2405, D2407, D2409, D2411). With the config **byte-identical** to what the check found, the failed
  command's **own** log — the newest `<command>-<14 digits>-<pid>.log` whose closing line is `Failed in …` or
  `Left for you in …`, the CLI's own rule, and never a log this check wrote — is diagnosed with **no local
  login**, which is the only state the cloud tier answers in (`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` and
  `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` unset and `claude` off PATH; D2400). The rows are: a **cloud** answer (`tier: cloud`,
  `offline: false`, exit 0), the **cost** the answer printed held against the run record's own **`cost_usd`**
  in `runs/<slug>/<id>/result.json` (read out of the bucket rather than taken from the answer — the figure the
  tier itself reads back, D2407), the **record** on the run's prefix (its `outcome` and its artifact rows), the
  answer read back out of the run's **own artifacts** (`artifacts/diagnosis.json`, `artifacts/diagnosis.md`,
  D2404), the **bundle gone** (no object under `inputs/diagnose/` — the evidence this machine uploaded is
  deleted once the answer is read, D2405), **exactly one** execution more than the baseline (D2407's one job
  and no retry), and the stored **task**'s own `review_class: true` — **T-TC12**'s marker. The marker's row is
  the one that needs an argument rather than a reading: an answer **exists at all** only if the run was
  admitted to the review-only variant, because a task without the marker is **halted at bootstrap** before its
  first stage, so the marker is read from the task the launch stored and the answer is what proves it took
  effect.

**The command.** It is **one command**, run at your own terminal **from the sandbox checkout** — the checkout
whose `origin` is the repository the diagnosis is scoped to:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check680.sh
```

It prompts for nothing and needs no flag on a machine with one installation: the installation (its name, its
GCP project, its region and the checkouts it remembers) is read with `fugaro config list --json`, which is
read-only, offline and needs no credential, and so is the repository, from the checkout's own `origin`.
Every flag overrides a value the installation supplies: `--name` the installation (project config) name,
`--config` its config file, `--checkout` a directory inside the checkout (default: this directory), `--repo`
the repository as `owner/name`, `--project`, `--region`, `--bucket`, `--subject` the failed log to diagnose,
`--bad-release` the release the base image is rolled back to (default `0.1.0`), `--absent-project` the project
part (b) points the tier at (it must not exist, and the check asks `gcloud` to confirm that), `--task` the text
of the deliberately refused launch, `--executions-limit` how many executions each `gcloud` read asks for
(default 200: a read `gcloud` fills is widened — ×2 at a time, at most 8× that — because the count parts (a)
and (c) compare has to be the **exact** one, and a project still full at the widest read is a row that could
not be measured rather than a pass), and `--cloud-seconds` the bound, in seconds, on **every call of this check
that reaches the cloud**: the deliberately refused launch of (a), the diagnosis of (c), and the two `troubleshoot`
reads of (a) and (b), each of which launches a job execution whenever its tier answers instead of declining. It
is `timeout`'s own (default 1500: the tier's own fifteen-minute timeout and slack; `0` for no bound).
`--dry-run` prints the
plan — the one job, the one refused launch and the three parts as commands — and every row as `not reached`,
calls nothing and writes nothing; `--help` prints the script's header.

**Prerequisites.** `bash`, `python3` (every document and every rewrite is read and written with it), `git`,
`gcloud` — authenticated: it lists the project's executions and reads the runs bucket — and `fugaro`, the
binary of the release under test, since the gates, the tier and the recipe are its own; a missing one stops
the run with one line naming it. `timeout` is **not** one of them: it is what the `--cloud-seconds` bound is
made of, and on a machine without one — macOS ships none, GNU coreutils has it, which is Check 310's own caveat
— every call of this check that reaches the cloud is unbounded and yours to interrupt, which is what they were
before
there was a bound at all. A **failed command already logged** on the machine is the premise of part
(c) — the tier explains a failure this machine wrote, and a check that invented one would be diagnosing
itself — so run a sandbox command that fails (a `fugaro run` whose launch the installation's gates refuse is
the one this check is written around) before running it, or pass `--subject <run id>`. A log that already
carries a `[fugaro-cause: …]` marker is refused as a subject: the **rules** tier answers that one from the log
alone, with no model call, and none of D2408's three parts is about it.

**Reading the `CHECK 680 RESULT` block.** Progress goes to stderr; ONE block on stdout, headed
`CHECK 680 RESULT` and ending `CHECK 680 RESULT END (exit N)`, is what you copy back. Its keys, in the order
it prints them, are `xtrace`, `agent-session`, `project`, `belong`, `checkout`, `config`, `login`, `subject`,
`baseline`, `a-config`, `a-decline`, `a-launch`, `a-executions`, `b-config`, `b-tier`, `c-answer`, `c-run`,
`c-cost`, `c-marker`, `c-artifacts`, `c-bundle`, `c-executions`, `restore`, `scratch` and `left-behind`,
followed by `aborted` if a guard or an internal error ended the run: the guard rows first, so a refusal says
what it refused, then (a), (b), (c) in the order they were measured. A criterion the check never reached
prints `FAIL — not reached` with the reason, so a block is never short. The last line is the verdict and it is
the exit status: **0** when every criterion that was measured held; **1** when a criterion was measured and
failed — the tier launched a job over a broken launch path, the decline carried a sentence the gate did not
write, an execution appeared where none may, the answer was not a cloud one, the record held no cost, the
class marker was missing, the bundle survived the answer — or when a guard refused the run; **2** when a row
could **not** be measured, for a reason that is this check's arrangement or the installation: no failed
command is logged, the workflow's image is judged from the build record rather than the local config, the
config file is not there or does not read as the CLI reads it, the executions could not be listed, the project
part (b) would use exists. Exit 2 is **NOT MEASURED and never a pass**: only an all-PASS block is a PASS.

**What it reads, and what it never reads.** Names, ids, stages, status words, a tier, a cost, a count and the
gates' own sentences: the installation and its project, the checkout's `origin`, the config's own dotted keys,
the run's reference, the record's `cost_usd` and outcome, the artifact names, the execution count and the
class marker. **No credential, token or secret value is read at all** — the check reads none, and the one
sentinel its own test plants in a config fixture must never reach the block — and no value of the answer is
printed beyond its **first line**, the tier, the cost and the run's own reference. And no trace: `bash -x`
prints every command as it runs, so the check **refuses** a shell that arrived with tracing on rather than
printing the installation's own names.

**Restore.** The check writes **one file** — the installation's own project config — and it takes a copy of it
beside it, `<config>.check680-backup` (mode 0600), **before the first write**. Every write replaces **one
literal value on one line** and nothing else moves: `base_images.base`'s release tag for part (a), then
`gcp_project`, `budget.firebase_project` and `budget.rtdb_url` for part (b), with the roll-back of (a) put
**back** before (b)'s writes. The exit trap puts the file back and removes the sidecar — on a clean end, on a
failed assertion and on a Ctrl-C alike — and the `restore` row reads the file's own hash against the one it
recorded first, so a check whose put-back did nothing is a FAIL and not a quiet success. A check killed
outright (SIGKILL, a power cut) leaves the sidecar, and the restore is **one command**:

```sh
cp <config>.check680-backup <config>
```

Nothing else in the installation is written: no task, no run, no policy and no budget. What is left behind is
what a diagnosis leaves anywhere — the run's record and its two answer artifacts in the runs bucket, which
`fugaro diagnose <ref>` explains and the bucket's lifecycle expires — and parts (a) and (b) leave nothing at
all: no execution, no run, and the file they arranged put back. The scratch directory (holding the task file
and every document the check read) is removed from the exit trap, and the `scratch` row says whether it really
went.

**The knobs.** `CHECK680_NAME`, `CHECK680_CONFIG`, `CHECK680_CHECKOUT`, `CHECK680_REPO`, `CHECK680_PROJECT`,
`CHECK680_REGION`, `CHECK680_BUCKET`, `CHECK680_SUBJECT`, `CHECK680_BAD_RELEASE`,
`CHECK680_ABSENT_PROJECT`, `CHECK680_TASK`, `CHECK680_EXECUTIONS_LIMIT` and `CHECK680_CLOUD_SECONDS` are the
inputs, beside `CHECK680_LOGS_DIR`, `CHECK680_DRY_RUN` and `CHECK680_KEEP_SCRATCH`. None of them can point a
call at another project or another host — the project and the bucket come from the installation or the flags
above — and none is needed to run the check as the register writes it. The `belong` refusal and the
`fugaro-prod` refusal are **not** knobs: they are the reason a value this check was given is checked before
the first call.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** Its own automated proof is
`scripts/live-checks/check680_test.sh`, which drives every step of it against fake `fugaro`, `gcloud` and
`git` — no cloud, no installation and no run — and is run by `go test ./scripts`.


## Check 341: the reports job's first firing, and what it stored (an installation and its own project, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by the task that registered Check 341 of [periodic-reviews/implementation-plan.md](periodic-reviews/implementation-plan.md)
§P8 — the plan names the number and leaves the row and this section to the task that implements the
check, which is the register's own rule for a work that reserved none — and **no step of it has been
run, and nothing here is a claim that the job fires or that what it stores is right.** It is the check
the reports job's own Terraform (**R12**) and plan (**R7**) are read by: the module plans the job
**paused** (`jobs.reports.paused`, the setting **R13** puts on the project layer), so this check is
the one that turns it on, watches it fire and reads what landed. It is also the check that settles
the question **R10** is blocked on — **Open item 5** of the plan: whether `fugaro runs digest` may
write to `reports/` at all, since **E4** makes the reports job its only writer.

**What the check confirms.** With `jobs.reports.paused: false` in the project layer and `fugaro
update` applied, the schedule fires once, and what it stored is what the plan's **E1** and **E3**
say: **one report per repository** under `reports/<slug>/<YYYY>/<key>.md`, **the project aggregate**
at `reports/<YYYY>/<key>.md` beside them, and the `reports/` objects **still there after the run
records' own 90 days** — which is the **18-month `reports/` lifecycle rule** (E3) doing what it is
for, and the half no hermetic test holds, because the bucket's own rule is read from the installed
bucket rather than from a plan. And the second reading: whether the stored report **reads back** —
`fugaro runs digest --stored` (**R10**) against what the job wrote — which is Open item 5's question
and the reason R10's own write half is held.

**What you do.** **You** run every step and **no agent runs any step of it**; point it at an
installation whose project the job may write into, and **never at a project whose name contains
`belong`** — this check turns the job on, and the job writes.

1. In the project layer, set `jobs.reports.paused: false` and run `fugaro update`. Record what it
   prints for the reports job, its account, its schedule and its grants.
2. Let the schedule fire once. The job's own command is `fugaro runs reports --job`, and it
   **refuses outside the job's environment** (a person writes one repository's report into a
   checkout with `fugaro runs digest`), so the schedule is the way to make the firing; record the
   execution and when it ran.
3. Read what landed under `reports/`: one report per repository at `reports/<slug>/<YYYY>/<key>.md`,
   and the project aggregate at `reports/<YYYY>/<key>.md`.
4. Read one stored report back — `fugaro runs digest --stored <period>` — and record what it prints.

**Expected.** One report per repository that ran in the period, each under its own slug and year; the
project aggregate beside them; the objects still present after the run records' own 90 days, which is
the bucket's own `reports/` rule and not a plan; and the stored report reading back as the report the
job wrote, with no launcher having written to `reports/` to make that so.

**Refutation.** A period with no report where a repository ran, an aggregate whose figures disagree
with the repository reports beside it, a `reports/` object gone with the run records' 90 days, or a
stored report that does not read back — the last of which is the reading that answers Open item 5
**no**, and holds R10's write half where it is.

**Restore.** Set `jobs.reports.paused: true` again and run `fugaro update`, which plans the job paused
— that is the whole of putting it back. The stored reports it wrote are ordinary reports in the
project's own `reports/` prefix and are meant to stay: the bucket's own 18-month rule reaps them, and
removing them by hand would take the very reading this check exists to take. Nothing else is created:
no account of the check's own, no binding and no credential.

**A script is not written yet.** The register's own rule ([CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md))
asks a new owner-run check to ship as ONE runnable script under `scripts/live-checks/` with a
hermetic test beside it, and **that script does not exist for this check**: what is written here is
the step list, the row above names no command, and the task that converts this check owes the script,
its test and the one command in the row.

**Paste back:** the execution's id and when it fired, the keys under `reports/` with the ones the
repositories' own runs would predict, the aggregate's figure beside the repository reports' own, and
what `fugaro runs digest --stored` printed — and **never a credential and never `belong`'s project**.

## Check 342: the failures report reproduces a window a person built by hand (an installation with stored reports, your own machine; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by the task that registered Check 342 of [periodic-reviews/implementation-plan.md](periodic-reviews/implementation-plan.md)
§P8 — the same rule as Check 341's, the task that implements the check writing its row and its
section — and **no step of it has been run.** It is the one check that says whether the **failure
classes** mean what [failure-classes/design.md](failure-classes/design.md) says they mean: a
vocabulary can be internally consistent, and every hermetic test can pass, while the word it puts on a
run is not the word a person who watched the run would use. Nothing here is a claim that it does.

**What the check confirms.** A window whose causes **you already know** — the design's own seven-day
table is one — read back two ways that must agree with each other and with what you know happened:
`fugaro runs ls --group-by failure_class` (**FC6**, the live reading of the window) and the
**Failures table** of the period's stored report (**R8**'s aggregate, which by **D1432**'s
recommendation carries the period's table beside its figures). **Including the runs whose class the
legacy reader read from `reason`** (**FC5**): a run that predates the `failure_class` field carries
none of its own, and the reader derives one from its `reason` rather than writing anything back — so
the check is also the reading that says the derivation lands on the class a person would give the run.

**What you do.** **You** run every step and **no agent runs any step of it** — both reads are yours,
and the account of the window is what only a person has.

1. Take a window you already know the causes of. The design's own seven-day table is one; a window
   you watched run is another.
2. Run `fugaro runs ls --group-by failure_class` over that window and record the table. If you use
   the design's table, compare row by row.
3. Read the same period's stored report — the Failures table under `reports/<YYYY>/<key>.md`, or
   `fugaro runs digest --stored <period>` in a checkout — and record it.
4. Put the two tables beside your own account of the window: each class's runs and the counts.

**Expected.** The two tables agree with each other and with the causes you know; the runs that
predate the field sit in the class their `reason` implies rather than in a class of their own or in
none; and the period's report and the live listing of the same period name the same runs under the
same classes.

**Refutation.** A class whose runs a person would not put there, a run that predates the field
falling out of every class, the live table and the stored table disagreeing over the same period, or
a class the design names that no window ever produces — any of which is a reading about the
**vocabulary**, and none of which the hermetic tests can take.

**Restore.** Nothing to undo: two reads and a comparison. No run is launched, nothing is written,
nothing is granted and no credential is minted, and there is nothing to paste back but the two
tables and the account of the window they are checked against.

**A script is not written yet.** The register's own rule ([CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md))
asks a new owner-run check to ship as ONE runnable script under `scripts/live-checks/` with a
hermetic test beside it, and **that script does not exist for this check**: what is written here is
the step list, the row above names no command, and the task that converts this check owes the
script, its test and the one command in the row.

**Paste back:** the window, the account of its causes, the two tables — the grouped listing and the
stored report's Failures table — and where they disagreed, if they did.

## Check 343: the opt-in commit into the designated repository (the designated repository's checkout, your own launcher account, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by the task that registered Check 343 of [periodic-reviews/implementation-plan.md](periodic-reviews/implementation-plan.md)
§P8, the number claimed for **R9**'s own live check by the designation design of 2026-11-17
([reconciliation.md](periodic-reviews/reconciliation.md) §7.3) — and, as with 341 and 342, the plan
names the number and leaves the row and this section to the task that implements the check. **No
script is written, and none is needed**: unlike Check 340 this check creates no account, writes no
IAM and needs no teardown, because the read is the launcher's existing bucket-wide `objectViewer`
and the write is the ordinary push path — the check is **one command** and the pull request it
opens. **No step of it has been run**, and nothing here is a claim that the commit works.

**What the check confirms.** The whole of the opt-in commit: that with `reports_commit` named — the
designated repository, and `dir` if the reports do not go to the default folder — **one**
`fugaro run --recipe commit-reports --commit-reports "commit the stored reports"` in that repository's
checkout carries the stored reports into it, that
a second run with nothing new in the store ends **without** a pull request, and that a file the
folder holds and the store does not is **still there** and named in the run's own record. It is
**R9**'s check and the last of the reports job's: the read of `reports/` is the starting person's own
launcher account (**D2754**), so no new credential and no new grant exists for it.

**The one command:**

```bash
fugaro run --recipe commit-reports --commit-reports "commit the stored reports"
```

**The two flags go together.** `--commit-reports` is what hands the stored reports to the run, and
the recipe is what reads them: a launch carrying it on any other recipe is refused at your terminal,
by name, before anything runs, so the command above is the whole of it — one line, one run.

**What you do.** **You** run every step and **no agent runs any step of it**; the run reads the
project's own `reports/` prefix with your launcher account and opens its pull request in the
designated repository, so **never point the installation at a project whose name contains `belong`**.

1. Name `reports_commit` (the `repo`, and `dir` if the reports do not go to the default folder) in
   your local project config and publish it — or let `fugaro update`'s policy stage carry it.
2. In the designated repository's checkout, run
   `fugaro run --recipe commit-reports --commit-reports "commit the stored reports"` with the
   starting person's own launcher account. Record the run's id and what it printed.
3. Read the pull request it opens: **one file per stored report** under `<dir>/<slug>/<YYYY>/<key>.md`,
   **the project aggregate** at `<dir>/<YYYY>/<key>.md` beside them, and the **index regenerated**
   over the whole folder.
4. Run `fugaro run --recipe commit-reports --commit-reports "commit the stored reports"` again with
   nothing new in the store: it must end **without** a pull request.
5. Leave a file in the folder the store does not hold, run
   `fugaro run --recipe commit-reports --commit-reports "commit the stored reports"` once more, and
   check the file is still there and named in the run's own record.

**Expected.** Step 2 opens one pull request carrying exactly the store's reports and the index over
the whole folder; step 4 ends with no new pull request; step 5 leaves the folder's own file where it
was and names it in the record rather than removing it.

**Refutation.** A file the store does not hold that the run removes or rewrites, an index that does
not cover the whole folder, a second run that opens a pull request over nothing new, or a pull
request that carries a report the store does not have — any of which is a reading about the commit
step, and none of which the hermetic tests can take of a real repository.

**Restore.** Nothing the check itself creates has to be put back: no account, no binding and no
credential is made, and the read is the launcher's existing bucket-wide `objectViewer`. What it
leaves is one branch and one pull request in the **designated repository**, which you merge or close
the way you would any other — and the stored reports under `reports/` are untouched, because the
check reads them.

**Paste back:** the run's reference, the pull request's URL and the files it carried, what the second
and third runs printed — and **never a credential and never `belong`'s project**.

## Check 750: a review judged against its task (a scratch installation you name, never `belong`; run by you; NOT RUN)

**NOT RUN.** Written by the "## Checks" section of
[docs/review-against-task/implementation-plan.md](review-against-task/implementation-plan.md) — its **Check 750** — and
**run by the owner**, at their own terminal, **after the release and after `fugaro update`**, on a scratch installation
they name (**never `belong`**, the owner's own development installation). It is the live half of the review-against-task
work: **D2930** to **D2939** and **RA10**'s two end-to-end files are merged, every review stage resolves the task a pull
request was written for through the runs bucket alone (`launchSpecForPR`), and every offline test of that resolution runs
against fake providers and a fake store. **No agent runs any step of it** — it launches real review jobs on the owner's
installation — and the script refuses a coding agent's session by name (`CLAUDECODE` and the four other markers that say
an agent, and not a person, is driving the shell; the editor extension's own marker is dropped rather than refused),
refuses `belong` whether it arrives as the installation name or as the GCP project `fugaro doctor --json` reports, and
refuses a shell that arrived with tracing on.

**What it settles.** Three readings, and nothing else in this repository takes any of them:

- **The against line names the run that opened the pull request** (steps 3 and 4). `fugaro review show RUN` prints what
  the review judged the change against on one line (**R8**, `reviewAgainstLine`): `against: run <bare-run-id>` for the task
  of the run that opened the pull request, `against: file <sha256>` for a task a person supplied with `--spec`, and
  `against: none (<why>)` when there was nothing to check against. The check reads the opening run **for itself** — the
  rows of `fugaro runs ls --pr N --json` (with `--repo .`, so the repository listed is this checkout's, resolved
  from its origin by `fugaro` — the one `fugaro review --pr` takes from there — and never a guess at the local
  config's repositories), where a candidate is a row whose branch names the run itself, which is not a
  follow-up, and whose record delivered **no artifact**, because a run that opens a pull request writes none — and then
  requires the review's own line to be exactly `against: run <that run>`. The launcher's answer is never the evidence for
  the launcher: a line naming another run, or none at all, is this row failing. The row that matters most is
  `against: none (no run found)` on a pull request a Fugaro run really opened: that is a launcher which lost the task, or
  **D2933**'s older job image, where a review launched before `fugaro update` rebuilt the images runs code-only whatever
  the launcher wrote. A pull request no Fugaro run opened — zero candidates, or several that disagree — is **refused
  before the first launch**, because the check's whole first reading is about a pull request that has an opening run.
- **A change that misses an item of its brief is reported as `unmet`, not shipped** (step 5). This is the half that needs
  a **second** pull request, and only the owner can arrange it: `--unmet-pr <M>` names one a Fugaro run opened whose head
  deliberately leaves out one item of the brief the run was given. Its review's artifact must list an issue with scope
  `unmet` and its verdict must be `fix first` — the one verdict that holds a change back. No offline test can force that
  out of a real model, which is why it is here. Without `--unmet-pr` the reading is **not taken**, the row reads
  `UNVERIFIED` and the check ends **INCOMPLETE (exit 3)** — never a pass.
- **`--code-only` says so** (step 6). `fugaro review --pr <N> --code-only` on the first pull request must print exactly
  `against: none (--code-only)`. The whole point of the flag is that a reader can tell a review handed **no** task from one
  whose launcher lost the task, so what is compared is the exact line and not merely that it says none.

**The command.** It is **one command**, run at your own terminal, from a checkout of the repository the pull request is in:
the check passes `--repo .` to its own `runs ls --pr` read, which the CLI resolves from that checkout's origin — the
repository `fugaro review --pr` takes from the same place — so a local config that lists several repositories neither
refuses the read nor gets rows from another one:

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check-750-review-against-task.sh --installation <name> --pr <N>
```

`--unmet-pr <M>` adds the second reading, on the second pull request (it must differ from `--pr`: a pull request that does
its task reports no unmet issue by construction). `--dry-run` prints the plan and makes no call at all, and `--help` prints
the script's header. **Prerequisites.** `fugaro`, `bash`, `mktemp` and `python3` on PATH (a missing one stops the run with
one line naming it), and the installation at the release or later: `fugaro version` and `fugaro review --help` are probed
**first**, and a build whose `review --help` does not name `--code-only` and `--spec` is stopped before anything is
launched, because the against line could not be there at all. **No `gcloud` is needed**, and the check runs no `git`
itself: every reading this check takes comes from `fugaro` itself (its `--repo .` is resolved by `fugaro` from the
checkout's origin), which is also what makes "no secret on any command line or in any output" easy to hold.

**Reading the `CHECK 750 RESULT` block.** Progress goes to stderr; ONE block on stdout, headed
`CHECK 750 RESULT` and ending `CHECK 750 RESULT: <verdict> (exit N)`, is what you copy back. Its keys, in
the order it prints them, are `installation`, `belong`, `release`, `pr-opened`, `bound`, `against-run`,
`unmet`, `code-only`, `agent-session`, `xtrace` and `restore`, followed by `fugaro-version`, `cap` and — if
an internal error ended the run — `aborted`. A criterion the check never reached prints `FAIL — not reached`
with the reason, so a block is never short and a key missing from it is a key the version you ran does not
know. The last line is the verdict and it is the exit status: **0** when every criterion passed; **1** when
a criterion was measured and failed; **2** when the check stopped before it could measure everything (a
guard stopped it, a tool is missing, an error ended it); **3** when it ran to the end with at least one row
**UNVERIFIED**. Only an all-PASS block is a PASS: a check that measured most of its criteria and left one
unmeasured is INCOMPLETE, not a pass.

**What it reads, and what it never reads.** Names, ids, status words, a verdict word, a scope word, a count and a
number: the installation and its GCP project, a pull request's rows (a run id, its repository, its status, whether it
is terminal), an artifact's own `against` record and its issues' scopes, and the ceilings the project publishes.
**No credential value is read by any step** — the check calls no cloud tool at all — and no task **text** is
printed: the artifact carries only the `against` record, the reader prints a fixed vocabulary, and every value is
clipped to it with `[A-Za-z0-9 ._/@:()+-]`, so a document that echoed back something else (a token in an error
body, a repository's own text) cannot reach the block. And no trace: `bash -x` prints every command as it runs, so
the check **refuses** a run whose shell arrived with tracing on rather than printing the installation's own names.

**What it does not put back.** It launches **two real review jobs** — the review of the pull request you name and
the `--code-only` one — and **three** with `--unmet-pr <M>`: each is a launch of its own with a review stage's model
spend, bounded by the project's per-run ceiling and the gateway's accounting. The check prints the ceiling it read
from `fugaro project show --json` before the first launch, and then which review it is about to pay for, and
launches: nothing asks you to confirm it, and a launch the gateway refuses past the ceiling is written as the row's
own reason rather than retried. Everything else it does is a read — `fugaro doctor`, `fugaro version`, `fugaro review
show`, `fugaro runs ls`, `fugaro project show` — and no review posts a comment or a review on the pull request. It
**writes nothing anywhere else**: the review runs it launched stay, as every run does, and the `restore` row says
whether its scratch directory (holding the doctor's answer, the listings, the launch results and the artifacts)
really was removed from the exit trap, on a failed assertion and on a Ctrl-C as well.

**The knobs.** `CHECK750_INSTALLATION`, `CHECK750_PR`, `CHECK750_UNMET_PR` and `CHECK750_DRY_RUN` are the inputs,
beside the bindings this check's own test and an owner's own patience use: `CHECK750_CALL_SECONDS`,
`CHECK750_LAUNCH_SECONDS`, `CHECK750_RUN_SECONDS`, `CHECK750_POLL_SECONDS` and `CHECK750_RUNS_LIMIT`. None of them
can point a call at another project or another host, and none is needed to run the check as the register writes it.

**OWNER-RUN, NOT RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** Its own automated proof is
`scripts/live-checks/check-750-review-against-task_test.sh`, which drives every step of it against a fake `fugaro`
— no cloud, no installation and no review job — and is run by `go test ./scripts`.

## Check 890: the data layout of a real project (installation `fugaro`, never `belong`; run by you; RUN 2026-11-23: FAIL on one path, now RC106)

**RUN 2026-11-23 on `fugaro`: FAIL on one UNNAMED path, `creds/current/<slug>/<run>`, which #3700 then named RC106 in
the script. The result is in [report.md](repo-coupling-audit/report.md) §1, "Live result".** Written by tasks **K1** and **K4** of
[docs/repo-coupling-audit/implementation-plan.md](repo-coupling-audit/implementation-plan.md). Its output fills
the live columns of the storage-path rows of [report.md](repo-coupling-audit/report.md) (task **R1**, the
reconciliation's **O2**). It only reads, and **no agent runs any step of it**.

**What it measures.** The audit names every storage path a project keys by repository: rows **RC40**–**RC50**
and **RC52**–**RC56**, and **RC99**–**RC102** and **RC106** for the five per-repository `creds/` paths
(`creds/workflowsecrets`, `creds/leases`, `creds/review-signs`, `creds/issuance` and `creds/current`). A reading of the code
cannot say whether a real project holds anything else keyed by a repository, so the check lists the
project's three stores, **keys only**, and compares what it finds with those rows:

- `rtdb`: the Realtime Database's top-level keys, one level under each of them, one level under each child of
  `config/` and `creds/`, and the parent of the slug segment of every RTDB row of the report. Every read is
  `shallow=true`, and the check prints keys, never a value.
- `gcs`: the runs bucket's root, and two levels under `runs/`, `builds/`, `cache/`, `locks/`, `tokens/` and
  `reports/` (one level under any other top-level prefix).
- `firestore`: the Firebase project's Firestore collection ids, and the first page of `spendDaily`'s document
  ids, through a list whose mask names no field.
- `layout`: every listed path with a repository slug in it must match one of the report's patterns; one that
  matches none is printed **UNNAMED**, and the row is a FAIL naming it.
- `restore`: the scratch directory, which held the token file and every response body, is gone.

A level keyed per repository or per run is sampled: the check descends into at most `--sample N` of its keys
(default 3) and prints at most N of them with the count, so `runs/` does not enumerate every run.

**The command.**

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check-890-data-layout.sh fugaro
```

The argument is the Fugaro project's name; its local config
(`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/fugaro.yaml`, or `--config <file>`) names the GCP project, the runs bucket,
the database and the Firebase project. `--dry-run` prints the plan and calls nothing, and `--help` prints the
usage. `CHECK890_DAY` sets the day key the `spend/<day>` and `outcomes/<day>` reads use (default today), and
`CHECK890_CURL_SECONDS` each read's time limit (default 30). It needs `bash`, `mktemp`, `python3`, `gcloud` and
`curl`. It refuses to start in a coding agent's session (`CLAUDECODE`, `CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT`,
`CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE`, `CURSOR_AGENT`, `AI_AGENT`) and in a shell that arrived tracing (`bash -x`), whose trace
would print the access token.

**What it reads, and what it never prints.** `gcloud auth print-access-token`, `gcloud storage ls`, shallow
RTDB GETs, Firestore's `documents:listCollectionIds` (a POST only by the API's shape) and a `spendDaily` list
GET whose mask reads no field: a few hundred reads at most. Every call runs with stdin from `/dev/null`, and
nothing is written, launched or deleted. The access token goes into a 0600 curl config file inside a 0700
scratch directory that the exit trap removes; it never reaches an argv.

**Reading the result.** Progress goes to stderr; ONE block on stdout, headed `CHECK 890 RESULT`, is what you
copy back. Its last line is the verdict, and the verdict is the exit status:

- **PASS** (exit 0): every row passed, so every slug-keyed path the check listed is one a report row names.
- **FAIL** (exit 1): a row was measured and failed: a slug-keyed path no row names (each printed
  **UNNAMED**), or a scratch directory still there.
- **INCOMPLETE** (exit 2): the run stopped before it measured: a guard refused it, a tool is missing, the
  local config does not name what it needs, or no access token could be minted.
- **INCOMPLETE** (exit 3): it ran to the end and at least one row reads **UNVERIFIED**: a store, or some of
  its reads, did not answer.

**OWNER-RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** Its own automated proof is
`scripts/live-checks/check-890-data-layout_test.sh`, which drives it against a fake `gcloud`, `curl` and
`fugaro` (no cloud) and is run by `go test ./scripts`.

## Check 891: where `fugaro update` and a launch read repository context (installation `fugaro` and its checkouts, never `belong`; run by you; RUN 2026-11-23: PASS)

**RUN 2026-11-23 on `fugaro` with three checkouts: PASS. The result is in [report.md](repo-coupling-audit/report.md) §1,
"Live result".** Written by tasks **K2** and **K4** of
[docs/repo-coupling-audit/implementation-plan.md](repo-coupling-audit/implementation-plan.md). It settles the
reconciliation's **U4** (whether a member-run command triggers Terraform on `fugaro` today), and its output
fills the report's live columns (task **R1**). It launches nothing, applies nothing, and **no agent runs any
step of it**.

**What it measures.** The audit's question is whether one admin, from anywhere, can run the whole update.
[report.md](repo-coupling-audit/report.md) §4 names the stages that read the working directory; this check
measures it on the real installation:

1. It runs `fugaro update --plan-only --json --events --project fugaro` once from an empty temporary
   directory and once from each checkout you name. `--project` is always passed, so a checkout's own
   `project:` cannot switch the comparison to another project; a checkout whose `fugaro.yaml` names another
   project (or none) is reported and skipped.
2. It prints, per stage, the `stage` line's state and detail in each place, and marks every stage whose state
   or detail differs between the empty directory and a checkout. The stages §4 allows to differ are
   `repository`, `images`, `policy`, `plugin`, `checkout` and `secrets` (the last is **RC98**, the stage that
   reads the working directory's origin and default branch); any other stage that differs is a FAIL.
3. It reads the newest `launch.json` of each repository with runs in the runs bucket
   (`runs/<slug>/<run-id>/launch.json`) and prints its `job`: a shared project job (`fugaro-p-…`) or the
   repository's own, which is the launch's repository coupling (**RC76**).

**The command.**

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check-891-update-trace.sh fugaro <each checkout>
```

Every argument after the project is a checkout of one of its repositories; name each one you have.
`CHECK891_BUCKET` overrides the runs bucket (default `fugaro-runs-<gcp_project>`, the GCP project read from
`fugaro doctor --json --project fugaro`), and `CHECK891_RUNS` is how many of a repository's newest runs are
tried for a `launch.json` (default 5). It needs `bash`, `mktemp`, `python3`, `fugaro` and `gcloud`; no token is
minted, since `gcloud` reads the bucket with its own credential. It refuses to start in a coding agent's
session and in a traced shell.

**Two accepted side effects.** `update --plan-only` is not a pure read, and the plan accepts two things it
does inside itself:

- **The Terraform state lock.** Terraform's plan takes the state lock: it writes, then deletes, a `.tflock`
  object in the state bucket, once for each root the run plans (`internal/infra` passes no `-lock=false`).
- **Remembered checkouts.** The run records the checkouts it ran from in the local config.

Nothing else is written. Every call has its stdin on `/dev/null` and every `gcloud` call carries `--quiet`.

**What it never prints.** A stage detail and a job name pass through a redactor that masks opaque mixed-case
runs and `key=value` secrets, and a `launch.json` contributes its `job` only.

**Reading the result.** Progress goes to stderr; ONE block on stdout, headed `CHECK 891 RESULT`, is what you
copy back. Its last line is the verdict and the exit status:

- **PASS** (exit 0): every stage that differs between the empty directory and a checkout is a §4 blocker.
- **FAIL** (exit 1): a stage differs that §4 does not name, which is what this check exists to find.
- **INCOMPLETE** (exit 2): the run stopped before it could compare: a guard refused it, a tool is missing, or
  an argument after the project is not a directory.
- **INCOMPLETE** (exit 3): it ran to the end and a row is **UNVERIFIED**: no checkout of `fugaro` was given
  (or every one named another project), or no `launch.json` could be read.

**OWNER-RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** Its own automated proof is
`scripts/live-checks/check-891-update-trace_test.sh`, which drives it against a fake `fugaro`, `gcloud` and
`curl` (no cloud, no installation) and is run by `go test ./scripts`.

## Check 892: the IAM a member and an admin hold (installation `fugaro`, never `belong`; run by you; RUN 2026-11-23: PASS)

**RUN 2026-11-23 on `fugaro`: PASS. The result is in [report.md](repo-coupling-audit/report.md) §1, "Live result".**
Written by tasks **K3** and **K4** of
[docs/repo-coupling-audit/implementation-plan.md](repo-coupling-audit/implementation-plan.md). It settles the
reconciliation's **U3** (the real IAM a member holds on `fugaro`) and confirms the Perms column of
[report.md](repo-coupling-audit/report.md) live (task **R1**). It only reads, and **no agent runs any step of
it**.

**What it measures.** The report names three permission sets a row needs:

- **TF-admin**: an admin in the grants node `config/admin/access`, from which `fugaro update` derives the
  local `terraform.admins`; applies Terraform.
- **DB-admin**: `roles/firebasedatabase.admin` on the Firebase project: the GCP project's owners and editors
  plus the budget admins.
- **operator**: an operator or admin in the grants node (`terraform.operators`): starts runs, and acts as a
  repository's build and job service accounts.

It reads the installation's local config (`terraform.admins`, `operators`, `budget_admins`,
`budget.rtdb_url`, `budget.firebase_project`), the IAM policies of the GCP project, the Firebase project and
every per-repository build and job account, and the grants node **with its values**, which are the
principals and roles it compares and hold no secret. For each member you name it prints which of TF-admin,
DB-admin and operator it holds and the report rows it can therefore exercise, then the whole matrix:
principal, role in the node, local lists, and the project and account roles held.

It **fails on one rule**: a principal the node places as `operator` or `viewer`, or scopes to repositories,
that holds `roles/owner`, `roles/editor` or `roles/resourcemanager.projectIamAdmin` on the GCP project, an
admin in all but name. A grant whose role is not viewer, operator or admin is a FAIL too. An owner or editor
the node does not place is an implicit admin (**D1592**) and is reported, never failed; a local
`terraform.admins` that differs from the node's project admins is reported as **DIFFERS**, not failed,
because the next `fugaro update` rewrites it from the node.

**The command.**

```sh
bash scripts/live-checks/check-892-iam.sh fugaro <a member's address>
```

A member is an address (`ada@example.com`) or an IAM member (`user:…`, `group:…`, `serviceAccount:…`); name
as many as you want read. `CHECK892_CONFIG` names the local config when it is not
`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/fugaro/projects/fugaro.yaml`. It needs `bash`, `mktemp`, `python3`, `gcloud` and `curl`. It
refuses to start in a coding agent's session and in a traced shell. Every call runs with stdin closed and
every `gcloud` call with `--quiet`; nothing is written. The access token goes into a 0600 curl config file in a
0700 scratch directory the exit trap removes, and is never printed or put on an argv.

**Reading the result.** Progress goes to stderr; ONE block on stdout, headed `CHECK 892 RESULT`, is what you
copy back. Its last line is the verdict and the exit status:

- **PASS** (exit 0): no principal is an admin in all but name.
- **FAIL** (exit 1): at least one is, or the node holds a role the report does not name.
- **INCOMPLETE** (exit 2): the run stopped before it could compare: a guard refused it, a tool is missing, the
  local config names no valid GCP project or database, no access token could be minted, or the GCP project's
  policy or the grants node could not be read.
- **INCOMPLETE** (exit 3): it compared, and a read it needed for part of the matrix did not answer
  (**UNVERIFIED**): the Firebase project's policy, an account's policy, or a grants node that is absent.

**OWNER-RUN: no agent runs any step of it.** Its own automated proof is
`scripts/live-checks/check-892-iam_test.sh`, which drives it against a fake `gcloud`, `curl` and `fugaro` (no
cloud, no database) and is run by `go test ./scripts`.
